# The Alien's Guide to Earth: full text of every investor and trader page

Site: https://alienspacex.com · Updated 2026-11-28 · Education only, not advice. Text is CC BY 4.0; please cite the page URL.

# Warren Buffett

> Ran Berkshire Hathaway for sixty years and explained every decision in a yearly letter to its owners.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/buffett.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

You are buying a claim on what a company will earn.

## Summary

Buffett ran Berkshire Hathaway for six decades and wrote to its owners every year. The letters are free, plainly written, and among the best education in investing there is.

## Big ideas

### 1. A share is a slice of a business

You are buying a claim on what a company will earn. The price on the screen is an offer from a stranger, and it carries no information about the business.

- **Pick businesses, not tickers.** He buys on a view of how the company will do over many years. He holds no view on where the share price or the market goes next, and does not act as if he had one. (2021 · 2022)
- **The farm and the shop.** In 1986 he bought a Nebraska farm, in 1993 a retail property in New York, knowing little about farming or real estate. He asked only two things: what will this asset earn over the years, and is the price sensible against that? Neither came with a daily quote, and he never missed having one. (2013)
- **Watch the field.** If you can enjoy a weekend without checking the price of something you own, you can do the same on a weekday. Results on the ground decide the outcome; the price catches up later. (2013)
- **Count the earnings you never see.** Your real income from a holding includes your share of the profit the company keeps. Accounts show only the dividend. At a business that reinvests well, the retained part is the more valuable half. (1999 · 2019 · 2020)
- **Popularity now, weight later.** Over months, price measures how liked a share is. Over years, it measures what the business is worth. This is Graham's idea, and he repeats it thirty years on because nothing has replaced it. (2022 · 2023)
- **Two doors into the same room.** Buying a whole company and buying 2% of a listed one are the same act of judgement. The listed route has two advantages: shares are sometimes offered at foolish prices, and a mistake can be sold in a day. (1995 · 2022)
- **Part of a gem beats all of a pebble.** A small piece of an outstanding business is worth more than full control of an average one, and it is far less work. (2013 · 2014 · 2020)
- **Keep an honest yardstick.** A rising market flatters everyone. The test is whether you beat a cheap index after costs and tax over several years, using a benchmark chosen in advance and never swapped after a bad stretch. (1997 · 2004 · 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-01-a-share-is-a-slice-of-a-business.html

### 2. Moats: what makes a business worth owning

A great business earns a high return on the money inside it, and can keep doing so because something stops competitors from taking it away.

- **Three kinds of savings account.** Great: pays a very high rate and needs few new deposits to grow. Good: pays a fair rate, but only on large new deposits. Gruesome: grows fast, demands ever more money and pays little on it. He names See's Candies, FlightSafety and airlines as the three. (2007)
- **See's in numbers.** Bought in 1972 for $25 million, when it earned under $5 million before tax on $8 million of capital. By 2007 it earned $82 million on $40 million. Along the way it sent $1.35 billion to the parent after keeping only $32 million for itself. That cash bought other businesses. (2007)
- **The word that matters is enduring.** A moat that must be rebuilt every few years is not a moat, which rules out industries prone to rapid change. And if results depend on one superstar, the star is great, not the business. (2007)
- **The Inevitables.** A handful of companies will almost certainly dominate their fields for decades. A larger group will probably do so. Leaders in fast-moving industries belong to neither group. Even with an Inevitable you can overpay, and the usual way they get hurt is management drifting away from the core. (1996)
- **Is the moat wider this year?** He asks managers to strengthen the competitive position every year, even at the cost of current profit. Earnings bought by squeezing customers or skimping on the brand are a withdrawal from the moat. (2005 · 2008)
- **Lowest cost wins slowly.** Where customers buy mainly on price, the operator with the lowest costs keeps taking share. GEICO is his thirty-year example. (1995 · 2000 · 2013)
- **Some trades demand brilliance daily.** A retailer has to be clever every single day, because rivals copy each good idea at once. Other businesses run for decades on one right decision made long ago. He prefers the second kind. (1995)
- **Moats can drain.** Newspapers were close to a local monopoly. Once readers and advertisers had alternatives, capable managers could only slow the decline. When industry economics and management pull in opposite directions, economics wins. (2006 · 2012)
- **Growth is a number, not a virtue.** Growth that needs capital earning a poor return destroys value. Seeing that an industry will grow is easy. Working out who will keep the profit is the hard part, and when he cannot do that he passes. (2007 · 2009)
- **Later, he bought capital-heavy.** With too much cash for small gems, he bought a railroad and utilities: huge capital needs, steady returns on very large sums. In 2023 he said the railroad must spend more than its depreciation just to stand still, and that utility regulation had turned out worse than he assumed. (2009 · 2010 · 2023)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-02-moats-what-makes-a-business-worth-owning.html

### 3. Price, value and the margin of safety

Value is the cash a business will hand its owners over time. Price is what you pay for that. The gap between the two is your return and your protection.

- **Aesop wrote the formula.** A bird in the hand against birds in the bush. To value anything you need three answers: how sure are you the birds are there, when will they appear and how many, and what does a risk-free bond pay meanwhile? Growth is one input among several, and it can subtract value. (2000)
- **A range, never a point.** Intrinsic value is an estimate. If the honest range is too wide to act on, move to something else. A rough figure that is about right beats an exact one that is wrong. (2000 · 2005 · 2010)
- **The two numbers are different things.** What you pay and what you get are separate questions. In the crisis he restated the aim: a good business at a fair price, ahead of a poor one at a low price. (2008)
- **Wonderful at fair beats fair at wonderful.** He began with statistically cheap, mediocre companies. Munger persuaded him that such bargains do not scale and seldom last. This is the largest single change in his method, and he credits it entirely to his partner. (2012 · 2014 · 2023)
- **Great companies at full prices earn ordinary returns.** Buy first-class businesses at rich valuations and you earn roughly their profit growth, nothing extra. A high price removes the margin of safety even when the business is superb. (2005 · 1997)
- **A stated hurdle.** He stayed out of shares unless he saw a high probability of at least 10% a year before tax. Idle cash was the accepted alternative. (2002)
- **Check expectations against arithmetic.** Shareholders together cannot earn more than businesses earn. Any return forecast has to fit economic growth plus inflation plus dividends, less costs. He ran this sum against the optimism of 1999 and against pension-fund assumptions in 2007. (1999 · 2007)
- **Value it as if it had no debt.** Cheap borrowing can make a poor purchase look fine per share. He prices every business on an all-equity basis, then decides. (2000 · 2017)
- **Size is an anchor.** As capital grows, the list of ideas that can move the total shrinks. A small investor has a real edge here, and it erodes with every doubling. (1997 · 1998)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-03-price-value-and-the-margin-of-safety.html

### 4. Mr. Market and temperament

Prices swing far more than values do. The swings are there to be used or ignored. They are never instructions.

- **The hamburger quiz.** If you will be eating burgers for life and do not raise cattle, you should want beef to get cheaper. If you will be a net buyer of shares for years, the same logic applies. Only someone about to sell gains from high prices. (1997)
- **If you must time, time against the crowd.** His advice to those who insist on timing: be cautious when others are eager, and eager only when others are afraid. (2004)
- **Two kinds of fear.** Fear across the market helps you, because it produces bargains. Fear inside you hurts you. An investor who keeps costs low and sits with large, soundly financed businesses will almost certainly do well. (2016)
- **Berkshire itself has halved, more than once.** He printed his own stock's four worst falls (chart below) as the case against borrowing to own shares. Nobody can say how far a price may drop in the short run, and debt forces a decision at the worst moment. Without debt, your mind stays clear. (2017)
- **Cinderella at the ball.** In a boom everyone plans to leave just before midnight. The trouble is that nobody in the ballroom can see a clock. (2000)
- **Bubbles move wealth; they do not create it.** A company that loses money over its lifetime has destroyed value, whatever its market value was at the peak. The gains of promoters came out of the pockets of late buyers. (2000)
- **Being out is the bigger risk.** The danger of sitting out of the game is far larger than the danger of staying in it. He does not step in and out on forecasts. (2012)
- **Bad news is the buyer's friend.** Pessimism lowers prices. Large opportunities are rare, and when one arrives he acts in size. (2008 · 2009)
- **Ignore the chatter.** He spends no time on forecasts of the economy or the market, his own or anyone else's. Beyond the wasted hours, they crowd out the handful of facts about a business that decide the result. (2013)
- **Expect to trail in a boom.** A quality-first approach lags when markets roar and leads when they are flat or falling. Know this ahead of time so a strong year for others does not push you into changing method. (2012)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-04-mr-market-and-temperament.html

### 5. Activity, costs and patience

The return from owning good businesses is earned by sitting. Almost everything an investor does beyond that subtracts from it.

- **Newton's fourth law.** Newton gave physics three laws of motion and then lost a fortune in the South Sea Bubble. Buffett supplies the missing law: for investors as a group, the more they move, the less they keep. (2005)
- **The Gotrocks family.** Imagine one family owns every business in the country. Its wealth grows by what the businesses earn. Then helpers arrive: brokers to trade between cousins, managers to choose the brokers, consultants to choose the managers, and finally hedge funds with a share of profits. Each layer is paid out of the same earnings. He guessed these frictional costs might reach a fifth of all corporate profit. (2005)
- **Three ways investors beat themselves.** High costs from trading and fees. Decisions made on tips and fashion in place of valuation. And stop-start timing: getting in after a long rise and out after a long fall. (2004)
- **Wait for the fat pitch.** Ted Williams cut the strike zone into cells and swung only at balls in his best one. An investor has it easier, because there are no called strikes. Standing with the bat on your shoulder costs nothing. (1997)
- **Doing nothing is a decision.** When you own pieces of excellent businesses, inactivity is the intelligent course. Nobody sells a wonderful subsidiary because of a rate forecast, so why sell a minority stake in one? (1996)
- **The movies would have paid better.** After selling McDonald's and trimming other holdings, he told shareholders they would have done better had he spent market hours at the cinema. (1998)
- **Lumpy beats smooth.** He takes the higher, bumpier return over the lower, steadier one. Most managers choose the reverse because smooth is easier to explain. (1995 · 1998)
- **A dozen decisions.** Looking back over 58 years he counted about twelve really good decisions, roughly one every five years. The record rests on those, plus avoiding ruin in between. (2022)
- **The ten-year bet.** A plain index fund against five funds-of-funds chosen by professionals, over 2008 to 2017. The index fund won by a wide margin (chart below). The managers were not stupid. Layers of fees were the difference. (2016 · 2017)
- **One per cent is not small.** On his 77-year example, an annual fee of 1% would have cut the ending sum in half. (2018)
- **Idle cash is the lesser evil.** Cash earning little is uncomfortable. A purchase made to relieve the discomfort is worse. (1998 · 2003)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-05-activity-costs-and-patience.html

### 6. Risk, debt and survival

Risk is the chance of losing capital for good. Price swings are something else. Stay in a position where no single event can end the game.

- **The one rule.** Among everything that changed at Berkshire over six decades, he names one investment rule that has not and will not: do not put capital at risk of permanent loss. (2023)
- **Volatility is not risk.** Risk is the probability of ending your holding period with less purchasing power. Over a day or a year, shares are riskier than cash. Over decades, cash and bonds are the riskier choice. The horizon decides which is safe. (2011 · 2014)
- **Investors make shares risky themselves.** By trading actively, trying to time moves, diversifying too little, paying high fees and borrowing. Each can turn a good long-run asset into a poor result. (2014)
- **One zero is enough.** A long run of fine numbers multiplied by a single zero is zero. Leverage wins most of the time, which is why it is addictive, and the rare loss is total. (2010)
- **Never rely on strangers.** Keep so much liquidity that any conceivable cash need is small beside it. This costs return in ordinary years. It buys sleep, survival and the means to purchase when others must sell. (2009 · 2010 · 2021)
- **The tide.** Only when conditions turn do you learn who was running without protection. Calm years hide weak practice. (2001)
- **The Noah rule.** He had foreseen the risk of a mega-catastrophe and done too little about it. Forecasting the flood earns nothing. The ark does. (2001)
- **Exposure, not experience.** Judge a risk by what could happen. A quiet record says little about a danger that has not struck yet. (2001)
- **Look for hidden links.** Many small, unrelated risks are safe to carry. One concentrated exposure, or several that turn out to move together, is not. (2001 · 2005)
- **History-fed formulas.** Models built on past data give precise answers and false comfort when the conditions that produced the data have changed. He warns in particular against handing risk decisions to people with formulas. (2008)
- **Derivatives.** Hidden leverage, chains of counterparties, and profits booked on models years before any cash arrives. He wound down General Re's book and admitted he took too long. (2002 · 2003)
- **Small odds, long time.** A one-in-thirty chance each year becomes about 97% over a century. A risk you would dismiss in any single year is close to certain across an investing life. (2015)
- **Low rates are no excuse.** When safe yields are poor, the temptation is to accept weaker credit or longer maturities. He holds Treasury bills and waits. (2003 · 2019 · 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-06-risk-debt-and-survival.html

### 7. Circle of competence

You do not need to understand many businesses. You need to know exactly which ones you do understand, and stay there.

- **Know the perimeter.** The size of the circle matters little. Knowing where it ends matters a great deal. You only ever have to value the companies you choose to value. (1996)
- **Why he skipped technology.** He did not think the industry was bad. He could not tell which companies would hold a durable advantage ten years out. In 1999 that discipline cost him his worst year against the index, and he gave his own stock-picking a D. He kept the rule. (1999)
- **Exciting is not the same as knowable.** The first item on his list of things Berkshire does not do: buy into businesses whose future he cannot assess, however thrilling the product. (2009)
- **Multiply the odds.** A plan that needs several separate things to go right has a low chance of success even if each step looks likely. He learned it from a zinc-recovery project. Simple propositions survive contact with reality better. (2004)
- **Passing is free.** If you cannot make a rough estimate of earnings five years ahead, move on. Nobody can call you out for not swinging. (1997 · 2013)
- **Know-nothing can beat know-something.** An investor who admits to knowing nothing about individual companies and buys a cheap index fund over time will beat most professionals. Trouble starts in between, with knowing a little and acting on a lot. (2013)
- **The circle can grow, slowly.** Apple entered the portfolio in 2016 and within five years was one of Berkshire's four giants. He treats it as a consumer franchise with loyal users and large buybacks, which is ground he knows. (2020 · 2021)
- **Keep learning.** Among the Munger sayings he passed on: the world changes, and your views must change with it. Staying inside the circle does not mean freezing it. (2022)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-07-circle-of-competence.html

### 8. Capital allocation: what happens to retained profit

Over a decade, what management does with the profit it keeps counts for more than the profit itself.

- **An order of preference.** First, reinvest in existing businesses where that widens the moat. Second, buy other businesses. Third, repurchase shares when they sell well below value. Dividends come when none of these can earn a good return. (2012)
- **Dividend or sell a little?** He worked an example: owners who keep everything reinvested and sell a small slice each year can end with more cash and more capital than under a payout, provided retained money earns well. Each owner also sets his own level of income. (2012)
- **Buybacks need two conditions.** The company has more cash than the business needs, and the shares trade below a conservative estimate of value. With both, buying back is the surest use of money. Without the second, it destroys value for those who stay. (1999 · 2011 · 2016)
- **The IBM paradox.** If you own a company that keeps buying its own shares, and you are not selling, you should hope the price stays low for years. Each repurchase then lifts your share of the business by more. (2011)
- **Ownership that grows by itself.** Apple's repurchases raised Berkshire's percentage stake year after year without Berkshire buying a share. (2020 · 2021)
- **Issuing shares is selling the family silver.** Paying for an acquisition with stock means handing over a slice of everything you already own. He paid for Dexter Shoe in shares; by 2007 those shares were worth $3.5 billion, for a purchase of about $400 million. (1997 · 2005 · 2009)
- **The 1924 insight.** Edgar Lawrence Smith set out to show bonds beat shares and found the opposite, because companies keep part of their profit and compound it. Retained earnings are the engine. Everything else is commentary. (2019)
- **Deferred tax is an interest-free loan.** Tax owed on unrealised gains stays invested and working until the day you sell. Each sale ends that loan. (2018)
- **Options that reward hoarding.** A fixed-price option gains value when a manager simply retains earnings, with no skill involved. Watch how pay is set where profits pile up. (2005)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-08-capital-allocation-what-happens-to-retained-profit.html

### 9. Acquisitions: a test for any company that buys others

Most deals help the seller and the adviser. Use his filters to judge every serial acquirer you own.

- **The seller knows more.** The seller picks the moment and writes the forecast. He treats sellers' projections as entertainment. Most acquisitions damage the buyer's shareholders. (1995)
- **Compare with the stock market.** Every proposed purchase has to beat the alternative of simply buying shares in the best listed companies. Many managements never run that comparison. (1995)
- **His six filters.** Large enough to matter. Consistent earning power already shown. Good returns on equity with little debt. Management in place. A simple business. A stated price. No turnarounds, no auctions, no hostile bids. (1999 · 2003 · 2008)
- **Be the buyer of choice.** Owners who care what happens to their company after the sale prefer a buyer with no exit plan and no debt-loading. That reputation took decades to build and wins deals money alone could not. (2000 · 2002 · 2008)
- **The spreadsheet never disappoints.** Once a chief executive wants a deal, the forecasts and the promised synergies will be found to support it. In 2017 he sat out because prices for decent businesses had reached records, pushed by cheap debt. (2017)
- **Who is advising?** An adviser paid only if the deal closes will favour closing. He proposed hiring a second adviser paid only if the deal fails. (2009 · 2019)
- **Like a marriage.** Surprises arrive after the ceremony. Most of his have worked out, and the good ones grow to become most of the value while the poor ones shrink in importance. (2019)
- **Overpaying, in his own words.** The $11 billion after-tax write-down on Precision Castparts was his error alone. He was too hopeful about its normal level of profit and so paid too much. Nobody misled him. (2020)
- **The handshake.** Some of his best purchases closed after one meeting with no formal checks. That works only when you know exactly who you are dealing with. (1997 · 2003)
- **Tuck-ins under proven managers.** Small additions to businesses run by tested people carry the least risk. They extend talent already proven. (2006)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-09-acquisitions-a-test-for-any-company-that-buys-others.html

### 10. Managers, pay and boards

He looks for people who run a company as if it were their family's only asset, and for pay and boards that keep them that way.

- **Three tests, in one sentence.** Good returns on the tangible capital the business needs, managers who are both able and honest, and a sensible price. (2019)
- **The hundred-year instruction.** His managers are told to run the business as if they owned all of it, it were the only asset their family would ever have, and it could not be sold for a century. (1998)
- **Choose carefully, then leave them alone.** He hires with great care and manages very little. Capital allocation and the choice of chief executive stay at the centre. Everything else is delegated. (2010)
- **Pay for what the manager controls.** Bonuses tied to the results of the manager's own unit. A share price moves for reasons outside any one person's control and makes a poor yardstick. (1996 · 1997 · 2006)
- **Options are a cost; bought shares are commitment.** Accounting long treated options as free. He counts them as pay and deducts them when valuing a company. He prefers managers who buy shares with their own money and carry the downside too. (1998 · 2001 · 2002)
- **Beware the chief executive who forecasts growth.** Very few large companies sustain 15% a year. A leader who promises it will eventually be tempted to manufacture it. (2000)
- **The company that always makes its number.** Business is too uneven for that. Consistently meeting expectations is evidence of management of the figures. (2002 · 2016 · 2022)
- **What a director is for.** Business sense, an owner's outlook, and shares bought with personal money. When the fee is a large part of a director's income, independence is hard to keep. The core job is choosing and overseeing the chief executive. (2002 · 2003 · 2019)
- **The ratchet.** Pay committees compare with peers, nobody wants to be below average, and so the average climbs every year. (2005)
- **Candour.** Spin travels inward: tell the public a flattering story for long enough and you start to believe it. He writes each letter as he would want to be written to if a relative ran the business and he were the absent owner. (1995 · 2023)
- **No thumb-sucking.** Munger's term for putting off the correction of a mistake. He calls delay the cardinal sin, worse than the original error. He adds that he never looks at where a candidate went to school. (2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-10-managers-pay-and-boards.html

### 11. Accounting: read like an owner

Reported numbers are where analysis starts. His letters are a thirty-year course in where they mislead.

- **Depreciation is real.** It is a worse cost than most, because the cash goes out first and the benefit arrives later. He is scathing about measures that leave it out. (2002)
- **Adjusted earnings.** Share-based pay is a cost. Restructuring that recurs every few years is a cost. Figures that strip them out flatter management. (2015 · 2016 · 2021)
- **Standing still costs more than the books say.** For capital-heavy businesses, real maintenance spending runs above the depreciation charge. Owner earnings are lower than reported profit. (2016 · 2018 · 2023)
- **The big bath.** Large one-time charges and reserves set up at acquisitions can be fed back into later years to smooth profit. He named the practice and declined to use it. (1998)
- **Not all amortisation is a cost.** Writing down software is a true expense. Writing down purchased customer lists or goodwill often is not, because the asset may be growing in value. Separate the two before judging earnings. (1999 · 2012)
- **The chosen base year.** A growth table that starts in a terrible year or ends in a wonderful one can make ordinary performance look brilliant. Check the endpoints. (2003)
- **Bottom-line noise.** Since unrealised gains on shares began flowing through profit, reported net income swings wildly and says little. He directs readers to operating earnings. (2017 · 2018 · 2019)
- **Book value retired.** After three decades as his yardstick, he dropped book value. It understates operating businesses, and buybacks above book reduce it while raising value per share. (2018)
- **Three warning signs.** Weak accounting choices, footnotes you cannot follow, and management that broadcasts profit forecasts. If you cannot understand a note, he assumes that was intended. (2002)
- **Self-graded exams.** An insurer's profit depends on its own estimate of future claims. Such estimates are usually too low. The same caution applies to any business where today's profit rests on a guess about tomorrow's losses. (1999 · 2001 · 2017)
- **Four questions for the auditor.** He drafted them for audit committees. The first: had the auditor alone prepared these accounts, what would have been done differently? (2002)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-11-accounting-read-like-an-owner.html

### 12. Insurance: float and the discipline of saying no

Every letter returns to insurance. The ideas carry over to any business that takes money today against a promise to pay later, such as lenders.

- **Float.** Premiums arrive now and claims are paid later. Meanwhile the insurer invests money it holds and does not own. If premiums cover claims and expenses, the float is free, or better than free. (1995 to 2024)
- **Three questions about float.** How much is there, what does it cost, and what is the long-run outlook for both? Size alone tells you nothing. (2002)
- **Four disciplines.** Understand every exposure. Assess the likelihood and cost of loss conservatively. Set a price that leaves a profit. Walk away if that price is not available. (2011 · 2014)
- **The fourth is where most fail.** National Indemnity let its volume shrink for years when prices were poor, and promised no layoffs so that staff would not write bad business to keep their jobs. Most insurers cannot bear to watch competitors take the business. (2004 · 2012)
- **Easy in, hard out.** A badly priced contract takes a moment to sign and can take decades to pay for. (1995)
- **Surprises go one way.** In long-dated promises, bad surprises far outnumber good ones. Reserve and price with that in mind. (2005)
- **Profit that is not profit yet.** Under-priced catastrophe cover can look like easy money for years before one event takes it all back. Judge such a business over a long span. (1996 · 1997)
- **A weak reinsurer is no protection.** Cheap cover from a party that may not pay is expensive. The same holds for any guarantee. (2002)
- **A revolving fund.** Accounts show float as a debt due. In practice it is replaced as it is paid out, so its economic burden is far lower than the stated figure, as long as underwriting holds. (2012 to 2016)
- **The long tail.** The true cost of some policies is not known for decades. Optimism has no place in pricing them. (2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-12-insurance-float-and-the-discipline-of-saying-no.html

### 13. Mistakes: his own list

Read what he took from each one. His costly errors fall into four groups: misjudging how long an advantage would last, paying with undervalued shares, paying an optimistic price, and waiting too long once the facts changed. Market crashes do not appear on the list. The other half of the picture came in 2022: about one good decision every five years has carried the record.

  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-13-mistakes-his-own-list.html

### 14. Productive assets, inflation and the long view

Wealth compounds in things that produce: businesses, farms, property. Claims on money and objects that produce nothing do not compound.

- **Three kinds of asset.** Claims on currency, such as deposits and bonds, look safe and lose purchasing power quietly. Assets that produce nothing depend on a later buyer paying more. Productive assets keep yielding whatever happens to the currency. He chooses the third by a wide margin. (2011)
- **The gold cube.** All the world's gold, about 170,000 tonnes, would make a cube 68 feet a side. At that year's price it equalled all the farmland in America plus sixteen Exxon Mobils, with about $1 trillion left over. A century on, the farms and companies will have produced enormous output. The cube will be the same cube. (2011)
- **The $114.75 example.** His first share purchase, in 1942, cost $114.75. Put into a no-fee index fund with dividends reinvested, that sum would have reached $606,811 by early 2019. In gold it would have been about $4,200. (2018)
- **What holds up in inflation.** The ideal asset can raise its prices with the currency and needs little fresh capital to do so. Farms, property and businesses such as See's pass both tests. (2011)
- **Cash: fortress, not home.** He holds very large amounts of Treasury bills so that Berkshire can never be forced. In his last letter he also wrote that he will never prefer cash-equivalents to ownership of good businesses. Both statements hold together. (2003 · 2024)
- **The tailwind.** Productivity gains have raised living standards for two centuries, and he expects that to continue. He says much of Berkshire's record came from this, as distinct from his own skill. (2015 · 2018 · 2020)
- **Japan.** Stakes in five trading houses, bought from 2019 and largely funded by borrowing in yen, so the currency risk is neutral. Simple businesses, low prices, sensible managements. The position was disclosed on his ninetieth birthday, a late lesson in looking abroad. (2020 to 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/buffett-14-productive-assets-inflation-and-the-long-view.html

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers.” (2021 letter)
- “Games are won by players who focus on the playing field” (2013 letter)
- “Price is what you pay; value is what you get.” (2008 letter)
- “nothing recedes like success” (1997 letter)
- “be fearful when others are greedy and greedy only when others are fearful” (2004 letter)
- “speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest” (2000 letter)
- “We do better when the wind is in our face.” (2012 letter)
- “When it's raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.” (2009 letter)
- “For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.” (2005 letter)
- “don't even think about owning it for ten minutes” (1996 letter)
- “Performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter.” (2017 letter)
- “we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%” (1998 letter)
- “Never risk permanent loss of capital.” (2023 letter)
- “Volatility is far from synonymous with risk.” (2014 letter)
- “Predicting rain doesn't count; building arks does.” (2001 letter)
- “derivatives are financial weapons of mass destruction” (2002 letter)
- “credit is like oxygen” (2010 letter)
- “Over time, bad relative numbers will produce unsatisfactory absolute results.” (1999 letter)
- “What is smart at one price is stupid at another.” (2016 letter)
- “Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut.” (2019 letter)
- “A bad reinsurance contract is like hell” (1995 letter)
- “You can fondle the cube, but it will not respond.” (2011 letter)
- “The babies being born in America today are the luckiest crop in history.” (2015 letter)
- “Never bet against America.” (2020 letter)
- “Mistakes fade away; winners can forever blossom.” (2024 letter)
- “The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom.” (2022 letter)

## Read the originals

Open Berkshire's letters page and pick the year. In each report, start reading at “To the Shareholders of Berkshire Hathaway Inc.”

- [The 1995 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Why most acquisitions fail. Retailing against one-decision businesses. The full purchase of GEICO.
- [The 1996 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The best single letter on how an individual should choose shares: circle of competence, the Inevitables, inactivity.
- [The 1997 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The hamburger quiz. Ted Williams and the fat pitch. What it costs to pay with shares.
- [The 1998 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): General Re. Options as a cost. Accounting games named. The McDonald's confession.
- [The 1999 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): His worst relative year. Why no technology shares. Rules for buybacks. Look-through earnings.
- [The 2000 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Aesop's formula for value. Investment against speculation. The bubble examined.
- [The 2001 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): After September 11: three underwriting rules, the Noah rule, the tide going out.
- [The 2002 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Derivatives. What directors are for. Three accounting warning signs.
- [The 2003 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The base-year trick. Lending in manufactured housing. Directors' independence. Index funds.
- [The 2004 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Three ways investors beat themselves. National Indemnity shrinking on purpose.
- [The 2005 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The Gotrocks family and frictional costs. Widening the moat. How pay ratchets up.
- [The 2006 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The fading moat of newspapers. Two-and-twenty fees. Walter Schloss.
- [The 2007 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Great, good and gruesome businesses. See's in numbers. Dexter's true cost.
- [The 2008 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The crisis. Price against value. Models and their limits. His own errors that year.
- [The 2009 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The list of things Berkshire does not do. Issuing shares for the railroad. Liquidity.
- [The 2010 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Leverage and liquidity: the clearest statement of why he avoids debt.
- [The 2011 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Three kinds of asset and the gold cube. The IBM buyback paradox. Four insurance disciplines.
- [The 2012 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Dividends explained with a worked example. The order of capital allocation.
- [The 2013 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The farm and the New York property. Advice for the non-professional. His will.
- [The 2014 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Fifty-year review: bargains to quality, the conglomerate form, volatility against risk.
- [The 2015 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Productivity and prosperity. The case against adjusted earnings. Small odds over long periods.
- [The 2016 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The logic of buybacks. The ten-year bet. Two kinds of fear.
- [The 2017 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Deal prices and cheap debt. Berkshire's four crashes. The bet's final lessons.
- [The 2018 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Forest and trees. Book value retired. The $114.75 example.
- [The 2019 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The power of retained earnings. What boards get wrong. Conflicted advice.
- [The 2020 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): The Precision Castparts confession. Conglomerates. Buybacks at Apple.
- [The 2021 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Business-pickers. The four giants. Why so much cash.
- [The 2022 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Coca-Cola and American Express dividends over three decades. A dozen decisions. Munger's sayings.
- [The 2023 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Munger the architect. Writing for an absent owner. The one rule. Japan. Errors in rail and utilities.
- [The 2024 letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): Mistakes and thumb-sucking. Cash against businesses. His last annual letter.

## Words to know

- **Intrinsic value**: The cash a business will hand its owners over its remaining life, valued today. Always an estimate, best held as a range.
- **Margin of safety**: The gap between that value and the price you pay. It protects you when your estimate is wrong.
- **Moat**: Whatever stops competitors from taking a business's profits: a brand, low costs, a network, a licence.
- **Mr. Market**: Benjamin Graham's imaginary partner who offers to buy or sell every day at prices set by his mood. Use his offers; never take his advice.
- **Circle of competence**: The businesses you genuinely understand well enough to value. Knowing its edge matters more than its size.
- **Retained earnings**: Profit a company keeps and reinvests instead of paying out. What it earns on that money decides the next decade.
- **Buyback**: A company buying its own shares. Sensible only with spare cash and a price below value.
- **Float**: Money an insurer holds between collecting premiums and paying claims, invested in the meantime.
- **Owner earnings**: Profit after the spending needed just to keep the business where it is.
- **Book value**: Assets minus liabilities in the accounts. Buffett's yardstick for decades, retired in 2018.

## Sources and scope

Every idea in this section comes from the chairman's letters published in Berkshire Hathaway's annual reports for 1995 to 2024, read at berkshirehathaway.com/reports.html. Figures (See's, Coca-Cola, the ten-year bet, Berkshire's price falls, the gold cube, the $114.75 example, Precision Castparts) were checked against the letter of the year shown. The wording is the compiler's own throughout, apart from the short phrases marked as his, one per letter. The letters are Warren Buffett's copyright; read them in full, because a summary cannot carry his voice or his humour.

Buffett wrote the annual letters through the 2024 letter. The 2025 letter, published in February 2026, was written by Greg Abel and is outside this section. A 2026 letter has not been published yet. Buffett's short farewell note of November 2025 is optional reading in week 12.

# Charlie Munger

> Buffett's partner for over forty years, and the clearest thinker on why smart people make bad decisions.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/munger.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Hang what you learn on a latticework of big ideas from many fields, and invert: ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid it.

## Summary

Charlie Munger was Buffett's partner and Berkshire's vice chairman from 1978 until his death in November 2023, at 99. He trained as a lawyer, and his talks are as much about how to think and live as about money.

## Big ideas

### 1. A latticework of models

Isolated facts do not stick and do not help. Hang them on a frame built from the big ideas of many fields, then use whichever ideas fit the problem.

- **The frame comes first.** If facts do not hang together on a latticework of theory, you cannot use them when you need them. Build a frame of models from several fields and attach your reading and experience to it. (USC 1994)
- **The man with a hammer.** A person who knows one model forces every problem into its shape. Narrow training makes this error common. (USC 1994)
- **Each field has a few big ideas.** The truly big ideas in each discipline, learned in essence, carry most of the load. Learning those is far less work than mastering any one field. (HLS 1998)
- **Learn it the way pilots do.** Pilots get training wide enough to cover nearly everything useful, use checklists every time, and keep skills fresh in simulators. He wanted professionals educated the same way. (HLS 1998)
- **Prefer the most basic explanation.** Give priority to the explanation from the most fundamental discipline, and credit each idea to the field it came from. (HLS 1998)
- **Be fluent with numbers.** Numerical fluency was one of his five helpful notions. Arithmetic shows what a goal really requires. (Practical 1996)
- **Big results have several causes.** Expect extreme outcomes from combinations of factors acting together, not from one lever. (Practical 1996)
- **Simple maths on the odds.** He judged bets with the elementary probability of Fermat and Pascal. Accounting helps as well, though it stops describing reality in some cases, such as a shrinking business. (USC 1994)
- **Don't worship what can be counted.** Almost everyone overweighs what can be numbered and neglects what cannot. (UCSB 2003)
- **Physics envy.** Hoping that economics will behave with the precision of physics gets clever people into terrible trouble. (UCSB 2003)
- **And then what?** Economics pays too little attention to second- and higher-order effects. Follow consequences further than the first step. (UCSB 2003)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-01-a-latticework-of-models.html

### 2. Invert, always invert

Many problems that resist a direct attack give way when turned round. Ask what would guarantee failure, and then avoid it.

- **A graduation speech about misery.** Asked to advise school leavers, he listed sure routes to a miserable life, adding his own to three that Johnny Carson had given years before. Avoiding them is most of the work. (HS 1986)
- **The rustic's question.** A countryman wished he knew where he was going to die, so he would never go there. Munger treats the joke as a serious method. (HS 1986)
- **Jacobi's rule.** The mathematician Carl Jacobi advised turning problems around. Munger points to Darwin and Einstein, who made breakthroughs by thinking in reverse. (HS 1986)
- **Forward and backward.** Get the needed models into your head, then think each problem through both forward and backward. (Stanford 1996)
- **Decide the no-brainers first.** Settle the big, obvious questions first. With those fixed, the rest of a problem often becomes simple. (Practical 1996)
- **Think in reverse.** When you cannot see how to reach a goal, ask what would make it impossible, and remove that. (Practical 1996)
- **Twenty-one years later.** He told law graduates the same thing: turn a problem around and you often think better. (USC Law 2007)
- **What to avoid comes first.** He usually decided what not to do before choosing what to do. Avoiding large errors beats occasional flashes of brilliance. (Almanack)
- **Three baskets.** For investments he kept three baskets: yes, no, and too tough to understand. The third basket is large, and he felt no duty to empty it. (Almanack)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-02-invert-always-invert.html

### 3. Incentives

To predict what people will do, look first at what they are rewarded for. He put this first in his list of 25 human tendencies.

- **The first tendency.** People respond to rewards and punishments far more strongly than they expect, and their beliefs drift to fit what pays. (PHM 2005)
- **Incentive-caused bias.** Decent people reach conclusions that serve their own income, often without knowing it. Take special care with advice from anyone paid by the action they recommend. (PHM 2005)
- **Pay for the result.** His example: a delivery company's night shift ran slow until workers were paid per shift and could go home once all the planes were loaded. Pay for time and you get time. (PHM 2005)
- **Controls are a kindness.** He called the cash register a great moral instrument. Systems that make cheating hard keep honest people honest. (PHM 2005)
- **Stop slop early.** Small dishonesty that is tolerated spreads, and becomes very hard to reverse. Stop it at the start. (Stanford 1996)
- **Granny's rule.** Make the pleasant thing the reward for doing the unpleasant thing first. (PHM 2005)
- **Keep advisers working for you.** Whoever pays the fees must control the advisers. Layers of consultants bring perverse incentives. (Foundations 1998)
- **Reasons work.** People comply more when given reasons, even weak ones. Give real reasons, and test the reasons you are given. (PHM 2005)
- **Choose your system.** Avoid perverse incentive systems, and avoid working directly under someone you do not admire and do not want to be like. (USC Law 2007)
- **Systems before villains.** He traced much corporate misconduct to standard incentive systems working on people below conscious awareness. Wrongdoing that is rewarded dies hard. (Scandal 2000)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-03-incentives.html

### 4. The psychology of misjudgment

He built a list of 25 mental tendencies that lead sensible people into error, and used it as a checklist. The danger peaks when several act at once.

- **Three talks became one.** Talks given in 1992, 1994 and 1995 became one. He rewrote it for the book in 2005, at 81, from memory and without fresh research. (PHM 2005)
- **Use it as a checklist.** He ran through his own list, tendency by tendency, to explain events that puzzled him. Do the same before an important decision. (PHM 2005)
- **Lollapalooza.** Extreme outcomes come from several tendencies pushing the same way. One of his examples is an airliner evacuation test, run in a darkened hangar with older volunteers, that ended in many injuries. (PHM 2005)
- **Authority can be fatal.** People defer to whoever is in charge, even when that person is plainly wrong. In one of his examples, that deference ended in a plane crash. (PHM 2005)
- **Know it; don't abuse it.** Not everything you know about psychology should be used to manipulate people. Anyone who sees through it will hate you for it. (Stanford 1996)
- **Crowd folly.** Under some conditions people behave like lemmings. He said this explains much foolish thinking, in markets as elsewhere. (Roundtable 2000)
- **Priced like paintings.** He described shares being valued partly like Rembrandt paintings: bought mostly because their prices had already risen so far. (Roundtable 2000)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-04-the-psychology-of-misjudgment.html

### 5. The inner life: envy, resentment, self-pity

Much of his life advice is about thoughts to refuse. A few emotions do more damage than bad luck, and they are under your control.

- **Three from Carson.** He began with Johnny Carson's prescriptions for misery: mood-altering chemicals, envy and resentment. (HS 1986)
- **Resentment costs the carrier.** He cites Disraeli, who learned to give up revenge as a motive, though he kept an outlet for resentment. A grudge mostly harms the person who carries it. (HS 1986)
- **Four to refuse.** Envy, resentment, revenge and self-pity: he named them together as disastrous ways of thinking. (USC Law 2007)
- **Envy is everywhere.** He said envy and jealousy are extreme in modern life. Expect them in others, and watch for them in yourself. (PHM 2005)
- **Defer the reaction.** The standard cure for overactive hostility is to train yourself to delay your response. (PHM 2005)
- **Denial.** The mind bends facts that are too painful to accept. Notice when you are doing it. (PHM 2005)
- **Light stress, heavy stress.** Light stress can slightly improve performance; heavy stress causes dysfunction. Make big decisions when calm. (PHM 2005)
- **Being right can cost you.** You can cause great offence by being right in a way that makes someone lose face in front of others. (USC Law 2007)
- **Avoid intense ideology.** He warned that extremely intense ideology clouds the mind. (USC Law 2007)
- **How to bear hard times.** Have low expectations, keep a sense of humour, and surround yourself with the love of friends and family. (Stanford 1996)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-05-the-inner-life-envy-resentment-self-pity.html

### 6. Reliability, trust and deserving

He thought most of what people want in life is earned by being someone others can rely on. Trust that is deserved is the strongest arrangement there is.

- **Be reliable.** First on his own list of routes to misery was being unreliable: not faithfully doing what you have promised. He said it can outweigh all your other virtues combined. (HS 1986)
- **Learnable by almost anyone.** In a 2006 note he repeated that reliability is essential for progress in life, and that almost anyone can learn it to great advantage. (HS 1986)
- **Deserve what you want.** The safest way to try to get what you want is to try to deserve it. (USC Law 2007)
- **Admiration-based love.** He thought no love is so right as love grounded in admiration, and that it should extend to the instructive dead. (USC Law 2007)
- **Three rules for a career.** Sell only what you would buy yourself. Work only for people you respect and admire. Work only with people you enjoy. (Stanford 1996)
- **A seamless web of deserved trust.** In your own life, what you want to maximise is trust that has been earned, all the way round. (USC Law 2007)
- **Choose clients like friends.** A rule from his years as a lawyer, and one that applies to partners, managers and investments too. (Almanack)
- **Liking distorts.** We overlook the faults of people and things we love. Love admirable people, and still check their work. (PHM 2005)
- **Records over impressions.** A face-to-face meeting carries too much weight. Underweigh the impression and overweigh the past record. (PHM 2005)
- **Fairness matters.** People react strongly when they are treated unfairly. Arrangements that feel unfair breed resentment that outlasts the gain. (PHM 2005)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-06-reliability-trust-and-deserving.html

### 7. Learning for life

He saw lifelong learning as a duty, and as the main reason ordinary people overtake cleverer ones over a working life.

- **Learning machines.** He kept seeing people rise who were not always the smartest, but who kept learning. They went to bed each night a little wiser than they were that morning. (USC Law 2007)
- **Wisdom is a moral duty.** He held that acquiring wisdom is an obligation, not a hobby. (USC Law 2007)
- **Skills expire.** Without lifetime learning you will not do well. Berkshire's skills from one decade would not have carried it through the next. (USC Law 2007)
- **Learn from other people's mistakes.** Learning everything from your own experience was on his list of routes to misery. The errors of others are cheaper teachers. (HS 1986)
- **The instructive dead.** Admire and learn from the great minds of the past. He counted them among the right objects of love. (USC Law 2007)
- **Keep curiosity alive.** Curiosity drives learning and protects against many other errors. (PHM 2005)
- **Use it or lose it.** Skills fade without practice. Skills practised to fluency last much longer. (PHM 2005)
- **Learning gets harder with age.** Ageing makes new, complex skills harder to acquire. Keep learning and practising, and learn the difficult things while you can. (PHM 2005)
- **Hunt for disconfirming evidence.** Darwin trained himself early to weigh seriously any evidence against his own hypotheses. Do the same with your beliefs. (PHM 2005)
- **Maintain what you know.** Pilots are made to practise in simulators so skills do not decay. Schedule your own refreshers. (HLS 1998)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-07-learning-for-life.html

### 8. Objectivity and the edge of what you know

Knowing the limits of your competence is worth more than its size. Self-regard and strong ideology are the usual ways people step over the edge without noticing.

- **Circle of competence.** Everyone has a circle of competence. Play where you have an edge, and stay out of games where others clearly have it. (USC 1994)
- **Know what you don't know.** Know what you know and what you do not. When you lack competence, say so. (Stanford 1996)
- **Use your advantages.** Work out where your talents lie and use them. Berkshire avoided high technology partly because it had no edge there. (Stanford 1996)
- **Change your mind.** He said he and Buffett were very good at changing their prior conclusions. (Stanford 1996)
- **Earn the right to an opinion.** He did not feel entitled to an opinion until he could state the arguments against it better than its supporters could. (USC Law 2007)
- **Self-serving bias.** It is in everyone. Use routines and checklists to keep yourself objective. (USC Law 2007)
- **Don't fool yourself.** He quoted Feynman: the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. (Foundations 1998)
- **Don't rush to decide.** Uncertainty is uncomfortable, so the mind grabs an answer early. Slow down before a big decision. (PHM 2005)
- **Overoptimism.** People expect better outcomes than the odds support. The antidote is habitual use of simple probability. (PHM 2005)
- **Vivid is not important.** What comes to mind easily gets too much weight. Look for the evidence that is dull but large. (PHM 2005)
- **Crowds and authority.** People copy others and defer to authority, most of all when confused or rushed. Those are the moments to slow down. (PHM 2005)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-08-objectivity-and-the-edge-of-what-you-know.html

### 9. Investing: few, great, and then sit

The big money comes from a handful of great businesses, bought when the odds are clearly favourable, then held for a long time.

- **The great businesses did it.** He said the great bulk of their money came from the great businesses. (USC 1994)
- **Bet heavily when the odds are clear.** The wise ones bet heavily when the world offers them the opportunity. The rest of the time, they wait. (USC 1994)
- **Twenty punches.** Imagine a ticket with only 20 slots for every investment you will ever make. You would think hard and bet big on each one. (USC 1994)
- **Quality compounds.** Over long periods a share earns roughly what the business earns. A business earning 18% on capital for 20 or 30 years gives a fine result even bought at an expensive-looking price. (USC 1994)
- **Taxes favour sitting.** The way income tax works alone gives a large edge to holding for a long time. (USC 1994)
- **The industry adds nothing, net.** The investment management business as a whole adds no value for all its clients combined. A select few managers can. (USC 1994)
- **Opportunity cost.** Judge every use of money against the next-best use available. (Almanack)
- **Resist the urge to act.** Patience means resisting the natural human bias to do something. (Almanack)
- **Concentration can be rational.** Someone with nearly all their wealth held long-term in three fine companies is securely rich. Heavy concentration can be a rational choice. (Foundations 1998)
- **Lumpy results are the price.** In super-cat reinsurance, huge swings in annual results, including some very unpleasant years, are inevitable. Judge it over many years. (Wesco 1996)
- **Need less.** In a 2006 note he worried about institutions imitating Harvard and Yale's investing out of envy, and favoured reducing one's perceived needs over taking more risk. (USC 1994)
- **Omissions cost most.** Among Berkshire's mistakes he named the failure to buy Walmart early. (BRK 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-09-investing-few-great-and-then-sit.html

### 10. Business models, moats and scale

He studied why some businesses compound for a century while others never earn their keep, and taught it through plain examples.

- **Scale isn't enough.** Sears's advantages of scale did not stop it losing heavily to Walmart. Bureaucracy did Sears terrible damage. (USC 1994)
- **Who keeps the gain?** In a commodity business, the advantages of great improvements flow through to customers, not to owners. (USC 1994)
- **Razor and blades.** Gillette began selling blades in multiple packages, with the razor handle a one-time purchase. Repeat purchases built the business. (USC 1994)
- **A gem under the mess.** GEICO had a magnificent business submerged in a mess, but still working. Clearing the mess released its value. (USC 1994)
- **Coca-Cola from scratch.** It is 1884 in Atlanta. You have $2 million and must build a business worth $2 trillion. How would you do it? (Practical 1996)
- **Start from the arithmetic.** He set the target first: 2.92 trillion eight-ounce servings in 2034. Netting 4¢ a serving would earn $117 billion. The numbers show what the business must become. (Practical 1996)
- **Many factors at once.** A strong trademark, Pavlovian conditioning, social proof and being always available, all working together. (Practical 1996)
- **Owners can wreck a brand.** With New Coke, the company's own executives came to the brink of destroying the most valuable trademark in the world. (Practical 1996)
- **Inflation sorts businesses.** Some businesses produce little cash even when volume holds steady. Borrowing short and lending long, the savings and loan model, can stop working and go into reverse. (Blue Chip 1982)
- **No jewel.** He told owners plainly that his savings and loan, as it then had to be run, was no jewel. Careful operators in that business earned very modest returns. (Wesco 1985)
- **Owners and managers.** In that industry, managers were mostly not owners, and their rewards were tied to size and recent numbers. (Wesco 1985)
- **A weaker vehicle, said plainly.** Each dollar of Wesco's book value, he wrote, gave much less intrinsic value than a dollar at Berkshire. (Wesco 2006)
- **Respect rivals you dislike.** People underrate both the competence and the morals of competitors they dislike. (PHM 2005)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-10-business-models-moats-and-scale.html

### 11. Costs, consultants and febezzlement

Fees and frictional costs look small each year and become enormous over time. He attacked them with arithmetic and with a word he coined.

- **Layers of consultants.** Large institutions hired consultants to choose managers, adding layers with perverse incentives and little clear benefit. (Foundations 1998)
- **Three per cent a year.** Counting every layer, total investment costs could easily reach 3% of a foundation's net worth each year. (Foundations 1998)
- **Half must be below the median.** After the croupiers' take, exactly half of investors get a below-median result. Yet nearly every expert says he is above average. (Foundations 1998)
- **Leverage plus overconfidence.** Long-Term Capital Management collapsed through overconfidence in its highly leveraged methods. (Foundations 1998)
- **Indexing for the average foundation.** He judged indexing a wiser choice for the average foundation than what it was doing. (Foundations 1998)
- **Febezzle.** The economist J. K. Galbraith wrote of the 'bezzle', wealth that has been embezzled but not yet missed. Munger coined 'febezzle' for wealth quietly lost to wasteful investment fees. (Roundtable 2000)
- **Switching is expensive.** Constantly pulling money from lagging managers is folly. He put investors' real performance lag at over 5% of assets a year. (Roundtable 2000)
- **Wealth effects.** Rising share prices make people feel and spend as if richer, which he warned could produce much mischief. (Roundtable 2000)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-11-costs-consultants-and-febezzlement.html

### 12. Accounting, honesty and candour

He wrote as a lawyer who distrusted flattering numbers. The test is always what an absent owner would want to be told.

- **A parable written in 2000.** He imagined Quant Tech, a prosperous company whose founder died in 1982, and traced how the managers who followed him ruined it by chasing reported earnings. (Scandal 2000)
- **Options counted as free.** Because share options were not counted as a cost, managers could add phony earnings to real ones. (Scandal 2000)
- **Dollops.** A moderate dollop of phony earnings each year is less likely to be noticed than one large one. (Scandal 2000)
- **A chain letter inside.** Inflated earnings brought a Ponzi or chain-letter effect into the share price, rewarding present holders at later buyers' expense. (Scandal 2000)
- **Professions pay the bill.** After the scandal, the public turned hard against the professions that had made it possible. (Scandal 2000)
- **Write for the absent owner.** Each year they tried to tell shareholders what they would want to be told if the roles were reversed. (Blue Chip 1982)
- **Repeat what matters.** Repetition is right where facts stay true and analytically important over many years. (Blue Chip 1982)
- **Flag the unusual.** He labelled a large gain as highly unusual and not likely to recur. (Wesco 1985)
- **Book profit when it is earned.** Super-cat underwriting profit was recognised only after the contracts expired. (Wesco 1996)
- **Ignore the windfall.** He told owners to ignore a large non-cash investment gain when judging the year's earnings. (Wesco 2006)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-12-accounting-honesty-and-candour.html

### 13. Adversity, patience and hard work

Setbacks are certain, and many are unfair. What decides a life is the response to them, and the steady work done in between.

- **Don't stay down.** Staying down after a setback was on his list of routes to misery. (HS 1986)
- **Unfair blows will come.** Life is very likely to deliver terrible, unfair blows. Some people recover and others do not. He cited Epictetus on using each setback well. (USC Law 2007)
- **Assiduity.** He liked the word because it meant sitting down and staying there until the job is done. (USC Law 2007)
- **Losses bite harder.** Losses and near misses provoke outsized reactions. The most addictive forms of gambling are built on near misses. (PHM 2005)
- **Small steps go unnoticed.** Change that arrives in small steps escapes notice, because each step is a small contrast with the last. (PHM 2005)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-13-adversity-patience-and-hard-work.html

### 14. The Berkshire system, in his words

In his 2014 essay, written directly to Berkshire shareholders for the first time, he explained why the company had worked.

- **Four causes.** He credited the constructive peculiarities of Buffett, the constructive peculiarities of the Berkshire system, good luck, and the intense devotion of some shareholders and admirers. (BRK 2014)
- **Focus, kept for 50 years.** Buffett's decision to limit himself to a few kinds of activity, and keep at them for 50 years, worked like a lollapalooza. Munger compared it to Roger Federer's tennis. (BRK 2014)
- **Each company keeps its own systems.** There is no group-wide personnel, stock option, incentive or retirement system. Subsidiaries run their own. (BRK 2014)
- **Keep head office small.** Buffett set out to minimise the bad effects that almost always come from a large bureaucracy at headquarters. (BRK 2014)
- **Win/win.** He wanted win/win results everywhere, for instance gaining loyalty by giving it. (BRK 2014)
- **A narrow job at the top.** The chairman keeps few tasks: managing nearly all the security investments, writing a long, useful letter as he would want it as a passive shareholder, answering questions for hours, and admiring what others achieve. (BRK 2014)
- **Rare elsewhere.** No other large company he knew had half these elements. Most have heavy bureaucracy and chief executives who arrive at about 59 and are soon retired by an age limit. (BRK 2014)
- **Successors.** He named Ajit Jain and Greg Abel as proven performers. (BRK 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/munger-14-the-berkshire-system-in-his-words.html

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “To the man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.” (USC 1994)
- “Broadscale problems, by definition, cross many academic disciplines.” (HLS 1998)
- “Invert, always invert.” (HS 1986, quoting Jacobi)
- “Incentives are superpowers.” (PHM 2005)
- “Generally speaking, envy, resentment, revenge, and self-pity are disastrous modes of thought.” (USC Law 2007)
- “Don't sell anything you wouldn't buy yourself.” (Stanford 1996)
- “The answer is I have a black belt in chutzpah.” (UCSB 2003, explaining why, with no economics training, he would lecture economists)
- “I think the orthodox view is grossly mistaken.” (Foundations 1998, on the view that wide diversification is a must)
- “super-cat reinsurance is not for the faint of heart” (Wesco 1996)
- “Whose bread I eat, his song I sing.” (Scandal 2000, the old saying he applies to compliant accountants)
- “if the roles were reversed and we were passive investors” (Blue Chip 1982)
- “the weirdly intense, contagious devotion of some shareholders” (BRK 2014)

## Read the originals

The talks are free to read in the publisher's online edition of Poor Charlie's Almanack. The letters link to published copies.

- [Letter to Blue Chip Stamps stockholders for 1982, signed by Munger as chairman, dated 17 February 1983](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/2135167/charlie-mungers-1982-letter-to-wesco-shareholders): Writing to owners candidly, and how inflation sorts businesses.
- [Letter to Wesco Financial shareholders for 1985, dated 13 February 1986](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/2136293/charlie-mungers-1985-letter-to-wesco-shareholders): A frank verdict on his own savings and loan business.
- [Harvard School commencement, Los Angeles, 13 June 1986](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): Prescriptions for a miserable life, and the habit of inverting problems.
- [A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): The latticework of models, great businesses, and few big bets.
- [Worldly Wisdom, Revisited, with questions from students](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): Knowing what you know, three rules for a career, bearing hard times.
- [Practical Thought about Practical Thought?](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): The Coca-Cola thought experiment and his five helpful notions.
- [Letter to Wesco Financial shareholders for 1996](https://gurufocus.com/news/2136790/charlie-mungers-1996-letter-to-wesco-shareholders): Super-cat reinsurance, lumpy results and conservative accounting.
- [Fiftieth reunion of the Harvard Law School class of 1948, 24 April 1998](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): Why professionals need the big ideas of many fields, taught as pilots are.
- [Investment Practices of Leading Charitable Foundations](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): Layers of fees, indexing and concentration.
- [Breakfast meeting of the Philanthropy Roundtable, 10 November 2000](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): Febezzlement, crowd folly and wealth effects.
- [The Great Financial Scandal of 2003](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): How a sound company is ruined by accounting games.
- [Academic Economics](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): Physics envy, counting what can be counted, second-order effects.
- [The Psychology of Human Misjudgment](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): The 25 tendencies that lead sensible people into error.
- [Letter to Wesco Financial shareholders for 2006, dated 27 February 2007](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/2135591/charlie-mungers-2006-letter-to-wesco-shareholders): Plain talk about a weaker vehicle, and ignoring windfalls.
- [USC Gould School of Law commencement, 13 May 2007](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): His fullest statement on how to live.
- [Vice Chairman's Thoughts, Past and Future](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/letters.html): What made Berkshire work, in his own account.
- [Poor Charlie's Almanack: the editor's chapters](https://stripe.press/poor-charlies-almanack/book): How he decided, in the book's own account.

## Words to know

- **Worldly wisdom**: Practical judgment built from the big ideas of many fields, used together on real problems.
- **Latticework of models**: The connected set of those big ideas you think with. Facts are hung on it so they can be used.
- **Man with a hammer**: The error of forcing every problem into the one model you know.
- **Inversion**: Solving a problem backwards: ask what would cause failure, then avoid it.
- **Circle of competence**: The area where you really know enough to judge. Knowing its edge matters more than its size.
- **Incentive-caused bias**: Drifting towards conclusions that serve your own pay, often without noticing.
- **Lollapalooza**: An extreme result produced when several psychological forces push the same way at once.
- **Too tough to understand**: His third basket for ideas, beside yes and no. You never have to decide on those.
- **Opportunity cost**: Judging any use of money against the next-best use available.
- **Febezzle**: His word for wealth quietly lost to wasteful investment fees, modelled on Galbraith's 'bezzle'.

## Sources and scope

The talks are read from Poor Charlie's Almanack, the collection of Munger's talks edited by Peter D. Kaufman, in the Stripe Press edition, which the publisher has put online in full. The Wesco letters and the 1982 Blue Chip Stamps letter are read from published copies of the original annual letters. His 2014 essay appears in Berkshire Hathaway's 2014 annual report. Items tagged Almanack come from the book's own account of his methods. Every exact phrase and every date and figure was checked a second time against these sources. The many Munger quotations that circulate online were not used unless they appear in them. The wording is the compiler's own, apart from the short phrases marked as his, one per source.

Munger wrote no yearly letter like Buffett's. This section uses the eleven talks collected in Poor Charlie's Almanack, his letters to Wesco Financial and Blue Chip Stamps shareholders, and his 2014 essay for Berkshire. Remarks reported from meetings are left out, because no official transcripts exist and many circulating quotes are wrong.
