# Peter Lynch

> Ran the Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, beat the market by a mile, and showed ordinary people how to find good stocks.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/lynch.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

An ordinary person who keeps their eyes open often spots a good company years before the professionals, but must still do the homework.

## Summary

Peter Lynch ran Fidelity's Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, averaging 29.2% a year, about double the S&P 500. He retired at 46 and spent the following decades teaching ordinary people to pick stocks the way he did: look around, sort, check, explain, then own.

## Record at a glance

- **13 years**: May 1977 to May 1990
- **29.2%**: average a year, about double the S&P 500
- **$18M → $14B**: fund size when he started and left
- **$1,000 → $28,000**: what $1,000 became over his tenure

## Big ideas

### 1. The amateur's edge

An ordinary person who keeps their eyes open often spots a good company years before the professionals do.

- **You start ahead.** He argued that any normal person can pick stocks as well as the average Wall Street expert, using what they already see at work and in the shops. (1989 One Up I)
- **Professionals play it safe.** Many fund managers fear looking bad more than they want to win, so they avoid small, unknown companies until everyone already knows them. (1989 One Up I)
- **Your edge is where you work and shop.** Your job, your industry and the products you use every day can show you which companies are winning before the numbers reach Wall Street. (1989 One Up I · 1993 Beating the Street)
- **Spotting is only the start.** He never said to buy a stock just because you like the product or the store. You still have to study the company's earnings, finances and competition. (2000 New intro)
- **Know what you own.** He called this the single most important thing, and reckoned about 80% of people own stocks they couldn't explain. (1994 Press Club)
- **Step one, then step two.** In 2023 he repeated that he never told people simply to put money into the market. Knowing a company is step one; reading its balance sheet is step two. (2023 Interview)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-01-the-amateurs-edge.html

### 2. Is it gambling? Stocks and your stomach

Stocks reward patient owners of good companies; the real test is your stomach, not your brain.

- **Owning, not betting.** Stocks are a gamble only if you pick them like lottery tickets. Behind every stock is a business, and businesses that earn more become worth more. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Why stocks beat bonds.** With a bond, the best you can hope for is your money back plus interest. Over the long run, stocks with dividends returned about 11% a year, against 5 to 6% for bonds. (1989 One Up I · 1996 PBS interview)
- **Profits are the engine.** Company profits have grown about 8% a year over time, which is why stocks rise in the long run, even after flat decades. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Bad picks are worse than cash.** Over the long run, a portfolio of poorly chosen stocks won't beat money left under the mattress. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **The stomach decides.** Markets fall often: he counted 53 declines of 10% or more in 95 years, 15 of them of 25% or more. If you can't sit through that, don't own stocks. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Only money you won't need.** Buy, hold and add when the market falls, but only with money you won't need soon. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Temperament as much as homework.** If a sharp drop would keep you awake at night, he said in 2023, you shouldn't be investing in stocks. (2023 Interview)
- **Start with how the world works.** His beginner's book opens with the history of companies and capitalism, because investing makes sense only once you see what a company is. (1995 Learn to Earn)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-02-is-it-gambling-stocks-and-your-stomach.html

### 3. Look in your own backyard

The best leads come from everyday life: the store you like, the product people keep buying, the trend at your job.

- **Start close to home.** He believed the best place to start looking for the next winner is your own backyard: home, work and the shops. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Watch what people keep buying.** A product that friends, family or colleagues keep coming back to is a clue worth following up. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **If you like the store…** One of his principles: if you like the store, chances are you'll love the stock. Then check the numbers. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Small companies, big gains.** His biggest wins often came from small companies with room to grow. In 2023 he cited Au Bon Pain, which bought St. Louis Bread for $23 million in 1993; it later sold for $7.5 billion. (2023 Interview)
- **A hit product is not enough.** The Cabbage Patch doll was a huge hit, but it couldn't save a mediocre company with a bad balance sheet. (1989 One Up I)
- **Turn over more rocks.** The more companies you look at, the more bargains you find. His early winners came from industries others ignored. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Know a few well.** An individual can do well by knowing three to five companies thoroughly and buying when one becomes attractive. (1996 PBS interview)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-03-look-in-your-own-backyard.html

### 4. The six kinds of stock

Before buying, decide which of six kinds of stock you are looking at; that tells you what to expect and when to sell.

- **Sort before you buy.** Every company fits one of six kinds: slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds and asset plays. (1989 One Up II)
- **Slow growers.** Large, ageing companies growing about as fast as the economy. You own them mainly for the dividend: low risk, low gain. (1989 One Up II)
- **Stalwarts.** Big, established companies growing earnings about 10 to 12% a year: low risk, moderate gain. He expected perhaps 30 to 50% from them, and liked them for protection in recessions. (1989 One Up II)
- **Fast growers.** Small, aggressive companies growing 20 to 25% a year. His favourites and the land of ten- to forty-baggers, but the riskiest when growth stops. (1989 One Up II)
- **Cyclicals.** Companies whose profits rise and fall with the economy. With these, timing matters more than anywhere else. (1989 One Up II)
- **Turnarounds.** Battered companies that might recover. They can make big gains, as Chrysler did in the early 1980s, but many never come back. (1989 One Up II · 1996 PBS interview)
- **Asset plays.** Companies sitting on something valuable the market has missed, such as property, cash or a business inside the business. (1989 One Up II)
- **Kinds change.** Fast growers eventually slow down and become stalwarts or slow growers, so check the label again from time to time. (1989 One Up II)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-04-the-six-kinds-of-stock.html

### 5. The perfect stock, and the ones to avoid

He looked for dull, overlooked companies in boring niches, and stayed away from the hottest story in town.

- **Dull is beautiful.** The perfect company has a boring, even ridiculous name and does something dull or disagreeable, so the crowd ignores it. (1989 One Up II)
- **Overlooked is better.** Big institutions don't own it and analysts don't follow it. A spinoff, or a company with a depressing or rumour-ridden image, often qualifies. (1989 One Up II)
- **Niche and repeat buyers.** A no-growth industry, a protected niche and a product people have to keep buying are all good signs. (1989 One Up II)
- **Insiders and buybacks.** When insiders buy their own shares, or the company buys back stock, management is showing confidence. Heavy insider buying makes a near-term bankruptcy very unlikely. (1989 One Up II)
- **Use technology, don't sell it.** He preferred companies that use technology to cut their costs over companies racing to sell it. (1989 One Up II)
- **Avoid the hottest stock.** The hottest stock in the hottest industry, the one everyone talks about, is the one he would avoid most. (1989 One Up II)
- **Beware “the next” and diworseification.** Stocks touted as the next big name rarely are, and profitable companies that buy unrelated businesses usually make themselves worse. (1989 One Up II)
- **Beware whispers and exciting names.** Long shots with thrilling stories and no earnings, and companies with exciting names in hot fields, attract buyers for the wrong reasons. (1989 One Up II)
- **Fewer colour photos.** Half joking: all else equal, invest in the company with the fewest colour photographs in its annual report. (1993 Beating the Street)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-05-the-perfect-stock-and-the-ones-to-avoid.html

### 6. Earnings are the engine

Over months the price can do anything; over years it follows the company's earnings.

- **Short term, no link; long term, a full link.** Over months or even years there is often no connection between how a company does and how its stock does. Over the long term, the connection is complete. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Find what drives the profits.** Something has to keep the profits growing; the more you know about that something, the better. (1989 One Up II)
- **Price is not proof.** A rising price doesn't mean you were right, and a falling one doesn't mean you were wrong. Only the business can tell you that. (1989 One Up III)
- **Time favours good companies.** Time is on your side when you own shares of superior companies, and against you when you own options. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Even ten years late can be early.** Investors who bought Wal-Mart ten years after its 1970 listing could still have made about 30 times their money by following its expansion. (1996 PBS interview)
- **The stock doesn't know you own it.** Don't fall in love with a share. Stay while the company's fundamentals hold, and leave if they break. (1994 Press Club)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-06-earnings-are-the-engine.html

### 7. The famous numbers

A few simple numbers tell you whether a good company is also a good price.

- **P/E equal to growth is fair.** A fairly priced company's P/E roughly equals its earnings growth rate. A P/E well below the growth rate may be a bargain; well above it, a warning. (1989 One Up II)
- **Half is attractive, double is dear.** A P/E around half the growth rate looked very attractive to him; around twice the growth rate, very unattractive. (1989 One Up II)
- **Add the dividend.** For dividend payers, add the yield to the growth rate and divide by the P/E. Below 1 is poor, about 1.5 is okay, and 2 or better is what you want. (1989 One Up II)
- **Cash minus debt.** Check how much cash the company holds against its long-term debt. Plenty of net cash cushions the bad years. (1989 One Up II)
- **Who owns it?** The fewer institutions own it and the fewer analysts follow it, the more room there is for discovery. (1989 One Up II)
- **Do the arithmetic, even without earnings.** For a company with no profits yet, work out what it would need to earn later to justify today's price. (2000 New intro)
- **Cheap is not safe.** A $3 stock can go to zero just like a $50 one. A lousy cheap stock is as risky as a lousy expensive one. (1989 One Up III)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-07-the-famous-numbers.html

### 8. Balance sheet first

The biggest losses come from weak balance sheets; know a company's finances before you risk money on it.

- **Finances before faith.** Never invest in a company without understanding its finances. The biggest losses come from companies with poor balance sheets. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Two losers, one bargain.** In 2023 he compared two loss-making companies: one with $300 million of debt, one with no debt and $200 million in cash. (2023 Interview)
- **Debt decides who survives.** In a downturn, a company with little debt can wait; one with heavy debt may not. That matters most for turnarounds and cyclicals. (1993 Beating the Street · 2023 Interview)
- **Read the numbers yourself.** His beginner's book teaches how to read a stock table, an annual report and a balance sheet, before trusting anyone else's summary. (1995 Learn to Earn)
- **The homework list.** Before buying, check the earnings prospects, financial condition, competitive position and plans for expansion. (2000 New intro)
- **Fancy offices are a warning.** A lavish head office can signal managers who care more about themselves than about shareholders. (1993 Beating the Street)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-08-balance-sheet-first.html

### 9. The two-minute drill

If you can't explain why you own a stock in two minutes, simply enough for a child, you don't know enough to own it.

- **Give the monologue.** Before buying, he talked himself through why he was interested, what had to happen for the company to succeed, and what could get in the way. (1989 One Up II)
- **Simple enough for a child.** If you can't explain to a ten-year-old, in two minutes or less, why you own a stock, he said, you shouldn't own it. (1994 Press Club)
- **The crayon test.** If you couldn't draw the idea with a crayon, he wouldn't invest in it. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Each kind has its own story.** For a slow grower the story is the dividend; for a fast grower, where it can still expand; for a turnaround, how it will fix itself; for an asset play, what the assets are worth. (1989 One Up II)
- **Write it down.** For beginners in 2023 he suggested a paper portfolio of at least ten stocks, a few written reasons for each, reviewed every three months. (2023 Interview)
- **“It's going up” is not a reason.** Pressed, many owners admit their real reason is that the stock is rising, which is no reason at all. (1994 Press Club)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-09-the-two-minute-drill.html

### 10. Ten-baggers: let the winners run

You only need a few big winners in a lifetime, so let them run and don't cut the flowers to water the weeds.

- **A ten-bagger.** His baseball term for a stock that goes up tenfold: two home runs and a double. (1996 PBS interview)
- **A few are enough.** You don't need many. A handful of tenfold winners in a lifetime makes investing worthwhile. (1996 PBS interview · 1993 Beating the Street)
- **Right six times in ten.** A good stock picker is right about six times in ten, so the winners must be allowed to outgrow the losers. (1996 PBS interview · 2023 Interview)
- **Flowers and weeds.** Selling your winners and keeping your losers is like pulling out the flowers and watering the weeds. Buffett liked the image enough to use it in his 1988 letter. (1989 One Up III)
- **Add to the winners.** He did well by owning many stocks, letting winners run and adding to them, even though Magellan missed more than a hundred ten-baggers. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Look at what you own first.** The best stock to buy may be one you already own; check it before hunting for something new. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Lose 100%, gain 900%.** Whatever you pay, picking the wrong stock costs at most the same 100%. A ten-bagger gains 900%. (1989 One Up III)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-10-ten-baggers-let-the-winners-run.html

### 11. Don't time the market

Nobody can predict the economy or the next fall; study companies, not forecasts.

- **Thirteen minutes.** Spend little time on economic forecasts: he joked that 13 minutes a year on economics wastes ten of them. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Facts, not forecasts.** Watch the facts in the industries you own, such as used-car prices for carmakers or new hotel building for hotel chains. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Nobody saw 1982 coming.** In 1982 inflation was 14%, the prime rate 20% and over half his companies were losing money. The great bull market began that year. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Timing barely matters.** Investing every year at the year's high from 1965 to 1995 earned about 10.6% a year; at the year's low, about 11.7%. (1996 PBS interview)
- **Declines are normal.** Falls happen and no one knows when. People who say they predicted one predicted many others too. (1994 Press Club)
- **The cocktail party.** Half joking, he described four stages of a market, from guests avoiding him at parties to everyone giving him tips. He did not use it to predict. (1989 One Up I)
- **Pessimism rarely pays.** Unless you sell short for a living, it rarely pays to be a pessimist about the long run. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **History says: markets fall.** Study history to learn that markets go down, and decide in advance that a fall is a chance to buy, not a reason to run. (1994 Press Club)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-11-dont-time-the-market.html

### 12. Keep checking the story

Hold as long as the story holds; recheck it every few months, and sell when the story, not the price, changes.

- **Check the story regularly.** Even a long-term owner has to keep following the company. Stories end, for example when a business saturates its market. (2023 Interview)
- **Know the stage.** Companies pass through stages, from start-up to fast growth to maturity. The key question is which stage yours is in. (2023 Interview · 1995 Learn to Earn)
- **Sell by kind.** The right exit depends on the kind of stock: a stalwart after a solid rise, a fast grower when its room to expand runs out, a turnaround once it has turned around. (1989 One Up II)
- **Boredom is expensive.** Give up on a stock because nothing is happening and, all too often, things start to happen the day after you sell. (1989 One Up III)
- **Don't be a trader.** Cheap commissions are no reason to trade. Buying three stocks a day and selling them on Friday is gambling, not investing. (2023 Interview)
- **Few holdings for part-timers.** A part-time picker can follow eight to twelve companies, with no more than five in the portfolio at any one time. (1993 Beating the Street)
- **Beware buying after the leap.** In 2000 he warned that few dot-com buyers get the full ride, because the early gains happen before most people can buy. (2000 New intro)
- **Stocks are like children.** Don't take on more than you can handle. (1993 Beating the Street)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lynch-12-keep-checking-the-story.html

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “The p/e ratio of any company that's fairly priced will equal its growth rate.” (One Up on Wall Street, 1989)
- “Never invest in any idea you can't illustrate with a crayon.” (Beating the Street, 1993)
- “the single most important thing … is to know what you own” (National Press Club, 1994)
- “if you spend 13 minutes a year on economics, you've wasted 10 minutes.” (PBS interview, 1996)
- “That's not investing. That's gambling.” (Yahoo Finance interview, 2023, on frequent trading)
- “very few dot.com investors benefit from the full ride” (One Up on Wall Street, introduction to the 2000 edition)
- “Capitalism happens when people make things and sell them for money.” (Learn to Earn, 1995)

## Read the originals

The books are in print; borrow or buy them. The 1996 interview transcript is free at PBS and the 2023 interview at Yahoo Finance.

- [One Up on Wall Street, Part 1: Preparing to invest](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/One-Up-On-Wall-Street/Peter-Lynch/9780743200400): Why an ordinary person has an edge over the professionals, whether stocks are gambling, and the temperament it takes.
- [One Up on Wall Street, Part 2: Picking winners](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/One-Up-On-Wall-Street/Peter-Lynch/9780743200400): The heart of his method: the six kinds of stock, the perfect stock and the ones to avoid, the two-minute drill and the famous numbers.
- [One Up on Wall Street, Part 3: The long-term view](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/One-Up-On-Wall-Street/Peter-Lynch/9780743200400): Building a portfolio, when to buy and sell, and the silliest things people say about stock prices.
- [One Up on Wall Street: Introduction to the millennium edition](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/One-Up-On-Wall-Street/Peter-Lynch/9780743200400): His view of the dot-com boom: do the homework, do the arithmetic, and remember few buyers get the full ride.
- [Beating the Street](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Beating-the-Street/Peter-Lynch/9780671891633): His Magellan years, a class of seventh graders who picked stocks, 21 Peter's Principles and 25 golden rules.
- [Talk at the National Press Club](https://novelinvestor.com/peter-lynch-single-important-thing/): Know what you own, explain it in two minutes, ignore forecasts, and expect the market to fall.
- [Learn to Earn](https://www.simonandschuster.ca/books/Learn-to-Earn/Peter-Lynch/9780684811635): A beginner's guide, for anyone of high-school age or older, to capitalism, companies and the basics of investing.
- [Interview for PBS Frontline, “Betting on the Market”](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/betting/pros/lynch.html): His life story in his own words: caddying, his first ten-bagger, Magellan, 1987, and why timing the market doesn't pay.
- [Interview with Yahoo Finance](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/fidelity-legend-peter-lynch-i-never-said-to-invest-in-the-stock-market-120755736.html): Thirty-four years after his first book: balance sheets, company stages, regrets, and why cheap trading isn't investing.

## Words to know

- **Ten-bagger**: A stock that rises tenfold. His baseball term: two home runs and a double.
- **Slow grower**: A large, mature company growing about as fast as the economy, owned for its dividend.
- **Stalwart**: A big, established company growing earnings about 10 to 12% a year.
- **Fast grower**: A small, aggressive company growing 20 to 25% a year. His favourite kind.
- **Cyclical**: A company whose profits rise and fall with the economy.
- **Turnaround**: A battered company that might recover.
- **Asset play**: A company sitting on something valuable that the market has missed.
- **PEG ratio**: The P/E divided by the earnings growth rate. Around 1 is fair; well below 1 may be a bargain.
- **Diworseification**: His word for a profitable company buying unrelated businesses and making itself worse.
- **Two-minute drill**: A short spoken case for a stock: why you like it, what must happen, what could go wrong.

## Sources and scope

Only Peter Lynch's own words: his three books (written with John Rothchild), his 1994 National Press Club talk, his 1996 PBS interview and his 2023 Yahoo Finance interview. Ideas are summarised in our own words. Each source gives at most one short exact line, checked against the original text or a published copy. Magellan's record is as reported by Fidelity and repeated by Lynch; it covers his 13 years only, and fund size includes new money from investors, not just gains. The sorting game uses invented companies. Facts were checked against at least two sources.

Lynch wrote three books, all with John Rothchild. One Up on Wall Street is split here into its three parts plus the new introduction of 2000. Three recorded talks and interviews add his own spoken words. Magazine columns and paraphrased quotes found online are left out.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- The tools (sorting game, price check, checklist, ten-bagger maths) are teaching aids built from his published rules of thumb. They are not valuation models and must not be used as the basis for a decision.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Peter Lynch, Fidelity Investments, Simon & Schuster, PBS, Yahoo or any company named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.

Text written for this site is CC BY 4.0. Please cite https://alienspacex.com/lynch.html when you use it.

# Benjamin Graham

> Taught Buffett, wrote the two founding books of value investing, and turned a near-ruinous 1929 into rules for never being ruined again.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/graham.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Investing, not speculating. An investment protects your money and earns a fair return. Anything else is speculation.

## Summary

Benjamin Graham taught Warren Buffett, wrote Security Analysis (1934) and The Intelligent Investor (1949), and is called the father of value investing. The 1929 crash nearly ruined him, and he spent the rest of his life working out how an ordinary person could invest without being ruined. His answers: know the difference between investing and speculating, treat the market as a moody partner, and always insist on a margin of safety.

## Record at a glance

- **−70%**: his account, 1929 to 1932, against −74% for the Dow: the crash nearly wiped him out
- **17.4% a year**: Graham-Newman, 1945 to 1956, leaving out GEICO; the S&P 500 did 18.3%, but with far bigger swings
- **≈ $0.7m**: paid in 1948 for half of GEICO ($712,500 to $720,000, by source); it outgrew everything else he owned
- **1934**: Security Analysis, with David Dodd; The Intelligent Investor followed in 1949

## Big ideas

### 1. Investing or speculating?

An investment, after careful study, protects your money and promises a fair return. Anything else is speculation, and you should know which you are doing.

- **His definition.** After thorough analysis, an investment promises safety of the money you put in and an adequate return. Whatever fails that test is speculative. (Book, 1934)
- **Two faces of a share.** A share has one investment side, the business growing over decades, and one speculative side, prices swinging with hope, fear and greed. (Interview, 1976)
- **Speculation isn't a crime.** He did not forbid speculation; he asked that you do it knowingly, with money you can afford to lose, and keep it apart from your investments. (Book, 1973)
- **Your worst enemy.** The investor's main problem is usually himself: his moods, not the market. (Book, 1973)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-01-investing-or-speculating.html

### 2. Mr Market

Picture a partner who offers every day to buy your share or sell you his, at a price that depends on his mood. You may take his offer or ignore it.

- **The parable.** Mr Market turns up daily with a price. Some days he is euphoric and asks too much; some days gloomy and sells too cheap. (Book, 1973 · Buffett, 1987)
- **Ignore him freely.** You are never obliged to trade. His offers are there to use when they suit you. (Buffett, 1987 · Book, 1973)
- **One meaning only.** For a true investor, price swings mean one thing: a chance to buy wisely after sharp falls and sell wisely after big rises. Otherwise, forget the market. (Book, 1973)
- **Buffett's debt.** Buffett wrote that this picture of Mr Market describes the attitude to price swings he finds most useful for investing. (Buffett, 1987)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-02-mr-market.html

### 3. Margin of safety

Pay well below what something is worth. The gap protects you from your own mistakes, bad luck and the unknown.

- **The central idea.** He called the margin of safety the central concept of investment, the closing chapter of his book. (Book, 1973)
- **Every purchase justified.** In his last interview: every purchase, and the price paid, should be justified by a margin of safety in value terms. (Interview, 1976)
- **Dollars for 40 cents.** Buffett summed up Graham's school as buying a dollar of value for 40 cents, then waiting. (Buffett, 1984)
- **Safety in numbers.** A margin of safety works on average, not every time, which is why he spread his money across many holdings. (Book, 1973)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-03-margin-of-safety.html

### 4. Know which investor you are

He split investors in two. Defensive investors want safety and little effort; enterprising ones will put in time and skill. Mixing the two is the danger.

- **Defensive.** A defensive investor wants freedom from bother and serious mistakes. Simple rules and a balanced portfolio suit him. (Book, 1973)
- **Enterprising.** An enterprising investor is willing to spend real time and care to earn more than average, and must have the knowledge to do it. (Book, 1973)
- **Effort, not courage.** The difference is the work you will do, not how much risk you will take. (Book, 1973)
- **Good enough is easy.** A sound, if unspectacular, result needs little effort. Doing better than that takes much more work and some wisdom. (Book, 1973)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-04-know-which-investor-you-are.html

### 5. Seven tests for the defensive investor

For investors who want safety, he set seven plain tests: size, strong finances, steady earnings, dividends, growth, and moderate prices against earnings and assets.

- **Size and strength.** A large company, with current assets at least twice current liabilities and long-term debt no larger than working capital. (Book, 1973)
- **Record.** Earnings in each of the past ten years, dividends paid without a break for twenty, and earnings up at least a third over ten years. (Book, 1973)
- **Price.** No more than 15 times average earnings of the past three years, and no more than 1.5 times book value, or a product of the two no higher than 22.5. (Book, 1973)
- **Strict on purpose.** Few companies pass all seven. The tests are meant to keep a defensive investor away from trouble, not to find the next great growth story. (Book, 1973)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-05-seven-tests-for-the-defensive-investor.html

### 6. Buying below working capital

His favourite bargain: shares selling for less than the company's current assets minus all its debts, giving nothing at all for factories or brands.

- **The method.** Buy shares priced below net current asset value: current assets minus every liability, with fixed assets counted as zero. (Interview, 1976)
- **His own result.** He said this method had earned about 20% a year over more than 30 years. (Interview, 1976)
- **They come and go.** Such bargains grew scarce in the boom years, then returned after the 1973 to 1974 crash: in January 1976 he counted over 300, about a tenth of listed shares. (Interview, 1976)
- **Buy a group.** He applied it to a spread of such shares, not one or two, so that the winners outweighed the disappointments. (Book, 1973)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-06-buying-below-working-capital.html

### 7. Simple rules, many stocks

Late in life he decided that detailed analysis rarely paid any more. Better to buy groups of cheap shares by simple rules, and to sell by rules too.

- **Analysis no longer pays.** Elaborate research rewarded investors forty years earlier; by 1976 he thought it rarely justified its cost. (Interview, 1976)
- **A second simple rule.** Buy groups of shares at no more than seven times the past year's earnings. He said tests of this kind showed 15% a year or better from 1925 to 1975. (Interview, 1976)
- **A rule for selling.** Set a profit target of 50% to 100%, and sell anything that has not reached it within two or three years. (Interview, 1976)
- **The small investor's edge.** Institutions are limited to some 300 to 400 huge companies; an individual can choose from about 3,000. (Interview, 1976)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-07-simple-rules-many-stocks.html

### 8. Stocks and bonds: the 25–75 rule

Keep at least a quarter of your money in shares and at least a quarter in bonds, always. Rebalance as markets move.

- **Floors on both sides.** Hold no less than 25% in shares and no less than 25% in bonds or their equivalent; a 50–50 split is a sensible default. (Interview, 1976 · Book, 1973)
- **Rebalance.** After a big rise in shares, move some into bonds; after a fall, do the reverse. (Interview, 1976)
- **Bonds of moderate length.** He suggested bond holdings averaging seven or eight years to maturity. (Interview, 1976)
- **A rule against moods.** A fixed rule stops you buying more just because prices rose and selling just because they fell. (Book, 1973)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-08-stocks-and-bonds-the-25-75-rule.html

### 9. The market catches up with value

Prices can stray far from value for a long time. But, as he told the Senate, the market eventually catches up.

- **A mystery, he admitted.** Asked by a senator how a cheap share ever reaches its value, he called it one of the mysteries of the business, but said experience shows it does. (Senate, 1955)
- **His students.** In 1984 Buffett showed nine investors from Graham's school beating the market over long periods with different stocks. (Buffett, 1984)
- **Not luck.** Buffett's point: if the winners all come from one small village of thinking, the method matters, not chance. (Buffett, 1984)
- **Index-level results.** Graham doubted most professionals could beat the averages, and thought clients should expect roughly index results. (Interview, 1976)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-09-the-market-catches-up-with-value.html

### 10. Loss, luck and generosity

The crash taught him caution, GEICO taught him how much luck matters, and his friends remembered his generosity.

- **The crash.** From 1929 to 1932 his account fell about 70%. He blamed his own borrowing, not the crash. (Study, 1977)
- **The measured record.** From 1945 to 1956, leaving out GEICO, Graham-Newman earned 17.4% a year against 18.3% for the S&P 500, with far smaller swings. (Study, 1977)
- **One lucky decision.** GEICO, bought against his own rule of wide diversification, made more than all his other decisions together. He drew the lesson himself in his book. (Book, 1973 · Study, 1977)
- **A generous man.** He quietly helped refugees from Nazi Germany, read Greek and Latin, and translated a Spanish novel into English. (Study, 1977)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/graham-10-loss-luck-and-generosity.html

## Special section

**Try his seven tests on a company** 

**A quick price check** Tests 6 and 7 together cap the price at the square root of 22.5 × earnings per share × book value per share. People now call this the Graham number. Enter a company's figures to see it.

Graham called himself a defensive investor's teacher first. These tests protect; they do not promise big gains.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “promises safety of principal and an adequate return” (Security Analysis, 1934, defining an investment)
- “The investor's chief problem—and even his worst enemy—is likely to be himself.” (The Intelligent Investor, 1973)
- “a margin of safety, in value terms, to protect his commitment” (Financial Analysts Journal interview, 1976)
- “We know from experience that eventually the market catches up with value.” (Testimony to the US Senate, 1955)

## Read the originals

Start with chapters 8 and 20 of The Intelligent Investor, on Mr Market and the margin of safety. Then read his short 1976 interview, free online.

- [Security Analysis](https://www.ivey.uwo.ca/bengrahaminvesting/resources/ben-graham-collection/): The textbook that founded the profession: how to study a company's accounts, and his definition of an investment.
- [The Intelligent Investor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Intelligent_Investor): His book for ordinary investors: investment versus speculation, Mr Market, the defensive and enterprising investor, and the margin of safety.
- [Testimony on the stock market](https://novelinvestor.com/graham-mysteries-stock-market/): Asked why the market was booming, he explained why prices wander from value, and why value wins in the end.
- [A conversation with Benjamin Graham](https://bylo.org/bgraham76.html): His last views: why detailed analysis no longer pays, two simple methods for individuals, selling rules, and the stock-bond balance.
- [Benjamin Graham, the father of financial analysis](https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/research/foundation/1977/benjamin-graham-the-father-of-financial-analysis-full-pdf): His life, a March 1976 conversation, his character, and a careful measurement of how Graham-Newman really performed.
- [The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Superinvestors_of_Graham-and-Doddsville): Nine investors from Graham's school, each beating the market with different stocks, and why that rules out luck.
- [Berkshire Hathaway letter to shareholders](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1987.html): Buffett retells his teacher's parable of Mr Market and explains why it shaped his own investing.

## Words to know

- **Speculation**: Buying in the hope that the price will rise, without a margin of safety in value.
- **Margin of safety**: The gap between a cautious estimate of value and the price you pay.
- **Mr Market**: Graham's picture of the market as a moody partner offering prices you may take or ignore.
- **Current ratio**: Current assets divided by current liabilities.
- **Working capital**: Current assets minus current liabilities.
- **Net current asset value**: Current assets minus all liabilities, with nothing for factories or brands.
- **Book value**: A company's assets minus its liabilities, as shown in its accounts.
- **Price to earnings (P/E)**: The share price divided by the profit per share.
- **Rebalancing**: Selling some of what has risen and buying what has fallen, to return to a set mix.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Security Analysis (1934), The Intelligent Investor (1973 edition), his Senate testimony (1955), his 1976 interview with the Financial Analysts Journal, Kahn and Milne's study for the CFA Institute (1977), and Buffett's 1984 talk and 1987 letter. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Graham's books are long and were revised several times; we use the 1973 edition of The Intelligent Investor. The often-repeated claim that he earned 20% a year for decades is not supported by the best study of his fund, so we show the measured figures instead.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by the estate of Benjamin Graham, Columbia University, CFA Institute, the publishers of his books, Berkshire Hathaway, GEICO or any company named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.

# Philip Fisher

> Ran his own firm for 68 years, found great companies by talking to everyone around them, and held Motorola for nearly half a century.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/fisher.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Scuttlebutt. Learn about a company from its customers, suppliers, rivals and former staff.

## Summary

Philip Fisher ran his own investment firm in San Francisco from 1931 until he retired at 91. Where Graham looked for cheap shares, Fisher looked for outstanding companies, found out everything about them by talking to the people around them, and then held on, in Motorola's case for nearly fifty years. Buffett once said he was 15% Fisher.

## Record at a glance

- **1955 → 2004**: bought Motorola when it made radios; he still owned it when he died
- **15 points**: his checklist for an outstanding company, from his 1958 book
- **68 years**: running his own firm, from 1931 until he retired at 91 in 1999
- **1958**: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits, one of the first investing books on the New York Times bestseller list

## Big ideas

### 1. Scuttlebutt

Find out about a company from the people around it: customers, suppliers, competitors, former employees and scientists. Only then visit the managers.

- **The grapevine.** He found the business grapevine remarkably informative: put together many small views and a clear picture forms. (Book, 1958)
- **Ask about the others.** Ask five companies in an industry about the strengths and weaknesses of the other four, and you will learn a great deal about all five. (Book, 1958)
- **Then the managers.** Meet management only after the scuttlebutt, so you know which questions matter. (Book, 1958)
- **Buffett learned it.** Buffett said that from Fisher he learned the value of the scuttlebutt approach. (Obituary, 2004)
- **Learned at Stanford.** His habit began at business school, visiting companies each week with a professor. (Book, 1980)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-01-scuttlebutt.html

### 2. The fifteen points

He listed fifteen questions an outstanding company should answer well. A company need not pass all, but must pass most.

- **Room to grow.** Products or services with enough market to lift sales sizably for years, and a management determined to find the next ones. (Book, 1958)
- **Research and selling.** Effective research for its size, and a sales organisation better than average. (Book, 1958)
- **Margins.** A worthwhile profit margin, and a plan to keep or improve it. (Book, 1958)
- **Inside the company.** Good relations with staff and among executives, depth of management, and sound cost controls. (Book, 1958)
- **Most, not all.** A company that fails one or two points can still be outstanding; one that fails many is not. (Book, 1958)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-02-the-fifteen-points.html

### 3. Ability and integrity

Two traits in the people who run a company are essential: business ability, and honesty. Without both, he would not invest.

- **Two traits.** He learned early that the people running a company need two things: business ability and integrity. (Book, 1980)
- **Unquestionable integrity.** His last point asks whether management has unquestionable integrity. Managers are far closer to the assets than shareholders are. (Book, 1958)
- **Candour when it hurts.** Beware managers who talk freely when things go well but clam up when trouble comes. (Book, 1958)
- **No needless dilution.** Ask whether growth will need so many new shares that existing owners gain little. (Book, 1958)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-03-ability-and-integrity.html

### 4. Growth that lasts

Look for companies that can keep growing for years, because they keep developing new products. Fortunes come from seeing big changes early.

- **The next product.** Ask what the company will sell once today's products are fully exploited. (Book, 1958)
- **Big shifts.** Now and then a deep change, in technology or in society, lifts or sinks a whole group of companies at once. (Book, 1960)
- **Early is everything.** The big gains go to those who see what such a change means before everyone else does. (Book, 1960)
- **Motorola.** He bought Motorola in 1955, when it was still a radio maker, and held it for the rest of his life. (Obituary, 2004)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-04-growth-that-lasts.html

### 5. Conservative investors sleep well

A conservative investment keeps your purchasing power with the least risk. He defined it in four dimensions.

- **Low costs and skill.** To be truly conservative, a company must be the lowest-cost producer, or close to it, and strong in marketing, research and finance. (Book, 1975)
- **People.** Second, the people: able and honest managers. (Book, 1975)
- **Above-average earnings.** Third, a business whose nature lets it earn better than average returns. (Book, 1975)
- **A sensible price.** Fourth, the price: a great company can still be a poor buy if the market already prices it for perfection. (Book, 1975)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-05-conservative-investors-sleep-well.html

### 6. When to sell: almost never

If you bought the right company, the time to sell is almost never. He gave three reasons to sell, and dismissed the rest.

- **Reason one.** You made a mistake: the company is not what you thought. (Book, 1958)
- **Reason two.** The company has changed and no longer passes the fifteen points as it did. (Book, 1958)
- **Reason three.** A clearly better opportunity appears; he thought this should be rare. (Book, 1958)
- **Not a reason.** A big rise in price, or fear of a market fall, is not a reason to sell an outstanding company. (Book, 1958)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-06-when-to-sell-almost-never.html

### 7. Own the best, not the most

Over-diversifying into companies you don't know well is riskier than owning a few you know thoroughly.

- **Don't overstress diversification.** Owning too many companies means owning ones you cannot follow properly. (Book, 1958)
- **Quality over count.** Spread enough that one mistake cannot cripple you, then take care to own the best, not the most. (Book, 1958)
- **His own practice.** He held a small number of companies for very long periods, Motorola above all. (Obituary, 2004)
- **Buffett's mix.** In 1969 Buffett described himself as 85% Graham and 15% Fisher: cheapness from one, quality from the other. (Forbes, 1969)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-07-own-the-best-not-the-most.html

### 8. Don't follow the crowd

Prices swing with fashion. Look years ahead, buy when fear runs high, and judge price by tomorrow's earnings, not today's.

- **War scares.** Don't be afraid of buying when war fears push prices down. (Book, 1958)
- **Time as well as price.** With a true growth company, waiting for a perfect price can cost more than paying a fair one. (Book, 1958)
- **Years ahead.** He came to see that a company's price against its earnings a few years out matters far more than today's figure. (Book, 1980)
- **Against fashion.** Good moments to buy often come when a passing problem makes the market think less of an outstanding company than it deserves. (Book, 1958)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-08-dont-follow-the-crowd.html

### 9. Dividends matter less

He thought investors made too much fuss about dividends. A company that can reinvest profits well usually serves owners better by doing so.

- **The hullabaloo.** He devoted a chapter to what he saw as excessive attention to dividends. (Book, 1958)
- **Reinvestment first.** A fast-growing company that reinvests profits at high returns may do far more for owners than one that pays them out. (Book, 1958)
- **A clear policy.** What matters is a dividend policy that is clear and consistent, so owners know what to expect. (Book, 1958)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-09-dividends-matter-less.html

### 10. Lessons from his own mistakes

He saw the 1929 crash coming and still lost money. He started his firm in the Depression with almost nothing, and built his method from mistakes.

- **A first job he disliked.** He later called his first job, as a bank's securities analyst, intellectually dishonest, and resolved to work differently. (Book, 1980)
- **Right, and still wrong.** In August 1929 he warned his bank of the worst bear market in 25 years, then bought shares he thought cheap and lost money in the crash. (Book, 1980)
- **A tiny start.** He opened his firm with costs of $25 a month and made $3 a month in the first year. (Book, 1980)
- **Judge me in three years.** He told clients to fire him if he had not produced worthwhile results within three years. (Book, 1980)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/fisher-10-lessons-from-his-own-mistakes.html

## Special section

**Tick the points a company passes**

- Its market can lift sales sizably for years
- Management is set on finding the next products
- Its research is effective for its size
- Its sales organisation is better than average
- It earns a worthwhile profit margin
- It has a plan to keep or improve that margin
- Relations with its staff are outstanding
- Its executives work well together
- It has depth of management, not one star
- It controls and understands its costs
- It is strong in the ways that matter in its industry
- It thinks long term about profits
- Growth won't need so many new shares that owners gain little
- Managers speak as openly about bad news as good
- Management has unquestionable integrity

**His three reasons to sell**

- A mistake: the company was never what you thought.
- A change: it no longer passes the points as it did.
- A much better use: a clearly superior company appears. This should be rare.

**His ten don'ts, in brief**

- Don't buy promotional companies with no record yet.
- Don't ignore a good share just because it trades off the main exchange.
- Don't buy for the tone of the annual report.
- Don't assume a high P/E means the growth is already priced in.
- Don't haggle over tiny sums on an outstanding company.
- Don't overstress diversification.
- Don't fear buying on a war scare.
- Don't be swayed by irrelevant past prices and earnings.
- Don't forget time as well as price for a true growth share.
- Don't follow the crowd.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “the time to sell it is—almost never” (Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits, 1958)
- “those who appreciated the significance of what was happening early” (Paths to Wealth through Common Stocks, 1960, on who makes fortunes)

## Read the originals

Start with the first three chapters of Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits: the scuttlebutt method and the fifteen points.

- [Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits](https://www.fool.com/specials/2001/01/18/fishers-investing-criteria-sp010118.aspx): His main book: the scuttlebutt method, the fifteen points, when to buy and sell, dividends, and ten don'ts for investors.
- [Paths to Wealth through Common Stocks](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Philip_Arthur_Fisher): How big changes in technology and society affect whole groups of companies, and how inflation shapes investing.
- [Conservative Investors Sleep Well](https://www.morningstar.com.au/personal-finance/bookworm-an-essential-quality-conservative-investments-phil-fisher): What makes an investment conservative: low costs and strong skills, good people, a business that earns above average, and a sensible price.
- [Developing an Investment Philosophy](https://www.fool.com/archive/portfolios/rulemaker/2001/03/23/eight-principles-of-investing.aspx): His own story: Stanford, a dishonest first job, the 1929 crash, starting his firm, and the lessons behind each part of his method.
- [Philip A. Fisher, 96, is dead; wrote key investment book](https://www.nytimes.com/2004/04/19/business/philip-a-fisher-96-is-dead-wrote-key-investment-book.html): His life and family, Motorola and Texas Instruments, and what Buffett said he learned from him.
- [How Omaha beats Wall Street](https://hedgefundalpha.com/strategies/forbes-warren-buffett-omaha-beats-wall-street/): The young Buffett explains his approach, and how much of it comes from Graham and how much from Fisher.

## Words to know

- **Scuttlebutt**: Information gathered informally from people who deal with a company.
- **Growth stock**: A share in a company expected to grow sales and profits much faster than average.
- **Profit margin**: Profit as a share of sales.
- **Research and development**: Spending on new products and processes.
- **Dilution**: When a company issues new shares, each existing share owns less of it.
- **Diversification**: Spreading money across many holdings to reduce the harm of any one mistake.
- **Low-cost producer**: A company that can make its product more cheaply than its rivals.
- **Dividend**: Part of a company's profit paid out to shareholders.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits (1958), Paths to Wealth through Common Stocks (1960), Conservative Investors Sleep Well (1975), Developing an Investment Philosophy (1980), his New York Times obituary (2004) and Forbes's 1969 profile of Buffett. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Fisher published no audited record of his results, so we show none. His books are short and still in print together in one volume; his own story is in Developing an Investment Philosophy (1980).

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by the family of Philip Fisher, Fisher & Co., John Wiley & Sons, Stanford University, Motorola, The New York Times, Forbes or any company named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.

# John Templeton

> Bought 104 cheap shares as war broke out in 1939, then searched the whole world for bargains at the point of maximum pessimism.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/templeton.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Maximum pessimism. The best bargains appear when almost everyone is selling.

## Summary

John Templeton grew up in a small town in Tennessee, won a Rhodes scholarship, and in 1939 borrowed $10,000 to buy every cheap share he could as war broke out. His Templeton Growth Fund, started in 1954, looked for bargains across the world long before that was usual. His creed: buy at the point of maximum pessimism, search everywhere, stay humble, and never think you know it all.

## Record at a glance

- **14.5% a year**: Templeton Growth Fund, 1954 to 1992, as reported by AP and the New York Times
- **$10,000 → $2m**: what $10,000 put into the fund in 1954 had grown to by 1992
- **104 stocks**: bought in 1939 at $1 or less, 34 of them in bankruptcy (some say 37); only 4 became worthless
- **$90m**: profit on bets against overpriced technology shares in 2000, according to his great-niece

## Big ideas

### 1. Buy at maximum pessimism

Shares only become bargains when people sell them, and people sell when they are gloomy. So the best time to buy is when almost everyone else is pessimistic.

- **Buy low.** Buy when others are despondently selling, and sell when they are greedily buying. Following the crowd means buying what is already expensive. (Rules, 1993)
- **Why bargains exist.** The only way a share gets cheap is that people sell it, and the usual reason they sell is pessimism. (Book, 2008)
- **The four moods.** A line widely credited to him describes a bull market's life: born on pessimism, growing on scepticism, maturing on optimism, dying on euphoria. (Book, 2008)
- **Prepare in calm times.** He kept a wish list of quality companies, with orders ready to buy if prices collapsed, so fear could not stop him acting. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-01-buy-at-maximum-pessimism.html

### 2. The 1939 basket

As war broke out in Europe, he borrowed $10,000 and bought 100 shares in each of 104 companies trading at $1 or less. Nearly all of them made money.

- **The order.** In 1939 he bought 100 shares in each of 104 companies selling at $1 or less, including 34 in bankruptcy. (Morningstar · Irish Times, 2008)
- **Only four failed.** Just four of the 104 let him down; after repaying the loan he had a handsome profit. (Morningstar · Irish Times, 2008)
- **Why war helped.** He reasoned that in wartime, things that were in surplus and unprofitable become scarce and profitable. (Morningstar)
- **A borrowed stake.** He borrowed the money, a big risk for a young man; he spread it across 104 companies so no single failure could sink him. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-02-the-1939-basket.html

### 3. Search the whole world

He looked for bargains in every country, not just at home. That was rare in the 1950s, and it gave him far more choices.

- **A global fund.** He launched the Templeton Growth Fund in 1954, incorporated in Canada, and it searched for bargains across the world. (Obituary, 2008)
- **Japan.** He bought large holdings in Japan while its economy was still recovering from the war, and sold them in the boom years of the 1980s. (interactive investor)
- **More places, more bargains.** Diversify by country as well as industry: more markets mean more chances to find something cheap. (Rules, 1993)
- **Travel first.** After Oxford he spent seven months travelling the world with a friend, on very little money, before starting work in New York. (Irish Times, 2008)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-03-search-the-whole-world.html

### 4. Bargains among quality

Cheap is not enough. He looked for good businesses, with strong market positions and capable managers, at low prices.

- **Quality first.** Search for bargains among quality companies: a strong market position, capable management and enough capital. (Rules, 1993)
- **Earnings five years out.** He judged price against estimated earnings about five years ahead, and avoided shares above roughly 12 to 14 times. (LGT)
- **About four years.** He held shares for about four years on average. (LGT)
- **Ford near bankruptcy.** From 1978, when Ford looked headed for bankruptcy, he bought and kept buying as the shares fell further. By 1987 they were worth many times his price. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-04-bargains-among-quality.html

### 5. Value, not forecasts

Buy individual companies on their own merits, not on what you think the economy or the market will do.

- **Not the outlook.** Buy value, not market trends or the economic outlook. Individual shares can move against the market. (Rules, 1993)
- **Do your homework.** Study a company carefully before you buy, or hire wise experts to do it for you. (Rules, 1993)
- **Flexible.** No type of investment is always best. Stay open to shares, bonds and cash, and hold cash when bargains are scarce. (Rules, 1993)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-05-value-not-forecasts.html

### 6. Diversify, and keep watching

There is safety in numbers. Spread your money by industry, by risk and by country, and keep checking what you own.

- **Safety in numbers.** Diversify by industry, by risk and by country, so that one setback cannot ruin you. (Rules, 1993)
- **Not buy and forget.** Monitor your investments: markets change, companies rise and fall, and no share should be bought and forgotten. (Rules, 1993 · Morningstar)
- **Real returns.** Aim for the best total return after tax and inflation; anything else is not a real return. (Rules, 1993)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-06-diversify-and-keep-watching.html

### 7. Don't panic

When markets crash, don't sell in fear. And don't be gloomy too often: over time, optimism has paid.

- **Hold your nerve.** In a crash, don't sell just because everyone else is. Sell only if you find something clearly more attractive. (Rules, 1993)
- **This time is different?** He warned against investors who think this time is different when it is really a repeat of the past. (Rules, 1993)
- **Not too fearful.** His last rule: do not be fearful or negative too often. Over decades, shares have risen despite many falls. (Rules, 1993)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-07-dont-panic.html

### 8. Selling into euphoria

The mirror of buying at maximum pessimism is selling at maximum optimism. In 2000, aged 87, he bet heavily against overpriced technology shares.

- **Insane prices.** He said technology shares had reached 100 times earnings, or 20 times sales where there were no earnings. (Morningstar)
- **The trade.** He bet against dozens of newly listed technology shares that had soared, timed for just before insiders were free to sell. (Financial Advisor)
- **The result.** According to his great-niece, he put about $185 million into these bets and made about $90 million. (Financial Advisor)
- **A rare move.** He usually bought; betting on falls was something he did only when prices looked truly absurd. (Book, 2008)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-08-selling-into-euphoria.html

### 9. Humility

Invest, don't speculate. Learn from mistakes, accept there is no free lunch, and never think you know it all.

- **Invest, don't trade.** Frequent trading and speculation tend to lose money in costs and mistimed moves. (Rules, 1993)
- **Learn from mistakes.** Study your errors, forgive yourself, and don't try to win losses back with bigger risks. (Rules, 1993)
- **No free lunch.** Don't invest on tips or sentiment; there is no free lunch. (Rules, 1993)
- **Begin with a prayer.** An active Presbyterian, he began meetings with a prayer, which he believed clears the mind and reduces mistakes. (Rules, 1993 · Irish Times, 2008)
- **All the answers.** An investor who has all the answers doesn't even understand all the questions. (Rules, 1993)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-09-humility.html

### 10. Distance, thrift and giving

He did his best work far from Wall Street, lived frugally, and gave much of his fortune to the study of the spiritual side of life.

- **Away from the noise.** His record improved after he moved away from Wall Street to the Bahamas in 1968, where he worked largely by fax. (Blog · Irish Times, 2008)
- **Thrift.** He paid part of his way through Yale with poker winnings after the Depression hit his father, and in the Bahamas he drove old cars. (Irish Times, 2008)
- **The Prize.** In 1972 he created the Templeton Prize, meant as a Nobel-style award for progress in religion. (AP, 2008)
- **Giving.** He was knighted in 1987 for his philanthropy, and set up the John Templeton Foundation the same year. (Obituary, 2008 · AP, 2008)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/templeton-10-distance-thrift-and-giving.html

## Special section

**Tap a stage to see what he did** 

**His 16 rules, in brief**

- Aim for real returns, after tax and inflation.
- Invest; don't trade or speculate.
- Stay flexible about types of investment.
- Buy low.
- Look for bargains among quality companies.
- Buy value, not trends or forecasts.
- Do your homework, or hire wise experts.
- Diversify by industry, risk and country.
- Keep watching what you own.
- Don't panic.
- Learn from your mistakes.
- Begin with a prayer.
- Accept that beating the market is hard.
- Stay humble: nobody has all the answers.
- There is no free lunch.
- Don't be fearful or negative too often.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “An investor who has all the answers doesn't even understand all the questions.” (16 rules for investment success, 1993)
- “It was insane, and I took advantage of the temporary insanity.” (On the technology bubble of 2000, quoted by Morningstar)

## Read the originals

Start with his 16 rules for investment success, free as a short brochure from Franklin Templeton.

- [16 rules for investment success](https://www.franklintempleton.com/forms-literature/download/TL-R16): His rules in his own words: real returns, investing not trading, buying low, bargains among quality stocks, diversifying, not panicking, humility and prayer.
- [Billionaire investor dies at 95](https://www.americanrhodes.org/news-123.html): His Tennessee childhood, Yale and Oxford, why the Growth Fund was set up in Canada, and its long-term record.
- [Legendary investor Templeton dead at 95](https://www.startribune.com/legendary-investor-templeton-dead-at-95/24090479/): The fund's 14.5% average yearly return from 1954 to 1992, the sale of his firm, and his philanthropy.
- [Investment guru once dubbed the greatest global stock-picker](https://www.irishtimes.com/news/investment-guru-once-dubbed-the-greatest-global-stock-picker-1.944579): Poker at Yale, a year travelling the world, the 1939 trade, and the man behind the fund.
- [John Templeton: how to be a bargain hunter](https://www.morningstar.com.au/personal-finance/john-templeton-how-to-be-a-bargain-hunter): The 1939 trade, buying Ford near bankruptcy, his view of the 2000 bubble in his own words, and why buy-and-hold is not buy-and-forget.
- [How to invest like the best: John Templeton](https://www-warranty.ii.co.uk/analysis-commentary/how-invest-best-buy-low-and-sell-high-john-templeton-ii538493): His Japan holdings bought after the war and sold in the 1980s boom, and the research behind his bargain hunting.
- [How John Templeton reconciled God and Mammon](https://www.lgt.com/de-en/market-assessments/insights/financial-knowledge/how-john-templeton-reconciled-god-and-mammon-301902): His price discipline, using earnings five years ahead, how long he held shares, and his faith.
- [The making of Templeton](https://www.fa-mag.com/news/making-templeton-1966.html?page=3): His approach to bubbles, and the size of his bets against technology shares in 2000, as told by his great-niece.
- [John Templeton's 16 rules for investment success](https://awealthofcommonsense.com/john-templetons-16-rules-for-investment-success/): A walk through his rules, and how his results improved once he moved away from Wall Street.
- [Investing the Templeton Way](https://moiglobal.com/lauren-templeton-investing-the-templeton-way/): His bargain-hunting method, with his most famous trades explained.

## Words to know

- **Contrarian**: Deliberately going against the crowd.
- **Bargain hunting**: His own name for his style: buying shares far below what they are worth.
- **Real return**: Your return after tax and inflation.
- **Short selling**: Borrowing shares to sell them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price.
- **Lock-up**: A period after a share's first listing when insiders may not sell.
- **Initial public offering (IPO)**: A company's first sale of shares to the public.
- **Mutual fund**: A pooled fund that invests many people's money together.
- **Diversification**: Spreading money across many holdings to reduce the harm of any one mistake.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his 16 rules (World Monitor, 1993), obituaries in the Washington Post, the Irish Times and by AP (2008), Morningstar and interactive investor profiles, Financial Advisor magazine, an LGT study of his method, and Investing the Templeton Way (2008). Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Templeton was born and built his career in the United States; in the 1960s he gave up US citizenship, became British and later lived in the Bahamas. He wrote mostly about life and faith, and less about investing, so his 16 rules are the main source in his own words.
