# John Bogle

> Launched the first index fund for ordinary investors, was mocked for it, and spent his life cutting the costs that eat savers' returns.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/bogle.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Buy the haystack. Own the whole market instead of hunting for the few winners.

## Summary

John Bogle, called Jack, founded Vanguard in 1974 and in 1976 launched the first index fund for ordinary investors. Critics called it Bogle's folly. His idea was simple: most investors cannot beat the market after costs, so own the whole market as cheaply as possible and hold it. Warren Buffett later said that if anyone deserves a statue for helping American investors, it is Bogle.

## Record at a glance

- **1976**: launched the first index fund for ordinary investors; it raised only about $11 million at launch
- **Owned by its investors**: Vanguard is owned by its funds, and so by the people who invest in them
- **12 books**: selling more than 1.1 million copies
- **$854,000 vs $220,000**: gain on $1 million by 2016 in Buffett's ten-year bet: an index fund against five funds of hedge funds

## Big ideas

### 1. Buy the haystack

Instead of searching for the few stocks or funds that will beat the market, buy the whole market through a low-cost index fund, and hold it.

- **His corollary.** Don't hunt for the needle; buy the whole haystack. An index fund owns every company, so it is sure to own the winners. (Book, 2007)
- **Simple, not easy.** Successful investing is simple, he wrote, but it takes discipline and patience to stick with it. (Book, 2007)
- **A fair share.** The book's subtitle promised only your fair share of the market's return, which most investors fail to get. (Book, 2007)
- **Not his invention.** Index funds already existed for big institutions; his was the first one ordinary savers could buy. (AP, 2019 · Vanguard, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-01-buy-the-haystack.html

### 2. Costs matter

Returns are uncertain; costs are certain. Every fee and commission comes straight out of what you earn, and over decades the damage compounds.

- **Two forces.** He set the magic of compounding returns against the tyranny of compounding costs. Over long periods costs can eat a large part of your gains. (Book, 2007)
- **You get what you don't pay for.** In most things you get what you pay for; in fund investing, he argued, the money you don't pay in fees is what you keep. (Book, 2007)
- **Pick the cheapest.** One chapter tells investors simply to focus on the lowest-cost funds. (Book, 2007)
- **A lifelong fight.** His obituaries describe a career spent pushing for lower fees for ordinary investors. (AP, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-02-costs-matter.html

### 3. The simple arithmetic

All investors together own the market. So, before costs, they earn the market's return; after costs, they must earn less. Beating the market is a loser's game for most.

- **Before and after costs.** As a group, investors earn exactly the market's return before costs, and less after them. Someone's gain over the average is someone else's loss. (Book, 2007)
- **A loser's game.** Trying to beat the market is a loser's game for most, he wrote: the more the managers and brokers take, the less investors make. (Book, 2007)
- **Buffett's bet.** Buffett bet that an S&P 500 index fund would beat five funds of hedge funds over ten years. By 2016, $1 million in the index fund had gained $854,000; the hedge funds, $220,000. (Buffett, 2017)
- **Buffett agrees.** Buffett told both large and small investors to stick with low-cost index funds. (Buffett, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-03-the-simple-arithmetic.html

### 4. Bogle's folly

His first index fund was mocked and nearly failed to launch. He stood behind it for years until the idea won.

- **A thin start.** First Index Investment Trust launched on 31 August 1976 with only about $11 million (sources say $11 million to $11.4 million). (AP, 2019 · NAPA, 2019)
- **The jeers.** Rivals called it Bogle's folly and said it aimed only for average results. (AP, 2019)
- **He held on.** Vanguard says he stood behind the idea, in the face of sceptics, until it was widely accepted. (Vanguard, 2019)
- **Its descendant.** The fund became the Vanguard 500 Index Fund and a huge success. (Telegraph, 2019 · Vanguard, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-04-bogles-folly.html

### 5. Owned by its investors

After losing his job in 1974, he built Vanguard differently: the fund company is owned by its funds, and so by their investors, not by outside shareholders.

- **Fired, then free.** He lost his job running Wellington after the falling stock market of the early 1970s and a quarrel with his partners. (AP, 2019 · Morningstar, 2019)
- **A new structure.** In most fund companies an outside management firm runs the funds for its own profit. At Vanguard the funds own the manager. (Vanguard, 2019)
- **Still unique.** Morningstar called Vanguard the first, and still the only, mutually owned fund family. (Morningstar, 2019)
- **The name.** He named it after Nelson's flagship at the Battle of the Nile. (Telegraph, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-05-owned-by-its-investors.html

### 6. Time is your friend

Buy, hold, and stay the course. Trading in and out, and chasing what has done well, is how investors lose the market's return.

- **Hold forever.** His simplest strategy: buy and hold all of a nation's listed businesses, at very low cost, for good. (Book, 2007)
- **Business beats the market.** In the long run, he argued, the returns of businesses, their dividends and earnings growth, matter more than the market's moods. (Book, 2007)
- **Expenses and emotions.** He saw the two great enemies of investors as expenses and emotions. (Book, 2007)
- **Bogleheads.** Followers who share his buy-and-hold approach call themselves Bogleheads. (AP, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-06-time-is-your-friend.html

### 7. Yesterday's winners, tomorrow's losers

Funds that topped the charts rarely stay on top. Chasing past performance means buying high and paying for luck.

- **Regression.** A chapter titled Yesterday's Winners, Tomorrow's Losers shows how top funds tend to sink back towards the average. (Book, 2007)
- **Fooled by randomness.** He warned that a hot record is often luck, and luck does not repeat. (Book, 2007)
- **Funds disappear.** Many funds that once looked good were later closed or merged out of existence. (Book, 2007)
- **Look before you leap.** Even advisers picking funds for you face the same problem, he wrote, so be wary of paying for selection. (Book, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-07-yesterdays-winners-tomorrows-losers.html

### 8. Taxes and trading

Trading costs money twice: in commissions and in taxes. Low turnover keeps more of the return working for you.

- **Uncle Sam.** One chapter's title tells investors not to pay the tax authorities any more than they should. (Book, 2007)
- **Turnover.** Funds that trade a lot pass on costs and taxes that an index fund, which rarely sells, largely avoids. (Book, 2007)
- **A trader's tool.** He was wary of exchange-traded funds when they were used for frequent trading rather than holding. (Book, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-08-taxes-and-trading.html

### 9. A duty of trust

He believed managing other people's money is a duty, not just a business, and spent his later years saying so.

- **The 1987 speech.** He told the fund industry it must change its pricing, products and promotion, and hold itself to higher standards of trust and fiduciary duty. (Vanguard, 2019 · NAPA, 2019)
- **A profession first.** He argued fund management should behave like a profession rather than a mere industry. (NAPA, 2019)
- **Integrity.** Morningstar wrote that admirers and critics alike agreed he was a man of irreproachable integrity. (Morningstar, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-09-a-duty-of-trust.html

### 10. A statue, a heart, and enough

He took far less from his work than he could have, survived years of heart disease, and was honoured by Buffett as the person who did most for American investors.

- **The statue.** Buffett wrote that if a statue is ever built for the person who did most for American investors, it should be of Bogle. (Buffett, 2017)
- **A modest fortune.** Buffett noted that Bogle's low-cost funds earned him only a tiny share of the wealth that flowed to managers who charged far more. (Buffett, 2017)
- **A new heart.** He received a heart transplant in 1996, a month after handing Vanguard to John Brennan. (Vanguard, 2019)
- **No more to give.** In 2012 he said his one regret was not having more to give away. (Telegraph, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bogle-10-a-statue-a-heart-and-enough.html

## Special section

**See what a fee costs you** 

**His rules, in brief**

- Own the whole market through a low-cost index fund.
- Keep costs low: every fee is a certain loss.
- Hold for the long run; impulse is the enemy.
- Don't chase last year's winners.
- Trade rarely: turnover costs you twice, in fees and taxes.
- Stay the course when markets fall.
- Remember the arithmetic: investors as a group earn the market, minus costs.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “Don't look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack!” (The Little Book of Common Sense Investing, 2007)
- “We must hold ourselves to higher standards, standards of trust and fiduciary duty.” (Speech to the fund industry, 1987, quoted by Vanguard)

## Read the originals

Start with The Little Book of Common Sense Investing. It is short, and each chapter makes one point.

- [The Little Book of Common Sense Investing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Little_Book_of_Common_Sense_Investing): His case for low-cost index funds: the arithmetic of costs, why yesterday's winning funds disappoint, taxes, and staying the course.
- [Vanguard announces the passing of its founder](https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/vanguard-announces-the-passing-of-founder-john-c-bogle-869516972.html): His two great achievements, the first index fund and Vanguard's ownership structure, his 1987 speech, his heart transplant, and his successor.
- [John Bogle dies at 89; fought for lower fees for investors](https://triblive.com/news/world/john-bogle-dies-at-89-fought-for-lower-fees-for-investors): Losing his job in the early 1970s, the launch of the first index fund, the jeers of Bogle's folly, and the Bogleheads.
- [John Bogle, champion of the small investor](https://uk.news.yahoo.com/john-bogle-champion-small-investor-060000466.html): His family, why he named his firm Vanguard, his heart troubles, and his views on wealth and giving.
- [Vanguard founder Jack Bogle dies](https://morningstar.co.uk/uk/news/180816/vanguard-founder-jack-bogle-dies.aspx): His Princeton thesis, the break with Wellington, and why Vanguard's mutual ownership is still unique.
- [Investment legend Bogle dies](https://www.napa-net.org/news/2019/2/investment-legend-bogle-dies/): A short record of his career, his speeches and his twelve books.
- [Berkshire Hathaway letter for 2016](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2016ltr.pdf): The result of his ten-year bet that an index fund would beat hand-picked hedge funds, and his tribute to Bogle.

## Words to know

- **Index fund**: A fund that simply owns all the shares in a market index, such as the S&P 500, instead of picking.
- **Expense ratio**: A fund's yearly running costs, as a percentage of the money invested.
- **Active management**: Picking investments in an attempt to beat the market.
- **Turnover**: How much of a fund's holdings it sells and replaces in a year.
- **Fiduciary duty**: A legal and moral duty to act in someone else's best interest.
- **Mutual fund**: A pooled fund that invests many people's money together.
- **Compounding**: Earning returns on past returns, so growth speeds up over time.

## Sources and scope

Sources: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (2007), Vanguard's 2019 announcement of his death, obituaries by the Associated Press, the Telegraph and Morningstar, a trade-press obituary, and Buffett's letter for 2016. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Bogle wrote twelve books; we use The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (2007, revised 2017) as the main one. Vanguard's own funds are mentioned for history only, not as a recommendation.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.

# Howard Marks

> Has written memos since 1990 that Buffett opens first: on risk, cycles, and thinking differently from the crowd.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/marks.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Second-level thinking. Ask not just what is good, but what everyone else already thinks.

## Summary

Howard Marks co-founded Oaktree Capital in 1995 and is best known for his memos to clients, which he has written since 1990. Buffett says they are the first thing he opens. Marks's message: you cannot predict the future, but you can know where you stand in the cycle, avoid big losses, and think differently from the crowd.

## Record at a glance

- **1990**: his first memo to clients; he has written them ever since, and they are free online
- **4th percentile**: where a pension fund ranked over 14 years though never in the top quarter in any year: the lesson of his first memo
- **≈ $6 billion**: invested by his partner's team from mid-September to the end of 2008, about $400 million a week, as panic peaked
- **1995**: co-founded Oaktree Capital in Los Angeles

## Big ideas

### 1. Second-level thinking

To do better than others you must think differently, and better. First-level thinking asks whether something is good; second-level thinking asks what is already in the price.

- **The first chapter.** His book opens with second-level thinking: a simple, obvious view cannot beat the market, because everyone already holds it. (Book, 2011)
- **Different actions.** If you think like everyone else you will act like them and get the same results; you have to think differently from the norm. (Talk)
- **The example.** A first-level thinker says a company is good, so buy. A second-level thinker asks whether everyone agrees, and whether the price already reflects it. (Book, 2011)
- **Not simple.** He warns that second-level thinking is hard work and that easy formulas are a sign of first-level thinking. (Book, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-01-second-level-thinking.html

### 2. Risk means losing money

For Marks, risk is not the jiggling of prices. It is the chance of a permanent loss, and it is hardest to see when times are good.

- **The risk that matters.** The most important risk is the chance of losing money, not short-term volatility. (Book, 2011)
- **Three chapters.** He devotes three chapters to risk: understanding it, recognising it and controlling it. (Book, 2011)
- **Good times teach bad lessons.** Easy markets teach investors that risk doesn't matter, just before it does. (Book, 2011)
- **Risk and return.** Riskier assets must appear to offer higher returns, but that is a promise, not a guarantee. (Book, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-02-risk-means-losing-money.html

### 3. It's what you pay

There is no such thing as a good or bad asset in itself, only a good or bad price. A great company bought too dear can be a poor investment.

- **Price and value.** He gives separate chapters to value and to the relationship between price and value. (Book, 2011)
- **Quality can be risky.** A high-quality asset bought at too high a price can be risky; a low-quality one bought cheaply can be safe. (Book, 2011)
- **Below value.** His answer to when to buy is simple: when the price is below intrinsic value. (Book, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-03-its-what-you-pay.html

### 4. The pendulum

Investor psychology swings like a pendulum between greed and fear, optimism and despair. It spends little time at the sensible midpoint.

- **A chapter of its own.** His book has a chapter on awareness of the pendulum. (Book, 2011)
- **Rarely in the middle.** Moods overshoot in both directions; the extremes are where mistakes, and opportunities, are made. (Book, 2011 · Book, 2018)
- **Many cycles.** His second book traces the cycles in the economy, in profits, in attitudes to risk, in credit and in investor psychology. (Book, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-04-the-pendulum.html

### 5. You can't predict. You can prepare.

Nobody can forecast the economy or the market reliably. But you can know roughly where you are in the cycle and prepare for what usually follows.

- **Forecasts don't help.** He dismisses economic forecasts, which he thinks add no value, but believes deeply in cycles. (Memo, 2001)
- **Where you are.** The key is to know where you are, even if you cannot know exactly where you are going. (Memo, 2001)
- **Borrowed words.** He took the memo's title from an insurance company's advertising slogan. (Memo, 2001)
- **Scenarios.** Since we never know what will happen, consider the likely scenarios and prepare for them. (Memo, 2001)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-05-you-cant-predict-you-can-prepare.html

### 6. Take the temperature

Watch how people around you behave. When everyone is eager and careless, be careful; when everyone is frightened, look for bargains.

- **Read the mood.** He judges the market by its psychology: is it buoyant and greedy, or depressed and fearful? (Memo, 2023)
- **Excess and correction.** A strong move one way is more likely to be followed by a correction than to grow to the sky. (Memo, 2023)
- **Two extremes.** Beware optimism so strong that no price seems too high, and look for despair so deep that any sale seems good. (Memo, 2023)
- **Resist your own mood.** Stand apart from the crowd, and act when you see something illogical. (Memo, 2023)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-06-take-the-temperature.html

### 7. bubble.com

In January 2000, near the peak of the technology bubble, he warned that internet and telecom shares had become a bubble. It burst within weeks.

- **The memo.** His January 2000 memo, bubble.com, warned of a bubble in technology, internet and telecom shares as it peaked. (Memo, 2023)
- **Little exposure.** Oaktree owned little technology at the time. (Memo, 2023)
- **Then defence.** From 2004 to 2007 he grew steadily more cautious, selling assets and raising the bar for new investments before the crisis. (Memo, 2023)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-07-bubble-com.html

### 8. Buying in the panic

Being prepared paid off in late 2008. When panic was at its worst, Oaktree had money ready and spent it.

- **Ready money.** Oaktree had raised a large fund for distressed debt before the crisis, so it could buy when others were forced to sell. (Memo, 2023)
- **$400 million a week.** From mid-September to the end of 2008 his partner Bruce Karsh's team invested about $400 million a week, about $6 billion. (Memo, 2023)
- **Not the bottom.** In 2020 he again bought as markets fell, accepting it might not be the lowest point. (Memo, 2023)
- **Fear as a signal.** Extreme pessimism, in his view, is when risk is lowest and bargains are best. (Memo, 2023 · Book, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-08-buying-in-the-panic.html

### 9. Avoid the losers

Superior results over time come less from big wins than from avoiding big losses. His very first memo made the point.

- **The pension fund.** A pension fund he met was never in the top quarter in any of 14 years, yet ranked in the top 4% over the whole period. (Memo, 1990)
- **Why.** It never had a disastrous year, never falling below the middle of its peers. (Memo, 1990)
- **Bold steps.** He argued that bold moves aimed at great performance are as likely to be wrong as right. (Memo, 1990)
- **Oaktree's creed.** He later said the memo set out what became a core part of Oaktree's investment philosophy. (Memo, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-09-avoid-the-losers.html

### 10. Writing to think, and saying 'I don't know'

His memos are how he thinks. He is candid about uncertainty and avoids flat predictions.

- **Since 1990.** He has written memos to clients since 1990, and they are posted publicly on Oaktree's website. (Memo, 1990 · Memo, 2023)
- **Never 'get out'.** He says he never tells clients anything as flatly negative as to get out of the market. (CFA, 2019)
- **Admit ignorance.** When asked something he can't answer, he says he doesn't know. (CFA, 2019)
- **Buffett reads first.** Buffett has written that Marks's memos are the first thing he opens in his mail. (Book, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/marks-10-writing-to-think-and-saying-i-dont-know.html

## Special section

**Pick one side of each pair for today's market** 

**Four memos to start with**

- The Route to Performance (1990): his first memo, on avoiding losers.
- bubble.com (2000): the warning at the peak of the technology bubble.
- You Can't Predict. You Can Prepare. (2001): cycles, and why forecasts don't help.
- Taking the Temperature (2023): five market calls looked back on.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “You can't predict. You can prepare.” (Title of his memo, 2001, borrowed from an insurance advert)
- “You have to do different things and think differently from the norm” (Talks at Goldman Sachs)

## Read the originals

Start with his first memo, The Route to Performance (1990), three pages long, then the book The Most Important Thing (2011).

- [The Route to Performance](https://www.oaktreecapital.com/docs/default-source/memos/1990-10-12-the-route-to-performance.pdf): His first memo: the pension fund that reached the top 4% over 14 years by never having a bad year.
- [You Can't Predict. You Can Prepare.](https://www.oaktreecapital.com/docs/default-source/memos/2001-11-20-you-cant-predict-you-can-prepare.pdf): Why he ignores economic forecasts but takes cycles seriously, and why knowing where you are matters more than knowing where you are going.
- [Taking the Temperature](https://www.oaktreecapital.com/docs/default-source/memos/taking-the-temperature.pdf): Five market calls from 2000 to 2020, from bubble.com to the 2008 crisis and Covid, and how he reads the market's mood.
- [The Most Important Thing](https://news.columbia.edu/node/2519): His memos distilled: second-level thinking, price and value, understanding and controlling risk, cycles and the pendulum.
- [Mastering the Market Cycle](https://books.google.com/books?id=8hhDDwAAQBAJ): The cycles in the economy, profits, credit and investor psychology, and how to position yourself as they turn.
- [Talks at Goldman Sachs](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/talks-at-gs/howard-marks.html): Marks on second-level thinking and on cycles.
- [The Best of](https://cnt.oaktreecapital.com/insights/memo/the-best-of): Marks picks his favourite memos from 35 years and says why each matters.
- [Getting the odds on your side](https://blogs.cfainstitute.org/investor/2019/02/19/howard-marks-cfa-getting-the-odds-on-your-side/): His cautious memos, why he never says 'get out', and being honest about what he does not know.

## Words to know

- **Second-level thinking**: Thinking about what others think, and what is already reflected in the price.
- **Distressed debt**: Bonds and loans of companies in, or close to, financial trouble.
- **High-yield bond**: A bond from a riskier company that pays more interest; also called a junk bond.
- **Cycle**: The repeated rise and fall of economies, profits, credit and moods.
- **Percentile**: A ranking out of 100: the 4th percentile means better than 96% of the group.
- **Intrinsic value**: What an asset is really worth, based on what it will earn.
- **Volatility**: How much and how fast a price moves up and down.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his memos The Route to Performance (1990), You Can't Predict. You Can Prepare. (2001), Taking the Temperature (2023) and The Best of (2025); his books The Most Important Thing (2011) and Mastering the Market Cycle (2018); a Goldman Sachs talk; and a CFA Institute report of a 2019 talk. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Marks is still working and writing; facts are as of late 2026. Oaktree's funds are mentioned for history only; this page says nothing about investing with any firm.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Howard Marks, Oaktree Capital Management, Brookfield, Columbia University Press, Goldman Sachs, CFA Institute or any company named. Memos are linked, not copied. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.

# Seth Klarman

> Wrote a book that sold 5,000 copies and became a legend, and built a firm on one rule above all: avoid losing money.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/klarman.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Avoid loss first. The first goal is not to lose money; returns come second.

## Summary

Seth Klarman has run the Baupost Group in Boston since 1982, when four families hired him at 25 to manage about $27 million. In 1991 he wrote Margin of Safety, which sold few copies, went out of print and became a cult classic. His creed is Graham's, pushed further: avoid losing money first, value things cautiously, and wait for the market to offer a big discount.

## Record at a glance

- **1982**: founded Baupost with about $27 million from four families
- **≈ 20% a year**: the reported net return of Baupost's largest partnership, with one losing year from 1983 to the late 2000s
- **5,000 copies**: the first print run of Margin of Safety at $25; used copies later sold for over $1,000
- **$22 billion**: Baupost's assets by 2026, as reported

## Big ideas

### 1. Avoid loss first

Klarman puts avoiding loss ahead of everything. A big loss takes a long time to recover from, so protecting money comes before chasing returns.

- **The primary goal.** The book argues that avoiding loss should be every investor's first goal. (Summary · Book, 1991)
- **Risk-averse.** The book's own subtitle describes its strategies as risk-averse. (Book, 1991)
- **Survive the worst.** He tests each holding against severe scenarios, asking whether it would survive a collapse like 1933. (Interview, 2026)
- **Strength in bad times.** Protecting the downside lets you keep buying when weaker investors are forced to sell. (Interview, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-01-avoid-loss-first.html

### 2. Margin of safety

Valuation is never precise, the future is unknowable and people make mistakes. So buy only at a price far enough below value to absorb all three.

- **Three reasons.** A margin of safety is needed because valuation is imprecise, the future is unpredictable and investors are human. (Summary)
- **Graham's idea.** He took the title from Graham, who made the margin of safety the central idea of The Intelligent Investor. (Book, 1991)
- **Haircut your value.** Do the work to estimate value, assume you are wrong and cut the estimate, then wait for that lower price. (Summary)
- **Strong in declines.** Value investing with a margin of safety has tended to hold up well when markets fall. (Summary)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-02-margin-of-safety.html

### 3. Investors and speculators

Investors buy businesses below their value; speculators bet on which way prices will move. Wall Street, he argues, mostly serves the speculators.

- **Where investors stumble.** The book's first part covers speculators and unsuccessful investors and how they go wrong. (Book, 1991)
- **Wall Street's interest.** He argues that Wall Street makes money from activity and fees, so its interests often work against investors. (Book, 1991)
- **Price is not value.** Separate price movements from the reality of the business behind them. (Summary)
- **Feels like gambling.** Once you adopt a value approach, he wrote, other kinds of investing start to look like gambling. (Summary)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-03-investors-and-speculators.html

### 4. The performance derby

Many professional investors are judged every quarter against an index. That pushes them to follow the crowd, which creates chances for investors who don't have to.

- **The client loses.** A chapter on the institutional performance derby argues that short-term relative performance contests hurt clients. (Book, 1991)
- **Constraints create bargains.** Rules and habits that limit institutions can push prices away from value. (Summary)
- **Absolute, not relative.** Baupost judges itself on absolute returns, aiming to beat inflation by a wide margin rather than beat an index. (Interview, 2026 · Book, 1991)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-04-the-performance-derby.html

### 5. Value it three ways

No single method gives the true value. He discusses several, from future cash flows to break-up value to what similar companies fetch, and urges conservatism.

- **Several methods.** The book discusses valuing a business by the present value of its future cash, by its liquidation or break-up value, and by stock market comparisons. (Book, 1991)
- **Conservative always.** Since no one can predict when values will rise or fall, value conservatively, giving real weight to worst-case liquidation value. (Summary)
- **A range, not a number.** Value is better thought of as a range than a precise figure, so leave room for error. (Book, 1991 · Summary)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-05-value-it-three-ways.html

### 6. Look where others aren't

Bargains are most common in complicated, unpopular or forced-sale situations that most investors avoid.

- **His hunting grounds.** The book discusses bankruptcies and financially distressed companies, thrift conversions and other neglected areas. (Book, 1991)
- **Complexity.** He still looks in complicated corners such as distressed debt, real estate and private deals, where competition is thin. (Interview, 2026)
- **Forced sellers.** When others must sell, for rules or lack of cash, prices can fall well below value. (Interview, 2026 · Summary)
- **Bottom-up.** He relies on studying individual investments, not big economic forecasts. (Interview, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-06-look-where-others-arent.html

### 7. Cheap isn't enough

A cheap share can stay cheap for years. He looks for a catalyst, an event that can close the gap between price and value.

- **Not a strategy.** In 2026 he said simply buying cheap things is not a strategy on its own. (Interview, 2026)
- **A catalyst.** Baupost wants an identifiable event that can drive a turnaround within a year or two. (Interview, 2026)
- **In the book too.** One chapter on where to look starts with catalysts, alongside market inefficiencies and institutional constraints. (Book, 1991)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-07-cheap-isnt-enough.html

### 8. Patience and cash

When there is nothing good to buy, hold cash rather than take more risk. But he admits that holding too much cash for too long was a mistake.

- **Cash as an option.** He has said that, rather than take more risk, Baupost holds cash when opportunities are scarce. (Profile)
- **Not paid to hold cash.** Cash is meant to be spent when bargains appear, not kept forever. (Interview, 2026)
- **His own mistake.** He now says Baupost almost certainly held too much cash for too long, and has made its holdings more liquid so it needs less. (Interview, 2026)
- **Also missed.** He says he should have paid more attention to venture capital. (Interview, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-08-patience-and-cash.html

### 9. Fear is useful

Klarman sees fear as protective. Being worried keeps you prepared; the danger is when everyone feels safe.

- **Scared, not sorry.** He has said Baupost is a fan of fear: better to be scared than sorry. (Profile)
- **Stretched today.** In 2026 he described the market as feeling stretched, expensive and speculative. (Interview, 2026)
- **Forced selling.** Avoiding situations where you must sell at the worst time is essential. (Interview, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-09-fear-is-useful.html

### 10. A book that landed with a thud

His one book sold poorly, went out of print and became one of the most sought-after investing books in the world. His career began with two mentors and four families.

- **Mentors.** He learned the trade working for Max Heine and Michael Price at Mutual Shares. (Interview, 2026)
- **Four families.** Baupost began in 1982 with about $27 million from four families who had sold businesses; he was 25. (Interview, 2026)
- **A flop, then a legend.** The book sold about 5,000 copies at $25. Used copies later sold for more than $1,000. (Book, 1991 · Profile)
- **The e-book.** In 2018 a $9.99 e-book briefly appeared on Amazon and sold thousands before vanishing. (Money, 2018)
- **Graham's heir.** He edited the 2023 edition of Graham and Dodd's Security Analysis. (Profile)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/klarman-10-a-book-that-landed-with-a-thud.html

## Special section

**Value a business three ways** 

**Where he looks for bargains**

- Distressed and bankrupt companies, which many funds are not allowed to hold.
- Complicated situations that take real work to understand.
- Forced sellers, who must sell for rules or cash, not value.
- Unpopular areas that the crowd has given up on.
- Situations with a catalyst that can close the gap between price and value.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “cheap is not really a strategy” (Masters in Business interview, 2026)

## Read the originals

If you can find it, read Margin of Safety, chapters 5 and 6. Otherwise, start with his 2026 interview on Masters in Business.

- [Margin of Safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margin_of_Safety_(book)): Why most investors stumble, the value-investing philosophy built on a margin of safety, how to value a business, and where to look for bargains.
- [Margin of Safety: a book summary](https://jamesclear.com/book-summaries/margin-of-safety): A short summary of the book's main points: loss avoidance, conservative valuation, and institutional constraints.
- [Masters in Business: Seth Klarman](https://ritholtz.com/2026/06/transcript-seth-klarman/): His mentors, how Baupost began, absolute returns, catalysts, his mistakes with cash, and his view of today's market.
- [Seth A. Klarman](https://ivey.uwo.ca/bengrahaminvesting/resources/interviews-notes/seth-a-klarman): A short profile: Baupost's approach, its reported long-term record and his education.
- [The investing book that sells for thousands](https://money.com/seth-klarman-margin-of-safety-author-value-investing/): Why used copies of Margin of Safety cost so much, and the brief appearance of a $9.99 e-book.
- [Seth Klarman](https://www.hks.harvard.edu/about/seth-klarman): His book and his role as editor of the 2023 edition of Security Analysis.

## Words to know

- **Margin of safety**: The gap between a cautious estimate of value and the price you pay.
- **Absolute return**: A return judged on its own, not against an index.
- **Liquidation value**: What a business would fetch if its assets were sold off and debts paid.
- **Present value**: What future cash is worth today, after allowing for time and risk.
- **Catalyst**: An event that can make the market recognise value.
- **Distressed debt**: Bonds and loans of companies in, or close to, financial trouble.
- **Thrift conversion**: When a savings bank owned by its depositors sells shares to the public.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Margin of Safety (1991) and a summary of it, his 2026 Masters in Business interview, the Ivey Business School and Harvard profiles, and a 2018 report on the book. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Klarman is still working, and Baupost is private; its returns are not published, so the figure we show is the reported one. His letters to clients are private and are not used here.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Seth Klarman, the Baupost Group, HarperCollins, Bloomberg, Ivey Business School, Harvard University or any company named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.

# Walter Schloss

> Never went to college, never visited a company, owned a hundred cheap shares at a time, and beat the market for 47 years.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/schloss.html · Section: the United States · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Price first. Price, compared with value, is what matters most.

## Summary

Walter Schloss never went to college. He started as a Wall Street runner at 18, learned from Benjamin Graham at evening classes and worked for him before starting his own partnership in 1955. For 47 years he bought cheap shares by simple rules, owned around a hundred at a time, never visited managements and beat the market by a wide margin. Buffett called him one of the good guys of Wall Street.

## Record at a glance

- **21.3% a year**: his partnership, 1956 to 1984, before his share (16.1% for his partners), as Buffett reported
- **47 years**: 1956 to 2002, about 15% to 16% a year, by different counts
- **$100,000**: the money 19 investors gave him to start in 1955
- **≈ $11,000**: his office costs in a year when his partnership earned $19 million, as Buffett noted

## Big ideas

### 1. Price comes first

His first factor: price, compared with value, is the most important thing. A share is part of a business, not a piece of paper.

- **Factor one.** Price, set against value, is the most important factor of all. (Note, 1994)
- **A real business.** Try to work out what the company is worth, remembering that a share is a piece of a business. (Note, 1994)
- **Cheap against value.** Buffett said Schloss simply buys businesses selling for less than they are worth, and that's all he does. (Buffett, 1984)
- **Graham's methods.** He picked shares by simple statistical methods learned while working for Graham. (Buffett, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-01-price-comes-first.html

### 2. Assets over earnings

He preferred buying assets at a discount to buying earnings. Earnings can change fast; assets usually change slowly.

- **Start with book value.** Use book value as the starting point for estimating what a business is worth. (Note, 1994)
- **Watch the debt.** Make sure debt is well below the shareholders' equity. (Note, 1994)
- **Assets change slowly.** Earnings can change dramatically in a short time; you need to know far more about a company to buy its earnings. (Note, 1994)
- **Not growth or managers.** Unlike most analysts, he paid little attention to earnings growth or to management. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-02-assets-over-earnings.html

### 3. Buy near the lows

He liked shares trading near the bottom of their range of recent years, and he was patient once he had bought.

- **Near the low.** He found it helpful to buy near the low of the past few years. (Note, 1994)
- **Check the history.** A share that has fallen from 125 to 60 may look cheap, but if it was 20 three years ago, it may still be vulnerable. (Note, 1994)
- **Patience.** Stocks don't go up immediately; give them time. (Note, 1994)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-03-buy-near-the-lows.html

### 4. Own many, buy in steps

He spread his money across around a hundred shares and bought and sold gradually rather than all at once.

- **Over a hundred.** Buffett noted that Schloss owned well over 100 stocks at a time. (Buffett, 1984)
- **On a scale.** Buy on a scale and sell on a scale: in steps, not all at once. (Note, 1994)
- **No single bet.** A few big winners did not explain his success; it came from many modest ones. (Buffett, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-04-own-many-buy-in-steps.html

### 5. Public numbers only

He never visited managements or chased inside information. He read the published numbers, sent for annual reports and decided for himself.

- **Never near inside information.** Buffett wrote that Walter and Edwin never came within a mile of inside information and used outside information only sparingly. (Buffett, 2007)
- **The manuals.** He looked up the numbers in the manuals and sent for the annual reports. (Buffett, 1984)
- **A tiny office.** He worked without a secretary, clerk or bookkeeper; his only associate was his son. (Buffett, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-05-public-numbers-only.html

### 6. Keep emotions out

Fear and greed are the worst emotions for an investor. Have your own method, follow it calmly, and don't be swayed by tips or crowds.

- **Fear and greed.** Try not to let emotions affect your judgment; fear and greed are the worst of them. (Note, 1994)
- **No tips.** Don't buy on tips or for a quick move, and don't sell on bad news. (Note, 1994)
- **Be a loner.** Don't be afraid to stand alone, but look hard for weaknesses in your own thinking. (Note, 1994)
- **Have a philosophy.** Have a method of investing and stick to it once you have decided. (Note, 1994)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-06-keep-emotions-out.html

### 7. Don't sell too soon

Many investors sell after a quick gain. He re-checked the company's value first, and watched the level of the whole market.

- **Not in a hurry.** A 50% gain is not by itself a reason to sell; re-check the company's value against its book value first. (Note, 1994)
- **The market's level.** Before selling, ask whether yields are low, prices high and people very optimistic. (Note, 1994)
- **Advice is optional.** Listen to people you respect, but remember it's your money and the decision is yours. (Note, 1994)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-07-dont-sell-too-soon.html

### 8. Compounding, shares and leverage

Let returns compound, prefer shares to bonds over the long run, and be careful with borrowed money.

- **The rule of 72.** At 12% a year, money doubles in about six years: divide 72 by your return. (Note, 1994)
- **Shares over bonds.** Bonds limit your gains and inflation eats their value, so he preferred shares. (Note, 1994)
- **Leverage.** Be careful with borrowed money; it can go against you. (Note, 1994)
- **Keep what you make.** It is harder to keep money than to make it, and a big loss is hard to recover. (Note, 1994)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-08-compounding-shares-and-leverage.html

### 9. Paid only when partners gained

He charged no management fee. He took a share of profits only, and kept his costs tiny.

- **No fee.** He charged no management fee, taking a 25% share of the profits instead. (Morningstar)
- **Not a dime.** Buffett wrote that he took nothing unless his partners made money. (Buffett, 2007)
- **$11,000.** Buffett once pointed out that his office costs were about $11,000 in a year when the partnership earned $19 million. (Morningstar)
- **Skin in the game.** He invested his own money alongside his partners. (Morningstar · Buffett, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-09-paid-only-when-partners-gained.html

### 10. A quiet life on Wall Street

He came in as a teenage runner, learned from Graham, served in the war and ran his partnership for 47 years with his son. Buffett used his record to show that skill, not luck, can beat the market.

- **No college.** He started as a runner at 18 in 1934; his firm paid for two courses with Graham at the New York Stock Exchange Institute. (Obituary, 2012)
- **War and Graham-Newman.** He served four years in the Army, kept in touch with Graham, and joined Graham-Newman in 1946. (Obituary, 2012)
- **His own firm.** He left in 1955 and started with $100,000 from 19 investors; his son Edwin joined in 1973. (Obituary, 2012 · Interview, 1989)
- **Not luck.** Buffett wrote that there was no possibility his 47-year record was due to chance, and that it involved no real risk of permanent loss. (Buffett, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/schloss-10-a-quiet-life-on-wall-street.html

## Special section

**His 16 factors, in our words** 

**Would it pass a look in his style?**

- The price is at or below book value
- The price is near the low of the past few years
- Debt is well below shareholders' equity
- The company has a long record, good and bad years included
- You can judge it from published reports alone
- It would be one of many holdings, not a big bet

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “Price is the most important factor to use in relation to value.” (Factors needed to make money in the stock market, 1994)

## Read the originals

Read his one-page 1994 note, Factors Needed to Make Money in the Stock Market, then Buffett's 2006 letter where he writes about Schloss.

- [Factors needed to make money in the stock market](https://novelinvestor.com/walter-schloss-investing-stocks/): His 16 factors on one page: price and value, book value, patience, emotions, selling, compounding and leverage.
- [The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Superinvestors_of_Graham-and-Doddsville): Schloss as one of nine investors from Graham's school who beat the market, with his record and his method.
- [Berkshire Hathaway letter for 2006](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2006ltr.pdf): Buffett's tribute to Schloss at 90: his 47-year record, his fees, his son Edwin, and why luck cannot explain it.
- [Walter & Edwin Schloss](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5886cbc4a5790a5c18741c5a/t/5a82161e9140b7fe8b250bf3/1518474785579/Schloss+-+OID+1989.pdf): Father and son on their method, with their record for the 33 years to 1988.
- [Graham disciple and Buffett favourite dead at 95](https://www.investmentnews.com/industry-news/legendary-graham-disciple-and-buffett-favorite-dead-at-95/42387): His early years, his Army service, Graham-Newman, how his partnership began, and his family.
- [16 guidelines that stock investors must adhere to](https://www.morningstar.in/posts/50090/equity-6.aspx): His factors with examples, and how he charged his partners.
- [Walter Schloss: a maverick on Wall Street](https://www.morningstar.in/posts/31470/3/a-maverick-on-wall-street.aspx): His low-key style, his tiny office costs and his distance from the market's emotions.

## Words to know

- **Book value**: A company's assets minus its liabilities, as shown in its accounts.
- **Runner**: A junior clerk who carried papers and messages between Wall Street firms.
- **Partnership**: A pooled investment fund run by a manager for a group of partners.
- **Leverage**: Investing with borrowed money.
- **Rule of 72**: Divide 72 by a yearly return to find roughly how many years money takes to double.
- **Inside information**: Important facts about a company not yet made public; trading on it is illegal.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his 1994 note of 16 factors, Buffett's 1984 talk and 2006 letter, an Outstanding Investor Digest interview (1989), obituaries in InvestmentNews/Bloomberg (2012) and Morningstar profiles. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Schloss wrote little; his 1994 note is the main source in his own words. Sources give slightly different figures for his long-term record, so we show the range.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.

# Anthony Bolton

> Ran Fidelity Special Situations for 28 years, about 19.5% a year, by buying good companies the crowd had given up on.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/bolton.html · Section: the United Kingdom · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Go against the crowd, with a reason. He bought what others disliked, but only once he understood why the gloom was overdone.

## Summary

Anthony Bolton ran Fidelity Special Situations from December 1979 to December 2007, about 19.5% a year, well ahead of the UK market. His method: buy good companies the crowd has given up on, write down why you own each one, meet the managers, and sell when the reason breaks.

## Record at a glance

- **19.5% a year**: Fidelity Special Situations, Dec 1979 to Dec 2007
- **£1,000 → £147,000**: over his 28 years, dividends reinvested
- **about 13.5% a year**: the UK stock market over the same 28 years
- **£6bn**: the fund's size when it was split in two, 2006

## Big ideas

### 1. The contrarian's edge

The best bargains are usually in companies the crowd has given up on. The hard part is buying when it feels uncomfortable.

- **Popular means pricey.** When everyone likes a share, the good news is already in the price. When everyone hates it, a little good news can lift it a lot. (Podcast, 2025 · Morningstar)
- **Discomfort is a signal.** He bought recovery shares before all the information was in, a place he called the discomfort zone. (Morningstar)
- **But don't rush.** He warned that buying too early is a common mistake. Be patient with your entry, and add more only when conviction is high. (Morningstar)
- **The tech bubble test.** In the late 1990s he refused internet shares. His fund lagged the market by almost 20% before the bubble burst and proved him right. (Morningstar)
- **Unloved is not enough.** Going against the crowd only pays when you know why the crowd is wrong. A share can be unpopular for good reasons. (Book, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-01-the-contrarians-edge.html

### 2. Write down why you own it

Every share you own needs a reason you can write in a few lines, and a written case against it.

- **A reason for every holding.** Know what you own and why, in words simple enough to explain to a friend. (Morningstar · Book, 2009)
- **Retest it.** He went back to each thesis at regular intervals to check that it still held. (Morningstar)
- **Write the counter-thesis.** He also wrote down what could make the share a bad investment, and worked out why he disagreed with the doubters. (Morningstar)
- **Seek out the other side.** He made a point of listening to people with the opposite view, to stress-test his own. (Podcast, 2025)
- **Forget what you paid.** The price you paid says nothing about what a share is worth today. (Book, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-02-write-down-why-you-own-it.html

### 3. What is already in the price

Look for a gap between price and value, measured in several ways, then give it time to close.

- **Hunt for anomalies.** He bought where the price looked out of line with what the company was worth, then waited for the gap to close. (Morningstar)
- **Several measures, no favourite.** Price to earnings, company value to cash profits, free cash flow yield, price to sales and cash returns on investment, each against history and against other companies. (Morningstar)
- **The right tool for the job.** For housebuilders he thought price to earnings nearly useless, because one-off land sales distort profits. Price to adjusted book value worked better. (Morningstar)
- **Spotting beats timing.** Seeing a mispricing is easier than knowing when it will correct. Some ideas took one year, some several. (Morningstar)
- **Stand firm through noise.** Share prices and profits can drift apart for a year or two. Keep testing the idea rather than giving up on it. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-03-what-is-already-in-the-price.html

### 4. Meet the managers

He learnt most by meeting the people who run companies, again and again, and writing everything down.

- **Two or three a day.** He met two or three companies every working day and valued hearing from managers directly. (Article, 2007)
- **Keep the notes.** He handwrote notes in every meeting and kept them all from the late 1980s onwards. (Article, 2007)
- **Candour counts.** He looked for managers who were candid and consistent. Like Buffett, he believed a boss who misleads shareholders may end up misleading himself. (Article, 2007)
- **The second meeting matters.** Repeated follow-up meetings, not first impressions, uncovered the occasional gem. (MoneyWeek)
- **Owners have a voice.** In the 2003 Carlton–Granada merger he pressed for an independent chairman. The press nicknamed him the Quiet Assassin, a name he disliked. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-04-meet-the-managers.html

### 5. What makes a good company

Start with the quality of the business, then ask whether it will be worth more in ten years.

- **Franchise first.** Begin by judging how strong the business franchise is. (Book, 2009)
- **Ten years from now.** Ask whether the company will still be here in ten years, and be more valuable. (Book, 2009)
- **Master of its own fate.** Prefer companies in control of their own destiny, rather than at the mercy of others. (Book, 2009)
- **Managers who know the detail.** Check that the people in charge understand the business strategically, operationally and financially. (Book, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-05-what-makes-a-good-company.html

### 6. Where the analysts are not

Medium and smaller companies, and those analysts have given up on, are where mispricing lives.

- **Less crowded corners.** He leaned towards medium and smaller companies, which fewer analysts followed. (Book, 2004)
- **No forecasts, no fans.** He liked companies that analysts had given up on, with few or no profit forecasts. (Morningstar)
- **Takeovers as a bonus.** Owning many cheap, mid-sized companies meant some would be bid for. His book has a whole chapter on why it is good to have your shares bought out. (Book, 2009)
- **Information is everywhere.** His book has chapters on where to find information and on the value of good brokers: do the reading others skip. (Book, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-06-where-the-analysts-are-not.html

### 7. Charts as a second opinion

Research comes first. He used price charts to confirm it and to time his buying and selling, never on their own.

- **Fundamentals first.** He used charts to confirm his research, not to replace it. (MoneyWeek)
- **Mostly for timing.** He found charts most useful on bigger companies, to time buying and selling once the research was done. (MoneyWeek)
- **A health check.** He compared checking a chart to a visit to the doctor: being too early in a share can be costly. (MoneyWeek)
- **Reading the crowd.** Charts, shareholder lists and directors' dealings all helped him judge where the crowd already stood. (Podcast, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-07-charts-as-a-second-opinion.html

### 8. When to sell

Sell when the reason for owning breaks, when the price reaches your target, or when you find something better.

- **Three reasons to sell.** Something breaks the thesis; the share reaches his valuation target; or he finds a better idea. (Morningstar)
- **Don't chase your losses.** Holding a loser just to win back what you lost, or to prove the original idea right, is dangerous. (Morningstar)
- **A broken thesis means sell.** Even if the share now looks cheap, a broken reason is a reason to go. (Morningstar)
- **Popularity is risk.** When a share becomes everyone's favourite, the risk has risen even if the story has not changed. (Podcast, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-08-when-to-sell.html

### 9. Know yourself

Temperament matters more than intelligence. Find an approach that fits your nature, then stick with it.

- **Temperament over IQ.** He believed emotional people do not make good investors, however clever they are. (Morningstar)
- **Your own style.** Find an approach that suits your personality, and keep to it through good and bad years. (Morningstar)
- **Ignore the benchmark.** He ran the fund on his own judgement rather than hugging the index, which is why it could look so different from the market. (Book, 2004)
- **Decide alone.** He drew on the widest possible range of facts and opinions, but the final call was always his own judgement. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-09-know-yourself.html

### 10. Even legends stumble

His China fund went badly at first. How he explained it teaches as much as his years of success.

- **The comeback.** In 2010 he came out of retirement to launch a China fund, a market he had not invested in before. (interactive investor)
- **What went wrong.** He blamed a focus on smaller companies, too much weight in consumer shares, and borrowing to invest, all of which hurt in a falling market. (Trustnet, 2012)
- **New market, new rules.** Accounting scandals at some Chinese companies listed in the US also hurt. Familiar methods need new checks in an unfamiliar market. (Trustnet, 2012)
- **He said sorry.** He apologised to investors for poor results. By the time he retired in 2014 the trust had just about turned a profit. (interactive investor)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/bolton-10-even-legends-stumble.html

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “I value very highly hearing directly from management” (The Spectator, 2007)
- “I've found charts very useful, particularly on bigger companies, especially for timing.” (MoneyWeek interview)
- “easier to spot an anomaly than knowing exactly when it is going to correct” (as quoted by Morningstar)

## Read the originals

Both books are in print or easy to find second-hand. The Spectator article, the MoneyWeek interview and the 2025 podcast are free online.

- [Investing Against the Tide](https://www.pearson.com/store/p/investing-against-the-tide/P200000009635/9781292129280): His own book: the principles he used for 28 years, then stories of memorable meetings and of his best and worst investments. Short and practical.
- [Investing with Anthony Bolton](https://harriman-house.com/investing-with-anthony-bolton): A study of his methods and record by the financial writer Jonathan Davis, with a chapter of lessons in Bolton's own words.
- [Remember the wisdom of Keynes and Mark Twain](https://archive.spectator.co.uk/article/9th-june-2007/22/remember-the-wisdom-of-keynes-and-mark-twain): In his own words: meeting two or three companies a day, keeping notes, and what candid managers look like.
- [The guru who believes in charts](https://moneyweek.com/10642/anthony-bolton-the-guru-who-believes-in-charts): How he combined meetings with management, going against the herd, and charts as a second opinion.
- [What he learnt in three decades of investing](https://www.morningstar.in/posts/35426/investing-against-the-tide.aspx): His three big lessons, the valuation measures he used, recovery shares, and his three reasons to sell.
- [The mindset of a contrarian investor](https://www.nbim.no/en/news-and-insights/podcast/2025/the-mindset-of-a-contrarian-investor--anthony-bolton/): A long, free conversation on why popularity is risk, why the best opportunities feel uncomfortable, and how he reads the crowd.
- [The reasons for my underperformance](https://www.trustnet.com/News/386663/fund/sectors): Bolton explains what went wrong in his first years running a China fund.
- [Five fund managers who said sorry](https://ii.co.uk/analysis-commentary/five-fund-managers-who-said-sorry-and-what-happened-next-ii515118): How his China fund ended, set beside other managers who apologised for poor results.

## Words to know

- **Contrarian**: An investor who deliberately goes against the crowd: buying what is unloved and selling what is loved.
- **Investment thesis**: The short written reason for owning a share.
- **Counter-thesis**: The written case against your own idea: what would make it a bad investment.
- **Recovery share**: A company in trouble whose shares are priced as if it will never recover.
- **Company value to cash profits (EV/EBITDA)**: The value of a whole company, shares plus debt minus cash, divided by profits before interest, tax and depreciation.
- **Free cash flow yield**: Cash a company has left after investing, as a percentage of its value.
- **Technical analysis**: Studying price charts and trading patterns, rather than the business itself.
- **Special situations**: Companies going through change: recovery, takeover, restructuring or neglect.
- **Gearing**: Borrowing money to invest more than you have. It magnifies both gains and losses.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his book (2009), Jonathan Davis's study with his own lessons chapter (2004), his Spectator article (2007), interviews with MoneyWeek and Norges Bank's In Good Company podcast (2025), and press coverage of his China fund. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Bolton wrote one book of his own and contributed a chapter of lessons to Jonathan Davis's study of his career. Articles and interviews add his spoken words. Where a point comes from a journalist's summary rather than his own text, the source is named.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.

# Terry Smith

> Exposed creative accounting and lost his job for it, then built Fundsmith on three rules: buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/smith.html · Section: the United Kingdom · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Buy good companies. Companies that earn high returns on their capital, in cash, year after year, without much debt.

## Summary

Terry Smith exposed creative accounting in 1992 and was sacked for refusing to withdraw his book. In 2010 he founded Fundsmith on three rules: buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing. Since launch it has returned 13.8% a year against 12.1% for world shares, though it trailed the market every year from 2021 to 2025.

## Record at a glance

- **13.8% a year**: Fundsmith Equity, Nov 2010 to Dec 2025
- **12.1% a year**: world shares (MSCI World) over the same years
- **+613%**: total gain since launch, against +468% for world shares
- **+0.8%**: in 2025: his weakest year, and the fifth in a row behind the index

## Big ideas

### 1. Buy good companies

A good company earns a high return on the money tied up in it, in cash, and keeps doing so for decades.

- **Return on capital is the test.** A good business makes a high return on the capital it uses, in cash, and can sustain it. (Owner's Manual)
- **Hard to copy.** Its advantages should be difficult for rivals to replicate. (Owner's Manual)
- **Little debt needed.** It should not need heavy borrowing to earn its returns. (Owner's Manual)
- **Room to reinvest.** It should be able to reinvest its cash at high rates, so growth compounds. (Owner's Manual)
- **Built to last.** It should be resilient to change, especially technological change. (Owner's Manual)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-01-buy-good-companies.html

### 2. The numbers that show quality

Every year he publishes the same few measures for his companies beside the market's. Quality shows up in the numbers.

- **Returns.** In 2025 his companies averaged a 31% return on capital, against 17% for both the S&P 500 and the FTSE 100. (Annual letters)
- **Margins.** Gross margin 62% against 45% and 43%; operating margin 28% against 18% and 17%. (Annual letters)
- **Cash.** They turned 94% of their profits into cash. (Annual letters)
- **Safety.** Median interest cover was 29 times, against 9 and 8: profits dwarf interest bills. (Annual letters)
- **Durability.** The average company in the fund was founded in 1919. (Annual letters)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-02-the-numbers-that-show-quality.html

### 3. Don't overpay

Even the best company can be a bad investment at the wrong price. He checks how much cash you get for what you pay.

- **Cash for your money.** He tracks free cash flow yield, the cash a company produces against its price. At the end of 2025 his portfolio's was 3.7%, against 2.8% for the S&P 500. (Annual letters)
- **No greater fools.** Buy only what you would happily own at a price you accept. Profits that depend on someone paying more later rely on a greater fool. (FT article, 2013)
- **Quality earns its price.** He argues that the market tends to underestimate how long great companies keep compounding, so paying up for them can still work. (Book, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-03-dont-overpay.html

### 4. Do nothing

Once you own good companies at sensible prices, the hardest and best thing is to leave them alone.

- **Deal rarely.** Frequent trading adds costs that steadily eat into returns. (FT article, 2013)
- **Low turnover.** In 2025 the fund's turnover was 12.7%, and voluntary dealing cost 0.008% of the fund. (Annual letters)
- **Don't time the market.** Most people buy after rises and sell after falls. Guessing the turns rarely works. (FT article, 2013)
- **Switch off the screen.** If you own good companies at sensible prices and dislike what the price is doing, stop looking. (FT article, 2013)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-04-do-nothing.html

### 5. Read the accounts

His first fame came from showing how companies dressed up their profits. Reported profit can mislead; cash is harder to fake.

- **Profits that weren't.** In 1990 several big British companies went bust while reporting healthy profits. Their real problem was cash. (Book, 1992)
- **The book that cost his job.** In 1992 he expanded his research into a book. His employer, UBS Phillips & Drew, asked him to withdraw it; he refused and was sacked. (Book, 1992)
- **The usual tricks.** Acquisition accounting, deferred payments, exceptional items, off-balance-sheet debt, hidden liabilities, brand values, changed depreciation, capitalised costs and currency mismatches. (Book, 1992)
- **It changed the rules.** Many of the practices he exposed were later curbed or stopped. (Book, 1992)
- **Habits stick.** Managers who flatter their earnings rarely change, so treat it as a lasting warning sign. (Book, 1992)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-05-read-the-accounts.html

### 6. You are the biggest risk

Most damage to investors' returns is self-inflicted: chasing fashion, trading too much, buying what they don't understand.

- **Look in the mirror.** His Owner's Manual warns that the greatest threat to your returns is your own behaviour. (Owner's Manual)
- **Not because it's fashionable.** The fund will not own something because it is in fashion and might go up, because eventually it goes down, usually by a lot. (Owner's Manual)
- **Understand it or skip it.** If you can't explain how an investment works, don't buy it. Complexity often hides risk. (FT article, 2013)
- **Tax is not a reason.** Never invest just to avoid tax. Tax-driven schemes often carry high fees and weak returns. (FT article, 2013)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-06-you-are-the-biggest-risk.html

### 7. Costs come out of your pocket

Fees, charges and dealing costs are certain; returns are not. Keep the certain losses small.

- **Minimise fees.** Charges from advisers, platforms and funds can swallow most of an investment's income. (FT article, 2013)
- **Show the full bill.** Fundsmith reports a total cost of investment that includes dealing costs: 1.06% a year for its main share class in 2025. (Annual letters)
- **Small numbers compound.** A cost of 1% a year sounds small, but over decades it takes a large share of the final pot. (Book, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-07-costs-come-out-of-your-pocket.html

### 8. Don't over-diversify

Twenty or so well-chosen companies give most of the safety of spreading out. More than that, and you know each one less well.

- **About twenty is enough.** Around 20 well-chosen shares capture most of the benefit of diversification. (FT article, 2013)
- **A concentrated fund.** At the end of 2025 Fundsmith Equity held 29 companies. (Annual letters)
- **The 80th company.** His Owner's Manual asks how much a manager can really know about the 80th company in a portfolio. (Owner's Manual)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-08-dont-over-diversify.html

### 9. Avoid poor businesses and star bosses

Stay away from companies that earn poor returns, and from companies that only work with a genius in charge.

- **Never own poor quality.** Companies that earn weak returns on their capital destroy value over time; strong ones compound it. (FT article, 2013)
- **A business an idiot could run.** Avoid companies that depend on one brilliant or charismatic leader who may not stay. (FT article, 2013)
- **Everyday, repeated sales.** He favours businesses built on many small, predictable purchases, such as household goods and medical supplies. (Owner's Manual)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-09-avoid-poor-businesses-and-star-bosses.html

### 10. When it doesn't work

From 2021 to 2025 his fund trailed the market five years running. How he explained it is a lesson in honesty and patience.

- **Five years behind.** The fund lagged world shares in every calendar year from 2021 to 2025. (Annual letters)
- **A weak 2025.** It returned 0.8% while world shares rose 12.8%; even cash did better. (Annual letters)
- **His explanation.** A market led by a handful of giant technology shares, money pouring into index funds, and a weak dollar. His biggest single drag was Novo Nordisk, which cost the fund about 3 points. (Annual letters)
- **Still ahead since launch.** Over 15 years the fund remains ahead: 13.8% a year against 12.1%. (Annual letters)
- **Judge over decades.** A sound approach can trail for years. Decide in advance how long you will give a strategy, and judge it honestly. (Owner's Manual)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/smith-10-when-it-doesnt-work.html

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “The greatest threat you face to your investment performance is from you.” (Fundsmith Owner's Manual)
- “Buy good companies. Don't overpay. Do nothing.” (Annual letter, 2025)
- “If you don't fully understand it, don't invest” (Ten golden rules, Financial Times, 2013)

## Read the originals

Start with the Owner's Manual (about twenty pages) and the latest annual letter. Both are free.

- [Fundsmith Equity Fund Owner's Manual](https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/mv3abv1h/owners-manual.pdf): The rulebook: what the fund buys, what it never does, and why the biggest risk to your returns is you.
- [Annual letters to fund owners](https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/4hcfd1pg/2025-fef-annual-letter-web.pdf): Each letter gives the results, the portfolio's quality numbers, the biggest winners and losers, and plain explanations when things go wrong.
- [Ten golden rules of investment](https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/news/2013/2070-financial-times-ten-golden-rules-of-investment/): His ten rules for private investors, from 'if you don't understand it, don't invest' to 'switch off the screen'.
- [Accounting for Growth](https://www.worldofbooks.com/en-au/books/terry-smith/accounting-for-growth/9780712657648): The book that exposed how British companies of the 1980s flattered their profits, and cost him his job.
- [Investing for Growth](https://www.panmacmillan.com/authors/terry-smith/investing-for-growth/9780857199010): Ten years of his writing in one place, including the golden rules and his case for buying only the best companies.

## Words to know

- **Return on capital employed (ROCE)**: Operating profit as a percentage of the money tied up in a business. His main test of quality.
- **Gross margin**: Sales minus the direct cost of making them, as a percentage of sales.
- **Operating margin**: Profit after running costs, before interest and tax, as a percentage of sales.
- **Cash conversion**: How much of the reported profit actually arrives as cash.
- **Interest cover**: How many times profits cover the interest bill.
- **Free cash flow yield**: The cash a company produces after investment, as a percentage of its value.
- **Turnover**: The share of a portfolio bought and sold in a year.
- **Total cost of investment**: All the costs of owning a fund, including dealing costs, not just the headline charge.
- **Index fund**: A fund that simply buys a whole market index rather than choosing companies.
- **Creative accounting**: Legal but misleading ways of making profits look bigger or smoother than they are.

## Sources and scope

Sources: the Fundsmith Owner's Manual (2010), the annual letters (2010 to 2025, figures from the 2025 letter), 'Ten golden rules of investment' (Financial Times, 2013), Accounting for Growth (1992) and Investing for Growth (2020). Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Smith writes plainly and often. The Owner's Manual and the annual letters are free on Fundsmith's website; his Financial Times columns and letters to 2020 are collected in Investing for Growth. Accounting for Growth (1992) is out of print but easy to find second-hand.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Terry Smith, Fundsmith LLP, the Financial Times, the publishers or any company named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.
