# John Maynard Keynes

> The century's most famous economist failed at forecasting markets, changed his method, and beat the UK market for a quarter of a century.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/keynes.html · Section: the United Kingdom · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

In 1938: choose a few cheap investments carefully, hold them steadfastly, and balance the risks.

## Summary

John Maynard Keynes was the most famous economist of the 20th century. He also ran King's College, Cambridge's investments for 25 years. He failed as a market forecaster in the 1920s, changed his method, and from 1922 to 1946 his fund averaged about 16% a year against 10.4% for the UK market.

## Record at a glance

- **16.0% a year**: his King's fund's average yearly return, 1922 to 1946
- **10.4% a year**: the UK stock market's average over the same years
- **+8 points**: a year ahead on his UK shares (Chambers & Dimson)
- **½ hour**: a day on it, usually in bed each morning

## Big ideas

### 1. The forecaster who failed

In the 1920s he tried to profit from the ups and downs of the economy. Even he could not time them.

- **The plan.** At first he believed profit could be made by holding shares in slumps and selling them in booms, which he called a credit cycle policy. (Memo, 1938)
- **The result.** Looking back in 1938, he admitted the fund had not managed to profit from moving in and out of shares as a whole. (Memo, 1938)
- **Why it fails.** He found that people who try usually move after the turn, both in and out, and trade too often, which piles up costs and makes them jumpy. (Memo, 1938)
- **After the 1929 crash.** Having suffered heavy losses, he sold a fifth of his UK shares and moved into government bonds, the conventional response. (Chambers & Dimson)
- **Currencies too.** In 354 currency trades he was usually right about direction but struggled with timing. (Currency study, 2016)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-01-the-forecaster-who-failed.html

### 2. From forecaster to stock picker

In the early 1930s he stopped forecasting the market and started choosing individual companies. His results improved dramatically.

- **The switch.** From the early 1930s he moved from top-down market timing to bottom-up stock picking. (Chambers & Dimson)
- **Less trading.** His yearly turnover fell from about 55% in the 1920s to 30% in the 1930s and 14% in the 1940s. (Chambers & Dimson)
- **What did work.** Even in his 1938 review, buying particular shares when their prices were greatly depressed had done well. (Memo, 1938)
- **He changed his mind in writing.** His 1938 memo openly drew the opposite lesson from the one he had set out to prove. Admitting it is the first step. (Memo, 1938)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-02-from-forecaster-to-stock-picker.html

### 3. His three principles

In May 1938 he summed up successful investment in three principles: careful selection, steadfast holding, balance.

- **1. Careful selection.** A few investments, picked because they are cheap compared with what they are likely to be worth over the next few years, and compared with the alternatives. (Memo, 1938)
- **2. Steadfast holding.** Own them in size and refuse to be shaken out, for years if needed, until they deliver or you can see you were wrong. (Memo, 1938)
- **3. Balance.** Mix your risks even though each holding is big, ideally with some that tend to move the other way, as gold-mining shares often did against other shares. (Memo, 1938)
- **The £1 note.** Selling something worth £1 for 15 shillings (75p), hoping to buy it back for 12s 6d (about 62p), is a poor trade. So is refusing to buy it at 15 shillings because it looks too good to be true. (Memo, 1938)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-03-his-three-principles.html

### 4. A few big bets you understand

He thought spreading money across many things you know little about was a mistake. Better a few large holdings you understand.

- **Know the business.** In 1934 he told a colleague it is better to invest decent amounts in a few businesses you understand and whose managers you believe in. (Letter, 1934)
- **Two or three at a time.** He reckoned that at any one moment only two or three companies earned his complete confidence. (Letter, 1934)
- **Concentrated in practice.** His holdings grew from about 20 to over 60, yet at times more than half the fund sat in five shares. (CFA Institute, 2014)
- **A bold position.** In 1936, 66% of the fund was in mining shares. (CFA Institute, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-04-a-few-big-bets-you-understand.html

### 5. Shares over bonds, for the long run

He moved a centuries-old college endowment from land and bonds into shares, decades before other institutions.

- **Ahead of his time.** He moved King's into shares while most institutions still relied on bonds and property. (Chambers & Dimson)
- **Shares for the long run.** For investors with very long horizons, he favoured shares over bonds. (CFA Institute, 2014)
- **Look abroad.** By the late 1930s his fund held less in Britain than in the US or Africa. (CFA Institute, 2014)
- **Value and dividends.** He leaned towards cheap shares with high dividend yields. One famous buy, the mining group Union Corporation, cost 30% less than its estimated break-up value. (CFA Institute, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-05-shares-over-bonds-for-the-long-run.html

### 6. The beauty contest

He compared the stock market to a newspaper contest where you win by guessing what others will pick, not what you think is best.

- **The contest.** Readers had to pick the six prettiest faces from a hundred photographs. The prize went to whoever picked closest to the average choice. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Second and third guesses.** So each player picks not the face he finds prettiest, but the one he thinks others will pick, and some go further still. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Professionals do the same.** Many professional investors focus on guessing how market opinion will shift in the coming months, not on a business's long-run worth. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Your edge.** Prices can drift far from value for a long time. Thinking about the business, not the crowd, is what lets you profit when they meet again. (CFA Institute, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-06-the-beauty-contest.html

### 7. Convention and reputation

Most people assume tomorrow will look like today, and most professionals would rather be wrong with the crowd than right alone.

- **The convention.** Lacking real knowledge of the far future, we assume the present will continue unless we have a specific reason to expect change. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Safety in numbers.** He saw that for a professional's reputation, failing with everyone else is safer than succeeding alone. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Liquid but jumpy.** Because shares can be sold at any moment, their prices are revalued daily, letting short-term mood dominate. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Someone must back you.** He could be unconventional because the Fellows of King's trusted him. Long-term investing needs patient backers. (Chambers & Dimson)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-07-convention-and-reputation.html

### 8. Animal spirits

Much of what drives business and markets is not calculation but a spontaneous urge to act, which can switch off suddenly.

- **Not just arithmetic.** Many decisions to invest rest on spontaneous optimism, which he called animal spirits, rather than on careful calculation. (General Theory, 1936)
- **When spirits fade.** If optimism dims, investment can collapse even with no new facts. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Speculation and enterprise.** He warned that when a nation's investment is driven by casino-like speculation, the job is likely to be done badly. (General Theory, 1936)
- **Use the mood, don't share it.** His own best buys came when prices were greatly depressed: when animal spirits were at their lowest. (Memo, 1938)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-08-animal-spirits.html

### 9. Holding through the falls

Long-term investing means sitting through sharp falls. He did, and it cost him a chairmanship.

- **Two big falls.** In nine years his whole share portfolio had twice fallen 20 to 25% within a few months, and he could not escape either fall. (Memo, 1938)
- **1937–38.** When London shares fell sharply he stayed invested, and resigned as chairman of an insurance company whose board would not stick with his strategy. (Chambers & Dimson)
- **Half an hour a day.** He spent no more than about half an hour each morning on it, usually before getting out of bed. You don't need to watch every price. (CFA Institute, 2014)
- **The reward.** By his death, King's had drawn level with Trinity, the wealthiest college in Cambridge. (Chambers & Dimson)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-09-holding-through-the-falls.html

### 10. Words he never said

Keynes is the most misquoted investor of all. Checking who really said what is a good habit for every investor.

- **Not his line.** "The market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent" has no solid source in Keynes's writings. The earliest record found is the American adviser Gary Shilling, in 1986. (Quote Investigator)
- **Nor this one.** "When the facts change, I change my mind" is also widely credited to him, but scholars of his papers have found no primary source. (Quote Investigator)
- **What he did write.** His real words, in chapter 12 of The General Theory, the 1938 memo and the 1934 letter, are sharper than the invented ones. Read them. (General Theory, 1936 · Memo, 1938 · Letter, 1934)
- **Check before you share.** If a quote is too perfect and has no date or source, it is probably not genuine. (Quote Investigator)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/keynes-10-words-he-never-said.html

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “it is better for reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally” (The General Theory, 1936)
- “a steadfast holding of these in fairly large units through thick and thin” (Memo to King's College, 1938)
- “put fairly large sums into enterprises which one thinks one knows something about” (Letter to F. C. Scott, 1934)

## Read the originals

Chapter 12 of The General Theory is free online. The 1934 letter is reproduced in Warren Buffett's 1991 letter. The research summaries are free on the Cambridge Judge Business School and CFA Institute websites.

- [Post-mortem memo to the King's College Estates Committee](https://novelinvestor.com/john-maynard-keyness-investment-policy/): His own review of his record: why timing the market failed, and the three principles that replaced it.
- [Letter to F. C. Scott](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1991.html): Why he preferred a few large holdings in businesses he understood, run by people he trusted.
- [The General Theory, chapter 12](https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/economics/keynes/general-theory/ch12.htm): The most quoted pages ever written about stock markets: convention, the beauty contest, animal spirits, speculation and enterprise.
- [Keynes the stock market investor](https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/insight/2013/investing-in-2013-ask-john-maynard-keynes): His record rebuilt from the King's archives: what he owned, how it did, and how he changed his method.
- [Keynes the investor: lessons to be learned](https://blogs.cfainstitute.org/eic/2014/10/20/keynes-the-investor-lessons-to-be-learned/): The numbers behind his record and eight lessons for investors today.
- [If you're so smart: Keynes and currency speculation](https://www.jbs.cam.ac.uk/2016/if-youre-so-smart/): A study of his 354 currency trades from 1919 to 1939: usually right on direction, poor on timing.
- [Maynard Keynes in King's College](https://www.kings.cam.ac.uk/node/16149): His life at the college: student, Fellow, Bursar from 1919 and First Bursar from 1924 to 1946.
- [The market can remain irrational…: who said it?](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2011/08/09/remain-solvent/): Why the most famous 'Keynes' line about markets probably isn't his.
- [Keynesian eugenics and the goodness of the world](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/1D1FE14255DA18E1DA28ED94E9680198): Research on Keynes's long involvement with eugenics, including as director of the Eugenics Society.

## Words to know

- **Bursar**: The college officer in charge of its money and property.
- **Endowment**: A fund given to an institution, invested so that it can pay for its work for ever.
- **Discretionary fund**: Money the manager may invest freely, without fixed rules on what to buy.
- **Credit cycle policy**: His 1920s attempt to buy shares in slumps and sell them in booms: market timing.
- **Intrinsic value**: What a business is really worth, judged from what it will earn, as opposed to its price.
- **Turnover**: The share of a portfolio bought and sold in a year.
- **Beauty contest**: His picture of a market where people guess what others will think, not what is good.
- **Animal spirits**: The spontaneous urge to act, rather than calculation, that drives much investment.
- **Shilling**: An old British coin worth one twentieth of a pound; 15 shillings was 75p.
- **Liquidity**: How easily something can be sold for cash at a fair price.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his May 1938 memo to the King's College Estates Committee, his letter to F. C. Scott of 15 August 1934, The General Theory (1936), research by Chambers, Dimson and Foo (Cambridge, 2013–14), a study of his currency trading (2016), King's College and Quote Investigator. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Keynes left no book on investing. His views come from his memos and letters (printed in his Collected Writings), from The General Theory, and from the King's College archives studied by David Chambers and Elroy Dimson. Famous lines often credited to him that he never wrote are flagged.

# Li Lu

> Heard Buffett speak by chance, founded Himalaya Capital, and became the only outside manager Charlie Munger said he ever invested with.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/lilu.html · Section: China · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

A share is part of a business. Returns come from the business growing in value, not from guessing prices.

## Summary

Li Lu reached the United States in 1989 with little money and less English, heard Warren Buffett speak at Columbia in 1993, and founded Himalaya Capital in 1997. Charlie Munger later called him the only outside manager he had ever invested with. His method: treat a share as part of a business, know exactly where your knowledge ends, buy with a margin of safety, and wait for the rare great bet.

## Record at a glance

- **29%+ a year**: his fund, January 1998 to 2009, after all expenses, in his own words (not independently audited)
- **36% a year**: the same fund from late 2004, when Munger joined, to 2009
- **−19%**: his first year, on paper; a large investor left the following year
- **10% of BYD**: bought by Berkshire for about $230m in 2008, after Li Lu brought the company to Munger

## Big ideas

### 1. A share is a piece of a business

Value investing rests on four ideas. The first is that a share is part-ownership of a real business, so your return comes from the business growing.

- **Four ideas, one road.** He sums up value investing as four ideas: a share is part of a business; the market is there to serve you; buy with a margin of safety; stay inside your circle of competence. (Lecture, 2015 · Lecture, 2019)
- **The lecture that changed his life.** A classmate took him to hear Buffett at Columbia. He found the case clear and convincing: shares are pieces of businesses, and over time prices follow what those businesses are worth. (Foreword, 2010 · Interview, 2013)
- **Two years of reading.** He then spent nearly two years reading about Buffett, Berkshire and Munger before buying his first share, while his own net worth was still below zero. (Foreword, 2010)
- **Owning changes how you look.** Once he owned a company he became curious about every part of it, and that curiosity taught him the whole industry. (Lecture, 2019)
- **Win-win, not zero-sum.** He likes investing in businesses because owner and company can both win. Trading against other traders is a zero-sum game. (Interview, 2013 · Talk, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-01-a-share-is-a-piece-of-a-business.html

### 2. Know where your circle ends

Your circle of competence should be small and clearly drawn. The skill is knowing where it ends, and what would prove you wrong.

- **The edge matters most.** What counts is not how much you know but knowing exactly where your knowledge stops. (Lecture, 2015 · Talk, 2026)
- **Say when you would be wrong.** You should be able to state the conditions under which your view of a company would fail. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Small and hard-won.** A real circle is built over years and stays small. Most people cannot see five or ten years ahead for most companies. (Lecture, 2015 · Lecture, 2019)
- **Don't fool yourself.** Intellectual honesty comes first: you are the easiest person to fool, and people tend to believe whatever suits them. (Lecture, 2015 · Lecture, 2019)
- **Argue the other side first.** From Munger he took the rule of holding no opinion until he can state the opposing case better than its supporters. (Foreword, 2010)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-02-know-where-your-circle-ends.html

### 3. The market serves you

Prices are there to use when they suit you. The market cannot tell you what a company is worth, and it punishes anyone who forgets that.

- **Servant, not master.** Use market prices to buy and sell when they suit you; never take them as a verdict on value. (Lecture, 2015 · Talk, 2026)
- **You cannot have both.** Many investors want the benefits of value investing and good results every quarter. Chasing both pushes you into speculation. (Talk, 2026)
- **The market finds your weak spots.** Act outside what you understand, or let fear and greed run you, and the market will expose it sooner or later. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Few play this game.** He estimates that only about one market participant in twenty invests this way. That is why the opportunity lasts. (Lecture, 2015 · Lecture, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-03-the-market-serves-you.html

### 4. Margin of safety

Because the future is uncertain, buy at a price far below your cautious estimate of value. He started with very cheap shares and moved, over time, to great businesses at fair prices.

- **Price is what you pay.** Since value can only be estimated, buy at the lowest price you can, and study the parts of a business that bear on your margin of safety. (Lecture, 2019)
- **His first big find.** As a student he bought a holding company whose stake in a large cable firm was alone worth about three times the whole company's market value. (Lecture, 2019)
- **Sold when the gap closed.** He sold once the margin of safety had gone. The shares kept rising for years afterwards. (Lecture, 2019)
- **From cheap to good.** A beginner with little money, he first bought very cheap shares, the safest choice. In time he moved to strong businesses at reasonable prices. (Interview, 2013)
- **Go and look.** Early on he visited nearby companies to check that their assets were real and the business was running. (Lecture, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-04-margin-of-safety.html

### 5. Research like an owner

Study a company as if you had just inherited it and had to run it. Talk to everyone, from the boss to the security guard.

- **Imagine you inherited it.** He suggests picturing that the company has just become yours and you must learn everything about it. (Lecture, 2019)
- **Talk to everyone.** He talks to people at every level, down to security guards, and asks about hiring, pay and how staff are treated. (Lecture, 2019)
- **The two petrol stations.** Two identical petrol stations drew very different custom, one about four times the other. The difference was an owner who ran his with care. So ask: do managers think like owners? (Lecture, 2019)
- **Talk to operators.** His ideas come from wide reading, newspapers and annual reports, and from people who run businesses, more than from other investors. (Interview, 2013)
- **When you can't judge the boss.** Management matters but is hard to assess. When he cannot judge it, he leans on the quality of the business and the price. (Interview, 2013)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-05-research-like-an-owner.html

### 6. Why he gave up short selling

He calls short selling one of his worst mistakes. The maths, the frauds and the distraction all work against you.

- **His worst mistake.** He ran a long-short fund in his early years, then stopped shorting around 2004 and calls it one of his worst mistakes. (Interview, 2013 · Foreword, 2010)
- **Small gain, unlimited loss.** A short can make at most 100% but can lose without limit, and you can be forced out before you are proved right. (Interview, 2013 · Foreword, 2010)
- **Frauds can last.** The best shorts often involve fraud, and frauds can survive long enough to squeeze you out. (Interview, 2013)
- **It steals your attention.** Constant short-side trading left no time to study his best long-term ideas. (Foreword, 2010 · Interview, 2013)
- **Growth favours owners.** Over long periods, a growing economy works for those who own businesses, not for those betting against them. (Interview, 2013)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-06-why-he-gave-up-short-selling.html

### 7. Patient, then decisive

Great opportunities are rare. Wait calmly while nothing happens, then act firmly when one appears.

- **One idea in decades.** Munger read Barron's for decades and found just one big idea in it. That is how rare the best chances are. (Lecture, 2019)
- **Both at once.** Patience and decisiveness have to live together: wait without fidgeting, then move in size. (Lecture, 2019)
- **Talent takes years to show.** It can take around fifteen years to tell real skill from luck; short-term results are often luck. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Each shot stands alone.** Like golf, a good hole does not guarantee the next. Judge each decision on its own merits. (Lecture, 2019)
- **BYD.** He was drawn to the battery and car maker by its founder's engineering record, its rise in a fierce market, and a margin of safety. Berkshire bought 10% in 2008 for about $230m and sold out by 2025 after a more than twentyfold rise. (Interview, 2013 · News, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-07-patient-then-decisive.html

### 8. A different road from Wall Street

Munger told him his problems were Wall Street's problems. He rebuilt his fund around long-term partners and a sense of duty to their savings.

- **Thanksgiving 2003.** He took Munger through every company he owned or followed. Munger said his problems came from the way Wall Street thinks, and offered to invest if he would take a different path. (Foreword, 2010)
- **A new structure.** With Munger's help he rebuilt the fund like Buffett's early partnerships: no shorting, long lock-ups for partners who stayed, and no new investors. (Foreword, 2010)
- **Your parents' savings.** He says a manager should treat clients' money like the lifetime savings of their own parents, and that people without that instinct should not be in the business. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Fees that favour managers.** He criticises the common hedge fund fee of 2% a year plus 20% of profits as serving managers better than clients. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Deserved trust.** He recalls Munger's ideal: a seamless web of deserved trust. Keep partners who share your approach, rather than chasing the most money. (Talk, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-08-a-different-road-from-wall-street.html

### 9. Own a slice of the world

Real wealth is your share of the world's buying power. Over two centuries, owning businesses beat cash, gold and bonds by a vast margin.

- **Fish where the fish are.** From Munger he takes the rule to look where others are not: less crowded markets, industries and countries. (Talk, 2026)
- **Wealth is a share of the world.** He measures wealth as your percentage of global buying power, not gold, cash or any currency, and keeps it by owning great businesses in growing economies. (Talk, 2026)
- **Two centuries of returns.** He cites US figures from 1802: a dollar in cash lost about 95% of its value, gold roughly tripled after inflation, and shares grew about a million times, roughly 6.7% a year after inflation. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Civilisation 3.0.** In his book he describes history in stages: hunting and gathering, farming, then free markets plus modern science, the stage in which businesses can compound. (Book, 2020 · Lecture, 2015)
- **China too.** In 2015 he argued value investing could work in China: its markets had risen about fifteenfold from 1991 to 2014, while short-term trading still dominated. (Lecture, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-09-own-a-slice-of-the-world.html

### 10. Mistakes, luck and compounding knowledge

He had a bad first year, sold winners too early and gave up shorting the hard way. He credits luck, and says knowledge compounds like money.

- **A bad start.** His first year ended 19% down on paper, and a large investor left the next year. (Foreword, 2010)
- **Sold too soon.** He was an early investor in Capital IQ, the data company, and sold; it later became far more valuable. (Interview, 2013)
- **Every mistake teaches.** He treats each mistake as a lesson, and names short selling as his biggest. (Interview, 2013)
- **Luck counts.** He credits part of his success to luck. (Talk, 2026)
- **Knowledge compounds.** Knowledge and trusted relationships compound like capital. Learning faster is how money, eventually, grows faster. (Talk, 2026 · Lecture, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/lilu-10-mistakes-luck-and-compounding-knowledge.html

## Special section

**Before you buy: eight questions**

- I can say what the business does and how it earns its money
- I would hold it even if no price were quoted for years
- The price is well below my cautious estimate of its value
- I know where my knowledge of it ends, and what would prove me wrong
- I have learned about it from people who work there, buy from it or compete with it
- Its managers think and act like owners
- I am buying to own it, not betting against anything
- Few other investors are looking at it closely

**His six principles, as he put them in 2026**

- A share is ownership of part of a real business.
- The market serves you it does not instruct you.
- Margin of safety because the future cannot be predicted.
- Circle of competence and above all, knowing where it ends.
- Fish where the fish are in less crowded markets, industries and countries.
- Wealth is a share of the world's buying power held through great businesses in growing economies, for a long time.

Li Lu was a student leader in the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. We mention it only as part of his life story; this site takes no political position.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “Shorting was one of the worst mistakes I've made.” (Graham & Doddsville interview, 2013)
- “the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you” (Graham & Dodd luncheon, Columbia, 2026)

## Read the originals

Start with the 2013 Columbia interview and the 2015 Peking University lecture. Both are free in English.

- [Foreword to the Chinese edition of Poor Charlie's Almanack](https://uploads-ssl.webflow.com/5ef3c7300432b40ed865991a/5ef3c7300432b4440a659983_Li%20Lu%20-%20Foreword%20to%20Chinese%20Edition%20of%20PCA%20(English%20translation).pdf): His own story: hearing Buffett, his first shares, a bad first year, meeting Munger, and how Munger changed his fund. Also what he learned from Munger about inversion, reading and character.
- [Know what you don't know](https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/imce-uploads/Graham%20%26%20Doddsville%20-%20Issue%2018%20-%20Spring%202013_0.pdf): A long interview in English: how he started, how he finds ideas, why he gave up short selling, and his early investment in BYD.
- [The prospects for value investing in China](https://www.himcap.com/publications): His fullest statement of the four core ideas, the qualities of a good investor, two centuries of returns, and whether value investing can work in China.
- [The practice of value investing](https://www.longriverinv.com/thought/the-practice-of-value-investing-by-li-lu): The practical side: his first investment as a student, how he researches a company like an owner, and why patience and decisiveness must go together.
- [Civilization, Modernization, Value Investing and China](https://www.himcap.com/publications): His view of history in stages, why modern economies let businesses compound, and how value investing fits China.
- [Fireside chat at the Graham & Dodd luncheon](https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/imce-uploads/36th%20Annual%20Graham%20%26%20Dodd%20Luncheon%20Transcript%20(20261005)%20CBS.pdf): His six principles, why you cannot want both value investing and good results every quarter, AI, China, and advice to young investors.
- [Berkshire exits BYD after 17 years](https://www.rte.ie/news/business/2025/0922/1534663-berkshire-hathaway-exits-byd): How Berkshire's 2008 purchase of 10% of BYD for about $230m grew more than twentyfold before it sold out.

## Words to know

- **Value investing**: Buying a share for less than the business is worth, and holding it while the business grows.
- **Circle of competence**: The area where you genuinely understand businesses well enough to value them.
- **Margin of safety**: The gap between a cautious estimate of value and the price you pay.
- **Mr Market**: Benjamin Graham's picture of the market as a moody partner offering prices you may take or ignore.
- **Short selling**: Borrowing shares to sell them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price.
- **Long-only fund**: A fund that only owns shares and never bets on prices falling.
- **Lock-up**: A period during which investors agree not to withdraw their money.
- **Intrinsic value**: What a business is really worth, judged from the cash it will produce.
- **Fiduciary**: Someone trusted to act in another person's interest, before their own.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his foreword to the Chinese edition of Poor Charlie's Almanack (2010), the Graham & Doddsville interview (2013), his Peking University lectures (2015 and 2019), his book (2020, in Chinese), his conversation at Columbia's Graham & Dodd luncheon (2026), and news reports on BYD. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Li Lu writes no yearly letters. His thinking is in a handful of speeches, one long interview and a foreword, most of them free on Himalaya Capital's website, plus a book in Chinese (2020). Some talks were given in Chinese; where we rely on a translation, the source says whose. He has published no fund figures since 2009.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.

# Duan Yongping

> Built the companies behind OPPO and vivo, then turned investor: buy businesses you understand, never borrow, and keep a list of things you won't do.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/duan.html · Section: China · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Buying a stock is buying the company. A company is worth the cash it will produce in future, discounted. Full stop.

## Summary

Duan Yongping built two electronics companies, Subor and BBK, whose offshoots grew into the phone makers OPPO and vivo. He stepped back in 2001, moved to California and turned to investing: a large bet on NetEase when it was in trouble, then Apple and Kweichow Moutai for many years. His rules: buying a stock is buying the company, buy only what you understand, never borrow, and keep a list of things you will not do.

## Record at a glance

- **about 100×**: his gain on NetEase, bought in its post-2000 crisis, by his own account (not audited)
- **$620,100**: his winning bid for lunch with Buffett in 2006, a record then; the money went to charity
- **1 → 3**: BBK split into three companies in 2001; they grew into OPPO, vivo and imoo
- **0**: interest-bearing loans: a fixed rule at BBK, OPPO and vivo

## Big ideas

### 1. Buying a stock is buying the company

One sentence from Buffett changed how he invested. A share is part of a company, and a company is worth the cash it will produce from now on.

- **The sentence that clicked.** In America he first tried charts and could make no sense of them, until Buffett's line that buying a stock is buying a company made everything clear. (Magazine, 2025)
- **Value is future cash.** A company is worth all the cash it will produce from now until it ends, discounted back to today. (Book, 2025)
- **Fewer than one in a hundred.** The idea sounds simple, he says, but perhaps fewer than 1% of investors truly understand it. (Interview, 2025)
- **The company's money, not the market's.** Investors earn what their companies earn. People forever talking about bull and bear markets are really hoping to win other traders' money. (Xueqiu replies)
- **No forecast needed.** He decides by comparing opportunities, not by predicting the economy. (Interview, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-01-buying-a-stock-is-buying-the-company.html

### 2. Only what you understand

Be honest about what you understand. He says he truly understands only a few companies, and his losses came when he strayed.

- **Know what you know.** Honesty with yourself is the heart of a circle of competence: know what you know and admit what you don't. (Talk, 2018)
- **A short list.** He says he understands Apple, Tencent and Moutai, only partly understands a few others, and avoids most of the rest. (Interview, 2025)
- **A grey zone.** He admits the line between understanding and not is blurry, which is why he keeps to the few he knows best. (Interview, 2025)
- **Games he knew.** He credits his NetEase success to knowing the games business from his Subor years. (Magazine, 2025 · Interview, 2025)
- **Others may understand what you don't.** Not understanding a company is no judgement on it; it simply isn't for you. (Talk, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-02-only-what-you-understand.html

### 3. The stop-doing list

Doing the right thing mostly means refusing to do wrong things. Most people know what is wrong; they do it anyway for a short-term gain.

- **Not doing wrong.** Most people can tell right from wrong. They do wrong things anyway because the short-term pull is strong, like smokers who know the harm. (Talk, 2018)
- **Stop early.** When you realise something is a mistake, stop at once. Stopping is cheapest at the start. (Talk, 2018)
- **BBK's list.** No selling on credit, no late payments to suppliers, no late wages, no haggling, no making products for others, no interest-bearing loans, no attacking rivals. (Magazine, 2025 · Talk, 2018)
- **Saying no to Walmart.** He once refused an order for a million VCD players without even discussing price: haggling would only waste everyone's time. (Magazine, 2025)
- **Learned the hard way.** Many items on the list came from painful lessons; each rule saves them from a class of mistakes. (Interview, 2025 · Magazine, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-03-the-stop-doing-list.html

### 4. Never borrow

His companies take no interest-bearing loans, and he never borrows to invest. Debt makes you faster in both directions.

- **No loans.** BBK, OPPO and vivo take no interest-bearing loans, so they cannot die from running out of cash. He cites Munger: most failures come from borrowing too much. (Talk, 2018)
- **One soaking.** Borrowing speeds up gains and losses alike. Getting your feet wet is unavoidable; getting soaked can be permanent. (Talk, 2018)
- **Crises as chances.** With ample cash, every crisis became a chance to act rather than a threat. (Talk, 2018)
- **Missing out is fine.** Missing some opportunities is acceptable, as long as you catch the right ones. (Talk, 2018)
- **Rivals gone, BBK still here.** Most of his old competitors have disappeared; he believes avoiding debt is a big part of why his companies survived. (Talk, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-04-never-borrow.html

### 5. Right business, right people, right price

Look at the business model and the culture first. Price comes last.

- **Three things, in order.** Right business, right people, right price, an order he credits to Buffett. Price matters least. (Talk, 2018)
- **Two filters.** He looks at two things, the business model and the corporate culture. If he dislikes either, he stops looking. (Review, 2026 · Interview, 2025)
- **Cheap, seen from ten years out.** Whether a share is expensive today is a short-term question. Look back from ten years ahead. (Talk, 2018)
- **Different, or nothing.** Products no different from rivals' can only compete on price and rarely make money. He calls 'value for money' an excuse for weak products. (Talk, 2018)
- **No cash flow, no investment.** He avoids anything that produces no cash flow, such as Bitcoin. (Talk, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-05-right-business-right-people-right-price.html

### 6. Benfen and a calm mind

Benfen means doing what you should, even when nobody asked. Add a calm, ordinary mind and, he says, you have the whole secret of BBK.

- **Their only secret.** Asked whether BBK's success came from advertising or incentives, he says no: it came from benfen plus a calm mind. (Talk, 2018 · Review, 2026)
- **Do the right thing, and do it right.** He came across Peter Drucker's line as a student; it became BBK's motto. (Interview, 2025 · Review, 2026)
- **What great bosses share.** He cites a study of top chief executives: their personalities differed in every way except one, integrity. (Talk, 2018)
- **Every word a promise.** Don't deceive customers or investors; what you say, you must do. (Talk, 2018)
- **Trust before money.** He left Subor because its owner broke promises about shares: a problem of trust, not money. (Interview, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-06-benfen-and-a-calm-mind.html

### 7. Hold great companies

Good companies rarely need selling. He sells when the business changes or something clearly better appears.

- **No need to sell.** By 2018 he had never sold Apple, saying good companies don't need selling. (Talk, 2018)
- **Two reasons to sell.** The company's earning power changes, or a clearly better company he understands appears at a good price. (Talk, 2018 · Interview, 2025)
- **Fully invested.** He calls himself a full-position investor and dislikes idle cash, since bank interest earns less than good companies. (Interview, 2025)
- **Moutai at half price.** When Moutai's shares fell by about half, he held on and kept buying. (Interview, 2025)
- **Trimming, not trading.** By 2025 he thought Apple's shares expensive and was trimming by selling call options. (Interview, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-07-hold-great-companies.html

### 8. NetEase, Apple and Moutai

Three bets made him famous as an investor. Each fits his rules: a business he understood, a culture he liked, a sensible price.

- **NetEase.** He bought heavily when the shares were in panic and the company held more cash than its market value. They rose about twentyfold in six months and more than a hundredfold in all. (Interview, 2025 · AFP, 2017)
- **Sold too early?** He later sold, saying he felt uneasy holding so much, and admits the later share price suggests he sold too soon. (Talk, 2018)
- **Apple.** He began buying in 2011, seeing the shift to software and the platform, and a culture that puts users first and refuses products that add too little. (Interview, 2025)
- **Moutai.** A unique product whose taste does not change, loyal customers, and steady dividends and buybacks. (Interview, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-08-netease-apple-and-moutai.html

### 9. The Buffett lunch and giving back

In 2006 he paid a record sum to lunch with Buffett, to charity. He plans to give most of his money away, and gives with conditions that make gifts last.

- **A record bid.** In 2006 he paid $620,100 at Buffett's charity lunch auction, the first winner from mainland China. (SCMP, 2006)
- **Giving most away.** He said he planned to follow Buffett by giving most of his money away. (SCMP, 2006)
- **Gifts that last.** In 2025 and 2026 he gave Moutai shares to education funds, on condition the shares are kept and only the dividends spent. (Review, 2026)
- **Three wishes for graduates.** At Zhejiang University in 2011 he told graduates: have no grand ambitions, keep a list of things you won't do, and be upright. (Review, 2026)
- **Improve yourself.** Asked about beating Apple, he said they think about improving themselves, not about surpassing anyone. (AFP, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-09-the-buffett-lunch-and-giving-back.html

### 10. The mistakes he admits

He is frank about his errors. Most came when he speculated or strayed outside what he understood.

- **Baidu.** A speculative bet on Baidu ended in a short squeeze that cost him $100 to 200 million. He calls it speculation, not investing. (Talk, 2018)
- **General Electric.** He bought GE in 2008, sold a few years later, and says he never really grasped its business model. (Interview, 2025)
- **Oil.** About $100 million put into an oil index lost more than $10 million before he sold. (Interview, 2025)
- **Smartphones.** BBK was slow to see the shift to smartphones; losses in 2012 and 2013 drained much of its cash. (Interview, 2025)
- **Speculation versus investing.** He says his real investing mistakes were few and small; the big losses came from speculation. (Talk, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/duan-10-the-mistakes-he-admits.html

## Special section

**Your own stop-doing list**

- I never borrow money to buy shares
- I never bet against a company by short selling
- I never buy a business I can't explain
- I never buy on a tip or a story alone
- I never trade to win other traders' money
- I never keep a mistake going just because stopping hurts
- I never buy a company whose culture I dislike
- I never pay for something that produces no cash

**BBK's stop-doing list, as reported**

- No selling on credit.
- No late payments to suppliers.
- No late wages.
- No haggling: one price for every customer.
- No making products for other brands.
- No interest-bearing loans.
- No attacking competitors.

His decision test, in his own description: first ask whether something is the right thing to do. Only then ask whether it makes money.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “能真懂这句话的人，可能不到1%” (On 'buying a stock is buying the company': “Perhaps fewer than 1% truly understand this.” Interview, 2025 (our translation))
- “投资赚的是公司赚的钱” (“Investing earns the money the company earns.” Reply on Xueqiu, 31 December 2023 (our translation))
- “我们不贷款，有充裕的现金流” (“We take no loans, and we have plenty of cash flow.” Stanford talk, 2018 (our translation))
- “the focus instead is to improve ourselves” (AFP interview, 2017, on competing with Apple)

## Read the originals

If you read Chinese, start with the Stanford talk, which is free online, then the 2025 book. Otherwise, browser translation of the free transcripts works reasonably well.

- [Talk and questions at Stanford](https://m.huxiu.com/article/265373.html): Fifty-odd questions answered: the stop-doing list, benfen and a calm mind, never borrowing, how he picks shares, Apple, NetEase and his own mistakes.
- [Interview with Fang Sanwen](https://finance.ifeng.com/c/8oChp5B5WMc): His life story, why so few people really understand that buying a stock is buying a company, which companies he understands, and a frank list of mistakes.
- [Da Dao: Duan Yongping's investing questions and answers](https://m.huxiu.com/article/4292824.html): Twenty years of his online answers, arranged by theme: investing, business models and culture, comments on companies, and life.
- [His replies on Xueqiu](https://www.xueqiu.com/3640871106/288907057): Short, blunt answers to readers' questions, including the difference between earning what a company earns and trying to win the market's money.
- [China's secretive billionaire reveals how he toppled Apple](https://www.malaymail.com/news/money/2017/03/20/chinas-secretive-billionaire-reveals-how-he-toppled-apple/1339087): A rare English-language interview: Subor, BBK, OPPO and vivo against Apple, NetEase, and his view of competition.
- [No shortage of tips at Buffett lunch](https://www.scmp.com/article/556023/no-shortage-tips-buffett-lunch): How a former electronics boss won the Buffett lunch auction, his background, and his plan to give most of his money away.
- [The two words that made Duan Yongping rich](https://www.36kr.com/p/3555484789095560): BBK's stop-doing list in practice, the Walmart order he refused, and how Buffett's line about buying companies changed his investing.
- [What the book Da Dao really teaches](https://finance.ifeng.com/c/8vOYN25Ve8V): His two filters for any company, his 2011 advice to Zhejiang University graduates, and his gifts of Moutai shares to education.

## Words to know

- **Benfen (本分)**: Doing what you should, honestly and without being asked; not taking advantage of others.
- **A calm, ordinary mind (平常心)**: Staying rational and returning to fundamentals whatever is happening around you.
- **Stop-doing list (不为清单)**: A written list of things a person or company will not do, whatever the short-term gain.
- **Discounted cash flow**: Valuing a company by adding up the cash it will produce in future, each year's cash shrunk back to today's money.
- **Short squeeze**: When a share that many have bet against rises fast, forcing them to buy back at high prices.
- **Call option**: A contract giving someone the right to buy a share at a set price. Selling one brings in cash now, but caps your gain.
- **Contract manufacturing (OEM)**: Making products for another company to sell under its brand.
- **Opportunity cost**: What you give up by choosing one use of money over the next best one.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his talk to Chinese students at Stanford (2018), his interview with Xueqiu's founder Fang Sanwen (2025), excerpts from the book of his answers (CITIC Press, 2025), his replies on Xueqiu, an AFP interview (2017), and press reports on his Buffett lunch (2006), BBK's stop-doing list and his gifts. Lessons are in our own words; short quotes are in the original language with our translation.

Duan writes in Chinese, mostly short answers on Xueqiu, where readers call him Da Dao. The 2025 book collects twenty years of them and is the only collection he has approved. Most sources here are in Chinese: lessons are our own English summaries, and short quotes are in the original with our translation. His investment results are personal and unaudited.

# Qiu Guolu

> Boiled investing down to three questions, why cheap, why good, why now, and built one of China's largest private fund firms on them.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/qiu.html · Section: China · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Cheapness is the hard truth. Even an ordinary company can pay well if bought cheaply enough.

## Summary

Qiu Guolu formed his approach during six years at Wedge Capital in the United States, ran investment at China Southern Asset Management from 2008, and in 2014 founded Gaoyi Asset Management, a home for several star managers that grew past 100 billion yuan. His bestselling book boils investing down to three questions: why is it cheap, why is it good, and why buy now?

## Record at a glance

- **3 questions**: why is it cheap, why is it good, why now: his whole method
- **about 10**: truly great companies, by his count, among roughly 2,500 then listed in China; so price must do much of the work
- **6 or 7 in 10**: years in which, he reckons, a sound method beats the market; a poor one manages 3 or 4
- **¥100bn+**: managed by Gaoyi, the firm he founded, by early 2021

## Big ideas

### 1. Three questions

All his analysis comes down to three questions: why is it cheap, why is it good, and why buy now?

- **Cheap, good, now.** Every analysis answers three questions: why the company is cheap, why it is good, and why now is the time to buy. (Book, 2014)
- **Valuation is the easy part.** Price to earnings, to book value and to sales are the most scientific measures, and the easiest to learn. (Book, 2014)
- **Quality is hard.** Few people can spot a truly great company before the market does, and many once-great companies lost their edge. (Book, 2014)
- **Good industry, good company, good price.** His whole approach: find good companies in good industries, then wait for a good price. (Book, 2014)
- **Simple tools.** Porter's five forces for the industry, DuPont analysis for how profits are made, and comparisons with peers and history for the price. (Book, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-01-three-questions.html

### 2. Cheapness is the hard truth

A low price is the investor's first protection. Even an ordinary company can pay well if bought cheaply enough.

- **Buy cheap to sell cheap.** He borrows a retailer's rule, Sam Walton's: you can only sell cheaply if you buy cheaply. In investing, buying cheaply matters even more. (Book, 2014)
- **Ordinary but cheap.** An ordinary company bought at a low enough price can still give a fine return. (Book, 2014)
- **Few true greats.** He reckoned that among about 2,500 Chinese listed companies perhaps ten were truly great, so most of the time price must do the work. (Book, 2014)
- **Wary of the next great thing.** He is suspicious of stories about the next great company, and admits he struggles even to pay a fair price for great ones. (Book, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-02-cheapness-is-the-hard-truth.html

### 3. Pricing power is the core advantage

A company with a real edge can raise prices without losing customers. That power comes from doing what you can repeat and others cannot copy.

- **Two tests.** A company with a real edge does something it can repeat again and again, and something others cannot copy. (Book, 2014)
- **Concentration is not enough.** He cares less about how few rivals there are than about the bargaining power and irreplaceability that brings. (Lecture, 2017)
- **Easy money versus hard work.** That power is the dividing line between businesses that earn easily and those that work hard for little. (Lecture, 2017)
- **Where it comes from.** Scarce resources, a strong brand, patents, a dominant position or a licence: in the end each shows up as pricing power. (Book, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-03-pricing-power-is-the-core-advantage.html

### 4. Count the moons, not the stars

Look at the whole industry, not just the company. The best skies have one bright moon; the worst are crowded with stars.

- **Best to worst.** One dominant firm is best; then one leader with a few strong rivals; then two or three equals; worst is a sky full of small competitors. (Lecture, 2017)
- **Define the sky.** The skill is drawing the right boundary: which firms are real rivals and which belong to a different sky. (Lecture, 2017)
- **Watch for invaders.** Firms from other industries can enter any sky. (Lecture, 2017)
- **A rising moon.** The prize is a company whose pricing power the market has not yet noticed. (Lecture, 2017)
- **Right track, wrong horse.** Investors often pick the right industry but the wrong company. (Lecture, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-04-count-the-moons-not-the-stars.html

### 5. Win first, then fight

Crowded, fast-growing industries make poor hunting grounds. Wait until the battle is over and back the winner.

- **Wait for the winner.** In a crowded industry it is hard to know whom to back, however fast it grows. Wait until the fighting ends and a winner emerges. (Book, 2014 · Lecture, 2017)
- **Fast change destroys moats.** In fast-moving technology, rivals simply build a new castle elsewhere. Televisions went through tubes, projection, LCD, plasma, LED and 3D in a few years; air conditioners changed far less. (Article)
- **A formula for a century.** Coca-Cola's formula has hardly changed in a hundred years, and China too has traditional products that last for centuries. (Article)
- **Scandals help leaders.** After food scandals, industry sales recovered within months and the big brands gained share, as buyers trusted known names. (Article)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-05-win-first-then-fight.html

### 6. Take what others discard

Go where the crowd is not, and be careful where it is packed. But cheap can stay cheap: check why the crowd left.

- **Twice a year.** Every January and July he adds up the industry weights of all fund companies, then grows cautious on the crowded industries and more hopeful on the shunned ones. (Article)
- **He has seen manias.** He lived through the 1992 rush for share certificates and the late-1990s Nasdaq boom and crash. (Profile, 2015)
- **Out of the crowded trade.** In 2020–21 he stayed out of the crowded trade in richly valued favourite shares, which then fell about 40% from early 2021. (Letter, 2022)
- **Beware value traps.** His book warns that some cheap shares stay cheap for good reasons, and describes the kinds most likely to become traps. (Book, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-06-take-what-others-discard.html

### 7. A lucky win is not a right bet

Judge your method, not this year's result. A sound process shows itself over five to ten years.

- **Two different things.** Winning a bet and betting right are not the same: a good process can give poor results for a while, and a bad one can get lucky. (Book, 2014)
- **Five to ten years.** A sound method gives good results with high probability over five to ten years, not six months. (Book, 2014)
- **Six or seven in ten.** He reckons a sound method beats the market in about six or seven years out of ten, a poor one in three or four. (Book, 2014)
- **Why it keeps working.** Citing Joel Greenblatt: value investing works over time precisely because it doesn't work every year. (Book, 2014)
- **Don't keep switching.** Investors who keep changing methods tend to fail; successful ones stick with one. (Book, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-07-a-lucky-win-is-not-a-right-bet.html

### 8. Clients first

A fund firm must put compliance before growth, clients before itself, and results before size.

- **Three priorities.** In 2017 he wrote to all staff: when growth clashes with compliance, compliance wins; when the firm's interest clashes with clients', clients win; when size clashes with results, results win. (Interviews, 2018–19)
- **Patient money.** Many Gaoyi funds lock investors in for two or three years, some for five or eight, because stable money lets managers think long term. (Interviews, 2018–19)
- **A home for managers.** He built Gaoyi to handle everything except investing, so its managers can concentrate on picking shares. (Interviews, 2018–19)
- **Shaped in America.** His first job was as a strategist and quantitative analyst; his approach took shape during six years at Wedge Capital. (Interviews, 2018–19)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-08-clients-first.html

### 9. Value investing works in China

He has tried most methods. For most people, he concluded, only value investing can really be learned and used, in China as anywhere.

- **First money in 1992.** At 19 he queued overnight for share subscription certificates and made his first stock market gains. (Profile, 2015)
- **Many methods tried.** Tips, charts, quant trading, concentrated picking, growth investing: he tried them all, and concluded that for most people only value investing can be learned and used. (Book, 2014)
- **Six strong years.** The 2015 profile credits him with six strong years at China Southern, using value methods in China's A-share market. (Profile, 2015)
- **The traits behind it.** The same profile sums up his habits: independent judgement, faith in common sense, a contrarian streak and patience for delayed rewards. (Profile, 2015)
- **Simple, not easy.** The point of the sequel: the principles are simple; holding to them, and applying them flexibly in a noisy market full of traps, is not. (Book, 2018)
- **Always learning.** He enjoys investing as a search for the truth, with new industries to learn every year. (Interviews, 2018–19)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-09-value-investing-works-in-china.html

### 10. Even legends stumble

After two hard years he wrote to investors about his mistakes, and what he would watch more closely.

- **Three lessons.** Too much in Hong Kong shares, cutting holdings too early in 2020, and too little attention to policy, especially the regulation of internet companies. (Letter, 2022)
- **Buying too soon.** After China's internet shares halved in late 2021 he added more, and they fell further. (Letter, 2022)
- **Look up at the sky.** His conclusion: keep your eyes on the road, but look up at the sky too, meaning watch policy as well as companies. (Letter, 2022)
- **Still a value investor.** He kept his faith in low valuations and his refusal to chase crowded favourites. (Letter, 2022)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/qiu-10-even-legends-stumble.html

## Special section

**Three questions, eight checks**

- Cheap: low against its own history and its peers, on more than one measure
- Good: it does something it can repeat, and others cannot copy
- Good: its industry has one or two clear leaders, and it is one of them
- Good: its products don't change every two or three years
- Good: I know how it makes its profits, and its strategy fits
- Now: the crowd is avoiding it, not chasing it
- Now: the industry's battle is over, and I am buying the winner
- I will judge this decision over five to ten years, not six months

**Count the moons: industries from best to worst**

- One moon. A single dominant firm.
- A moon with bright stars. One leader and a few strong rivals.
- Two or three moons. A handful of equals.
- A sky full of stars. Many small firms fighting on price.

**His four principles**

- Cheapness is the hard truth.
- Pricing power is the core advantage.
- Win first, then fight.
- Take what others discard.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “便宜才是硬道理” (“Cheapness is the hard truth.” A principle from his 2014 book (our translation))
- “定价权是核心竞争力” (“Pricing power is the core competitive advantage.” Gaoli lecture, 2017 (our translation))
- “不只是低头看路，也要抬头看天” (“Don't only look down at the road; look up at the sky too.” Letter to investors, 2022 (our translation))

## Read the originals

If you read Chinese, start with The Simplest Things in Investing: short chapters in plain language. Otherwise, the free articles linked below carry the core ideas, and browser translation works reasonably well.

- [The Simplest Things in Investing](https://news.cnyes.com/news/id/3568837): His bestseller: the three questions, cheapness, pricing power, winning first, contrarian buying, value traps and the difference between luck and skill.
- [The Not-So-Simple Things in Investing](https://www.36kr.com/p/1722207780865): Gaoyi's managers on putting simple principles into practice in a noisy market.
- [Crazy only for value](https://finance.ifeng.com/a/20150226/13514764_0.shtml): His path from the 1992 share certificate rush to the US and back, and his years at China Southern.
- [Interviews with Smart Investor](https://m.gelonghui.com/p/266308): How Wedge Capital shaped him, why Gaoyi locks in client money, and his 2017 letter setting the firm's three priorities.
- [Counting the moon](https://m.gelonghui.com/p/186330): Why industry structure decides pricing power, how to rank industries by their moons and stars, and how to define the sky.
- [Why fast-changing industries make poor investments](https://m.gelonghui.com/p/156733): His examples of televisions against air conditioners and Coca-Cola, and what food scandals did to industry leaders.
- [Letter to investors](https://wallstreetcn.com/articles/3659973): A frank look back at 2020–21: why he stayed out of the crowded trades, three mistakes, and what he would watch more closely.

## Words to know

- **A shares**: Shares of Chinese companies listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, traded in yuan.
- **Price to earnings (P/E)**: The share price divided by the profit per share.
- **Price to book (P/B)**: The share price divided by the company's net assets per share.
- **Pricing power**: The ability to raise prices without losing customers.
- **Porter's five forces**: A way to judge an industry: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, and the bargaining power of suppliers and customers.
- **DuPont analysis**: Splitting return on equity into profit margin, asset turnover and borrowing.
- **Value trap**: A share that looks cheap but stays cheap, because the business keeps getting worse.
- **Contrarian**: Deliberately going against the crowd.
- **Private fund**: A fund sold only to qualified investors, with fewer public reporting rules than a public fund.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his books (2014, updated 2020; and 2018 with Gaoyi colleagues), a 2015 newspaper profile, interviews in 2018 and 2019, a 2017 lecture at the Gaoli value investing institute, and press reports of his 2022 letter to investors. Lessons are in our own words; short quotes are in Chinese with our translation.

Qiu writes in Chinese. His first book gathers essays and posts written mostly before 2013; the sequel draws on Gaoyi's internal discussions. Neither has an English edition. Lessons are our own English summaries; short quotes are in Chinese with our translation. His funds report returns only to their investors, so we show none we cannot check.

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.

- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Qiu Guolu, Gaoyi Asset Management, China Southern Asset Management, Wedge Capital, the publishers, the publications quoted or any company named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners.

# Zhang Lei

> Learned investing at Yale under David Swensen, founded Hillhouse with $20 million, and preaches long-term bets on great entrepreneurs.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/zhanglei.html · Section: China · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Long-termism. Put time and conviction into things that create value over many years.

## Summary

Zhang Lei learned investing as an intern under David Swensen at Yale's endowment, then founded Hillhouse in 2005 with $20 million from Yale. He backed Tencent early, put $300 million into JD.com in 2010, and built one of Asia's largest investment firms. His creed: think long term, research deeply, back entrepreneurs with great vision, and be a friend of time.

## Record at a glance

- **$20m**: Yale's seed money when he founded Hillhouse in 2005
- **$2.4bn**: gains Hillhouse had made for Yale by 2020, according to David Swensen
- **$300m**: invested in JD.com in 2010, in one go
- **¥41.66bn**: paid in 2019 for 15% of Gree Electric; the shares were still below that price in early 2026

## Big ideas

### 1. Long-termism

Put your time and conviction into things that create value over many years. A long horizon is an edge from the starting line.

- **His compass.** Long-termism means putting time and conviction into things that keep creating value, learning the most effective ways of thinking, and always seeking the truth. (Preface, 2020)
- **An edge from the start.** A long horizon gives you an advantage before you begin, because so few investors can afford to wait. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Not about the shortest path.** Yale taught him that investing is not a race for quick returns but working with the best people to build lasting organisations. (Yale Daily News)
- **Holding long is a result.** Long holding periods are the result of backing companies that keep creating value, not a goal in themselves. (Book, 2020)
- **A friend of time.** He sums up his approach in three phrases: long-termism, walking with people of great vision, and being a friend of time. (Book, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-01-long-termism.html

### 2. Swensen's lessons

David Swensen was his first teacher. He learned what it means to be a fiduciary, to think truly long term, and to build an organisation with a soul.

- **A student who couldn't pay.** Short of money for his second year at Yale, he got an internship in Swensen's office. His first task was translating Swensen's book into Chinese. (Tribute, 2021)
- **Hundreds of basic questions.** Swensen answered hundreds of his questions, on the trading floor and over squash and softball. (Tribute, 2021)
- **Fiduciary.** Swensen showed him what a fiduciary is: someone who puts the interests of those who trust him first. He struggled to find a Chinese word for it. (Tribute, 2021)
- **A bet on a person.** Yale backed him when he was 32 and had never managed a portfolio. Swensen's reason: work with the right people and good things tend to follow. (Tribute, 2021)
- **A soul.** Swensen spoke of organisations with a soul, driven by a mission. Zhang came to believe such teams innovate more and last longer. (Tribute, 2021)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-02-swensens-lessons.html

### 3. Research is the base

Deep research comes first, and few bets. Understand real businesses the way a field researcher studies a village.

- **Few, deep bets.** Make deep fundamental research the basis of every decision, and place a few bets rather than chase many ideas. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Like fieldwork.** Value investing is not maths on paper. Like a sociologist doing fieldwork, you must see how people really live and buy. (Book, 2020)
- **Generalists.** His team works as generalists, and he counts himself one of the analysts. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Ask the basic questions.** Success comes down to stripping an investment to its most basic questions. (CFA Institute, 2018)
- **Ahead of the crowd.** Qiu Guolu recalls Zhang convening top scientists in 2015 on cancer immunotherapy, before most Chinese investors knew the field, and backing BeiGene in eight rounds. (Review, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-03-research-is-the-base.html

### 4. People first

Hillhouse's growth came mainly from people: the managers it hires and the entrepreneurs it backs.

- **Owners aligned with customers.** Before investing, find out whether owners, directors and managers are long-term, intelligent and aligned with their customers' needs. (CFA Institute, 2018)
- **Who he hires.** Intelligence, independent thinking and honesty count for more than experience or background. (CFA Institute, 2018)
- **Three intellectual habits.** Curiosity, independence and honesty, plus empathy: qualities he looks for in people. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Quality time with quality people.** Swensen's reason for backing him became Hillhouse's motto: spend quality time with quality people. (Tribute, 2021)
- **Entrepreneurs who invest.** He describes Hillhouse as entrepreneurs who happen to be investors. (Lecture, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-04-people-first.html

### 5. Backing great vision

He looks for entrepreneurs with great vision, which he defines in four parts.

- **Four signs.** Long-term thinking amid uncertainty; deep insight into the industry; focused execution; and strong empathy that brings people and resources together. (Excerpt, 2020)
- **The secret handshake.** He calls great vision Hillhouse's secret handshake with companies: founders who want to build something great make the best partners. (Excerpt, 2020)
- **Ten or twenty years.** Good entrepreneurs see ten or twenty years ahead, sometimes beyond their own lives. (Excerpt, 2020)
- **Choose the person, then the project.** When Swensen backed him, it was a bet on a person. Zhang applies the same logic to founders. (Tribute, 2021 · Excerpt, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-05-backing-great-vision.html

### 6. Moats must keep moving

Static moats erode. The lasting edge belongs to companies that keep innovating and rebuilding their advantage.

- **A dynamic moat.** Long-termism helps companies escape zero-sum games and keep rebuilding a dynamic moat through constant innovation. (Preface, 2020)
- **Value investing evolves.** As markets grow more efficient, deeply undervalued companies become rare. Investors must find new, forward-looking drivers of value. (Book, 2020)
- **Invest in change.** He looks for industries being changed by technology and new ways of doing business. (Lecture, 2015 · Review, 2020)
- **Technology and tradition.** He invests in both new technology and traditional industries, public or private, large or small. (CFA Institute, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-06-moats-must-keep-moving.html

### 7. Create value, don't just find it

Hillhouse tries to help good companies get better, rather than planning the exit first.

- **The exit looks after itself.** Unlike buyout firms that plan the exit first and lean on debt and cost cuts, he backs good people and solid cash flow and lets the exit take care of itself. (CFA Institute, 2018)
- **Belle.** In 2017 Hillhouse led the $6.8 billion purchase of the shoe retailer Belle, aiming to use technology for online sales, stock control and better service in shops. (CFA Institute, 2018)
- **Not the format, the substance.** With freedom to invest in public shares, venture and private equity, he focuses on the substance of a deal, not its form. (Lecture, 2015)
- **Go big when you know.** In 2010 he put $300 million into JD.com in one go, backed by years of studying retail around the world. (Review, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-07-create-value-dont-just-find-it.html

### 8. Fire cannot burn it

As a student he decided that what fire can burn, money and houses, matters least. What lasts is knowledge, ability and values.

- **Three fires.** Things fire can burn, such as money and houses, are not what matters. What matters is what fire cannot burn: knowledge, ability and values. (Book, 2020)
- **First principles.** Don't reason by analogy. Peel back the surface to see what a thing really is, then build up from there. (Book, 2020)
- **Education never ends.** He has given generously to Yale and, inspired by Swensen, founded an institute to teach long-term investing. (Yale Daily News · Tribute, 2021)
- **A teacher's example.** Swensen saw teaching as one of his most important duties; Zhang took that as the clearest sign of a long-term mind. (Tribute, 2021)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-08-fire-cannot-burn-it.html

### 9. Patience with big bets

Long-term bets can stay underwater for years. Gree shows both the patience and the risk.

- **Gree.** In 2019 a Hillhouse fund paid 41.66 billion yuan, partly borrowed, for 15% of Gree Electric and became its biggest shareholder. (Caixin, 2019–26)
- **Still underwater.** By early 2026 Gree's shares were nearly 20% below the purchase price, a paper loss partly offset by about 15 billion yuan of dividends. (Caixin, 2019–26)
- **Debt has a cost.** In 2026 Hillhouse planned to sell about 2% of Gree to repay bank loans from the deal. (Caixin, 2019–26)
- **Yale's gain.** By 2020, Swensen said, Hillhouse had made about $2.4 billion of gains for Yale. (Bloomberg, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-09-patience-with-big-bets.html

### 10. The LONGi investigation

In 2023 China's securities regulator investigated a Hillhouse unit over undisclosed share sales. Here are the facts, so you can judge for yourself.

- **What happened.** HHLR, Hillhouse's public-markets unit, owned 5.85% of the solar company LONGi. In March 2023 it lent out shares, taking its stake below 5%, the level above which sales must be announced. (News, 2023–24)
- **The gap.** When the loan ended, its stake was only 4.98%, implying it had sold about 0.9% of the company without an announcement. (News, 2023–24)
- **The probe.** In November 2023 the regulator opened an investigation for suspected breaches of share-transfer rules, and the exchanges soon closed the loophole. (News, 2023–24)
- **The response.** In April 2024 HHLR began buying the shares back, promising to hand any gain to LONGi. We have found no published final penalty decision. (News, 2023–24)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/zhanglei-10-the-longi-investigation.html

## Special section

**Four signs of an entrepreneur with great vision**

- Long-termism: seeking the long run amid uncertainty.
- Deep insight: into the industry, spotting key trends through constant innovation.
- Focused execution: doing things to the highest standard.
- Strong empathy: bringing people and resources together to make ideas real.

**What he looks for in people**

- Curiosity.
- Independence of mind.
- Intellectual honesty.
- Empathy.
- Long-term and aligned with customers, for the owners and managers he backs.

**An honest note.** In November 2023 China's securities regulator opened an investigation into HHLR, the public-markets unit of Hillhouse. HHLR owned 5.85% of the solar company LONGi. In March 2023 it lent out shares, taking its stake below 5%, the level above which sales must be announced; when the loan ended its stake was only 4.98%, implying it had sold about 0.9% of the company without an announcement. In April 2024 HHLR began buying the shares back and promised to hand any gain to LONGi. The case concerned the rules on announcing share sales; we have seen no allegation that clients' money was misused, and we have found no published final penalty decision. We include Zhang Lei for his long record and ideas, and state this plainly so you can judge for yourself.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “investing is not about chasing the shortest path to returns” (Email to Yale Daily News)
- “Spend quality time with quality people.” (Hillhouse's motto, in his tribute to Swensen, 2021)
- “Success ultimately comes down to asking the basic questions” (As reported by CFA Institute, 2018)

## Read the originals

Start with his tribute to David Swensen, free in English and a five-minute read, then the CFA Institute report of his 2018 talk. If you read Chinese, the book Value is the fullest account.

- [Value: My Thoughts on Investing](https://book.douban.com/subject/35188914/): His life, his idea of long-termism, how Hillhouse researches and backs companies, his four signs of a great entrepreneur, and more than ten case studies.
- [Preface to Value: long-termism](https://www.yicai.com/news/100751845.html): In his own words: why long-termism is the compass for investors, companies and society, and what a dynamic moat is.
- [Investing and entrepreneurship both need long-termism](https://www.36kr.com/p/852939339586439): Why choosing entrepreneurs with great vision is central, and his four-part definition of that vision.
- [Lecture at Columbia Business School](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/349678/notes-from-hillhouse-capitals-lei-zhangs-lecture-at-columbia-business-school): Why a long horizon is an edge from the start, deep research and few bets, the generalist team, and the qualities he hires for.
- [Lei Zhang on Hillhouse Capital's success equation](https://blogs.cfainstitute.org/blog/2018/05/14/lei-zhang-on-hillhouse-capitals-success-equation/): People first, asking basic questions, a long view that lets exits look after themselves, and using technology to improve good companies.
- [Remembering my legendary mentor David Swensen](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2021-05-09/obituary-remembering-my-legendary-mentor-david-swensen-101708563.html): His internship, what Swensen taught him about being a fiduciary and building an organisation with a soul, and why Yale backed him.
- [Profile of Lei Zhang, Yale trustee](https://yaledailynews.com/?p=152260): His Yale years, Hillhouse's name and its $20m start, his gifts to Yale, and what he says Yale taught him about investing.
- [Yale's $2.4 billion profit machine Hillhouse is ready to reload](https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/yale-s-2-4-billion-profit-machine-hillhouse-ready-to-reload-1.1427668): How much Hillhouse made for Yale, according to David Swensen, and why other endowments back Zhang personally.
- [Practising value investing: a review of Value](https://cs.com.cn/xwzx/jr/202009/t20200921_6096372.html): A fellow investor on what is new in his approach: research ahead of the crowd, as in biotech, and large, patient bets such as JD.com.
- [Hillhouse and Gree Electric](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-02-27/hillhouse-to-cut-gree-stake-in-first-move-since-landmark-buyout-102417309.html): How a Hillhouse fund won 15% of Gree in 2019, and its first planned sale of shares in 2026 with the stake below its purchase price.
- [The HHLR investigation over LONGi shares](https://yicaiglobal.com/news/hillhouse-unit-is-probed-by-chinese-regulators-for-allegedly-breaking-bourse-rules): Why China's securities regulator investigated a Hillhouse unit's LONGi shares, and how the unit responded.

## Words to know

- **Endowment**: A fund given to a university or charity and invested so it can pay for its work for ever.
- **Fiduciary**: Someone trusted to act in another person's interest, before their own.
- **Private equity**: Buying stakes in companies, often unlisted, usually with a view to improving them.
- **Venture capital**: Investing in young companies in return for a stake.
- **Take-private**: Buying all the shares of a listed company so it leaves the stock market.
- **Dynamic moat**: A competitive edge that a company keeps renewing through innovation, rather than a fixed advantage.
- **First principles**: Reasoning from what a thing fundamentally is, rather than by comparison with something else.
- **Disclosure threshold**: The shareholding, 5% in China, above which an investor must announce changes in its stake.
- **Securities lending**: Lending shares to another investor for a fee, to be returned later.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his book Value (2020) and its preface, notes from his Columbia Business School lecture (2015), CFA Institute's report of his 2018 talk, his 2021 tribute to David Swensen, Yale Daily News, Bloomberg (2020), Qiu Guolu's review of his book (2020), and press reports on Gree and LONGi. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

His main work is the book Value: My Thoughts on Investing (2020), in Chinese. In English there are reports of his talks, a few interviews and his tribute to Swensen. Hillhouse's returns are private, so we show only figures others have published. This page includes an honest note on a 2023 investigation into a Hillhouse unit.
