# Chandrakant Sampat

> India's original value investor: left the family business in the 1950s, bought the Indian arms of global companies cheaply, and taught a generation.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/sampat.html · Section: India · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Own businesses, not factories. Buying shares lets you share a business's growth without running it.

## Summary

Chandrakant Sampat is called India's original value investor. He left his family's business in the 1950s to buy shares, made his fortune owning the Indian arms of global consumer companies when few others saw their worth, and taught a generation, including Parag Parikh and Radhakishan Damani. He wrote no books and gave few interviews; he jogged, read, lived simply and kept to a handful of strict rules.

## Record at a glance

- **Mid-1950s**: began investing, when the Controller of Capital Issues still governed India's new share issues
- **₹16**: the price at which he bought Gillette's Indian arm, then called Indian Shaving Products
- **8–10 years**: his signal to buy a good company: its share price at an eight- or ten-year low
- **7 km**: his daily jog, from Haji Ali to Marine Drive, well into old age

## Big ideas

### 1. Own businesses, don't build factories

He left his family's business in the 1950s, drawn to shares. Buying a slice of a good listed business, he believed, beats the struggle of building one from scratch.

- **A first-generation investor.** He began in the mid-1950s, when the Controller of Capital Issues still oversaw new share issues, after leaving his family's business. (ET, 2015)
- **Advice to a young man.** When a young Parag Parikh's plan to make toothpaste tubes was rejected, Sampat told him to buy shares in good businesses instead: share the growth, skip the factory. (Obituary, 2015)
- **Easy to exit.** In those days, closing a business in India could drag on endlessly. A share could simply be sold. (Obituary, 2015)
- **A reader.** He read The Economist and Fortune closely, keeping an eye on business far beyond India. (Obituary, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-01-own-businesses-dont-build-factories.html

### 2. The FERA windfall

In the 1970s, India's Foreign Exchange Regulation Act forced many foreign companies to sell shares to Indian investors, often cheaply. Sampat bought the best of them and held for decades.

- **Forced sellers.** FERA required foreign companies to dilute their holdings at prices below their real value. He made a killing. (Obituary, 2015)
- **Hindustan Lever in the teens.** He bought Hindustan Lever when its shares were priced in the teens. (Obituary, 2015)
- **Gillette at ₹16.** Later he bought Gillette's Indian arm at ₹16 a share, when it was still called Indian Shaving Products. (Obituary, 2015)
- **Decades of holding.** He held his consumer companies for decades; a profile names Hindustan Lever and Nestlé among his picks. (Profile)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-02-the-fera-windfall.html

### 3. Cash flow and durability

For Sampat a good investment had to throw off cash, year after year, and last. He judged businesses by their cash, not their story.

- **Three tests.** He looked for positive cash flow, cash flow that lasts, and barriers that keep rivals out. (Round table, 2000)
- **The 2003 definition.** A business qualifies as a good investment only if it generates cash and shows durability. (Interview, 2003)
- **His screens.** He favoured high return on capital employed, a long record of dividends and little need for capital spending. Few companies passed. (ET, 2015)
- **Not the spreadsheet.** He warned people to beware of those he called spreadsheet specialists. (Tribute, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-03-cash-flow-and-durability.html

### 4. Buy at the lows

Find good companies with good managements, then wait until their share price sinks to an eight- or ten-year low. Buy from pessimists; sell to optimists.

- **His rule.** Pick up good companies with good managements when the share price is at an eight- or ten-year low. (Profile)
- **A second rule.** If you must act sooner, buy good companies about 40% below their 52-week high. (Profile)
- **Pessimists and optimists.** Buy from pessimists, sell to optimists, and be patient in between. (Tribute, 2015)
- **Not rigid.** He preferred a P/E of 15 or less, but said to focus on the quality and longevity of the business, and not to be rigid about the number. (Tribute, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-04-buy-at-the-lows.html

### 5. Simple, with little debt

He wanted businesses simple enough for anyone to understand, carrying little debt and needing little new money to grow.

- **Even a fool.** He bought only businesses that even a fool could understand, with very little debt. (Profile)
- **Capital-light.** A great business needs little extra capital to grow; a weak one needs capital forever. (Tribute, 2015)
- **Drucker's reader.** He was strongly influenced by the management thinker Peter Drucker. (ET, 2015 · Tribute, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-05-simple-with-little-debt.html

### 6. Muscle, fat or cancer

Not all growth is good. He sorted it into muscle, fat and cancer, and warned that nothing grows exponentially for long.

- **Three kinds of growth.** Good growth is muscle, bad growth is fat, and some growth ultimately kills, like cancer. (Tribute, 2015)
- **Value, not volume.** Gillette was his example: the number of razors sold grows slowly, but the value of each sale grows a lot. (Tribute, 2015)
- **Nature's accountant.** He compared nature to a miserly accountant that punishes even the smallest extravagance. Businesses, he implied, are no different. (Tribute, 2015)
- **No exponential forever.** In 2000 he told the software enthusiasts that nothing grows exponentially for long. (Round table, 2000)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-06-muscle-fat-or-cancer.html

### 7. Technology and creative destruction

He believed new technology destroys old businesses ever faster. That made him wary of fashionable shares and focused on durability.

- **Software in 2000.** At the height of the technology boom he argued that Indian software firms lacked free cash flow. (Round table, 2000)
- **Shorter lives.** In 2003 he said faster technology would shorten the lives of companies and the business cycle. (Interview, 2003)
- **Creative destruction.** He drew on Joseph Schumpeter, the economist who described how innovation keeps destroying old businesses. (Tribute, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-07-technology-and-creative-destruction.html

### 8. Integrity: humility plus courage

Sampat defined integrity as humility plus courage, and lived it. His four touchstone values were high enlightenment, high integrity, low expectation and hard work.

- **His definition.** Integrity, he said, is humility plus courage. (Tribute, 2015)
- **Thought, speech, action.** A friend described his ethics as complete harmony between what he thought, said and did. (Tribute, 2015)
- **An open letter.** In 2006 he wrote an open letter to the directors of Wyeth India over the transfer of a drug's marketing rights. (ET, 2015)
- **Old wisdom.** He drew on the Bhagavad Gita and Jain scriptures, as well as on Drucker and Schumpeter. (Tribute, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-08-integrity-humility-plus-courage.html

### 9. How many things can you do without?

One of India's richest investors lived simply, jogged daily and asked how little he needed, not how much he could have.

- **His question.** Parag Parikh said Sampat's philosophy was how many things you can do without. (ET, 2015)
- **The morning run.** For years he jogged about seven kilometres a day, from Haji Ali to Marine Drive. (ET, 2015 · Profile)
- **Against excess.** He objected to excessive consumption, debt, money-printing and short-termism. (Tribute, 2015)
- **Think for yourself.** Take the best ideas from great thinkers in every field, connect them yourself, and take nothing and nobody for granted. (Tribute, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-09-how-many-things-can-you-do-without.html

### 10. A teacher, and his blind spot

He shaped some of India's best investors. But his caution in later years also cost him, which he would have wanted us to learn from too.

- **Teacher.** Parag Parikh said he always walked away wiser after sitting with Sampat. (Obituary, 2015)
- **Sitting it out.** In his last years he stayed out of the market, worried that cheap money had inflated prices, and missed a strong rally in shares like Hindustan Unilever and Nestlé. (ET, 2015)
- **Right idea, wrong timing.** A friend wrote that he foresaw a credit-driven bubble but may have misjudged when it would end. (Tribute, 2015)
- **A bold forecast.** In 2003 he feared fast-changing technology could spell doom for capital markets within a few years. That did not happen. (Interview, 2003)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sampat-10-a-teacher-and-his-blind-spot.html

## Special section

**Try his screen on a company** 

**His touchstone**

- High enlightenment: keep learning from every discipline.
- High integrity: humility plus courage.
- Low expectation: expect little, and you're rarely disappointed.
- Hard work: there is no substitute.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security. This site is not registered with SEBI as an investment adviser or research analyst. Companies are named for history and education only.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “nothing in this world grows exponentially for a long time.” (Investor round table, January 2000)
- “Technology can alter anything and everything.” (Business Standard interview, 2003)
- “Don't be rigid on the P/E ratio.” (A saying recorded by Rohan Shah, Outlook Business, 2015)

## Read the originals

Start with the January 2000 investor round table, where he speaks at length, then Rohan Shah's notes of his sayings in Outlook Business (2015).

- [Investor Round Table](https://www.flame.edu.in/pdfs/fil/articles/Capital-Ideas-Online-Investor-Conference-Jan-2000.pdf): Sampat argues with fellow investors at the height of the technology boom: on free cash flow, durability, creative destruction and the multinationals.
- [There will be no capital formation](https://www.business-standard.com/article/markets/-8220-there-will-be-no-capital-formation-8221-103031701010_1.html): Why technology shortens business cycles, what a good investment must have, and his fears for capital markets.
- [Chandrakant Sampat: his philosophy in his words](https://hedgefundalpha.com/?p=34371): His buying rules in his own words: eight- to ten-year lows, simple businesses, little debt, free cash flow.
- [Chandrakant Sampat: grand old man of Dalal Street](https://www.business-standard.com/article/markets/chandrakant-sampat-grand-old-man-of-dalal-street-115020201089_1.html): FERA, Gillette at ₹16, Hindustan Lever in the teens, his reading, and the advice that sent Parag Parikh into shares.
- [A life spent spotting value in Indian markets](https://amc.ppfas.com/media/quotes/chandrakant-sampat-a-life-spent-spotting-value-in-indian-markets.php): His start in the 1950s, his screens for return on capital, dividends and low capital spending, his open letter on governance, and his simple life.
- [A man of value and wit](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/perspective/a-man-of-value-and-wit-596): His sayings on investing, on growth, on central banks, and the four values he called his touchstone.
- [In a class of his own](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/perspective/in-a-class-of-his-own-595): His ethics, the thinkers he drew on from the Gita to Drucker and Schumpeter, and his warnings about debt and excess.

## Words to know

- **Dalal Street**: The Mumbai street of the Bombay Stock Exchange; shorthand for India's stock market.
- **FERA**: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act of 1973, which pushed many foreign companies to cut their stakes in Indian units.
- **Controller of Capital Issues**: The government office that approved and priced new share issues in India before 1992.
- **Return on capital employed (RoCE)**: Operating profit as a share of the money tied up in the business.
- **Free cash flow**: Cash a business generates after paying for the investment it needs.
- **Capex**: Capital expenditure: spending on plants, machines and other long-lived assets.
- **FMCG**: Fast-moving consumer goods: everyday items like soap, razors and food.
- **₹1 crore**: Ten million rupees; ₹1 lakh is one hundred thousand.

## Sources and scope

Sources: an investor round table (Capital Ideas Online, 2000), a Business Standard interview (2003), a profile collecting his quotes, obituaries in Business Standard and The Economic Times (2015), and tributes in Outlook Business by Rohan Shah and Chetan Parikh (2015). Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Sampat left no books or letters, and his returns were never published. So this page relies on his interviews and on notes kept by people close to him, and says so wherever it does.

# Parag Parikh

> Started as a sub-broker in 1979, became India's voice of behavioural finance, and built a fund with one scheme and his own money in it.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/parikh.html · Section: India · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Study the mind. Investor behaviour matters as much as the balance sheet.

## Summary

Parag Parikh started as a sub-broker on Dalal Street in 1979; later his wife and mother sold some of their jewellery to help him grow. He became India's pioneer of behavioural finance: the study of why investors make the same mistakes again and again. In 2013 he launched a mutual fund with just one scheme, put his own money in it, and later closed his broking business to avoid conflicts. He died in 2015 in Omaha, after attending Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting.

## Record at a glance

- **1979**: began as a sub-broker; his wife and mother later sold some of their jewellery to help fund him
- **1 scheme**: all his mutual fund offered at launch in 2013; he called fund houses' many schemes a fad
- **2 books**: Stocks to Riches (2005) and Value Investing and Behavioural Finance (2009)
- **1999**: kept telling clients to sell technology shares at the height of the boom, and lost business for it

## Big ideas

### 1. From toothpaste tubes to shares

As a young man he wanted to make toothpaste tubes. Chandrakant Sampat told him to buy shares in good businesses instead. He started as a sub-broker, with his family's help.

- **Sampat's advice.** When his manufacturing idea was rejected as unviable, Sampat pointed him to listed businesses: share the growth without running the factory. (BS, 2015)
- **Family jewellery.** He started as a sub-broker in 1979, aiming to become a full broker. When he needed capital, his wife and mother sold some of their jewellery to help. (BS, 2015 · BS, 2015)
- **Research first.** His firm was one of the first Indian brokerages to set up a formal equity research desk. (Talk, 2014)
- **Sampat's student.** He said that whenever he sat with Sampat, he walked away wiser. (BS, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-01-from-toothpaste-tubes-to-shares.html

### 2. Study the mind, not just the accounts

He believed investor behaviour moves markets as much as company results. Understanding emotions, yours and others', is half the job.

- **What makes investors tick.** Stocks to Riches set out to discover what makes investors tick, and what keeps the stock market alive. (Book, 2005)
- **Profit from biases.** Investors can profit from the mental and emotional mistakes of others, if they avoid their own. (Talk, 2014)
- **India's pioneer.** His two books applied behavioural finance to Indian investors and Indian market history. (Moneylife, 2015 · Book, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-02-study-the-mind-not-just-the-accounts.html

### 3. Leave the herd

Greed and fear make Indian markets swing. He urged investors to buy when others are fearful, and paid a price for it in the technology boom.

- **Greed and fear.** His second book argues that successful investing means restraining and channelling emotions like greed and fear. (Book, 2009)
- **1999.** In the technology boom he suffered not because he owned such shares, but because he kept telling clients to sell them. (Talk, 2014)
- **Self-doubt.** As prices kept rising he admitted he was unsure whether he or the world was sane, but he held to his principles. (BS, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-03-leave-the-herd.html

### 4. Mistakes with Indian faces

His books name the traps: loss aversion, sunk costs, the endowment effect, mental accounting, decision paralysis. He showed them in Indian investors and Indian markets.

- **The list.** Stocks to Riches covers speculation, loss aversion, the sunk cost fallacy, the endowment effect, decision paralysis, mental accounting and mental shortcuts. (Book, 2005)
- **Indian examples.** His second book uses Indian market history and Indian companies to show these mistakes at work. (Book, 2009)
- **Traps by name.** It gives chapters to IPOs and to the growth trap: paying too much for exciting growth. (Book, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-04-mistakes-with-indian-faces.html

### 5. The law of the farm

Value investing is boring. You plant, you wait for years, you harvest. He called it the law of the farm.

- **Boring on purpose.** Value investing, he said, is boring: you have to wait for years. (Talk, 2014)
- **No shortcuts.** You cannot sow today and reap tomorrow. He called this a law made by God, not by men. (Talk, 2014)
- **A prepared mind.** He kept a watchlist of sound companies and bought when they became cheap. Fortune favours the prepared mind. (Talk, 2014)
- **A business, not paper.** Buy a business, not a piece of paper whose price you hope will rise. (Talk, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-05-the-law-of-the-farm.html

### 6. What a good business looks like

He looked for four things: honest management that treats minority shareholders well, a simple business, a strong moat and pricing power.

- **Four qualities.** Credible management that is fair to minority shareholders, a business you can understand, strong competitive moats, and pricing power. (Talk, 2014)
- **Use and exchange.** He separated a thing's value in use, what it does for you, from its value in exchange, what someone will pay for it. (Talk, 2014)
- **No greater fool.** Never pay more than intrinsic value; doing so means relying on a greater fool to buy from you. (Talk, 2014)
- **Buffett's way.** He believed Buffett's style of value investing, buying with a margin of safety, works best in India. (Talk, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-06-what-a-good-business-looks-like.html

### 7. Skin in the game

He insisted that those who manage money should invest alongside their clients, and he removed every conflict he could, even at a cost.

- **Co-investors.** He promised that his senior team, including himself, would invest alongside outside investors in the fund. (Cafemutual, 2015)
- **Family and staff too.** He, his family and key employees put personal money into the fund. (Cafemutual, 2015 · Value Research, 2015)
- **Closing the broking.** He shut his broking business and surrendered the licence to avoid conflicts of interest with the mutual fund. (Value Research, 2015 · Moneylife, 2015)
- **What he refused.** He rejected quick-gain tactics such as futures and options trading, and upfront commissions to attract clients. (Talk, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-07-skin-in-the-game.html

### 8. One fund, not a grocery shop

While fund houses launched scheme after scheme, he launched one. One clear way of investing, he argued, serves investors better.

- **One scheme.** PPFAS launched just one fund, managed in a go-anywhere style, so as not to confuse investors. (Cafemutual, 2015 · Value Research, 2015)
- **One right way.** There is only one right way of investing, he said; you can't have twenty. (Cafemutual, 2015)
- **Look abroad.** His fund could also buy shares overseas, including in the US. (Value Research, 2015)
- **Dividends and AGMs.** He saw a fund's dividend as just your own money handed back, and his fund was the first to hold unitholder meetings like company AGMs. (Value Research, 2015 · Moneylife, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-08-one-fund-not-a-grocery-shop.html

### 9. Standing up to the system

He was outspoken about the failings of India's finance industry, and argued with the regulator when he thought a rule would hurt competition.

- **An iconoclast.** His firm's tribute page calls him an iconoclast. (PPFAS)
- **The 2010 fight.** When a SEBI committee proposed sharply raising the money needed to run a mutual fund, he argued it would shut out new, smaller competitors. (BS, 2015)
- **A pass-through.** A mutual fund, he insisted, merely passes investors' money through; it is not a bank. The proposal was shelved. (BS, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-09-standing-up-to-the-system.html

### 10. A firm built to outlast him

He died suddenly in 2015, in Omaha, after Warren Buffett's annual meeting. The firm he built, run on his principles, carried on without him.

- **Omaha.** He died in a road accident on 3 May 2015, travelling with colleagues after the Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting. (Moneylife, 2015 · Cafemutual, 2015)
- **Built to last.** He set out to build an organisation and a team able to run without him. (PPFAS)
- **A long commitment.** His fund asked investors to think in terms of at least five years, holding quality through market cycles. (Value Research, 2015)
- **Against the odds.** Business Standard described his life as a journey from a childhood with polio to one of India's best-regarded value investors. (BS, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parikh-10-a-firm-built-to-outlast-him.html

## Special section

**Which bias is this? Tap your answer**

- A WhatsApp group says a small company will double. Everyone you know is buying, so you buy too. Answer: Herd behaviour. Buying because others are buying. His books warn that the crowd is usually late.
- You bought at ₹500. It is ₹300 and the business has got worse, but you won't sell until it's back to ₹500. Answer: Loss aversion. Refusing to take a loss. The market doesn't know or care what you paid.
- Your Diwali bonus feels like free money, so you gamble it on options instead of investing it. Answer: Mental accounting. A rupee is a rupee, wherever it came from. Treat a bonus like any other savings.
- You keep shares your father left you, though you would never buy them at today's price. Answer: Endowment effect. Valuing something more because you own it. Ask: would I buy this today?
- You paid ₹50,000 for a trading course, so you keep trading to make it worthwhile, though you keep losing. Answer: Sunk cost fallacy. Money already spent is gone. Only future costs and benefits should decide.
- There are so many mutual fund schemes that you can't choose, so your savings sit idle for years. Answer: Decision paralysis. Too many choices freeze you. One reason he launched only one fund.

**His four marks of a good business**

- Credible management that treats minority shareholders fairly.
- A simple business you can understand.
- A strong moat that keeps competitors out.
- Pricing power, so profits can keep up with costs.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security. This site is not registered with SEBI as an investment adviser or research analyst. Companies are named for history and education only.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “Value investing is boring. You have to wait for years.” (Morningstar investment conference, 2014)
- “AMCs launch funds like a fad. We don't want to be grocery shop.” (Interview with Cafemutual, quoted 2015)
- “The dividend is just your returns being given back to you.” (Quoted by Value Research, 2015)
- “It is a pass-through!” (On mutual funds, 2010, recalled by Business Standard)

## Read the originals

Start with Stocks to Riches (2005). It is short, plain and full of Indian examples.

- [Stocks to Riches: Insights on Investor Behaviour](https://amc.ppfas.com/knowledge-center/parags-views/books/): Why investors fail: speculation, loss aversion, the sunk cost fallacy, the endowment effect, mental accounting, decision paralysis and rules of thumb, with Indian examples.
- [Value Investing and Behavioural Finance](https://amc.ppfas.com/knowledge-center/parags-views/books/): Three decades of Indian market history read through greed and fear, including chapters on IPOs and the growth trap, and a case for contrarian value investing.
- [What made Parag Parikh a great investor](https://morningstar.in/posts/32853/what-made-parag-parikh-a-great-investor.aspx): Value investing in India, patience, his watchlist, the qualities of a good business, and what to avoid.
- [Parag Parikh dies in a car accident in USA](https://cafemutual.com/news/industry/3744-parag-parikh-dies-in-a-car-accident-in-usa): His career, his single fund, co-investing with clients, and his views on fund houses that launch schemes like a fad.
- [RIP Parag Parikh, a true-blue value investor](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/27810/rip-parag-parikh-a-true-blue-value-investor/): One go-anywhere fund, overseas shares, closing the broking business, his view of dividends, and India's first unitholder meetings.
- [Remembrance: when Parag Parikh got (a little) angry](https://www.business-standard.com/article/opinion/remembrance-when-parag-parikh-got-a-little-angry-115050500344_1.html): His start in 1979, the technology boom, and his fight against higher entry barriers for new mutual funds.
- [Chandrakant Sampat: grand old man of Dalal Street](https://www.business-standard.com/article/markets/chandrakant-sampat-grand-old-man-of-dalal-street-115020201089_1.html): How Sampat steered a young Parikh from manufacturing to the stock market.
- [Parag Parikh, promoter of PPFAS Mutual Fund, dies in a crash](https://moneylife.in/article/parag-parikh-promoter-of-ppfas-mutual-fund-dies-in-a-crash/41556.html): The facts of his death, his books, surrendering his broking licence for the fund, and the industry's first unitholders' meeting.
- [Dalal Street veteran Parag Parikh killed in US car accident](https://www.business-standard.com/article/current-affairs/dalal-street-veteran-parag-parikh-dies-in-omaha-115050400135_1.html): His journey from a childhood with polio to one of India's best-regarded value investors, and his start as a sub-broker.
- [Remembering Parag Parikh](https://amc.ppfas.com/paragparikh/): How his firm remembers him: an iconoclast who built an organisation meant to outlast him.

## Words to know

- **Behavioural finance**: The study of how emotions and mental shortcuts shape investors' decisions.
- **Sub-broker**: An agent who dealt through a registered stockbroker, often a first step into broking.
- **AMC**: Asset management company: the firm that runs a mutual fund.
- **PMS**: Portfolio management service: a manager running a separate portfolio for each wealthy client.
- **Herd behaviour**: Doing what everyone else does because they are doing it.
- **Loss aversion**: Feeling a loss about twice as strongly as an equal gain.
- **Mental accounting**: Treating money differently depending on where it came from, such as a bonus.
- **Endowment effect**: Valuing something more just because you own it.
- **SEBI**: The Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Stocks to Riches (2005) and Value Investing and Behavioural Finance (2009), his views at a Morningstar conference (2014), interviews and obituaries in Cafemutual, Value Research, Moneylife and Business Standard (2015), and PPFAS's own tribute and books pages. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Parikh's returns as a broker and portfolio manager were not published in full, so we show none. His fund continues today; it is mentioned for history only, not as a recommendation.

# Radhakishan Damani

> Dalal Street's famous bear turned patient investor, then built DMart from one Mumbai store on low costs, owned shops and fast payments.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/damani.html · Section: India · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Leave the small pond. Be a small fish in a big sea rather than the biggest in a pond.

## Summary

Radhakishan Damani was a famous bear, or short seller, on Dalal Street in the Harshad Mehta years, then a patient long-term investor, and then, from 2000, the founder of DMart, one of India's most successful retailers. He almost never speaks in public. His lessons are in what he did: own quality, keep costs lower than anyone, pay suppliers fast, own the shop, and grow slowly until the model is proven.

## Record at a glance

- **2000**: conceived DMart, after leaving active stock market trading
- **365 stores**: by March 2024, from two in its first year
- **104 times**: how many times DMart's ₹1,870 crore IPO was subscribed in March 2017
- **≈ 85%**: share of DMart's stores it owned rather than rented in 2017, by one analyst's count

## Big ideas

### 1. Leave the small pond

He did not start in the market. He ran a ball-bearings business until an uncle asked him: how rich is the top ball-bearings trader, next to Dalal Street's biggest names?

- **Dalal Street family.** He grew up in Mumbai, where his father worked on Dalal Street, and left college after a year of commerce. (BS, 2020)
- **Ball bearings.** He first ran a ball-bearings business and had no interest in the stock market. (BS, 2020)
- **The uncle's lesson.** After his father died, an uncle reportedly persuaded him that real wealth meant leaving a small pond, even as its biggest fish. (BS, 2020)
- **Bull and bear.** On Dalal Street he became skilled at both kinds of bet: on rises and on falls. (BS, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-01-leave-the-small-pond.html

### 2. The bear in the Harshad Mehta years

In the early 1990s, while Harshad Mehta drove prices to dizzying heights with borrowed money, Damani bet on a fall. He was right, but it hurt before it paid.

- **On the short side.** He was a known bear, and twice took the other side of Harshad Mehta's rallies, winning both times. (BS, 2017)
- **The painful trade.** He sold ACC shares at about ₹3,000 and kept selling as they rose towards ₹10,000. Losses mounted until the prices finally cracked. (BS, 2020)
- **A bear's school.** He was a keen follower of Manu Manek, a famous short seller of his early years. (Profile)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-02-the-bear-in-the-harshad-mehta-years.html

### 3. From trader to owner

Influenced by Chandrakant Sampat, he moved from trading to owning quality businesses for years. Fund managers said they could never tell which hat he was wearing.

- **Sampat's influence.** He has often said he was inspired by Chandrakant Sampat, whom he met in the early 1990s. (Profile)
- **HDFC Bank.** By market folklore he was the largest individual shareholder of HDFC Bank at its 1995 listing, and kept buying. (BS, 2017)
- **Quality costs more.** He was willing to pay up for HDFC Bank; in his view, quality commands a premium. (BS, 2017)
- **Both at once.** A fund manager said it was impossible to follow him, never knowing whether he was investing or trading in a share. (BS, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-03-from-trader-to-owner.html

### 4. Listen more than you talk

He rarely speaks in public and has never appeared on television. Friends say he says little and listens a lot, asking people what they see.

- **Silence.** He rarely speaks publicly, has never appeared on television, and keeps his views to himself. (BS, 2017)
- **A listener.** People who know him say he listens far more than he speaks. (BS, 2017)
- **The shopper first.** When a friend complained that DMart staff hovered around him while he shopped, Damani told them never to do it again. (BS, 2017)
- **No interviews.** He did not respond to Business Standard's interview request for its 2020 profile. (BS, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-04-listen-more-than-you-talk.html

### 5. Why a shop?

In 2000, at the height of his market success, he turned to retailing, after studying how Indians shop.

- **Research first.** The company says he spent a couple of years in research and reflection, testing his ideas about the Indian consumer, before starting. (Annual report, 2023)
- **Apna Bazaar.** In the late 1990s he ran a franchise of Apna Bazaar, a cooperative store chain, in Navi Mumbai. DMart refined the idea. (BS, 2020)
- **Conceived in 2000.** DMart's own annual report says he conceived the chain in 2000. (Annual report, 2019)
- **Walmart.** He was reportedly inspired by reading about Walmart. (BS, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-05-why-a-shop.html

### 6. Everyday low cost, everyday low price

DMart's model is simple to say and hard to copy: keep costs lower than anyone, so prices can be lower than anyone's, every day, without flashy discounts.

- **EDLC/EDLP.** The company offers value retailing using its Everyday Low Cost, Everyday Low Price principle. (Annual report, 2019)
- **Buy direct, pay fast.** It buys directly from manufacturers and pays vendors early, which earns better purchase prices. (Research, 2017)
- **A week, not months.** It reportedly pays suppliers within about a week, against the usual three months. (BS, 2020)
- **Fast-moving goods.** It focuses on items that sell quickly, and on high sales from every square foot. (BS, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-06-everyday-low-cost-everyday-low-price.html

### 7. Own the shop

Most retailers rent. DMart prefers to buy land and build its own stores, which keeps costs stable and avoids rent shocks.

- **Buy, then build.** Its chief executive has said the company typically prefers to buy land and then construct the buildings. (Annual report, 2019)
- **Mostly owned.** In 2017 an analyst counted about 85% of its 131 stores as owned. (Research, 2017)
- **A model, not a policy.** Store ownership is part of the low-cost model that lets it keep prices low. (DSIJ, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-07-own-the-shop.html

### 8. Slow, then fast

He grew DMart slowly for years, proving the model in a few regions before expanding. Then it grew quickly, cluster by cluster.

- **Eight years, ten stores.** DMart took eight years to open its first ten stores. The company says he wanted to prove the model both profitable and scalable first. (Annual report, 2023)
- **Then faster.** It had about 25 stores by 2010, then sped up. (BS, 2017)
- **Clusters.** The company deepens its presence where it already operates before moving to new regions. (Annual report, 2019 · Annual report, 2023)
- **The count.** It had 176 stores in 11 states and a union territory in 2019, and 365 by March 2024. (Annual report, 2019 · DSIJ, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-08-slow-then-fast.html

### 9. Frugal at the top

The man who became one of India's richest kept DMart's head office in a corner of an early store and worked without hierarchy.

- **A corner of a store.** For years DMart's corporate office was a small space carved out of one of its early stores. (Annual report, 2019)
- **No hierarchy.** He and his early team worked as one unit, without hierarchy or barriers. (Annual report, 2019)
- **A shared room.** After the IPO he reportedly shared a budget hotel room with his buying team on a trip to China. (BS, 2020)
- **The founder's thinking.** The company credits its success to the values and way of thinking he instilled. (Annual report, 2023)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-09-frugal-at-the-top.html

### 10. Listing day, and an honest note

In 2017 DMart's listing showed what patient building can be worth. And since this library puts integrity first, we also set out the one regulatory matter on record.

- **The IPO.** Avenue Supermarts' ₹1,870 crore IPO, priced at ₹299 a share, was subscribed more than 104 times. (Listing, 2017)
- **First day.** The shares listed on 21 March 2017 at more than double the issue price. (Listing, 2017)
- **The 2007 order.** SEBI examined trading by three broking firms of the R.S. Damani group in 2001. It found no evidence of manipulation, but censured the firms for delays in moving shares to clients. (SEBI, 2007)
- **Not a party.** Damani appeared at the hearing as a director of one firm; the order was against the three companies, not him personally. (SEBI, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/damani-10-listing-day-and-an-honest-note.html

## Special section

**Tap each step of the DMart flywheel** 

**An honest note.** SEBI's order of 2 January 2007 concerned three broking firms of the R.S. Damani group: Damani Shares & Stock Brokers, Maheshwari Equity Brokers and Avenue Stock Brokers. SEBI examined their sales of Infosys shares on 23 February and 2 March 2001, and other dealings. It found no evidence of price manipulation, held that alleged links to two other market groups were not established, and found the firms had broadly complied with short-sale rules. The one violation upheld was that the firms had moved securities from their pool accounts to clients' accounts later than the 15-day limit. SEBI treated this as a technical violation with no bad intent, and imposed censure, a minor penalty. Radhakishan Damani appeared at the hearing as a director of one firm; he was not a party to the order. We include it because this library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security. This site is not registered with SEBI as an investment adviser or research analyst. Companies are named for history and education only.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “imagined the retail business with the same values of simplicity, speed and nimbleness” (Avenue Supermarts annual report 2018-19, on its founder)
- “the way of business thinking that our founder has instilled in us” (Avenue Supermarts annual report 2022-23)

## Read the originals

Start with the first pages of any recent Avenue Supermarts annual report, where the company describes its founder and its model, then Business Standard's 2020 profile.

- [Avenue Supermarts annual report 2018-19](https://bseindia.com/bseplus/AnnualReport/540376/5403760319.pdf): How the company describes its founder, its core values, the EDLC/EDLP principle, buying land for stores, and cluster-based expansion.
- [Avenue Supermarts annual report 2022-23](https://bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/73ffab69-cd41-4f5d-a4d4-0c1894813d31.pdf): The founder's slow, deliberate start, the early office in a store, his influence on the company, and its cluster-based growth.
- [Meet D-Mart's Radhakishan Damani, the silent giant of stock markets](https://business-standard.com/article/markets/meet-d-mart-s-radhakishan-damani-the-silent-giant-of-stock-markets-117032301462_1.html): The trader and the investor: shorting in the Harshad Mehta years, HDFC Bank, his long-term holdings, and his silence.
- [The rise of DMart's Radhakishan Damani](https://business-standard.com/article/markets/the-rise-of-dmart-s-radhakishan-damani-who-got-richer-during-lockdown-120042401376_1.html): His early life, the lesson that took him to Dalal Street, the costly short, Apna Bazaar, and the habits behind DMart.
- [Avenue Supermarts settles with stellar premium on debut](https://www.business-standard.com/article/news-cm/avenue-supermarts-settles-with-stellar-premium-on-debut-117032100698_1.html): The IPO at ₹299 a share, subscribed 104.59 times, and the first day's close at ₹640.75.
- [Avenue Supermarts: delivering value](https://www.motilaloswal.com/site/rreports/HTML/636337193984127111/index.htm): An analyst's account of the EDLC/EDLP model: store ownership, direct sourcing, and paying vendors early.
- [Avenue Supermarts (DMart)](https://insights.dsij.in/dsijarticledetail/avenue-supermarts-dmart-42221): DMart's ownership model, everyday low pricing, and its 365 stores at March 2024.
- [Radhakishan Damani's portfolio and lessons](https://equitymaster.com/timeless-reading/radhakishan-damani-portfolio): His mentors, his short-selling years, and his move to long-term investing.
- [Order in the matter of R.S. Damani Group](https://www.sebi.gov.in/enforcement/orders/jan-2007/order-in-the-matter-of-rs-damani-group_7804.html): SEBI's findings on three broking firms of the group: no manipulation proved; censure for delays in moving shares to clients.

## Words to know

- **Short selling**: Selling borrowed shares, hoping to buy them back cheaper after a fall.
- **Bear**: An investor who expects prices to fall.
- **EDLC/EDLP**: Everyday Low Cost, Everyday Low Price: keeping costs lowest so prices can stay low every day.
- **Cluster expansion**: Opening new stores near existing ones before entering new regions.
- **IPO**: Initial public offering: a company's first sale of shares to the public.
- **Subscribed 104 times**: Investors applied for 104 times as many shares as were on offer.
- **Censure**: A formal reprimand from a regulator; a minor penalty.
- **Pool account**: An account where a broker holds clients' shares before passing them on.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Avenue Supermarts annual reports (2018-19 and 2022-23), Business Standard profiles (2017 and 2020), reports of the 2017 listing, Motilal Oswal's 2017 research initiation, a 2024 DSIJ report, an Equitymaster profile, and SEBI's 2007 order on the R.S. Damani group. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

Damani has given almost no interviews and has written nothing for publication, so this page describes his record rather than his words. Where reports are only market folklore, we say 'reportedly'. DMart is named for history and education only.

# Seiroku Honda

> A poor farmer's son who saved a quarter of every pay cheque from 25, invested it, and gave almost all of it away when he retired.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/honda.html · Section: Japan · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Save first. Set aside a quarter the day the money arrives, before spending anything.

## Summary

Seiroku Honda was born poor in 1866, became Japan's first doctor of forestry, and designed the forest of Meiji Shrine and parks across Japan. From the age of 25 he saved a quarter of every pay cheque before spending a yen, invested the savings in shares and forest land, and by 40 earned more from interest and dividends than from his salary. When he retired he gave almost all of it away. His 1950 book, My Confession of Wealth, is still read by Japanese savers today.

## Record at a glance

- **¼**: of every pay cheque saved first, from age 25, plus every bonus and windfall
- **Age 40**: when interest and dividends passed his professor's salary
- **30+**: industries he owned shares in: railways, gas, power, paper, beer, spinning, cement and more
- **2,600 ha**: of Chichibu forest he gave to Saitama, whose income still funds student loans

## Big ideas

### 1. A poor farmer's son

He was born poor in 1866, studied his way up, and became Japan's first doctor of forestry and the designer of famous parks and forests.

- **Humble start.** He was born in 1866 into a poor farming family in what is now Kuki, Saitama, and studied through hardship. (JPX, education · Saitama, 2024)
- **First of his kind.** He became Japan's first doctor of forestry and a professor at the Imperial University in Tokyo. (Rakuten, 2018 · Saitama, 2024)
- **Father of parks.** He designed parks across Japan, including Hibiya Park in Tokyo, and the forest of Meiji Shrine. (MUFG Bank, 2020 · Saitama, 2024)
- **Remembered for money.** Today he is remembered at least as much for how he saved and invested as for his parks. (MUFG Bank, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-01-a-poor-farmers-son.html

### 2. The quarter rule

Every time pay arrived, he set aside a quarter before spending anything, and saved every bonus and windfall in full.

- **First, not last.** He saved a quarter of each pay cheque the day it arrived, treating it as money he had never received. (JPX, education · MUFG Bank, 2020)
- **Windfalls too.** Bonuses and other one-off income went entirely into savings. (JPX, education · President)
- **The harvest image.** In his words, if you earn 40 yen, think you received 30 and put 10 away. (JPX, education)
- **Doing, not knowing.** He insisted that saving is a matter of doing it, not of finding the right method. (Daiwa, 2021)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-02-the-quarter-rule.html

### 3. Hard years by choice

The rule hurt. With a large household, money ran out each month. He held firm, choosing hardship early rather than being forced into it later.

- **Salt and sesame.** At the end of some months the family ate rice with only salt and sesame, and the children cried. (JPX, education)
- **No exceptions.** He persuaded his family that the rule was right and would not let feeling override it. (JPX, education · Daiwa, 2021)
- **Thrift by choice.** He argued that you should not cut back because poverty forces you to, but save on purpose to overpower poverty. (President · JPX, education)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-03-hard-years-by-choice.html

### 4. Vanity is the enemy

He saw the wish to look well-off as the biggest obstacle to saving, and believed early hardship makes for a better life later.

- **Vanity.** Wanting to live better than others, or just to look as if you do, is what wrecks saving. (JPX, education)
- **Spoiled young, poor later.** He wrote that those raised in luxury tend to become poor, while those who meet poverty early do better later. (JPX, education)
- **Pass it early.** Since everyone goes through a poor stretch at some point, he thought it best to get it over with young. (JPX, education)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-04-vanity-is-the-enemy.html

### 5. The snowball

Savings, once they form a core, grow by themselves. By 40 his interest and dividends earned more than his salary.

- **Like a snowball.** He wrote that money is like a snowball: tiny at first, but once a core forms it grows remarkably. (President)
- **A small start.** His first monthly saving was 14 yen and 50 sen. (President)
- **Pay and interest together.** After two or three years, interest began to arrive, so life slowly became easier. (JPX, education)
- **The milestone.** Fifteen years in, at 40, his interest and dividends were far larger than his salary. (President · Rakuten, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-05-the-snowball.html

### 6. Own good businesses, widely

He put his savings into the sound companies of his day, starting with railways and spreading across more than thirty industries.

- **Thirty railway shares.** His first purchase was 30 shares of Nippon Railway at 12.50 yen each, on a professor's advice that railways had a future. (JPX, education)
- **Bought out.** When the railways were nationalised, his shares were bought at about 2.5 times what he paid. (JPX, education)
- **Spread out.** As railway prospects dimmed he moved on, owning good shares across more than 30 industries, from gas and power to beer and cement. (President · JPX, education)
- **No gambling.** He kept away from speculation and stuck to sound investment. (JPX, education)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-06-own-good-businesses-widely.html

### 7. Invest in what you know: his forest

As a forester, he understood land and trees. He bought natural forest in the Chichibu mountains, and it became part of his fortune, and later his gift.

- **His own field.** He bought natural forest in the Chichibu mountains, close to his expertise. (JPX, education · Saitama Pref.)
- **A timber boom.** After the Russo-Japanese War timber prices soared, and he sold part of his forest at about 70 times its cost. (JPX, education)
- **2,600 hectares.** His forest holdings near Nakatsugawa in Chichibu covered about 2,600 hectares. (Saitama Pref.)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-07-invest-in-what-you-know-his-forest.html

### 8. Take a modest profit, protect the principal

He followed a simple selling rule: take a 20% gain when it comes, and if a holding doubles, sell half so the original money is safe.

- **Twenty per cent.** On some positions, if he reached a 20% gain, he took it in full and put the money on deposit, without chasing more. (JPX, education)
- **Sell half at double.** If a holding more than doubled, he sold half at once, getting his original money back. (JPX, education)
- **Then relax.** With the principal safe, a later crash could not hurt him, and further gains were a bonus. (JPX, education)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-08-take-a-modest-profit-protect-the-principal.html

### 9. Patience, and no shame about money

He waited patiently for good chances, invested boldly when times were bad, and rejected the old samurai pose of looking down on money.

- **Three steps.** Save a quarter; invest once a little has built up; wait patiently for good chances without forcing anything. (MUFG Bank, 2020)
- **Bad times, good chances.** Downturns pushed share prices down, and he invested actively when they did. (MUFG Bank, 2020)
- **Money matters.** He criticised the feudal habit of pretending to scorn money, calling money useful and worth having. (JPX, education)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-09-patience-and-no-shame-about-money.html

### 10. Give it back

At 60 he retired and gave almost everything away, mostly anonymously. His forest still pays for students' education in Saitama.

- **Wealth is not happiness.** He concluded that great wealth and fame do not guarantee happiness. (JPX, education)
- **Almost everything.** On retiring in 1927 he gave nearly all his assets to public causes, mostly without his name. (JPX, education · Saitama Pref.)
- **A forest for students.** Saitama's scholarship in his name, funded by income from his donated forest, has lent to students since 1954. (Saitama Pref.)
- **Still lending.** In 2024 it still offered interest-free loans of up to 30,000 yen a month to Saitama students. (Saitama, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/honda-10-give-it-back.html

## Special section

**Try the quarter rule on your own pay** 

**His three steps**

- Save a quarter of income first, and every windfall in full.
- Invest once a little has built up.
- Wait patiently for good chances, without forcing anything.

**His selling rule**

- A 20% gain: take it, bank it, and don't chase more.
- A double: sell half at once, so the original money is safe.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Many sources for this page are in Japanese; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “金と言うものは雪達磨のようなもので” (“Money is like a snowball.” From My Confession of Wealth, 1950, as quoted by President (our translation))
- “貯金の問題は、方法の如何ではなく、実行の如何である” (“Saving is a question not of method, but of doing it.” From My Confession of Wealth, as quoted by Daiwa (our translation))
- “人生即努力、努力即幸福” (“Life is effort; effort is happiness.” His motto, cited by his publisher (our translation))

## Read the originals

If you read Japanese, start with 私の財産告白 (My Confession of Wealth, 1950). If not, start with the stock exchange's education article and the Saitama Prefecture story of his gifts.

- [私の財産告白 (My Confession of Wealth)](https://www.hanmoto.com/bd/isbn/9784408551227): His account of how he saved a quarter of his pay, invested it, built a fortune and gave it away, and what he learned about money and happiness.
- [Honda Seiroku's saving and investing](https://money-bu-jpx.com/news/article002718/): The quarter rule in practice, his family's hard years, vanity, his first shares and forest, his selling rule, and his gifts.
- [Honda Seiroku's way of building wealth](https://president.jp/articles/-/111122): His first savings, the industries he invested in, the age-40 milestone, and his snowball idea in his own words.
- [Learning from the 'father of parks'](https://www.bk.mufg.jp/column/shisan_unyo/0020.html): His three steps: save a quarter, invest once a little has built up, and wait patiently for good chances.
- [Life-plan column on the quarter method](https://www.daiwa.jp/lp_dc/ideco/column/article_159/): How he carried out the quarter rule with a large household, quoted from his book.
- [Japan's Buffett: Honda Seiroku's wealth-building](https://media.rakuten-sec.net/articles/-/29878): His life as professor and park designer, and how his savings became a fortune.
- [Dr Honda Seiroku: his scholarship work](https://www.pref.saitama.lg.jp/documents/231096/hondadouga_no5.pdf): How he gave most of his wealth to public causes, including the forest that still funds students from Saitama.
- [Honda Seiroku scholarship: call for applicants](https://www.pref.saitama.lg.jp/documents/257306/news2024082801.pdf): The scholarship today: interest-free loans for Saitama students, paid for by the forest he donated.

## Words to know

- **Tenbiki (天引き)**: Deducting money at source, before you can spend it.
- **Meiji era**: 1868 to 1912: Japan's rapid modernisation under Emperor Meiji.
- **Sen (銭)**: A hundredth of a yen, used in his day.
- **Nippon Railway**: A private railway company of the Meiji era, nationalised in 1906.
- **Hectare**: 10,000 square metres, about 2.5 acres.
- **Bushi kuwanedo takayōji**: 'A samurai picks his teeth even when he hasn't eaten': keeping up appearances while pretending to scorn money.
- **Dividend**: The share of profit a company pays to its shareholders.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his book 私の財産告白 (1950) as published and as quoted by Japanese financial firms; articles by Japan Exchange Group's education site, MUFG Bank, Daiwa Securities, Rakuten Securities and President; and Saitama Prefecture's official materials on his life, gifts and scholarship. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

His book is in Japanese and has no official English edition, so this page relies on Japanese summaries of it and translates short lines ourselves. Modern-money estimates of his wealth vary and are only rough.

# Wahei Takeda

> Made Japan's favourite baby biscuit, then became a patient shareholder in over a hundred companies, treating each as a field to tend.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/takeda.html · Section: Japan · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Investing, not speculating. Owning a company to support it is not the same as betting on its price.

## Summary

Wahei Takeda built Takeda Seika into Japan's biggest maker of tamago boro, the little egg biscuits Japanese babies grow up on. From 1956 he invested the company's spare cash, and after a painful lesson moved to small and mid-sized companies, becoming a large shareholder in more than a hundred of them. Japan called him its Warren Buffett. He called being a shareholder being the company's danna, its patron.

## Record at a glance

- **1956**: the year he began investing the company's spare cash, at 23
- **100+**: listed companies in which he became a large individual shareholder
- **P/E ≈ 10**: the price he liked to pay: about ten times earnings
- **Gold**: medals he sent companies to thank them for their dividends

## Big ideas

### 1. The biscuit maker

He was a confectioner first. He turned a sweet sold loose by weight into a bagged, machine-made product, and built Japan's biggest tamago boro maker.

- **A confectioner's son.** Born in Aichi in 1933 to a family of sweet makers, he was his father's right hand while still a teenager after the war. (MUFG, 2024)
- **A simple idea.** Tamago boro was sold loose by weight in sweet shops. He saw it could be sold in bags, and automated production before rivals did. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Takeda Seika.** He founded the company in 1952; it became Japan's largest tamago boro maker, also known for the Mugi Fah wafer. (Obituary, 2016 · MUFG, 2024)
- **A poor craftsman.** His interviewer described him as a once-poor confectioner who became Japan's biggest individual investor. (Book, 2008)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-01-the-biscuit-maker.html

### 2. From speculator to investor

He began by trading famous shares for quick profit. Later he called that speculation, and drew a sharp line between betting on prices and owning a business to support it.

- **Spare cash.** In 1956, at 23, once the company was stable, he began investing its surplus cash. (MUFG, 2024)
- **A friend's tip.** A friendship with a securities branch manager led to his first purchase, which rose quickly. (Interview, 2015)
- **Short-term at first.** He started with big blue chips and traded for quick gains, which he later called speculation, not investment. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Similar, not the same.** Gambling-style speculation and investing to support a company look alike, he said, but are different things. (Interview, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-02-from-speculator-to-investor.html

### 3. The lesson of a collapse

In the 1990s a large company in which he was the top individual shareholder went bankrupt, its managers insisting all was well to the end. He sold his large companies and turned to smaller ones he could understand.

- **Fine until it wasn't.** Management kept saying the business was fine right up to the bankruptcy. (MUFG, 2024)
- **A clean break.** He sold all his large-company shares and moved to small and mid-sized listed companies. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Faces, not size.** He came to prefer companies where you can see the manager's face over big, impressive ones. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Plain accounts.** He valued simple, easy-to-read financial statements and knowing the management directly. (MUFG, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-03-the-lesson-of-a-collapse.html

### 4. Be the danna

In old Japan a danna was a patron who stood behind a business or an artist. He said that becoming a shareholder means becoming the company's danna.

- **His motto.** To be a shareholder is to be the company's danna, its patron. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Nurture, then wait.** He held with a nurturing attitude, waiting for the price to rise; if it didn't, he was content with dividends from a cheap purchase. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Cheer them on.** He encouraged struggling managers to run their business joyfully and recover, so dividends would follow. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Gold for thanks.** To thank companies for their dividends he sent them pure gold medals, a habit he kept all his life. (MUFG, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-04-be-the-danna.html

### 5. Fields and harvests

He saw investing as farming. Shares are the field and dividends the harvest. A good farmer watches the harvest, not the price of the land.

- **The farm.** Stocks are the field and dividends the harvest; watch the yearly harvest, not the price of the land. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Sow and replant.** Plant seeds in companies likely to bloom, take your share of the fruit, then plant again. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Never withdrawn.** He reinvested his dividends again and again, and his holdings grew past 10 billion yen. (MUFG, 2024)
- **The right season.** His interviewer titled the book with a gardener's rule: don't sow flower seeds in midsummer. (Book, 2008)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-05-fields-and-harvests.html

### 6. Cheap, sound and generous

He wanted shares that were cheap against earnings, companies with strong balance sheets, and managers who shared profits with shareholders.

- **About ten times.** Ideally he paid about ten times earnings, which he linked to a roughly 10% earnings yield. (Interview, 2015)
- **Two numbers.** He watched the payout ratio, how much profit goes to dividends, and the equity ratio, a sign of financial strength. (MUFG, 2024)
- **Skill shows.** He used return on equity to find companies that were both profitable and cheap. (Interview, 2015)
- **Never overpay.** He warned that buying overpriced shares always loses money in the end. (Interview, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-06-cheap-sound-and-generous.html

### 7. Dividends first

Dividends, not price gains, were the core of his returns. He noted that dividends hold up far better than prices in bad times.

- **The main source.** Dividends were his main return; in 2015 he expected about 350 million yen of tax on them. (Interview, 2015)
- **Steadier than prices.** Even if a share price halved, he said, dividends usually fell by no more than about 10%. (Interview, 2015)
- **Steady growth.** He aimed for companies with steady future growth that would pay good dividends. (Profile, 2015)
- **Glad for them.** He chose companies whose rising profits he could be truly happy about. (Profile, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-07-dividends-first.html

### 8. Calm in storms

He used only spare money, never borrowed to the limit, and refused to panic. A share price, he said, may go up or down; either is fine.

- **Up or down.** He shrugged off falls with a short verse: a share price is fine going down and fine going up. (Interview, 2015)
- **Lehman.** In the 2008 crash his holdings showed large paper losses, and he held on. (Interview, 2015)
- **Spare money only.** He invested only surplus funds and warned never to use margin to the limit. (Interview, 2015)
- **One book.** He said his only information source was the Shikiho company handbook, with no special inside sources. (Interview, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-08-calm-in-storms.html

### 9. When to sell

He held for the long run, but sold when a share looked overvalued, and lost patience with companies that hoarded cash instead of rewarding owners.

- **No small gains.** He held for the long term and did not sell quickly to lock in small profits. (Interview, 2015)
- **No greed.** Sell when a share looks overvalued; don't wait for the top. (Interview, 2015)
- **Hoarders.** Profitable companies that keep piling up retained earnings show poor prospects and little respect for shareholders, he said. (Interview, 2015)
- **Fewer, later.** At 82 he had cut from over 130 holdings to about 25, citing a proposed tax on large holders, the need for global reach, and the time research takes. (Interview, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-09-when-to-sell.html

### 10. Sincerity, and giving back

He believed sincerity passed from person to person brings success and happiness, ran a circle to develop young people, and gave back much of what he gained.

- **A chain of sincerity.** His philosophy: a chain of sincerity brings success and happiness. (Interview, 2015)
- **Marowa-ko.** He led a group called Marowa-ko to develop people, and returned his experience and wealth to society. (MUFG, 2024)
- **A hundred heroes in gold.** He had gold coins struck of a hundred figures from Japanese history, displayed in a hall he planned in Nagoya. (Talk, 2011 · His book, 2005)
- **Remembered.** He died on 21 July 2016, aged 83; fans thanked him for the biscuits and investors called him a model. (Obituary, 2016)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/takeda-10-sincerity-and-giving-back.html

## Special section

**Would he be this company's danna?**

- The share is cheap: around ten times earnings, or less
- It pays a healthy share of its profit as dividends
- Its equity ratio is strong: little reliance on debt
- You can see the manager's face, and you know who runs it
- Its accounts are simple enough to read yourself
- Its success would make you genuinely glad
- It does not pile up cash it cannot use
- You are buying with spare money, not borrowed money

**The farmer's year**

- Sow in companies likely to bloom, when the season is right.
- Tend as a patron: encourage, don't harass.
- Harvest the dividends, year after year.
- Replant the harvest, and let it grow.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Many sources for this page are in Japanese; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “割高な株を買うといつか必ず損をします” (“Buy overpriced shares and you will lose, sooner or later.” Gendai Business interview, 2015 (our translation))
- “株主になるとはその会社の「旦那」になること” (“To become a shareholder is to become the company's danna.” His motto, from MUFG Securities' profile (our translation))

## Read the originals

If you read Japanese, start with 花のタネは真夏に播くな (Don't Sow Flower Seeds in Midsummer), a book of long interviews with him. If not, start with the MUFG Securities profile.

- [Japan's top individual shareholder speaks](https://gendai.media/articles/-/42374): His views at 82: investing versus speculation, the price he pays, dividends, staying calm, what he sells, and why he cut his holdings.
- [Learning from the masters: Wahei Takeda](https://www.sc.mufg.jp/market/mnl/pdf/mnl202406/mnl_moneyphil_202406.pdf): His life, how he began investing, the collapse that changed him, the danna idea, his farming image, and his gold medals.
- [花のタネは真夏に播くな (Don't Sow Flower Seeds in Midsummer)](https://books.bunshun.jp/ud/book/num/9784167756017): How a poor confectioner became Japan's biggest individual investor, and his 'danna-style' investing philosophy.
- [人生を拓く「百尊」の教え](https://www.kodansha.co.jp/book/products/0000182722): His teaching on virtue, built around gold coins he had struck of a hundred great figures from Japanese history.
- [How Wahei Takeda succeeded](https://life.oricon.co.jp/rank_certificate/news/2061107/): His aim of steady growth and dividends, and choosing companies whose success you would be truly glad of.
- [A conversation with Wahei Takeda](https://www.kenbiya.com/ar/cl/kenbiya-ac/2.html): His hall of gold coins honouring great figures of Japanese history, and his thoughts on rebuilding after the 2011 earthquake.
- [Tamago boro's Wahei Takeda dies](https://www.j-cast.com/2016/07/22273252.html): His death at 83, the company he founded in 1952, and how fans and investors remembered him.

## Words to know

- **Danna (旦那)**: A patron who supports a business or an artist; also a master of a household.
- **Tamago boro**: Small egg biscuits that melt in the mouth, a classic Japanese baby snack.
- **Shikiho (会社四季報)**: Japan's quarterly handbook of listed companies, a staple for individual investors.
- **Payout ratio**: The share of after-tax profit a company pays out as dividends.
- **Equity ratio**: Shareholders' equity as a share of total assets; higher means sturdier.
- **P/E**: Price to earnings: the share price divided by yearly earnings per share.
- **Retained earnings**: Profits kept in the company rather than paid out (naibu ryūho).
- **Margin trading**: Buying shares with borrowed money.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his 2015 interview in Gendai Business, a 2024 profile by MUFG Securities, Jun Mizusawa's book of interviews (2008), his own first book (2005), reports of his 2011 talk and a 2015 investor profile, and his 2016 obituary in J-CAST News. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

Takeda published no investment returns, and estimates of his holdings vary by source and year. Most sources are in Japanese; summaries and translations are ours. Companies are named for history only.
