# Atsuto Sawakami

> Founded Japan's first independent fund company in 1999 and preached long-term investing for decades, when few in Japan would listen.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/sawakami.html · Section: Japan · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Investing, not money-rolling. Buying and selling on price moves is not investing.

## Summary

Atsuto Sawakami ran the Japanese arm of the Swiss private bank Pictet, then in 1999 founded Japan's first fund company with no ties to a big financial group. He sold one fund, directly, with no up-front commission, and preached long-term investing through decades when few in Japan wanted to hear it. He refused pension money as too short-term. Bloomberg called him Japan's first evangelist of long-term investing.

## Record at a glance

- **1999**: founded Japan's first fund company independent of the big financial groups
- **1 fund**: sold directly, with no up-front commission
- **+9%**: his fund's gain in the year to March 2001, while the Nikkei fell 36%
- **10 years**: the shortest horizon he says an investor should think in

## Big ideas

### 1. The outsider from Pictet

He spent sixteen years at the head of a Swiss private bank's Japanese business, then left to build a fund company for ordinary savers, owned by no big group.

- **Geneva and Pictet.** Born in Nagoya in 1947, he studied international economics in Geneva and led Pictet's Japan business from 1980 to 1996. (Toyo Keizai, 2014)
- **On his own.** He set up an advisory firm in 1996 and the Sawakami Fund in 1999. (Toyo Keizai, 2014 · Bloomberg, 2016)
- **A first.** It was Japan's first fund company with no ties to a major financial institution. (Inst. Investor, 2001)
- **An evangelist.** Bloomberg later called him Japan's first evangelist of long-term investing, and an old rebel. (Bloomberg, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-01-the-outsider-from-pictet.html

### 2. Investing, not money-rolling

He divides the market in two: real long-term investing, and what he calls money-rolling, buying and selling on price moves.

- **Mostly money-rolling.** What most institutions, and many individuals, do is not investing but rolling money around, he told a 2015 audience. (Talk, 2015)
- **Opposite instincts.** Ordinary investors buy more as prices rise; long-term investors buy more as prices fall. (Talk, 2015)
- **The whole of it.** Buying low and selling high, he said, is the ideal and the whole of investing. (Talk, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-02-investing-not-money-rolling.html

### 3. Buy when they sell

His fund adds to holdings when others sell and trims when others buy. Most people, he says, do the reverse and pay for it.

- **Fear and chase.** In a crash most people fear further falls and don't buy; in a rally they keep buying, then panic-sell when prices collapse. (Talk, 2015)
- **The fund's habit.** The fund buys companies making what consumers will need in future, adds when others sell, and trims when others buy. (Bloomberg, 2016)
- **Unloved old Japan.** In 2001 he bought restructuring 'failed' old-industry companies, then beaten-down technology names. (Inst. Investor, 2001)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-03-buy-when-they-sell.html

### 4. Proof in a bad year, and the long record

In 2001, as Japanese shares crashed, his fund rose and gained customers. Over the long run its returns were steady rather than spectacular.

- **Up in a crash.** In the 12 months to early March 2001 his fund gained 9% while the Nikkei fell 36%, with much of it in cash. (Inst. Investor, 2001)
- **Money in, not out.** While other Japanese funds faced withdrawals, his kept attracting new money. (Inst. Investor, 2001)
- **The long run.** In 2015 he said the fund had returned about 5% a year over its 16 years. (Talk, 2015)
- **Since launch.** By 2016 Bloomberg put its total return since 1999 at 95%. (Bloomberg, 2016)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-04-proof-in-a-bad-year-and-the-long-record.html

### 5. Why even pensions turned short-term

He argues that pension funds, which should be the most patient money, became short-termist once they began judging managers every year. So he would not take their money.

- **Annual reviews.** From the mid-1970s pensions were managed for safety and checked every year, so short-term results came to matter most. (Talk, 2015)
- **Dancing to the music.** Managers who sell too early are blamed, so they keep buying in rallies and get caught by the crash. (Talk, 2015)
- **No, thank you.** He has refused to manage pension money, saying it doesn't give managers enough time. (Bloomberg, 2016)
- **No institutions.** He told Bloomberg he has basically no dealings with institutional investors, whom he calls short-termist. (Bloomberg, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-05-why-even-pensions-turned-short-term.html

### 6. Sell direct, charge little

He sold his fund straight to savers, with no up-front commission, a low fee, no advertising and no sales force.

- **Low cost.** No up-front commission and a 1% management fee, which meant he needed far more money to break even. (Inst. Investor, 2001)
- **No adverts.** He did not advertise; visitors to the office were offered wine and snacks. (Inst. Investor, 2001)
- **No salesmen.** He relied on no sales staff. (Japan Times, 2001)
- **Direct, or nothing.** He told a younger founder that selling through brokerages was a mistake; the only way was to sell directly. (Bloomberg, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-06-sell-direct-charge-little.html

### 7. Tell investors everything

He believed savers should be told more, not less, and reported on every move every month.

- **Monthly reports.** His fund issued monthly information on its movements and investment decisions. (Japan Times, 2001)
- **More, not less.** He criticised fund managers who put the sales side before the customers they serve. (Japan Times, 2001)
- **Customers.** The fund had about 27,000 customers in 2001 and more than 118,000 by 2016. (Japan Times, 2001 · Bloomberg, 2016)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-07-tell-investors-everything.html

### 8. Think in decades

Look at least ten years ahead, he says, and ask how a company helps people live now and will help them in future.

- **Ten years, at least.** Investors should look at least ten years ahead, and hold for about that long. (Toyo Keizai, 2014)
- **People's lives.** Ask how a company supports people's lives today and how it will tomorrow; avoid businesses built on chasing money. (Toyo Keizai, 2014)
- **185,000 a day.** With the world's population growing by about 185,000 people a day, demand for energy, food, materials and water must rise. (Toyo Keizai, 2014)
- **Don't fear pessimism.** He argued that 'Japan pessimism' was nothing to fear, and that it was the time for long-term investing. (Toyo Keizai, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-08-think-in-decades.html

### 9. Letting go

He hired a former part-time actor, handed him the fund, and promised to judge him only over years, even when investors left and the style changed.

- **An unusual hire.** In 2007 a 28-year-old part-time actor came to his seminar; he later gave him a job and watched him grow. (Bloomberg, 2016)
- **The handover.** In 2013 the young man became chief investment officer and Sawakami's son became president. (Bloomberg, 2016)
- **A hard start.** Investors withdrew ¥126.5 billion over three years after the handover. (Bloomberg, 2016)
- **Years, not months.** He said he would not judge his successor until five to ten years into the job. (Bloomberg, 2016)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-09-letting-go.html

### 10. NISA, Japan, and an honest note

He welcomed Japan's tax-free NISA accounts but warned about timing, and this library also sets out the one regulatory action on record against his firm.

- **Great system, bad timing.** He said the new NISA, launched in January 2024, was a great system started at the worst possible time. (President, 2024)
- **Don't fear the turn.** He expected the trend to turn over the following decade and found that exciting. (Toyo Keizai, 2014)
- **The 2006 order.** In 2006 Japan's regulator found his firm had placed share trades for overseas advisory clients, which the law then barred, and had kept incomplete records. (FSA, 2006)
- **The penalty.** It ordered a one-month halt to new advisory contracts and a plan to improve compliance. (FSA, 2006)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/sawakami-10-nisa-japan-and-an-honest-note.html

## Special section

**Investing or money-rolling? Tap your answer**

- The Nikkei falls 25% in three months. You add to the funds you already own. Answer: Long-term investing. Buying more as prices fall is exactly his description of the long-term investor.
- A share has tripled this year and everyone on TV is talking about it, so you buy. Answer: Money-rolling. Buying because the price has risen is the habit he says most people fall into.
- You switch to whichever fund topped last year's table, every year. Answer: Money-rolling. Chasing last year's winner is judging on short-term results, the trap he says even pensions fall into.
- You buy a company because people will need what it makes in ten years. Answer: Long-term investing. Asking how a company serves people's lives a decade ahead is his test.
- One bad quarter, and you sell a sound company you planned to hold for years. Answer: Money-rolling. Selling on short-term news is the opposite of thinking in decades.
- Your monthly NISA contribution keeps going through a crash, untouched. Answer: Long-term investing. Steady buying through falls lets you buy more when prices are low.

**An honest note.** On 30 March 2006 Japan's Financial Services Agency took action against Sawakami Investment Trust. It found that the firm had placed securities orders many times for overseas clients with whom it had investment advisory contracts, which the investment advisory law of the time prohibited, and that it had not kept or delivered certain required documents for that business. The agency ordered the firm not to take on new investment advisory contracts for one month, from 3 April to 2 May 2006, and to set up a proper compliance system, strengthen internal controls and report on its measures. We include it because this library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Many sources for this page are in Japanese; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “I basically have no dealings with institutional investors.” (To Bloomberg, 2018)
- “Why should more information be harmful?” (The Japan Times, 2001)
- “Children have to burn their fingers to learn.” (On his successor, Bloomberg, 2016)
- “機関投資家がやっているのは投資ではなく単なるマネー転がし” (“What institutions do is not investing, just rolling money around.” Talk at the Nikkei Money symposium, 2015 (our translation))
- “新NISAの制度は素晴らしいが、スタートのタイミングは最悪” (“The new NISA is a great system, but it started at the worst time.” President Online, 2024 (our translation))

## Read the originals

Start with Bloomberg's 2018 story of the people he inspired, then The Japan Times' 2016 piece on his handover. If you read Japanese, read his 2015 talk report.

- [Days of wine and grosses](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/b15134gys29nfc/days-of-wine-and-grosses): His contrarian year: a gain while the Nikkei collapsed, no up-front commission, no advertising, and wine for visiting clients.
- [Investors fume as Enron-linked funds bleed](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2001/12/01/business/investors-fume-as-enron-linked-funds-bleed): His case for telling investors more: no sales staff, and monthly reports on every move.
- [Long-term investing needs foresight and reasoning](https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/56222): Why short-termism took over, why Japan pessimism is not to be feared, and how to pick companies for the next decade.
- [What the Sawakami Fund chairman calls ideal investing](https://life.oricon.co.jp/rank_certificate/news/2061842/): Money-rolling versus long-term investing, buying as prices fall, how pensions became short-term, and his fund's record.
- [Bit actor-bum managing $2.7 billion Japanese fund](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/09/30/business/corporate-business/bit-actor-bum-managing-2-7-billion-japanese-fund): How he hired his successor, handed over, refused pension money, and waits years to judge.
- [One man's fight against the lions of Japanese investing](https://www.bloombergquint.com/amp/business/one-man-s-fight-against-the-lions-of-japanese-investing): Japan's first evangelist of long-term investing, through the eyes of a fund founder he pushed to keep going.
- [Long-term investing in the new NISA era](https://president.jp/growth/archives/133): His view of Japan's new tax-free accounts, index funds, and how beginners should think about long-term investing.
- [Administrative action against Sawakami Investment Trust](https://www.fsa.go.jp/news/newsj/17/syouken/20060330-3.html): The regulator's findings and orders: a one-month halt to new advisory contracts, and a business improvement order.

## Words to know

- **Investment trust (投資信託)**: Japan's name for a mutual fund, often shortened to tōshin.
- **Independent fund company**: A fund manager not owned by a bank, broker or insurance group.
- **Direct sales**: Selling a fund straight to savers, with no broker or bank in between.
- **Up-front commission**: A fee taken from your money the moment you invest.
- **Nikkei 225**: Japan's best-known share index; it peaked at the end of 1989 and took decades to recover.
- **NISA**: Japan's tax-free investment account, launched in 2014 and expanded in 2024.
- **Money-rolling (マネー転がし)**: His term for trading on price moves rather than owning businesses.
- **FSA**: Japan's Financial Services Agency, the financial regulator.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Institutional Investor (2001), The Japan Times (2001 and 2016), Bloomberg (2018), Toyo Keizai (2014), Oricon's report of his 2015 talk, President Online (2024), and a Financial Services Agency notice (2006). Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

His fund's returns are quoted only as the sources give them, for the periods they cover. The fund still operates; it is named for history, not as a recommendation. Some sources are in Japanese; summaries and translations are ours.

# Prem Watsa

> Reached Canada from Hyderabad with almost nothing, turned a failing insurer into Fairfax, and grew its book value 18.7% a year for forty years.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/watsa.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Value first. Buy below what a business is worth, as Graham and Buffett taught.

## Summary

Prem Watsa grew up in Hyderabad, studied chemical engineering at IIT Madras, and reached Canada in the early 1970s with almost no money. In 1985 he took control of a small, struggling trucking insurer and renamed it Fairfax Financial. He ran it on Ben Graham's value principles and wrote to its owners every year. Since 1985 Fairfax's book value per share has grown about 18.7% a year, and people call him Canada's Warren Buffett.

## Record at a glance

- **18.7%**: a year: growth in Fairfax's book value per share, with dividends, 1985 to 2025
- **11.5%**: a year: the S&P 500 with dividends over the same forty years
- **$2.1bn**: of gains on credit default swaps by September 2008, bought from 2003 as protection
- **15%**: the long-term yearly target in Fairfax's guiding principles

## Big ideas

### 1. Eight dollars and a degree

He grew up in Hyderabad, son of a teacher, studied engineering at IIT Madras, and arrived in Canada with almost nothing.

- **A teacher's son.** He was born in Hyderabad in 1950; his father taught English and maths and later ran a boys' school. (Encyclopedia · Horatio Alger)
- **IIT Madras.** He graduated in chemical engineering from IIT Madras in 1971. (Encyclopedia)
- **Almost nothing.** He reached Canada with only a few dollars and paid for his MBA by selling furnaces in winter and air conditioners in summer. (Encyclopedia)
- **Hard roots.** His father had lost both his own parents at the age of three. (Horatio Alger)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-01-eight-dollars-and-a-degree.html

### 2. A rescue becomes Fairfax

In 1985 he and his partners took over a small trucking insurer close to failure, renamed it Fairfax, and built it into a global insurance group.

- **His own firm first.** In 1984 he started an investment firm, Hamblin Watsa, with his former boss. (Encyclopedia)
- **A near-bankrupt start.** In 1985 they took control of Markel Financial, a struggling Canadian trucking insurer, and renamed it Fairfax. (Encyclopedia)
- **The insurance engine.** Like Berkshire, Fairfax invests the money it holds for future claims, called float. (Letter, 2025)
- **Forty years on.** By 2025 Fairfax earned a record $4.8 billion in a year. (Letter, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-02-a-rescue-becomes-fairfax.html

### 3. Graham's disciple

From his first letter he said Fairfax would follow the value approach of Benjamin Graham and his famous student, Warren Buffett.

- **The value approach.** Buy securities below what they are worth, with a margin of safety, and wait. (Letter, 2025 · Encyclopedia)
- **Called Canada's Buffett.** His record and his insurance-plus-investing model earned him the nickname. (Encyclopedia)
- **Graham's warning.** He has quoted Graham that only 1 in 100 survived the 1929–32 crash unless bearish in 1925. (Nasdaq, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-03-grahams-disciple.html

### 4. Book value per share, not quarters

He judges Fairfax by one long-term number: the growth of book value per share. The target has been 15% a year since the start.

- **One number.** The goal is to compound book value per share by 15% a year over the long term. (Principles)
- **Not quarterly profit.** The focus is long-term growth in book value, not quarterly earnings. (Principles)
- **The record.** Since 1985 book value per share has grown 18.7% a year with dividends, and the share price 19.5%. (Letter, 2025)
- **The yardstick.** Over the same forty years the S&P 500 returned 11.5% a year with dividends. (Letter, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-04-book-value-per-share-not-quarters.html

### 5. Insure against the storm

He treats the investment portfolio like an insurer treats risk: buy protection against disasters others think impossible.

- **From 2003.** Fairfax began buying credit default swaps, a kind of insurance against companies failing to pay debts. (Press, 2008)
- **Protection, not a bet.** He described the swaps as steps to protect the balance sheet from investment risks. (Press, 2008)
- **The payoff.** By September 2008 the swaps had produced about $2.1 billion of gains as the credit crisis broke. (Press, 2008)
- **CEO of the year.** The Globe and Mail's business magazine named him CEO of the year, partly for holding on to the swaps. (Globe, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-05-insure-against-the-storm.html

### 6. Early looks like wrong

Being right too soon is painful. While he waited for the crisis, Fairfax's shares fell by about half, and critics mocked him.

- **Three lean years.** Between mid-2003 and mid-2006 Fairfax's share price fell about 50% as the swaps held back profits. (Reuters, 2013)
- **Early, again.** In 2012 he wrote that Fairfax continued to be early, and bearish, citing Graham. (Nasdaq, 2017)
- **Survive to be right.** Staying soundly financed is what lets an early investor survive until the market comes round. (Principles)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-06-early-looks-like-wrong.html

### 7. When protection costs too much

From 2010 he hedged all of Fairfax's shares against a deflationary slump that never came. The hedges cost billions before he removed them in 2016.

- **Fully hedged.** From 2010 Fairfax hedged about 100% of its shares; by September 2016 the hedges were 112.7% of its holdings. (Press, 2016 · Nasdaq, 2017)
- **The cost.** When removed in late 2016, the index shorts had cost about $1.2 billion that year alone. (Nasdaq, 2017)
- **A change of view.** After the 2016 US election he judged the hedges no longer needed and took them off. (Press, 2016)
- **The lesson.** Protection that works once can be too expensive the next time; the cost must be weighed. (Nasdaq, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-07-when-protection-costs-too-much.html

### 8. Own your mistakes

His letters take the blame for what goes wrong and share the credit for what goes right, including public apologies.

- **Blame and credit.** In his letters he accepts the blame for disappointments and shares the credit for successes. (Encyclopedia)
- **A public apology.** In 2009 he told shareholders Fairfax should have been far more careful with three failed value investments. (Globe, 2009)
- **BlackBerry.** Fairfax was BlackBerry's top shareholder through its decline; he later wrote of it as a mistake. (Reuters, 2013 · Letter, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-08-own-your-mistakes.html

### 9. Integrity under scrutiny

In 2006 a Fairfax subsidiary restated its accounts and the SEC investigated. In 2009 the SEC closed its review with no enforcement action.

- **Restatements.** A subsidiary, Odyssey Re, restated results for errors in accounting for finite reinsurance. (SEC, 2009)
- **Subpoenas.** Fairfax and Watsa received SEC subpoenas in 2006 over an answer he gave on an investor call. (SEC, 2009)
- **No action.** In June 2009 the SEC said it did not intend to recommend any enforcement action. (SEC, 2009)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-09-integrity-under-scrutiny.html

### 10. Patient, quiet and decentralised

He avoids publicity, runs Fairfax through independent managers, and thinks in decades.

- **Decentralised.** Fairfax's companies are run by their own leaders, with the head office judging them over the long term. (Letter, 2025)
- **Soundly financed.** Always being soundly financed is one of the company's core principles. (Principles)
- **Honours.** He was appointed a Member of the Order of Canada in 2015. (Encyclopedia)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/watsa-10-patient-quiet-and-decentralised.html

## Special section

**Fairfax's guiding principles, in short**

- 15% a year: compound book value per share over the long term.
- Long term: focus on book value, not quarterly earnings.
- Soundly financed: always.
- Friendly growth: grow from within, and through friendly acquisitions.

**Protection or a bet? Tap your answer**

- You buy cheap insurance that pays if credit markets freeze, because a freeze would badly hurt your business. Answer: Protection. Insuring against the one thing that could sink you is how he described the swaps from 2003.
- You short the market with borrowed money because you think it will fall next month. Answer: A bet. A short-term call on direction, with borrowed money, is a bet, not insurance.
- You keep paying for a hedge for six years, though the danger you feared keeps not coming. Answer: A bet. When protection costs more than it could save, it becomes a costly view on the market: the 2010–2016 lesson.
- You keep enough cash and little debt so a crash can never force you to sell. Answer: Protection. Being soundly financed is the cheapest protection of all.

**An honest note.** In February 2006 Fairfax's subsidiary Odyssey Re restated its results for errors in accounting for finite reinsurance contracts. Fairfax and Prem Watsa received SEC subpoenas in March 2006 relating to an answer he gave on an investor call about the company's review of those contracts. In June 2009 Fairfax said the SEC had completed its investigation and did not intend to recommend any enforcement action. Separately, the 2010–2016 equity hedges and some investments, such as BlackBerry, lost Fairfax a great deal of money, which he has acknowledged. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “in an attempt to protect our balance sheet from investment risks” (On the swaps bought from 2003, September 2008, as reported by Investment Executive)
- “We continue to be early - and bearish!” (Letter to shareholders, 2012, as quoted by Nasdaq)
- “We should have been a lot more careful” (To shareholders at the 2009 annual meeting, as reported by the Globe and Mail)

## Read the originals

Start with his latest letter to shareholders, then the 2008 credit default swap update and the 2016 letter, where he explains the hedges that cost Fairfax dearly.

- [Fairfax letter to shareholders for 2025](https://www.fairfax.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/FFH_Fairfax-Financials-Shareholders-Letter-2025-with-attachments-092704.pdf): A record year, and the forty-year record: book value per share up 18.7% a year with dividends since 1985, against 11.5% for the S&P 500.
- [Guiding principles for Fairfax](https://www.fairfax.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/FFH_Fairfax-Financial-2025-Annual-Report-144860.pdf): The objectives he set for the company: compound book value per share by 15% a year over the long term, think long term, and always be soundly financed.
- [Prem Watsa](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/prem-watsa): His life: Hyderabad, IIT Madras, arriving in Canada with almost nothing, building Fairfax, and how his letters take blame and share credit.
- [V. Prem Watsa](https://horatioalger.org/members/detail/v-prem-watsa): His family, his father's early life, and the hard start that shaped him.
- [Fairfax sells credit default swaps](https://investmentexecutive.com/?p=309460): How swaps bought from 2003 as protection paid off as the crisis broke, and why Fairfax told shareholders early.
- [Reduction in defensive equity hedges](https://www.fairfax.ca/press-releases/fairfax-financial-holdings-limited-reduction-in-defensive-equity-hedges-2016-11-11/): After six years of hedges that covered more than all of Fairfax's shares, he began removing them.
- [Watsa's returns improve after dropping full hedges](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/prem-watsas-returns-improve-after-dropping-full-portfolio-hedges-2017-08-08): The hedges' cost, his 2012 letter's warning from Graham, and how returns changed once the hedges came off.
- [Win some, lose some](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/report-on-business/rob-magazine/win-some-lose-some-win-some/article1347711/): Named CEO of the year for holding the swaps, then apologising to shareholders for three value bets that failed.
- [Fairfax letter to shareholders for 2024](https://fairfax.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/FFH_Fairfax-Financials-Shareholders-Letter-2024-with-attachments.pdf): Thirty-nine years in: the record so far, a 600-fold gain since the 1985 listing, and a look back at mistakes including BlackBerry.
- [BlackBerry and Watsa: looking wrong today, right tomorrow](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2013/09/23/113421.htm): Fairfax as BlackBerry's top shareholder, and how its shares halved from 2003 to 2006 while he waited for the credit crisis.
- [SEC plans no enforcement action against Fairfax](https://www.canadianunderwriter.ca/insurance/sec-plans-no-enforcement-action-against-fairfax-related-to-finite-reinsurance-1000332293/): How a three-year SEC review of Fairfax's finite reinsurance accounting ended with no enforcement action.

## Words to know

- **Book value per share**: What a company's assets minus its debts are worth on paper, divided by the number of shares.
- **Float**: Money an insurer holds from premiums before it pays claims, which it can invest meanwhile.
- **Credit default swap (CDS)**: A contract that pays out if a borrower fails to repay its debts; a kind of insurance.
- **Hedge**: A position that gains when your main holdings fall, to cushion losses.
- **Deflation**: Prices falling across an economy, which makes debts heavier and profits harder.
- **Finite reinsurance**: A kind of reinsurance that transfers little real risk; its accounting drew scrutiny in the mid-2000s.
- **Decentralised**: Run by the managers of each business, not from head office.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Fairfax's 2024 and 2025 letters to shareholders, the 2025 annual report's guiding principles, Fairfax press releases of September 2008 and November 2016, the Canadian Encyclopedia, Horatio Alger Association, Canadian Underwriter, Investment Executive, Nasdaq and the Globe and Mail. Lessons are in our own words.

Fairfax is a large, listed company and its results depend on many people, not one. Book value growth is the company's own measure, reported in US dollars and including dividends; it is not a fund return. Figures change every year: check the latest letter.

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.

# Francisco García Paramés

> Taught himself value investing from Peter Lynch and Buffett's letters, then beat Spain's market for 21 years, survived his worst years, and kept going.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/parames.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Self-taught. Read the masters, then think for yourself.

## Summary

Francisco García Paramés taught himself value investing from Peter Lynch's book and a letter he requested from Warren Buffett. From 1993 to 2014 his Spanish fund at Bestinver returned about 15.7% a year, more than five times its benchmark in total. He left over a disagreement with the owners, started Cobas in 2017, lived through years of painful losses, and stuck to his method. Spain calls him its Warren Buffett.

## Record at a glance

- **15.7%**: a year: his Spanish fund at Bestinver, 1993 to 2014
- **2,279%**: the fund's total gain over that time, against 410% for its benchmark
- **−14.1%**: his first year running a global fund, 1998, while markets rose 16.5%
- **20%**: a year: Cobas's international fund over the five years to mid-2026

## Big ideas

### 1. An uninspired start

He was an average student and a reluctant shop trainee. A magazine review of Peter Lynch's book changed his life.

- **Galicia.** He was born in 1963 in El Ferrol, in north-western Spain, one of five children. (MOI Global)
- **A first job.** He spent 15 months as a graduate trainee at the retailer El Corte Inglés, then took an MBA. (MOI Global)
- **The spark.** After reading a review in Business Week he picked up One Up on Wall Street, and then the other masters. (MOI Global)
- **A letter from Omaha.** He wrote to Buffett's company to get a copy of the shareholder letter. (MOI Global)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-01-an-uninspired-start.html

### 2. Self-taught at Bestinver

He joined a small fund firm owned by an industrial group as a young analyst, and within two years was running its Spanish fund.

- **A quiet start.** He joined Bestinver, part of the Acciona group, as a young analyst. (Interview, 2017 · MOI Global)
- **Learning by doing.** When his first tasks slowed down he began analysing Spanish shares to keep busy. (CFA, 2013)
- **Fully invested.** His approach meant being fully in shares, not timing the market. (Interview, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-02-self-taught-at-bestinver.html

### 3. Twenty-one years of results

From 1993 to 2014 his Spanish fund returned about 15.7% a year: 2,279% in total, against 410% for its benchmark.

- **The record.** Bestinfond gained 2,279% from 1993 to 2014, about 15.7% a year, against 410% for its index. (Interview, 2017)
- **Thirty times.** That turned each euro into about thirty. (MOI Global)
- **Abroad too.** His global fund beat the world index even when the index went nowhere. (Interview, 2017)
- **A loyal following.** When he left Bestinver in 2014, its assets fell by about 30%. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-03-twenty-one-years-of-results.html

### 4. Austrian economics

Ten years into his career he discovered the Austrian school of economics. It became his compass: markets work, are never in balance, and growth comes from saving.

- **A turning point.** Finding the Austrian economists ten years in was, he says, a major turning point. (Book, 2018)
- **Markets work.** He starts from the idea that markets work, by definition, and are never in equilibrium. (Mises, 2018)
- **Saving drives growth.** Economic growth comes from rising productivity, financed by savings. (Mises, 2018)
- **No guessing.** He sees trying to guess the economy's next move as close to a stab in the dark. (Book, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-04-austrian-economics.html

### 5. Risk is losing money

He defines risk not as how much a price swings, but as the chance of losing money.

- **Not volatility.** Risk is the probability of losing money by holding an asset, not how much its price moves. (Mises, 2018)
- **Time helps.** His book sets out long-run data on shares against other assets to argue for a long view. (Mises, 2018 · Book, 2018)
- **Painful patches.** Even his best decades held hard stretches, such as a 22% fall in six months in 2011. (Letter, 2018)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-05-risk-is-losing-money.html

### 6. Quality at a low price

He looks for strong businesses with high returns on capital, growth and little debt, bought when they are cheap.

- **Return on capital.** Bestinver judged business quality by return on capital employed. (CFA, 2013)
- **Governance.** The managers paid special attention to how companies were governed. (CFA, 2013)
- **The 2019 portfolio.** Cobas described its holdings as businesses with strong competitive positions, average returns on capital of about 25%, growth, and little debt. (Letter, 2019)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-06-quality-at-a-low-price.html

### 7. Leaving, and starting again

In 2014 he left Bestinver over differences with its owners. After a two-year wait he launched Cobas in 2017.

- **A clean break.** He left Bestinver in September 2014 after disagreements with its owners. (MoneyWeek)
- **Two years out.** A non-compete agreement kept him out of fund management for two years. (MoneyWeek)
- **A first bet.** He later said he saw an extraordinary opportunity in a beaten-down miner in late 2015. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-07-leaving-and-starting-again.html

### 8. The hard years

Cobas had a brutal start: losses in 2018, then the worst period for value investing on record, and the Covid crash. He wrote honestly to his investors.

- **2018.** His funds fell sharply, hit by holdings such as shipping companies. (Letter, 2018)
- **It had happened before.** He reminded investors that his first global year, 1998, lost 14.1% while markets rose 16.5%. (Letter, 2018)
- **2020.** In the Covid crash he acknowledged that most of his investors were suffering big losses in hard-earned savings. (Letter, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-08-the-hard-years.html

### 9. The rebound

By mid-2026 his international fund had returned about 20% a year over five years, and Madrid had become Europe's value-investing capital.

- **Five good years.** Bloomberg reported his international fund up about 20% a year over the five years to July 2026. (Bloomberg, 2026)
- **His method.** He describes it simply: buy assets below their intrinsic value, and be patient. (Bloomberg, 2026)
- **Disciples.** Former colleagues and students run their own value funds, making Madrid a hub. (Bloomberg, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-09-the-rebound.html

### 10. We are qualified to wait

His last lesson is patience: the best returns come to those who can wait, and to managers whose clients let them.

- **Waiting.** He calls waiting the most important thing, and says his team is qualified to do it. (Mises, 2018)
- **No forecasts.** He does not try to predict markets or economies, only to understand companies. (Interview, 2017 · Bloomberg, 2026)
- **Patient clients.** In the 2020 crash he thanked unitholders who kept their trust, some of whom invested more. (Letter, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/parames-10-we-are-qualified-to-wait.html

## Special section

**Would it pass his checklist?**

- It earns a high return on the capital it uses
- It has a strong competitive position that rivals find hard to copy
- It is still growing, not shrinking
- It carries little debt, or none
- It is run well, with good governance
- Its price is well below what you think it is worth
- You can hold it for years without needing the money

**Two ways to see risk** 

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “The most important thing is to wait, and we are qualified to wait.” (From Investing for the Long Term, as quoted by the Mises Institute)
- “discovering them was a major turning point” (On the Austrian economists, Investing for the Long Term, chapter 4)
- “most of our investors are suffering significant losses in their savings” (Letter to Cobas investors, first quarter 2020)

## Read the originals

Start with Investing for the Long Term (Wiley, 2018), chapters 1 and 7. Then read the Cobas letters of late 2018 and early 2020, written during his worst years.

- [Investing for the Long Term](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/investing-for-the/9781119431190/): His life as an investor in part one; Austrian economics, risk, passive versus active, and how he picks shares in part two.
- [Francisco García Paramés: quotations and references](https://moiglobal.com/francisco-garcia-parames-quotations-references/): His path from an uninspired first job to Lynch, Buffett's letter and Bestinver, and his long record.
- [The treasure? Stay in the stock market](https://www.cobasam.com/wp-content/uploads/The-Treasure-Stay-in-the-stock-market.pdf): His record from 1993 to 2014, his 100% equity stance, and why he never predicts markets or economies.
- [What is the 'Warren Buffett of Europe' up to?](https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/blogs/enterprising-investor/2013/what-is-the-warren-buffett-of-europe-up-to/): How Bestinver judged quality with return on capital employed, and its focus on corporate governance.
- [Cobas comment, fourth quarter 2018](https://www.cobasam.com/wp-content/uploads/CAM_Coment_4T_2018_ENG.pdf): A bad year explained: why large losses and mispricing had happened before in his 30 years, and why he stayed the course.
- [Cobas comment, second quarter 2019](https://www.cobasam.com/wp-content/uploads/CAM_Coment_2T_2019_ENG_final.pdf): What the portfolio held: strong competitive positions and high entry barriers, average returns on capital near 25%, growth, and minimal financial risk.
- [Cobas comment, first quarter 2020](https://www.cobasam.com/wp-content/uploads/CAM-Coment-1T-2020.pdf): Writing to investors in the Covid crash: acknowledging their losses, and the case for patience.
- [Austrian economics can help investors look beyond short-term thinking](https://mises.org/mises-wire/austrian-economics-can-help-investors-look-beyond-short-term-thinking): His ten Austrian insights for investors, his view of risk as the chance of losing money, and the case for waiting.
- [The world's greatest investors: Francisco García Paramés](https://moneyweek.com/481749/the-worlds-greatest-investors-francisco-garcia-parames): His Bestinver years, the 30% fall in Bestinver's assets when he left, and an early Cobas bet on a beaten-down miner.
- [Spain's Warren Buffett followers score a rare win for value investing](https://www.cobasam.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Spains-Warren-Buffett-Followers-Score-a-R-are-Win-for-Value-Investing-Bloomberg_3849.pdf): Madrid as Europe's value capital, his followers, and the recent rebound of his international fund.

## Words to know

- **Value investing**: Buying shares for less than the business is worth, then waiting.
- **Austrian school**: A school of economics, from Mises and Hayek, that stresses markets, saving and the limits of forecasting.
- **ROCE**: Return on capital employed: profit as a share of the money tied up in a business.
- **Benchmark**: The index a fund is compared with.
- **Non-compete**: A contract term that bars someone from working for a rival for a period.
- **Intrinsic value**: What a business is really worth, based on the cash it will produce.
- **Volatility**: How much a price swings up and down.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his book Investing for the Long Term (2018), Cobas Asset Management letters and interviews (2017–2026), MOI Global's profile, the CFA Institute's Enterprising Investor blog, MoneyWeek, the Mises Institute's review, and Bloomberg's 2026 report as posted by Cobas. Lessons are in our own words.

Fund returns are as reported by his firms and the press, before personal taxes, and depend on the dates chosen. His later Cobas record had a very hard start. Some sources are in Spanish; summaries are ours.

# André Kostolany

> A speculator, not a value investor: rich twice, broke in between, and the man who taught Germany how crowds move markets.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/kostolany.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Money + psychology. Prices follow the supply of money and the mood of the crowd.

## Summary

André Kostolany was born in Budapest in 1906, learned the stock market in Paris, fled to America in 1940, and spent his last decades explaining markets to Germans in books, columns and on television. He was not a value investor but a speculator, and he said so. He grew rich twice, lost nearly everything in between, and claimed to be right only 51% of the time. His thirteen books sold about three million copies, yet the English-speaking world barely knows him.

## Record at a glance

- **1906–1999**: seventy-plus years in markets, from Paris in the 1920s to Munich in the 1990s
- **2×**: rich twice: betting on the 1929 crash, then on German bonds after the war
- **51%**: the share of his trades he said were right; 49% were wrong
- **3 million**: copies of his 13 books sold, plus over 400 magazine columns

## Big ideas

### 1. From Budapest to the Paris bourse

A wealthy boy who wanted to be an art critic, he was sent by his father to learn broking in Paris in the 1920s.

- **Not his first wish.** He studied philosophy and art history and hoped to become an art critic. (etf.capital · Kagels)
- **Paris.** His father sent him to Paris in the mid-1920s to train under the broker Adrien Perquel. (comdirect · etf.capital)
- **No economics.** He never studied classical economics and mocked economists' forecasts all his life. (comdirect)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-01-from-budapest-to-the-paris-bourse.html

### 2. Rich twice, broke in between

He made a fortune betting on falling prices around 1929, lost it, and came close to bankruptcy more than once.

- **1929.** He grew rich betting that share prices would fall around the 1929 crash. (Kagels · justETF)
- **Then lost it.** Big bets that went wrong wiped him out more than once. (justETF · Kagels)
- **51 to 49.** He admitted being right on 51% of his trades and wrong on 49%. (comdirect)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-02-rich-twice-broke-in-between.html

### 3. The German bond coup

After the war he bought old German bonds that almost no one wanted, betting that Germany would want its good name back. It did.

- **A cheap bet.** He bought pre-war German bonds in Paris for about 250 francs each. (HSBC)
- **The reason.** He reasoned that the new West Germany would repay to regain its creditworthiness. (comdirect)
- **1953.** The London Debt Agreement settled Germany's old foreign debts. (London 1953)
- **A hundredfold.** He later sold the bonds for about 35,000 francs each: his stake grew more than a hundred times. (HSBC · comdirect)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-03-the-german-bond-coup.html

### 4. Money plus psychology

He said market trends come from two things: how much money is available, and the mood of the crowd.

- **The formula.** Trend equals money plus psychology. (FBV, guide)
- **Not more informed.** Don't assume people buying in a frenzy know more than you. (justETF)
- **Crises and rescues.** He argued that in a crisis governments and central banks act, which is why to buy then. (justETF)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-04-money-plus-psychology.html

### 5. The egg

He drew the market cycle as an egg. Rises and falls each have three phases: correction, accompanying, exaggeration.

- **Three phases each way.** Every rise and every fall moves through correction, an accompanying phase, and exaggeration. (etf.capital · Kagels)
- **Buy in panic.** He bought in the exaggeration of a fall, when heavy selling signals panic, and added at the start of the rise. (extraETF · HSBC)
- **Sell in euphoria.** He sold in the euphoric last phase of a rise, at the latest early in the fall. (HSBC)
- **Wait in between.** In the middle phases he advised doing nothing. (extraETF)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-05-the-egg.html

### 6. The dog and its owner

Prices relate to the economy like a dog to its owner on a walk: running ahead, falling behind, but always coming back.

- **The walk.** The share price runs ahead of the economy or lags behind, but returns to it. (etf.capital)
- **Long walks.** Over time prices follow the economy, even when short swings are wild. (etf.capital · justETF)
- **Anything can happen.** On the stock market anything is possible, even the opposite. (justETF)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-06-the-dog-and-its-owner.html

### 7. The four Gs

He said a successful investor needs four Gs: Geld, Gedanken, Geduld and Glück. Money, thoughts, patience and luck.

- **Geld, money.** Your own money, never borrowed. (etf.capital)
- **Gedanken, thoughts.** A considered plan: goals, time span and how much risk you can take. (etf.capital · comdirect)
- **Geduld, patience.** The most important of the four. (etf.capital)
- **Glück, luck.** It cannot be forced, but without it you lose confidence, and then patience. (comdirect)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-07-the-four-gs.html

### 8. Shaky hands and hard-boiled ones

He split investors into the shaky, who buy in euphoria and sell in panic, and the hard-boiled, who do the opposite.

- **The shaky.** They buy when prices are high and the mood is euphoric, and sell at a loss in panic. (etf.capital · comdirect)
- **The hard-boiled.** They hold when others get nervous, and buy when sentiment is at its lowest. (etf.capital)
- **Missing a G.** Anyone lacking one of the first three Gs ends up among the shaky. (etf.capital)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-08-shaky-hands-and-hard-boiled-ones.html

### 9. Sleeping pills and trams

His most famous advice: buy good shares, take sleeping pills, and stop looking. And never chase a share, any more than a tram.

- **Sleeping pills.** Buy shares, take sleeping pills, don't look for years, and you will be rich. (extraETF · justETF)
- **Pain, then money.** Stock market profits are payment for pain: first comes the pain, then the money. (justETF)
- **Don't chase.** Never run after a tram or a share; another one always comes. (comdirect)
- **Patience pays.** He liked to quote old Frankfurt brokers: money is made by sitting still, not with the head. (FBV, guide)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-09-sleeping-pills-and-trams.html

### 10. Teacher of a nation

In later life he explained markets to millions of Germans in columns, seminars and television, and co-founded an early asset manager.

- **Columns.** He wrote over 400 columns for the business magazine Capital. (comdirect)
- **Books.** His 13 books sold about three million copies. (comdirect)
- **Fiduka.** In 1971 he co-founded Fiduka, one of Germany's first asset managers, with Gottfried Heller. (comdirect)
- **A last warning.** Shortly before his death in 1999 he warned against the dot-com mania. (comdirect)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/kostolany-10-teacher-of-a-nation.html

## Special section

**Shaky hands or hard-boiled? Tap your answer**

- Prices have doubled, everyone at dinner talks about shares, and you buy for the first time. Answer: Shaky hands. Buying in euphoria, when the crowd is already in, is his picture of shaky hands.
- The market has fallen 35% on panic headlines. You buy more with spare money. Answer: Hard-boiled. Buying in the exaggeration of a fall, with your own money, is what the hard-boiled do.
- You borrowed to buy, prices drop, and the lender forces you to sell. Answer: Shaky hands. Without your own money, the first G, you cannot hold: you become shaky whether you like it or not.
- You bought a year ago, nothing has happened, and you are still waiting calmly. Answer: Hard-boiled. Patience in the quiet middle phases is the third G.
- A share you follow jumps 20% in a day; you chase it before it 'gets away'. Answer: Shaky hands. Never run after a tram or a share: another one always comes.

**The four Gs**

- Geld (money): your own, never borrowed.
- Gedanken (thoughts): a plan you have thought through.
- Geduld (patience): the most important.
- Glück (luck): it comes more often to those with the first three.

**An honest note.** Kostolany was a speculator, not a value investor, and he did not hide it. In his early years he made and lost fortunes with large, sometimes borrowed bets, and he came close to bankruptcy more than once. He published no audited record, so his wealth and many trades are known only from his own books and later accounts. We include him for his lessons on crowd psychology and patience, which have lasted, and we recommend none of his speculative methods.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “First comes pain, then comes money.” (A saying of his, as translated by justETF)
- “Der Börsenkurs verhält sich zur Wirtschaft wie der Hund zum Spaziergänger” (“The share price relates to the economy as the dog does to the walker.” His image, as quoted by etf.capital (our translation))
- “Einer Straßenbahn und einer Aktie darf man nie nachlaufen.” (“Never run after a tram or a share.” As quoted by comdirect (our translation))

## Read the originals

If you read German, start with Die Kunst über Geld nachzudenken (The Art of Thinking about Money, 2000). If not, start with justETF's collection of his sayings, then the comdirect profile.

- [André Kostolany: gentleman and speculator](https://magazin.comdirect.de/maerkte-im-blick/andre-kostolany): His life from Budapest to Paris, New York and Munich; the four Gs; shaky and hard-boiled hands; his German bond coup; and his warnings at the end.
- [Who was André Kostolany, and what was his method?](https://etf.capital/andre-kostolany-methode/): His biography, the egg with its three phases up and down, shaky versus hard-boiled investors, the four Gs, and the dog and its owner.
- [André Kostolany: the stock market guru](https://extraetf.com/wissen/boersenguru-kostolany): The four Gs, his sleeping-pill advice, and where in the egg he bought and sold.
- [10 André Kostolany quotes that explain the stock market](https://www.justetf.com/uk/academy/10-quotes-kostolany.html): Ten of his sayings with plain explanations, plus his ups and downs as a speculator.
- [Investment gurus: André Kostolany](https://hsbc-zertifikate.de/dam/jcr:3791f779-482d-48e4-92e0-f399c2c8fe8c/Gurus_Kostolany.2016-12-02-14-37-18.pdf): His contrarian strategy, the egg in practice, and the German bonds he bought at 250 francs and sold at 35,000.
- [Alles, was Sie über André Kostolany wissen müssen](https://www.m-vg.de/mediafiles/Leseprobe/9783959722629.pdf): A friend's memories, his formula that trend equals money plus psychology, and the old brokers' line that patience makes the money.
- [André Kostolany: life, the egg and the four Gs](https://www.kagels-trading.de/andre-kostolany/): How he grew rich twice, lost his fortune in between, and why his ideas help to read a market phase rather than to time a trade.
- [London Agreement on German External Debts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Agreement_on_German_External_Debts): The treaty that settled West Germany's pre-war foreign debts and restored its credit, the event behind his greatest coup.

## Words to know

- **Speculator**: Someone who buys or sells expecting to profit from price moves, often over shorter periods.
- **Hausse and baisse**: French and German words for a rising market and a falling one.
- **Shaky hands (zittrige Hände)**: Investors who buy in euphoria and sell in panic.
- **Hard-boiled (hartgesottene)**: Investors who act against the crowd and hold through falls.
- **Bond**: A loan to a government or company that pays interest and is repaid at the end.
- **London Debt Agreement**: The 1953 treaty that settled West Germany's old foreign debts.
- **Margin**: Borrowed money used to buy securities.

## Sources and scope

Sources: comdirect magazine, extraETF, etf.capital, justETF, HSBC's investor-guru series, FinanzBuch Verlag's guide to his ideas, Kagels Trading, and the record of the 1953 London Debt Agreement. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

Kostolany published no audited record; his fortune and trades are known from his own books and later accounts, and figures vary. He speculated, often with borrowed money in his youth. Most sources are in German; translations are ours.

# Peter Cundill

> Read Graham on a plane in 1973, then hunted the world for shares below their liquidation value: the Indiana Jones of Canadian money managers.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/cundill.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Below liquidation value. Buy a dollar of assets for 40 or 50 cents.

## Summary

Peter Cundill was a Canadian accountant who read Ben Graham's Security Analysis on a flight home in December 1973 and changed his life. He took over a small fund that had lost two-thirds of its value and turned it into the Cundill Value Fund. He hunted the world for shares selling below their liquidation value, from Japan to Europe, and compounded about 22% a year for his first fifteen years without a losing year. They called him the Indiana Jones of Canadian money managers.

## Record at a glance

- **22%**: a year: the Cundill Value Fund's first fifteen years, with no losing year
- **30%+**: a year: the fund's compound return in its first decade, to 1985
- **37%**: of the fund in Japan in 2004, with a third in cash, when bargains were scarce elsewhere
- **$500**: his first investment, in a mining tip, lost within 48 hours

## Big ideas

### 1. A $500 lesson

His first investment, as a summer office boy, was a mining tip. He lost all $500 in under two days, and never forgot it.

- **Montreal.** He was born in Montreal in 1938 and studied commerce at McGill, graduating in 1960. (McGill, 2011)
- **The tip.** As an office boy in 1959 he put $500 into a speculative mining share and lost it all within 48 hours. (Globe, 2011)
- **An accountant.** He qualified as a chartered accountant before moving into investment work. (McGill, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-01-a-500-lesson.html

### 2. The eureka moment

On a flight home in December 1973 he read Graham's Security Analysis. It gave him the method he had been missing.

- **The flight.** Flying from Toronto to Vancouver for Christmas in 1973, he read Graham and found his road. (Book, 2011)
- **A fund to fix.** In 1975 he took control of a small fund whose shares had fallen from $6 to $2. (Book, 2011 · Biography, 2014)
- **A new name.** He renamed it the Cundill Value Fund and ran it on Graham's rules. (McGill, 2011 · Book, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-02-the-eureka-moment.html

### 3. A dollar for forty cents

He bought shares priced below the company's liquidation value: what it would be worth if it closed and sold everything.

- **Liquidation value.** A share is cheap when its price is below what the business would fetch if wound up. (Morningstar · Book, 2011)
- **Margin of safety.** That gap was the margin of safety he swore by. (Morningstar)
- **A dollar for forty cents.** He popularised the idea of buying a dollar of value for 40 cents. (Morningstar)
- **Net-nets.** His favourite was a share below working capital minus all debts, Graham's net-net. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-03-a-dollar-for-forty-cents.html

### 4. His six tests

He wrote down his criteria: cheap against value and book, profitable, paying dividends, well off its high, and on a low P/E.

- **Below value and book.** The price must be below intrinsic value and book value, ideally below net working capital less long-term debt. (Morningstar)
- **Profitable.** Ideally five years of growing earnings. (Morningstar)
- **Dividends.** Ideally a regularly rising dividend. (Morningstar)
- **Out of favour.** A price under half its former high, preferably near its all-time low, and a P/E under ten. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-04-his-six-tests.html

### 5. Hidden assets

He read accounts for what they hid: buildings at old costs, valuable leases, power plants. JWT was his textbook case.

- **JWT.** The advertising agency J. Walter Thompson listed above $20 in 1972 and fell to about $4. (Morningstar)
- **Not on the books.** Its book value of $18 a share left out freehold buildings in Tokyo and Paris and a London lease. (Morningstar)
- **The result.** He bought at about $8 on average and sold a year later above $20. (Morningstar)
- **Homework.** Very few investors do the homework, which is the edge. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-05-hidden-assets.html

### 6. Buy more as it falls

His best investment, Cleveland-Cliffs, fell by more than half after he bought. He kept buying.

- **Unloved.** An iron-ore pellet maker with a large market share, it fell from his first price of $15 to $6. (Morningstar · Globe, 2011)
- **He kept buying.** He bought and bought as the price dropped, though the supply seemed endless. (Morningstar · Globe, 2011)
- **Sold, then bought back.** He sold much of it in the 1986–87 rally and bought back after the October 1987 crash. (Globe, 2011)
- **The return.** When he finally sold in 1991 he had compounded at over 30% a year. (Morningstar)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-06-buy-more-as-it-falls.html

### 7. Indiana Jones

He searched the world for bargains, often starting with the country whose market had done worst that year.

- **The nickname.** He was nicknamed the Indiana Jones of Canadian money managers. (Morningstar)
- **The worst market first.** He would look at the country with the year's worst stock market and put some money there. (McGill)
- **Japan.** After the 1997 crash he found hundreds of Japanese shares selling below net cash, with strong balance sheets. (Interview, 2004)
- **37%.** In 2004 over a third of his fund was in Japan. (Interview, 2004)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-07-indiana-jones.html

### 8. Cash is a position

When few shares met his tests he simply held cash, sometimes up to 40%, and waited.

- **A third in cash.** In 2004 he held about 33% in cash because he was finding few bargains. (Interview, 2004)
- **Up to 40%.** In the past his cash had been as high as 40%. (Interview, 2004)
- **Flexibility.** Cash kept him free to buy when the next crisis came. (Interview, 2004)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-08-cash-is-a-position.html

### 9. The one that went wrong

His worst investment, Cable and Wireless, met every Graham test and still failed. Careful analysis guarantees nothing.

- **By the book.** He bought after the dot-com bust: a low price, no debt, lots of cash, profitable networks. (Globe, 2011)
- **It failed.** He called it the investment where he had his head handed to him. (Globe, 2011)
- **The lesson.** Even strict adherence to Graham's rules is no guarantee. (Globe, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-09-the-one-that-went-wrong.html

### 10. Patience, history and giving back

He ended advising patience, picking good managers, and studying history, and left a large prize for history writing.

- **Patience.** His mantra was patience, patience and more patience; the big rewards come from compounding. (Globe, 2011)
- **Good managers.** After selling his firm to Mackenzie in 2006 he picked few shares himself and backed managers who used his value approach. (Globe, 2011 · Inv. Executive)
- **History.** He saw history and investing as alike: both study the past to understand the present. (McGill, 2011)
- **The prize.** His foundation created the Cundill History Prize at McGill in 2008, the largest of its kind. (McGill, 2011)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cundill-10-patience-history-and-giving-back.html

## Special section

**Would it pass the Cundill screen?**

- The price is below your estimate of intrinsic value
- The price is below book value, ideally below working capital less long-term debt
- The company is profitable, ideally with five years of growing earnings
- It pays a dividend, ideally a rising one
- The price is under half its former high, ideally near its low
- The P/E is under ten

**Three trades, three lessons**

- J. Walter Thompson: the accounts left out buildings and a lease; homework found them.
- Cleveland-Cliffs: he kept buying as it halved, and earned over 30% a year.
- Cable and Wireless: every test passed, and it still failed.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “The mantra is patience, patience and more patience.” (His advice to investors, last interview, The Globe and Mail, 2011)
- “both study the past to understand the present and predict the future” (On history and investing, as quoted by McGill University)
- “buying a dollar for 40 cents” (The idea he popularised, as reported by Morningstar Canada)

## Read the originals

Start with There's Always Something to Do (Christopher Risso-Gill, McGill-Queen's University Press, 2011), then his last interview with the Globe and Mail.

- [There's Always Something to Do: The Peter Cundill Investment Approach](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt7zrfw): His eureka moment reading Graham, how he ran the fund, and his criteria and trades over three decades.
- [Routines and Orgies: The Life of Peter Cundill](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1287h4s): His life, his firm, and the fund's early decade of more than 30% a year with no down year.
- [An interview with Peter Cundill](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/report-on-business/rob-magazine/an-interview-with-peter-cundill/article566267/): His first loss, his best investment, his worst, how he invested in retirement, and his advice to ordinary investors.
- [Three lessons from a Canadian investing legend](https://www.morningstar.ca/ca/news/191149/three-lessons-from-a-canadian-investing-legend.aspx): His criteria, and the stories of J. Walter Thompson, Bethlehem Copper and Cleveland-Cliffs.
- [Peter Cundill of Ivy Cundill Global Value Fund](https://www.thinkadvisor.com/2004/11/17/peter-cundill-of-ivy-cundill-global-value-fund/): Why a third of the fund was in Japan and a third in cash, and why bargains were scarce.
- [Investor Peter Cundill shook up money management industry](https://www.mcgill.ca/desautels/node/59467): His education and career, the founding of his fund, his book, and the history prize his foundation created.
- [Desautels alumnus Peter Cundill was a Canadian Warren Buffett](https://mcgill.ca/channels/channels/news/desautels-alumnus-peter-cundhill-was-canadian-warren-buffett-268762): How he weighed share prices against liquidation value, bet on the year's worst market, and his career award.
- [Global value investor Peter Cundill dies](https://www.investmentexecutive.com/news/people/global-value-investor-peter-cundill-dies): The sale of his firm to Mackenzie in 2006, his later role, and his final book.

## Words to know

- **Liquidation value**: What a company would fetch if it stopped trading and sold everything, after paying its debts.
- **Net-net**: A share priced below current assets minus all liabilities: Graham's deepest bargain.
- **Working capital**: Current assets, such as cash, stock and money owed by customers, minus current liabilities.
- **Book value**: Assets minus liabilities, as shown in the accounts.
- **P/E**: Price to earnings: the share price divided by yearly earnings per share.
- **Net cash**: Cash minus all debt.
- **Margin of safety**: The gap between price and value that protects you if you are wrong.

## Sources and scope

Sources: There's Always Something to Do (2011) and Routines and Orgies (2014), both by Christopher Risso-Gill; The Globe and Mail's last interview (2011); ThinkAdvisor's 2004 interview; Morningstar Canada; McGill University; Investment Executive; GuruFocus. Lessons are in our own words.

Fund returns are as reported in books and the press; figures differ by period and by source. He died in 2011, and his later record was earned with a team. Companies are named for history only.

# Luiz Barsi Filho

> Shined shoes in a São Paulo tenement, then built his own pension one dividend share at a time, and became Brazil's biggest individual investor.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/barsi.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

A private pension. Build your own retirement out of dividend-paying shares.

## Summary

Luiz Barsi Filho lost his father at one and grew up in a São Paulo tenement, shining shoes and selling sweets. At 14 he found work at a stockbroker. Worried that Brazil's state pension would fail him, he began in the early 1970s to buy shares in one durable company a month and reinvest every dividend. Half a century later he is Brazil's biggest individual investor, said to receive more than a million reais a day in dividends, and he still rides the metro.

## Record at a glance

- **14**: his age when he started work at a stockbroker, after years shining shoes
- **~10 years**: until his dividends passed what a state pension would pay him
- **R$0.50**: his cost for Santander Brasil preferred shares later worth over R$25
- **R$1m+**: a day in dividends, as reported by Fast Company Brasil, from a portfolio near US$2 billion

## Big ideas

### 1. A tenement childhood

He lost his father at one, grew up with his mother in a São Paulo tenement, and worked from about seven.

- **Brás.** He was born in São Paulo in 1939 and raised by his mother in a tenement in the Brás district. (InfoMoney · Book, 2022)
- **Fatherless at one.** His father, an immigrant, died when he was a year old. (InfoMoney)
- **Small jobs.** From about seven he shined shoes, sold sweets at a cinema and helped his mother as a tailor's apprentice. (InfoMoney)
- **Never again.** His stated aim was never to be poor again. (InfoMoney)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-01-a-tenement-childhood.html

### 2. A stockbroker at fourteen

At 14 he got a job at a stockbroker and fell for company accounts. He went on to study accounting, law and economics.

- **The broker.** At 14 he started at a stockbroker, where he became fascinated by balance sheets. (InfoMoney)
- **Many degrees.** He trained as an accounting technician, then studied law and economics. (InfoMoney · Investidor10)
- **Many jobs.** He taught balance-sheet analysis, worked as an auditor and analyst, and was a newspaper's economics editor for 18 years. (InfoMoney · Investidor10)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-02-a-stockbroker-at-fourteen.html

### 3. Shares guarantee the future

Before 30 he feared Brazil's state pension would fail him. In 1970 he wrote a study of which sectors last longest, and built his own pension from their shares.

- **A worry.** He concluded that Brazil's social security system could not be relied on. (InfoMoney)
- **The study.** In 1970 he ranked sectors by how long they would last: food, sanitation, energy, mining and finance. (InfoMoney · Investidor10)
- **A name that stuck.** The study's title, Shares Guarantee the Future, now names an education company run by his daughter. (Investidor10 · Fast Company)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-03-shares-guarantee-the-future.html

### 4. One thousand shares a month

He chose São Paulo's power company and bought about a thousand shares every month until he reached his target.

- **A choice.** His first pick, a food company, was dropped because of succession worries; he chose the power company CESP instead. (InfoMoney)
- **A target.** He aimed for 100,000 shares and bought about 1,000 a month. (InfoMoney)
- **Salary, then dividends.** He bought from his salary and reinvested the dividends. (Investidor10)
- **A decade.** Within about ten years his dividends exceeded a state pension. (InfoMoney)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-04-one-thousand-shares-a-month.html

### 5. The pension portfolio

His method: own durable companies that pay good dividends, bought cheaply, held for decades.

- **Perennial.** He looks for companies in durable sectors that pay good dividends and trade below book value. (InfoMoney)
- **Quality tests.** He judges product longevity, governance, management, finances, profits and how regularly dividends come. (InfoMoney)
- **A shareholder's mind.** He saw himself as owning part of profitable businesses, not trading in and out. (Investidor10)
- **Decades.** Several of his holdings have been owned for more than 30 years. (InfoMoney)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-05-the-pension-portfolio.html

### 6. Banks, energy, sanitation, insurance, telecoms

His followers sum up where he starts looking with one word: BESST, the sectors whose services people always need.

- **BESST.** Banks, energy, sanitation, insurance and telecoms are the starting filter taught by his followers. (Investidor10)
- **Only a start.** The sector is where the analysis begins, not where it ends. (Investidor10)
- **What he avoids.** He has excluded the state oil company, airlines, tourism and appliance retail. (InfoMoney)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-06-banks-energy-sanitation-insurance-telecoms.html

### 7. What he never does

He never invests money he may need, never sells because he has to, and avoids leverage, options and futures.

- **Spare money only.** Never invest money you might need. (InfoMoney)
- **Never forced.** Never sell out of necessity. (InfoMoney)
- **No gambling tools.** He avoids leverage, futures and options. (InfoMoney)
- **Fixed loss.** He jokes that fixed income, renda fixa, is really perda fixa: a fixed loss. (InfoMoney)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-07-what-he-never-does.html

### 8. Patience pays

His best results came from holding for decades: shares bought for cents grew into fortunes and paid him every year.

- **Santander.** He bought Santander Brasil preferred shares for about R$0.50; in 2020 they traded above R$25. (InfoMoney)
- **One holding's income.** In 2019 one power company alone paid him about R$4 million in dividends. (InfoMoney)
- **A million a day.** His portfolio, near US$2 billion, is reported to pay him over R$1 million a day. (Fast Company)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-08-patience-pays.html

### 9. Mistakes and a clean verdict

He lost money in banks that failed in the 1990s. In 2024 Brazil's regulator unanimously cleared him of an insider-trading charge.

- **Failed banks.** He counts investments in banks that collapsed, including Banco Nacional, among his mistakes. (InfoMoney · Investidor10)
- **The charge.** The regulator examined Unipar shares he bought in May 2021 while on its board. (CVM, 2024)
- **The verdict.** In March 2024 it acquitted him unanimously. (CVM, 2024 · InfoMoney, 2024)
- **His defence.** He said the purchase was made to collect dividends, in line with his strategy. (InfoMoney, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-09-mistakes-and-a-clean-verdict.html

### 10. Rich, but simple

He still lives simply, rides the metro on a free senior pass, and asks what wealth means.

- **The metro.** He commutes by metro with a free pass for older people. (InfoMoney)
- **What is rich?** Asked if he is rich, he turns the question back: what does wealth mean to you? (Book, 2022)
- **A family method.** Two of his children work in investing, and one teaches his method. (Fast Company)
- **Still on boards.** In 2026 he became vice-chairman of Unipar's board. (Investidor10)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/barsi-10-rich-but-simple.html

## Special section

**Would it fit his pension portfolio?**

- It is in a durable, essential sector: banks, energy, sanitation, insurance or telecoms
- It has paid dividends regularly for years
- Its products will still be needed in decades
- It is well governed and well managed
- Its finances are sound and it makes a profit
- The price is reasonable, ideally near or below book value
- You are buying with money you will not need

**His three nevers**

- Never invest money you may need.
- Never sell because you have to.
- Never use leverage, futures or options.

**An honest note.** Brazil's securities regulator, the CVM, brought a case alleging that Luiz Barsi Filho traded on inside information when he bought Unipar shares worth about R$1.1 million on 28 May 2021, while he sat on the company's board, days before it announced a deal. On 26 March 2024 the CVM's board acquitted him unanimously. His defence was that the purchase was made to collect dividends, in line with his long-standing strategy. He has also lost money on banks that failed in the 1990s. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “nunca mais voltar a ser pobre” (“Never to be poor again.” His stated aim, as quoted by InfoMoney (our translation))
- “Quando alguém me pergunta se sou rico, devolvo a pergunta” (“When someone asks if I am rich, I turn the question back.” From O Rei dos Dividendos, 2022, as excerpted by InfoMoney (our translation))

## Read the originals

If you read Portuguese, start with his autobiography, O Rei dos Dividendos (2022). If not, start with InfoMoney's profile, then the regulator's 2024 decision.

- [Who is Luiz Barsi, and how he got rich](https://www.infomoney.com.br/?p=1487952): His childhood, his studies and jobs, his 1970 sector study, the CESP plan, his rules and favourite holdings, and his mistakes.
- [O Rei dos Dividendos (The King of Dividends)](https://www.infomoney.com.br/?p=1978736): The saga of a poor immigrants' son who became Brazil's biggest individual investor, in his own words.
- [Luiz Barsi: the history and strategy of the King of Dividends](https://investidor10.com.br/conteudo/luiz-barsi-o-maior-investidor-individual-do-brasil-103470/): His career, the principles of his pension portfolio, the sector filter now taught as BESST, and his board role at Unipar.
- [Who is Luiz Barsi? Brazil's biggest individual investor](https://fastcompanybrasil.com/money/quem-e-luiz-barsi-o-maior-investidor-individual-da-b3/): His portfolio's size, the dividends it pays, and how two of his children carry on his method.
- [Judgment extract, PAS CVM 19957.007375/2022-43](https://conteudo.cvm.gov.br/export/sites/cvm/sancionadores/sancionador/anexos/2024/SEI_19957007375_2022_43.pdf): The regulator's unanimous decision acquitting him of an insider-trading charge over Unipar shares bought in 2021.
- [CVM unanimously acquits Luiz Barsi](https://www.infomoney.com.br/?p=2414844): Why he was investigated, what he bought, and the defence that the purchase was for dividends.

## Words to know

- **Dividend**: A share of a company's profit paid to its shareholders.
- **Dividend yield**: Yearly dividends as a percentage of the share price.
- **Book value**: Assets minus liabilities, as shown in the accounts.
- **Preferred shares (PN)**: In Brazil, shares with priority on dividends but usually no vote.
- **INSS**: Brazil's state social security and pension system.
- **Renda fixa**: Fixed income: bonds and deposits. He calls it perda fixa, fixed loss.
- **CVM**: Comissão de Valores Mobiliários, Brazil's securities regulator.

## Sources and scope

Sources: InfoMoney's profile and its excerpt from his autobiography, Investidor10, Fast Company Brasil, and the Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM) decision of 26 March 2024, with InfoMoney's report on it. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

Barsi publishes no full portfolio or audited record; holdings and wealth figures come from press reports and filings and change over time. Most sources are in Portuguese; summaries and translations are ours. Companies are named for history only.
