# Allan Gray

> Rose 10% at Fidelity while the 1962 market crashed, founded South Africa's biggest private fund firm and Orbis, then gave his control to charity.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/gray.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Be contrarian. Look where others will not: cheap, neglected, unloved.

## Summary

Allan Gray grew up in South Africa, studied at Harvard, and made his name at Fidelity in Boston in 1962, when the market fell 21.7% in a month and his portfolio rose. In 1973 he went home to Cape Town and started a firm that became South Africa's largest private investment manager, then founded Orbis to invest worldwide. He shunned publicity, asked more questions than he answered, and gave his controlling stake in both firms to a charitable foundation.

## Record at a glance

- **+10%**: his Fidelity portfolio in 1962, while the market fell 21.7% in January
- **1973**: the year he started his own firm in Cape Town
- **19.2%**: a year: the firm's flagship equity fund since 1998, against 14.4% for its benchmark
- **100%**: of the family's controlling stake given to a charitable foundation in 2015

## Big ideas

### 1. Butterworth to Harvard

He came from a pioneering family in the Eastern Cape, overcame dyslexia, and studied at Rhodes, the LSE and Harvard.

- **Pioneers.** His family came from Aberdeen in the 1890s; his grandmother became South Africa's first woman mayor. (Daily Maverick)
- **Dyslexic.** He was dyslexic, and still went on to study accounting at Rhodes University. (Daily Maverick)
- **Abroad.** He studied at the London School of Economics and took an MBA at Harvard. (Daily Maverick · Wikipedia)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-01-butterworth-to-harvard.html

### 2. 1962

At Fidelity in Boston, the market fell 21.7% in January 1962 and stayed weak until October. His portfolio rose 10%.

- **Eight years.** He spent eight years at Fidelity in Boston. (Daily Maverick · Wikipedia)
- **The crash.** In 1962 the market fell 21.7% in January; his portfolio ended up 10%. (Daily Maverick)
- **A foundation.** The experience made contrarian thinking the base of his philosophy for life. (Daily Maverick)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-02-1962.html

### 3. Chosen, not sold

In 1973 he started his own firm in Cape Town, believing clients should choose its services rather than be sold them.

- **1973.** He founded Allan Gray Investment Counsel in Cape Town. (Letter, 2015 · Wikipedia)
- **Not sold.** He wanted services clients chose, so the firm's growth would prove it was helping them. (Letter, 2015)
- **The ghost.** So private was he that he was called the 'ghost of Cape Town'. (Daily Maverick)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-03-chosen-not-sold.html

### 4. Contrarian by nature

He looked for cheap, neglected companies others overlooked, and trusted his own judgment over the crowd's mood.

- **Neglected.** He hunted for cheap companies the market had forgotten. (Legacy)
- **Argue the bull case.** When a share was beaten down he pushed colleagues to make the case for it. (Legacy)
- **Not right more often.** Being contrarian does not make you right more often; it finds prices where bad news is already in. (Orbis)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-04-contrarian-by-nature.html

### 5. Cycles

He believed in cycles: good times breed bad times, and strong businesses bought near a cyclical low offer a discount and improving results.

- **Good times, bad times.** He often said that good times, by their nature, produce the tough times. (Legacy)
- **Buy near the low.** Strong businesses near a cyclical low give both a discount and better results ahead. (Legacy)
- **And compounders.** He also liked businesses that could compound for a very long time. (Legacy)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-05-cycles.html

### 6. Value, then dream a little

He stood firmly on what a business was worth, then looked for the upside the market was not pricing.

- **A firm base.** Investments rested on business value. (Legacy)
- **Blue sky.** He looked for undervalued potential the market had not priced. (Legacy)
- **Dream a little.** He encouraged younger colleagues to imagine what could go right. (Legacy)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-06-value-then-dream-a-little.html

### 7. Wrong, and changing your mind

He accepted being wrong sometimes, because good calls would more than pay for bad ones, and he changed his mind when the facts changed.

- **Asymmetry.** He accepted some mistakes because the right decisions could more than offset smaller losses. (Legacy)
- **Held lightly.** He sought out contrary evidence and reversed positions when the facts changed. (Legacy)
- **Ideas go stale.** He taught that a good investment idea loses its value quickly if not acted on. (Legacy)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-07-wrong-and-changing-your-mind.html

### 8. The price of being different

He warned that a long-term contrarian approach pays only for those who can bear long, uncomfortable spells of underperformance.

- **The catch.** Superior results come only if you can withstand uncomfortably long periods of lagging. (Letter, 2015)
- **Shared conviction.** Owners and decision-makers must share the conviction to stay the course. (Letter, 2015)
- **The record.** The firm's flagship equity fund has returned about 19.2% a year since 1998, against 14.4% for its benchmark. (Factsheet, 2026)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-08-the-price-of-being-different.html

### 9. Fees that serve clients

His firms tied their fees to results, so they earned more only when clients did, an idea Orbis took further with refundable fees.

- **Performance fees.** The flagship fund's fee rises and falls with its result against the benchmark. (Factsheet, 2026)
- **Refundable.** Orbis is known for client-aligned, refundable fees. (Orbis, 2021)
- **Client wealth.** Colleagues recall that he insisted good returns must turn into real wealth for clients. (Legacy)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-09-fees-that-serve-clients.html

### 10. Giving it all back

He funded students' education for years, then gave his family's controlling stakes in both firms to a charitable foundation.

- **Scholarships.** In 2005 he created a foundation for school and university scholarships across southern Africa. (Daily Maverick)
- **Control given away.** In 2015 the family gave its controlling stakes in Allan Gray and Orbis to a foundation. (Letter, 2015 · BusinessLive)
- **Why.** He said free enterprise had done much for many, and those it rewards should help others. (Daily Maverick)
- **Long-term owners.** He wanted the firms free from short-term pressure from outside owners. (Letter, 2015)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/gray-10-giving-it-all-back.html

## Special section

**Crowd or contrarian?** 

**Five lessons he left**

- Look where others won't: neglected, cheap, unloved.
- Think in cycles: good times make bad times.
- Stand on value, then dream a little.
- Expect to be wrong sometimes, and size for it.
- Bear the lean years: they are the price of being different.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “but only if one can withstand uncomfortably long periods of underperformance” (Letter to clients, 31 December 2015)
- “The prosperity of good times by definition produces the tough times.” (A saying of his, recalled by a colleague in 'Allan's legacy')
- “The free enterprise system has done so much for so many” (On his philanthropy, as quoted by Daily Maverick)

## Read the originals

Start with his letter to clients of 31 December 2015, then Allan Gray's 'Allan's legacy: investment thinking'.

- [A letter from our founder](https://www.allangray.co.za/globalassets/about-us/our-ownership/a-letter-from-our-founder.pdf): Why he started the firm, why a long-term contrarian approach works only for those who can bear long bad spells, and why he gave control to a foundation.
- [Allan's legacy: investment thinking](https://www.allangray.co.za/latest-insights/investment-insights/allans-legacy-investment-thinking/): Contrarianism, cycles, compounders, 'dream a little', independent judgment, accepting mistakes, changing his mind and serving clients.
- [Allan Gray: death of a gentleman](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2019-11-12-allan-gray-death-of-a-gentleman/): His family, schooling and dyslexia, the 1962 story, the 'ghost of Cape Town', Orbis, and his foundations.
- [Allan Gray (investor)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Gray_(investor)): Dates and outline of his life and the firms he founded.
- [Orbis Global Equity: enduring lessons that shape how Orbis invests](https://www.allangray.co.za/latest-insights/offshore-investing/orbis-global-equity-enduring-lessons-that-shape-how-orbis-invests/): Lessons drawn from him and other mentors, including what contrarian investing really buys you.
- [Orbis: President's letter 2021](https://www.allangray.co.za/latest-insights/offshore-investing/orbis-presidents-letter-2021/): Orbis's culture and its client-aligned, refundable fees.
- [Allan Gray Equity Fund factsheet](https://www.allangray.co.za/globalassets/documents-repository/fund/factsheet/Allan%20Gray%20Equity%20Fund/Files/AGEF%20-%202026-05.pdf): The flagship equity fund's record since 1 October 1998, after fees, against its benchmark, and how its performance fee works.
- [Allan Gray gives away controlling stake to charitable foundation](https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/companies/financial-services/2016-01-08-allan-gray-gives-away-controlling-stake-to-charitable-foundation/): How the family gave its entire controlling stake in Allan Gray and Orbis to a charity.

## Words to know

- **Contrarian**: Going against the crowd: buying what others avoid, selling what they chase.
- **Cycle**: The repeating rise and fall of an industry or market.
- **Compounder**: A business that keeps growing its value at a high rate for many years.
- **Benchmark**: The index or average a fund is compared with.
- **Performance fee**: A fee that rises when a fund beats its benchmark and falls when it lags.
- **Refundable fee**: A performance fee held back and returned if later results fall short.
- **Underperformance**: Doing worse than the benchmark.

## Sources and scope

Sources: his letter to clients (2015); Allan Gray's 'Allan's legacy: investment thinking' and Orbis articles; an Allan Gray Equity Fund factsheet (May 2026); Daily Maverick's obituary (2019); BusinessLive (2016); Wikipedia. Lessons are in our own words.

The firms' records belong to large teams, not to one man, and most of the fund records on this page were earned after he moved to Orbis. Fund figures are as published by the firm, after fees, and change monthly.

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Not registered: this site and its makers are not registered with SEBI, the SEC, any Canadian or European regulator, or any other regulator as an investment adviser or research analyst. Companies and funds are named for history and education only, never as a view on their shares or units.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by the family or estate of Allan Gray, Allan Gray Limited, Orbis Investment Management, the Allan & Gill Gray Foundation, the Allan Gray Orbis Foundation, Daily Maverick, BusinessLive, or any company or publication named. # Cheah Cheng Hye

> Sold pineapples as a boy in Penang, spent 17 years as a journalist, then built Value Partners from under US$5 million: Asia's Warren Buffett.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/cheah.html · Section: the wider world · Updated 2026-11-28

## Core idea

Do the legwork. Visit companies; spend little time in the office.

## Summary

Cheah Cheng Hye grew up poor in Penang, sold pineapples by the road after his father died, and never went to university. He became a financial journalist in Hong Kong, taught himself accounting, and in 1993 co-founded Value Partners with less than US$5 million. Its Classic Fund rose about 3,588% over the next 32 years, against 722% for the Hang Seng Index. Asia calls him its Warren Buffett.

## Record at a glance

- **< US$5m**: Value Partners' money under management when it opened in 1993
- **+3,588%**: Classic Fund, April 1993 to January 2025, against +722% for the Hang Seng Index
- **2,500**: company visits a year by his firm's analysts
- **7 of 25**: years in which the Classic Fund lost money, to 2018

## Big ideas

### 1. Pineapples in Penang

He grew up poor in Penang. When his father died he was nine, the eldest, and the family's breadwinner.

- **Poor and hungry.** He was born in Penang in 1954 to a poor family and often went hungry. (The Edge)
- **Breadwinner at nine.** His father died when he was nine; as the eldest he supported the family. (The Edge)
- **Street trades.** He sold pineapples by the road, folded newspapers, and sold joss sticks at a temple. (The Edge · Time, 2007)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-01-pineapples-in-penang.html

### 2. Seventeen years of journalism

At 17 he joined a Malaysian newspaper, moved to Hong Kong in 1974, and spent 17 years reporting on Asian business.

- **A folder first.** He joined The Star at 17 folding newspapers, then became a reporter. (The Star, 2019)
- **Hong Kong.** He moved to Hong Kong in 1974 and worked for the Asian Wall Street Journal and Asiaweek. (The Edge · The Star, 2019)
- **A scoop.** He was first to report that the Hong Kong dollar would be pegged to the US dollar in 1983. (China Daily)
- **Why it helps.** He has said being an ex-journalist helps in investing. (Inst. Investor)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-02-seventeen-years-of-journalism.html

### 3. Self-taught

With no university degree, he wrote himself a study plan in accounting, law and statistics, and read annual reports cover to cover.

- **No college.** He never went to university. (The Edge)
- **A study plan.** He set himself a course in accountancy, law and statistics. (The Edge)
- **Annual reports.** He read companies' reports from cover to cover and worked long hours. (The Edge)
- **A trader first.** In 1989 he became head of research and a trader at Morgan Grenfell in Hong Kong. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-03-self-taught.html

### 4. A hobby fund becomes a giant

In 1993 he and a partner started Value Partners with under US$5 million. In 2007 it became Hong Kong's first listed asset manager.

- **1993.** He co-founded Value Partners with V-Nee Yeh, with less than US$5 million. (The Star, 2019 · MoneyWeek)
- **A listing.** Its 2007 share offer drew demand for more than 300 times the shares available. (SCMP, 2007)
- **The record.** The Classic Fund rose about 3,588% from April 1993 to January 2025, against 722% for the Hang Seng. (Wikipedia)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-04-a-hobby-fund-becomes-a-giant.html

### 5. Graham, adapted for Asia

He calls himself an old-fashioned Graham-and-Dodd value investor, but puts more weight on cash flow and governance, which matter more in emerging markets.

- **Old-fashioned.** He describes himself as a value investor in the Graham-and-Dodd tradition. (MoneyWeek)
- **Cash flow.** He weighs cash flow more heavily than Graham did. (MoneyWeek)
- **Governance.** In emerging markets he gives corporate governance special weight. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-05-graham-adapted-for-asia.html

### 6. Two thousand five hundred visits

His firm's analysts make about 2,500 company visits a year and are told to spend little time in the office.

- **Legwork.** Value Partners makes about 2,500 company visits a year. (The Edge · MoneyWeek)
- **Out of the office.** Staff are encouraged to spend little time at their desks. (The Edge)
- **BYD.** After BYD's shares fell sharply he visited, judged it unfairly marked down, and became its second-largest shareholder. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-06-two-thousand-five-hundred-visits.html

### 7. Buy when others sell

He buys when people sell and sells when they buy, prefers dull shares, and stayed out of the dot-com mania.

- **The rule.** We buy when people sell and sell when people buy, he says. (The Edge)
- **Dull is good.** He prefers dull stocks when others chase exciting ones. (The Edge)
- **No dot-coms.** He bought no dot-com shares while the market chased them. (MoneyWeek)
- **Sold to Buffett's fans.** When Buffett invested in BYD in 2008 and the market followed, Value Partners sold for a large profit. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-07-buy-when-others-sell.html

### 8. Stupid-clever

He says ego is an investor's worst enemy, and that about a third of his decisions are mistakes, mostly about people.

- **Kill the ego.** He urges a 'stupid-clever' mindset that takes the self out of investment decisions. (MoneyWeek)
- **A third wrong.** He reckons about a third of his decisions are mistakes, mainly from misjudging managers. (The Edge)
- **Too trusting.** He admits his trusting nature can be a weakness in a fund manager. (The Edge)
- **An airline.** He put US$30 million into a Hong Kong airline that went bust within six months. (MoneyWeek)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-08-stupid-clever.html

### 9. Losing years, and the regulator

His fund lost money in seven of its first 25 years. His record also includes a 2000 public reprimand and a 2017 fine for the firm.

- **Seven bad years.** Value investing is not always in favour: the Classic Fund was in the red in seven of 25 years. (China Daily)
- **The 2000 reprimand.** Hong Kong's regulator reprimanded him and the firm over buy orders near the close in late December 1998. (SFC, 2000)
- **Unintentional, but.** It found the effect unintentional, but said he should have known it could affect prices. (SFC, 2000)
- **The 2017 fine.** The firm was fined HK$4 million when two funds issued more shares than allowed; no investor losses were apparent. (SFC, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-09-losing-years-and-the-regulator.html

### 10. The lucky unlucky boy

He credits luck and an era of fast growth as much as skill, and stepped back from the firm in 2025.

- **Luck.** He says the unlucky boy was very lucky, but did not know it then. (The Edge)
- **Hard work.** He believes working harder can make up for a rival's cleverness. (The Edge)
- **Stepping back.** In January 2025, as a Chinese broker took control of the firm, he stepped down as co-chairman. (Hedgeweek, 2025 · Wikipedia)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/cheah-10-the-lucky-unlucky-boy.html

## Special section

**Would he buy, or wait? Tap your answer**

- A sound company's shares have halved on bad news you think is overdone. You have visited and checked. Answer: Buy. Buying a sound business after an unfair markdown, having done the legwork, is the BYD pattern.
- Everyone wants a hot new sector, and prices have tripled in a year. Answer: Wait. He stayed out of the dot-com mania: the crowd's favourite is rarely cheap.
- A dull, cash-rich company trades cheaply, and nobody covers it. Answer: Buy. He prefers dull stocks when others chase exciting ones.
- The numbers look cheap, but you have doubts about whether the managers can be trusted. Answer: Wait. He says most of his mistakes came from misjudging management.

**An honest note.** On 5 October 2000 Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission publicly reprimanded Value Partners Limited and Cheah Cheng Hye, the person responsible for its investment decisions. It found that on 28, 29 and 31 December 1998 the firm had placed buy orders near the close of trading in five stocks, which left their closing prices higher than they might otherwise have been. The SFC found this unintentional but said he should have known it could affect prices, and cited inadequate controls. In January 2017 the SFC reprimanded two Value Partners companies and fined them HK$4 million in total because two funds had issued more shares than their constitutions allowed, and the firm reported this six months late; the SFC found no apparent investor losses, and he was not named. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “We buy when people sell and we sell when people buy.” (His rule, as quoted by The Edge Malaysia)
- “Being an ex-journalist helps” (Interview with Institutional Investor's Alpha, 2012)

## Read the originals

Start with The Edge Malaysia's profile, then MoneyWeek's, then the regulator's 2000 reprimand.

- [Instinct to be different pays Value Partners chief](https://theedgemalaysia.com/article/lead-story-instinct-be-different-pays-value-partners-chief): His Penang childhood, journalism, self-study, contrarian method, company visits, his mistakes and his luck.
- [The world's greatest investors: Cheah Cheng Hye](https://moneyweek.com/481353/the-worlds-greatest-investors-cheah-cheng-hye): Morgan Grenfell, the founding, his adapted Graham approach, BYD, a failed airline, and his 'stupid-clever' mindset.
- [Malaysia's richest: Cheah Cheng Hye](https://www.pressreader.com/malaysia/the-star-malaysia-starbiz/20190323/281938839257070): From newspaper folder at 17 to journalist for 17 years, and founding Value Partners with under US$5 million.
- [A life-long learner who puts knowledge to use](https://www.pressreader.com/china/china-daily-hong-kong/20180420/281861529100335): His Hong Kong dollar peg scoop, his rise in journalism, and the Classic Fund's losing years.
- [Value Partners](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/b18bk5jvryckp8/value-partners): From crime reporter to fund manager, and why journalism helps in investing.
- [Cheah Cheng Hye](https://content.time.com/time/specials/2007/article/0,28804,1705574_1705572_1704395,00.html): A rags-to-riches story: from selling pineapples to Hong Kong's most successful independent fund firm.
- [Small stocks, big ideas drive Value Partners boss](https://www.scmp.com/article/620635/small-stocks-big-ideas-drive-value-partners-boss): A one-time hobby fund that listed in Hong Kong with demand for 300 times the shares on offer.
- [Cheah Cheng Hye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheah_Cheng_Hye): His career, and the Classic Fund's record from 1993 to 2025 against the Hang Seng Index.
- [SFC takes action against Value Partners Limited and Cheah Cheng Hye](https://www.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/news-and-announcements/news/enforcement-news/doc?refNo=00PR127): A public reprimand over buy orders near the close on three days in December 1998.
- [SFC reprimands and fines Value Partners $4 million](https://mondovisione.com/news/hong-kongs-securities-and-futures-commission-reprimands-and-fines-value-partner-2017125/): Two funds issued more shares than their constitutions allowed; no apparent investor losses.
- [Value Partners founder steps down from co-chairman role](https://www.hedgeweek.com/value-partners-founder-steps-down-from-co-chairman-role/): How he stepped back as a Chinese broker, the firm's largest shareholder, took control.

## Words to know

- **Value investing**: Buying shares for less than the business is worth.
- **Graham and Dodd**: Authors of Security Analysis (1934), the founding text of value investing.
- **Cash flow**: Cash a business actually brings in, as opposed to accounting profit.
- **Corporate governance**: How a company is controlled and whether minority shareholders are treated fairly.
- **Hang Seng Index**: Hong Kong's main share index.
- **Public reprimand**: A formal, published rebuke from a regulator.
- **Closing price**: The last traded price of the day, used to value funds.

## Sources and scope

Sources: The Edge Malaysia, The Star (2019), China Daily (2018), MoneyWeek, Institutional Investor (2012), Time (2007), the South China Morning Post (2007), Wikipedia, the Securities and Futures Commission's announcements of 2000 and 2017, and Hedgeweek (2025). Lessons are in our own words.

Fund returns are as published by Value Partners and reported by the press; they cover a team, not one man. In 2000 Hong Kong's regulator publicly reprimanded him and his firm, and in 2017 it fined the firm: see the honest note.

# Paul Tudor Jones

> Lost most of his clients' money on one cotton trade in 1979, built his rules around defence, and made a reported 125.9% after fees in 1987, the year of the crash.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/ptj.html · Section: the traders · Updated 2026-11-28

**For adults (18+). Trading is risky.** This page is about a professional trader who uses futures, leverage and derivatives. It is for education, not a trading course or a recommendation. Most individuals who trade lose money. In India, SEBI found that 93% of individual equity F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24. Past results, his or anyone's, do not predict future ones. Never trade with money you cannot afford to lose.

## Core idea

Defence first. Protect what you have; profits follow.

## Summary

Paul Tudor Jones learned to trade in the cotton pits of the 1970s, nearly wiped himself out in 1979, and decided never again to risk everything on one trade. He founded Tudor Investment in 1980, expected the 1987 crash, and his main fund is reported to have made 125.9% after fees that year, the year the market fell 22.6% in a single day. His rules are about defence first: cut losses, never add to losers, and look for trades that could pay five times what they risk.

## Record at a glance

- **125.9%**: his flagship fund's reported gain after fees in 1987, the crash year
- **14 for 14**: years up in the employee fund he managed alone: part of 1990 (from July), then every year 1991 to 2003
- **5:1**: the reward-to-risk ratio he looks for before taking a trade
- **200 days**: the moving average he uses as his line between offence and defence

## Track record

Hedge funds rarely publish their results. But from 1990 Tudor ran a small fund for its own employees that was registered with the SEC, so its monthly returns sit in public filings. Paul Tudor Jones was its only manager. These charts use those figures, after fees, from July 1990 to April 2004.

| Year | Fund | S&P 500 |
|---|---|---|
| 1990 | 25.44 |  |
| 1991 | 20.13 | 30.47 |
| 1992 | 34.01 | 7.62 |
| 1993 | 1.88 | 10.08 |
| 1994 | 6.87 | 1.32 |
| 1995 | 30.26 | 37.58 |
| 1996 | 9.52 | 22.96 |
| 1997 | 27.05 | 33.36 |
| 1998 | 34.11 | 28.58 |
| 1999 | 7.35 | 21.04 |
| 2000 | 23.69 | -9.1 |
| 2001 | 25.83 | -11.89 |
| 2002 | 21.34 | -22.1 |
| 2003 | 9.38 | 28.68 |
| 2004 |  |  |

From 1991 to 2003 the fund compounded about 18.9% a year, against about 12.1% for the S&P 500 with dividends. It lagged the index in strong bull years such as 1995 and 1997, but it made money in 2000, 2001 and 2002, when the index fell three years running. It had no losing calendar year in this record.

Each dot is a Dow closing level; the dashed line jumps almost two years, to August 1989. The Dow closed at a record 2,722 on 25 August 1987. On Monday 19 October it lost 22.6% in one day, from 2,246.73 to 1,738.74, then bounced back above 2,000 within two days. It did not pass the old high until 24 August 1989. Market Wizards reported that his Tudor Futures Fund gained 62% in October 1987 alone, and his main fund is reported to have made 125.9% after fees that year.

Average yearly gains of the flagship Tudor BVI Global Fund as reported by Bloomberg from investor documents in August 2017. These are press-reported figures for a different, much larger fund, not audited by us. From the mid-2000s he made fewer of the fund's trading decisions himself: by 2014, investors told CNBC he accounted for about 20% of its positions.

- Monthly returns and annual rates of return, July 1990 to April 2004: Tudor Fund For Employees L.P., prospectus filed with the SEC in 2004.
- S&P 500 total returns: published yearly figures (Slickcharts and US500 agree); other datasets differ by a few tenths of a point.
- Statistics such as compound growth and the deepest fall from a high are our own calculations from the monthly figures.
- Dow closing levels: CNBC (August 1987 high), 24/7 Wall St (16 and 19 October), Benzinga (20 October), The Motley Fool (21 October), AP via Lincoln Daily News (24 August 1989).
- Flagship fund figures: CNBC (2014), Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance (August 2017), GuruFocus (2017); the 62% October figure is from Market Wizards as quoted by GuruFocus.

## Big ideas

### 1. From Memphis to the cotton pit

After university a relative in the cotton business sent him to the great cotton trader Eli Tullis, who hired him and taught him on the floor of the New York Cotton Exchange.

- **Memphis.** He was born in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1954 and graduated from the University of Virginia in 1976. (Wikipedia)
- **An introduction.** Billy Dunavant, a cotton merchant in his family (he calls him his uncle; Wikipedia says cousin), sent him to Eli Tullis in New Orleans. (Robbins, 2014 · Wikipedia)
- **The floor.** Tullis offered him a job on the floor of the New York Cotton Exchange. (Market Wizards)
- **Fired.** Tullis later fired him for falling asleep at his desk after a night out in New Orleans. (Wikipedia)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-01-from-memphis-to-the-cotton-pit.html

### 2. Mr. Stupid: the 1979 cotton loss

In 1979 a cotton trade went badly wrong and he lost 60 to 70% of his clients' money. It nearly ended his career and shaped every rule he made afterwards.

- **The loss.** He traded too many cotton contracts; the market went against him, costing 60 to 70% of the accounts he managed. (Benzinga · 7 Circles)
- **The question.** He said the trade nearly broke him, and asked himself why he would risk everything on one trade. (Market Wizards)
- **The change.** He decided to make trading a pursuit of happiness rather than pain, and to learn discipline and money management. (Market Wizards · 7 Circles)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-02-mr-stupid-the-1979-cotton-loss.html

### 3. Tudor Investment, 1980

In 1980 he started his own firm. Dunavant and Tullis were among his first clients, and Commodities Corporation gave him $30,000 to manage.

- **1980.** He founded Tudor Investment Corporation at 26. (Wikipedia)
- **First clients.** Dunavant and Tullis were among his first clients; Commodities Corporation gave him $30,000 to manage. (Wikipedia)
- **Long practice.** SEC filings say he traded for his own account from 1977 and for customers from 1981. (SEC, 2004)
- **A one-man fund.** For the employee fund on this page he was the only person making trading decisions. (SEC, 2004)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-03-tudor-investment-1980.html

### 4. 1987: the crash he expected

In 1987 his deputy Peter Borish mapped that year's market against the run-up to the 1929 crash, and the two expected a collapse. In October the Dow fell 22.6% in a day. His main fund is reported to have made 125.9% that year.

- **On camera.** The 1987 PBS documentary Trader showed him, at 32, managing $125 million; he later persuaded PBS to stop showing it. (CNBC)
- **The 1929 map.** Peter Borish laid the 1987 market over the market before the 1929 crash. (Wikipedia)
- **Flat at the top.** He told Tony Robbins that prices had fallen below his long-term trend line, and he was out at the top. (Robbins, 2014)
- **Black Monday.** On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% to 1,738.74, its worst day ever. (24/7 Wall St, 2020 · CNBC)
- **The month and the year.** Market Wizards reported 62% for his Tudor Futures Fund in October alone; his main fund reportedly made 125.9% after fees in 1987. (GuruFocus · CNBC, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-04-1987-the-crash-he-expected.html

### 5. Defence first

His most repeated lesson: protect what you have before trying to make more. Never add to a losing position.

- **Losers average losers.** Never add to a position that is losing money. (Benzinga)
- **Trade smaller when it hurts.** Cut your trading when you are trading badly; increase it when you are trading well. (Benzinga)
- **Stay in control.** Avoid trades where you cannot control your risk. (Benzinga)
- **A shallow worst month.** In nearly 14 years of SEC-filed monthly results, the employee fund's worst month was a fall of 9.62%, in July 1990. (SEC, 2004)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-05-defence-first.html

### 6. Five to one

He looks for trades that could make five times what they risk. That means he can be wrong most of the time and still come out ahead.

- **The ratio.** He risks one dollar to make five. (Robbins, 2014)
- **The arithmetic.** At five to one, he says, you can win just 20% of the time; one win pays for four losses, with a little left over. (Robbins, 2014 · 25iq)
- **Humility built in.** The rule assumes you will often be wrong, and plans for it. (Robbins, 2014 · 25iq)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-06-five-to-one.html

### 7. The 200-day line

He watches the 200-day moving average of closing prices. If something falls below it, he gets out and plays defence.

- **His metric.** The 200-day moving average of closing prices is his metric for everything. (Robbins, 2014 · 25iq)
- **Why.** He has seen too many stocks and commodities go to zero. (25iq)
- **The rule.** Get out of anything that falls below it. (Robbins, 2014)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-07-the-200-day-line.html

### 8. Everything is connected

He is a global macro trader: he reads currencies, bonds, stocks and commodities as one system and bets on big shifts.

- **Directional and short-term.** SEC filings describe his approach as directional, short-term and discretionary, guided by strict risk control. (SEC, 2004)
- **Japan, 1990.** He bought put options on Japan's stock market in February 1990; his main fund reportedly made 87.4% that year as the market collapsed. (GuruFocus, 2017 · CNBC, 2014)
- **The cotton chair.** He chaired the New York Cotton Exchange from 1992 to 1995. (SEC, 2004)
- **The fastest horse.** In May 2020 he argued that money printing could bring inflation, and said his main fund might trade bitcoin futures as a hedge. (The Block, 2020)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-08-everything-is-connected.html

### 9. Two eras

His flagship fund averaged about 26% a year from 1987 to 2007, then about 4.7% a year from 2008 to 2016. Even legends have long flat stretches.

- **The golden era.** Investor documents showed about 26% a year from 1987 through 2007. (Bloomberg, 2017)
- **The slowdown.** From 2008 through 2016 the average fell to about 4.7% a year, and clients withdrew money. (Bloomberg, 2017)
- **2008.** In the financial crisis his fund lost nearly 5%, about 32 points better than the S&P 500. (GuruFocus, 2017)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-09-two-eras.html

### 10. Robin Hood, and a reputation

After the 1987 crash he co-founded the Robin Hood Foundation to fight poverty. His record also includes a guilty plea over wetlands, an SEC settlement, and words he later regretted.

- **Robin Hood.** After the crash, which hurt so many others, he and friends set up the Robin Hood Foundation, in 1988. (Bridgespan · Wikipedia)
- **Wetlands, 1990.** He pleaded guilty after protected wetlands on his Maryland hunting estate were filled without a permit, paying a $1 million fine and $1 million to a wildlife foundation. (NWF, 1993)
- **An SEC settlement.** In 1996 Tudor paid $800,000 to settle SEC claims about short sales in 1994, without admitting or denying them. (SEC, 1996)
- **Regrets.** In 2013 he apologised for saying motherhood hurts women's trading; in 2017 he said he had defended Harvey Weinstein too long. (NPR, 2013 · CNBC, 2017)
- **Know the odds.** Most individuals who try trading lose money, as SEBI's 2024 study showed in India. (SEBI, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/ptj-10-robin-hood-and-a-reputation.html

## Special section

**What does five to one really mean?** Put in how often your trades win and how much they make compared with what they risk. The calculator shows the average result per trade and the win rate you need just to break even.

**His rules, in short**

- Defence first: protect what you have.
- Never average losers: do not add to a losing trade.
- Trade smaller when it is going badly, bigger when it is going well.
- Look for five to one: risk one to make five.
- Respect the 200-day line: below it, get out.
- Never risk everything on one trade.

**Defence or offence? Tap your answer**

- A trade is down 20%. You buy more so your average price is lower. Answer: Offence gone wrong. Adding to a loser is exactly what he calls averaging losers.
- Before you enter, you know where you will get out if you are wrong, and the target is five times that distance. Answer: Defence. Knowing your exit and your reward-to-risk first is his 5:1 discipline.
- Your account is down three weeks running, so you double your position size to win it back. Answer: Offence gone wrong. He does the opposite: trade smaller when trading badly.
- An index you hold falls below its 200-day average. You sell and wait. Answer: Defence. That is his 200-day rule: below the line, play defence.

**An honest note.** In 1990 he pleaded guilty in a federal case after 86 acres of protected wetlands on his Maryland hunting estate were filled without a permit; he paid a $1 million fine and $1 million to the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. In September 1996 Tudor Investment Corporation settled an SEC proceeding about alleged breaches of the 'uptick rule' in short sales over two days in March 1994, paying $800,000 without admitting or denying the findings. In April 2002 a private lawsuit claiming 'short-swing' profits under Section 16(b) was settled, with the Tudor defendants paying $1.45 million. In 2013 he apologised for saying that motherhood keeps women from being great traders, and in 2017, after a supportive email he had sent Harvey Weinstein was reported, he told staff he had believed and defended Weinstein too long. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or trade anything, and none of it is a trading system. Figures for funds other than the SEC-registered employee fund are as reported by the press and are not audited by us.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “Mr. Stupid, why risk everything on one trade?” (On his 1979 cotton loss, Market Wizards (1989), as quoted by TurtleTrader)
- “At the very top of the crash, I was flat.” (On 1987, to Tony Robbins, Money: Master the Game (2014))
- “Don't ever average losers.” (His first trading rule, as quoted by Benzinga)
- “How do I keep from losing everything?” (What he calls the whole trick in investing, as quoted by 25iq)
- “The best profit maximizing strategy is to own the fastest horse” (The Great Monetary Inflation, May 2020, as quoted by The Block)

- [Paul Tudor Jones: the global macro trader](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/601011/paul-tudor-jones-the-global-macro-trader): His macro style, tripling his money in 1987, Japanese put options in 1990, and a near-5% loss in 2008 that was 32 points better than the S&P 500.
- [The day after the crash: Paul Tudor Jones made a mint, and found a mission](https://www.bridgespan.org/insights/paul-tudor-jones/the-day-after-the-crash-paul-tudor-jones-made-a-m): How 1987 led him to found the Robin Hood Foundation.
- [True tales of eco-crimes](https://www.nwf.org/Magazines/National-Wildlife/1993/True-Tales-of-Eco-Crimes): The wetlands on his Maryland estate, his guilty plea, a $1 million fine and $1 million to the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation.
- [Paul Tudor Jones distances himself from Harvey Weinstein](https://www.cnbc.com/2017/12/06/paul-tudor-jones-distances-himself-from-harvey-weinstein.html): A supportive email he sent Weinstein in October 2017, and his later note to staff.
- [Hedge fund manager apologizes for comments on women traders](https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2013/05/24/186504874/hedge-fund-manager-apologizes-for-comments-on-women-traders): His remarks at the University of Virginia, and his apology.
- [Paul Tudor Jones makes the case for bitcoin](https://www.theblock.co/post/64398/paul-tudor-jones-says-he-is-buying-bitcoin-as-a-hedge-against-central-bank-money-printing): Why he compared bitcoin with gold in 1976, and why his main fund might trade bitcoin futures.
- [Paul Tudor Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tudor_Jones): Dates of his life, his early career, his first clients, and his deputy Peter Borish's 1929 comparison.
- [93% of individual traders lost money in equity F&O, FY22 to FY24](https://www.sebi.gov.in/media-and-notifications/press-releases/sep-2024/updated-sebi-study-reveals-93-of-individual-traders-incurred-losses-in-equity-fando-between-fy22-and-fy24-aggregate-losses-exceed-1-8-lakh-crores-over-three-years_86906.html): India's regulator on how individual derivatives traders fared over three years.

## Words to know

- **Futures**: Contracts to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date; traded with borrowed money (leverage).
- **Leverage**: Using borrowed money so gains and losses are larger than your own money alone.
- **Short selling**: Selling something you do not own, hoping to buy it back cheaper.
- **Global macro**: Trading on big economic shifts across currencies, bonds, stocks and commodities.
- **Moving average**: The average closing price over a set number of days, redrawn each day.
- **Reward-to-risk**: How much a trade could make compared with how much it could lose.
- **Drawdown**: How far an account has fallen from its last high point.
- **Uptick rule**: A US rule, since changed, limiting short sales to prices above the last trade.

## Sources and scope

Sources: Tudor Fund For Employees L.P. filings with the SEC (1996 and 2004); Market Wizards (1989) and Money: Master the Game (2014) as excerpted online; CNBC, CNN Money, Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance, GuruFocus, Insider Monkey, Benzinga, NPR, The Block, Bridgespan; SEBI (2024). Lessons are in our own words.

He is a trader, not a long-term investor: his methods use futures, leverage and short-term positions that can lose quickly. The SEC-registered fund's figures are audited filings; flagship-fund figures are press reports. Read the risk note at the top of the page first.

- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.

# Mark Minervini

> Lost all his capital in the 1980s, then studied history's biggest winning stocks and won the U.S. Investing Championship twice, in 1997 and 2021.

Source page: https://alienspacex.com/minervini.html · Section: the traders · Updated 2026-11-28

**For adults (18+). Trading is risky.** This page is about a professional trader who buys and sells fast-moving shares, often in large positions, and sells quickly when they fall. It is for education, not a trading course or a recommendation. Most individuals who trade lose money. In India, SEBI found that 93% of individual equity F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24. Contest wins are single years. Past results, his or anyone's, do not predict future ones. Never trade with money you cannot afford to lose.

## Core idea

Study the winners. Copy what the biggest winners looked like before they ran.

## Summary

Mark Minervini left school early, played music, bought his first stock in 1983 and made a quick profit on it. Then, for about six years, he kept losing money until his capital was gone. After that he studied the biggest winning stocks in history, built a method he calls SEPA, and won the U.S. Investing Championship twice, in 1997 and 2021. His trademark is a strict checklist: buy only leading stocks in strong uptrends, at a precise point, and cut every loss small.

## Record at a glance

- **Twice**: U.S. Investing Champion: 1997 (+155%) and 2021 (+334.8%)
- **About 6 years**: of losing money before his method worked
- **8 tests**: in his Trend Template before a stock is worth a look
- **10%**: the most he says any loss should ever reach

## Track record

There is no public, audited year-by-year record of his trading to chart. What can be checked are his two entries in the U.S. Investing Championship, a real-money contest whose organiser verifies each entrant's brokerage account. His earlier five-year run comes from his own published figures, as reported by Jack Schwager.

- **+155%** won the 1997 U.S. Investing Championship
- **+334.8%** won again in 2021, a contest record at the time
- **220%** a year over about five years to 1999, by his own published figures
- **+128%** his worst year in that stretch, as reported

| 2021 contest point | His account |
|---|---|
| Start | +0% |
| Mar | +111.4% |
| Jun | +223.4% |
| Sep | +277.0% |
| Nov | +325.2% |
| Dec | +334.8% |

His running total in 2021 as the contest published it each quarter (November was a mid-quarter update), against the S&P 500 with dividends at the points where we have a checked figure. He entered his own money in the $1 million-plus stock division.

| Year | His result | S&P 500 |
|---|---|---|
| 1997 | +155.0% | +33.4% |
| 2021 | +334.8% | +28.7% |

Each bar is one calendar year. The contest years are his best-known, so this is the best side of his record, not a typical year. In 2024 another trader, J Law of Hong Kong, set a new record of 353.9%.

This is only arithmetic: what 220% a year would do to $10,000 over five years. It is not his actual year-by-year record, which he has not published. His book describes five years at 220% (33,500% in total); Jack Schwager describes about five and a half years from mid-1994. The sources differ slightly, so treat these as his own approximate figures, not audited by us.

- Contest results: U.S. Investing Championship press releases on Business Wire (April, July, October and December 2021, January 2022) and the winner's press release on PR Newswire (January 2022).
- 1994 to 1999 figures: Jack Schwager, Stock Market Wizards (2001), as summarised by TradingMarkets and The 7 Circles; the 33,500% total is from his book's description.
- S&P 500 total returns: 1997 from Slickcharts and US500; 2021 from S&P Dow Jones Indices, FactSet via Fisher Investments, and Bloomberg via a market update.
- The 2024 record: the contest's 2025 first-half release, via Webull.

## Big ideas

### 1. A musician who lost it all

He wanted to be a musician, bought his first stock in 1983, and made money at once. Then he lost money for about six years, until his capital was gone.

- **The studio.** He sold his music studio and used the money to trade. (Elearnmarkets)
- **Easy money.** His first stock, Allis-Chalmers, bought at $4 near its yearly low, made a quick profit. (IBD)
- **Six bad years.** He says he made every mistake possible and lost money for almost six years. (MarketWatch)
- **Wiped out.** By the end of the 1980s all his trading capital was gone. (IBD)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-01-a-musician-who-lost-it-all.html

### 2. Study the winners

Instead of guessing, he studied what the biggest winning stocks in history looked like before their big moves, and built a 'leadership profile' to copy.

- **The books.** Richard Love's Superperformance Stocks and William Jiler's work became the backbone of his method. (Stockopedia)
- **Weinstein.** After meeting Stan Weinstein in 1990 he added trend analysis to his work. (Stockopedia)
- **The profile.** He reversed his old habits and copied what winning stocks looked like before they ran. (MarketWatch)
- **Two flaws.** Looking back, he found he let small losses grow and had no clear rules for buying. (IBD)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-02-study-the-winners.html

### 3. SEPA: a specific entry point

In 1993 he founded Quantech Research Group, selling research based on his method, Specific Entry Point Analysis, or SEPA.

- **The firm.** Quantech Research Group, founded in 1993, sold his research to professional investors. (TWST, 1998)
- **The name.** He called the method Specific Entry Point Analysis: SEPA for short. (TWST, 1998)
- **Both sides.** SEPA combines a stock's price trend with its earnings growth. (Stockopedia · Goodreads)
- **A fund.** In 2000 he started a hedge fund, also called Quantech. (7 Circles)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-03-sepa-a-specific-entry-point.html

### 4. Stage 2 only

Borrowing Stan Weinstein's idea that stocks move through four stages, he buys only in Stage 2: when a stock is already in a strong, rising trend.

- **Four stages.** Resting, rising, topping, falling: he wants only the rising stage. (Stockopedia · ChartMill)
- **No bottom-fishing.** He avoids shares that have fallen far from their highs, however cheap they look. (ChartMill)
- **Strength first.** A stock must prove itself by rising before he will look at it. (ChartMill · MarketWatch)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-04-stage-2-only.html

### 5. The Trend Template

His trademark filter: eight tests on price, moving averages and the yearly high and low. A stock that fails any of them is not a candidate.

- **The averages.** Price above its 50-, 150- and 200-day averages, stacked in that order, with the 200-day rising. (ChartMill)
- **Near the high.** Within 25% of its 52-week high, and well above its 52-week low. (ChartMill · MQL5)
- **Two versions.** His first book asks for 30% above the low; his second says 25%. (MQL5)
- **Relative strength.** It should be beating at least 70% of other stocks. (ChartMill)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-05-the-trend-template.html

### 6. The VCP

His favourite setup is the Volatility Contraction Pattern: a rising stock pauses, and each pullback is smaller than the one before, until the price breaks out.

- **Shrinking swings.** Pullbacks of, say, 25%, then 15%, then 8%, each one tighter. (ChartMill)
- **Quiet volume.** Trading volume dries up as the pattern tightens: sellers are running out. (ChartMill)
- **The pivot.** He buys as the price breaks above the final tight range, with a stop just below it. (ChartMill)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-06-the-vcp.html

### 7. Cut losses small

After losing everything once, he made one rule above all: cut losses while they are small. He says no loss should ever reach 10%, and the average should be far smaller.

- **Nicked to death.** If the market is to beat him, he says, it must do it one small loss at a time. (IBD)
- **10% at most.** He sets a firm maximum loss of 10%, with an average loss much lower. (Financial Wisdom)
- **Staggered stops.** He may split a position, with half stopped out at 6% and half at 10%. (Stockopedia)
- **Half right.** He expects to be right only about half the time, so losses must stay smaller than gains. (Stockopedia)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-07-cut-losses-small.html

### 8. 220% a year

Jack Schwager reported that from mid-1994 to 1999 he averaged about 220% a year, with only one small losing quarter. These are his own figures, not an audited fund.

- **The run.** About 220% a year compounded over five and a half years from mid-1994. (TradingMarkets)
- **Worst year.** His worst year in that stretch was a gain of 128%. (7 Circles)
- **One down quarter.** Only one quarter lost money, by less than 1%. (TradingMarkets)
- **The total.** His books describe this as five years of triple-digit returns, about 33,500% in total. (Goodreads)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-08-220-a-year.html

### 9. Two championships

To prove his method with real money, he entered the U.S. Investing Championship twice and won both times: +155% in 1997 and a record +334.8% in 2021.

- **1997.** He won with a 155% return, trading only shares. (PR Newswire, 2022)
- **2021.** He won the $1 million-plus stock division with +334.8%, then a contest record. (PR Newswire, 2022 · Business Wire, 2022)
- **The race.** He led all year: +111.4% after three months, +223.4% after six, +277% after nine and +325.2% after eleven. (Business Wire, Apr 2021 · Business Wire, Jul 2021 · Business Wire, Oct 2021 · Business Wire, Dec 2021)
- **Record broken.** In 2024 J Law of Hong Kong beat his record with +353.9%. (Webull, 2025)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-09-two-championships.html

### 10. Teacher, critics and the CNBC moment

He now writes books and sells trading education. His record has fans and critics, and a 2021 TV interview showed the limits of trading charts without knowing the business.

- **The books.** Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard (2013) and Think & Trade Like a Champion (2017) set out his method. (Goodreads · Stockopedia)
- **A business.** He runs Minervini Private Access, a paid platform where members follow his trades, and live workshops. (Author page)
- **Upstart.** In October 2021 a CNBC interview about Upstart, a stock he held, went badly, and his angry replies online drew more criticism. (investingLive, 2021)
- **Know the odds.** Most individuals who try trading lose money, as SEBI's 2024 study showed in India. (SEBI, 2024)
  Web page: https://alienspacex.com/ideas/minervini-10-teacher-critics-and-the-cnbc-moment.html

## Special section

**Run the Trend Template** Type in a stock's numbers from any charting site, or keep our made-up example. The checker runs his eight tests and shows which pass.

**The VCP in four steps**

- A Stage 2 stock: it must already pass the Trend Template.
- It pauses and pulls back, then each pullback is smaller than the last.
- Volume dries up as the swings tighten.
- Buy the breakout above the last tight range, with a stop just below it.

**Leader or laggard? Tap your answer**

- A share is down 60% from its high and looks cheap. Answer: Laggard. He avoids stocks far from their highs; the template wants within 25% of the 52-week high.
- A share is 5% below its yearly high, above its rising 50-, 150- and 200-day averages. Answer: Leader. That is the Trend Template's picture of a Stage 2 leader.
- A share's 200-day average has been falling for six months, but it jumped 10% today. Answer: Laggard. He wants the 200-day average rising for at least a month; one good day does not change the trend.
- A rising share pulls back 20%, then 10%, then 4%, on lighter and lighter volume. Answer: Leader. Shrinking pullbacks on drying volume are his VCP.

**An honest note.** Only two parts of his record are independently verified: his 1997 and 2021 wins in the U.S. Investing Championship, a contest that checks entrants' real brokerage accounts. The 220% a year from 1994 to 1999 is his own figure, reported by Jack Schwager; there is no public, audited fund record to chart. He sells trading education, including a paid service where members follow his trades, so he has a business interest in his reputation. In October 2021 a CNBC interview about Upstart, a stock he owned, went badly, and his combative replies online drew criticism. We found no regulatory action against him. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or trade anything, and none of it is a trading system. Contest figures are as published by the U.S. Investing Championship; his other performance figures are his own, as reported, and are not audited by us.

## In their own words (short quotes)

- “It's going to have to nick me to death.” (On cutting losses small, Investor's Business Daily)
- “you'll likely be correct only about 50 percent of the time.” (To Stockopedia, on being wrong)
- “called Specific Entry Point Analysis — SEPA, for short.” (On his method, The Wall Street Transcript, 1998)
- “Growth comes at the expense of comfort.” (Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard (2013), as quoted by Goodreads)

## Read the originals

Start with Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard (2013), then Think & Trade Like a Champion (2017). For his story, read his chapter in Jack Schwager's Stock Market Wizards (2001).

- [2021 United States Investing Championship winners](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220124005241/en/2021-United-States-Investing-Championship-Winners-%E2%80%94-Minervini-Smashes-Record): Final standings for 338 entrants; a real-money competition first run in 1983.
- [Records shattered in international investing competition](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210426005252/en/Records-Shattered-in-International-Investing-Competition): Leading the $1 million-plus stock division after three months with +111.4%.
- [2021 championship six-month results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210722005154/en): Leading after six months with +223.4%.
- [2021 championship nine-month results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20211026005502/en): Leading after nine months with +277%.

- [2025 U.S. Investing Championship first-half results](https://www.webull.com/news/13249512026235904): Notes that J Law set a new record of +353.9% in 2024, beating Minervini's +334.8%.
- [How early stock losses built a champion stock trader](https://inkl.com/news/how-early-stock-losses-built-a-champion-stock-trader): His first stock in 1983, losing all his capital by the end of the 1980s, and the rule he made afterwards.
- [Expanded MarketWatch interview with Mark Minervini](https://michaelsincere.com/articles/my-marketwatch-interview-with-stock-market-wizard-mark-minervini): Losing money for almost six years, and the 'leadership profile' of winning stocks he built.
- [Mark Minervini: lessons from a stock market wizard](https://www.stockopedia.com/academy/articles/secrets-stock-market-wizard-minervini): His influences (Richard Love, William Jiler, Stan Weinstein), and why he expects to be right only about half the time.
- [Mark Minervini interview: how to trade like a champion](https://stockopedia.com/blog/mark-minervini-interview-how-to-trade-like-a-champion-353963): Risk management and staggered stop losses.

- [Loren Fleckenstein chats with Jack Schwager](https://tradingmarkets.com/?p=665916): The 220% average yearly return over five and a half years from mid-1994, with one losing quarter.
- [Mark Minervini: stocks around the clock](https://the7circles.uk/?p=21165): His performance to 1999, his worst year of +128%, and the hedge fund he started in 2000.
- [Stock Market Wizards: Mark Minervini](https://elearnmarkets.com/school/units/stock-market-wizards/mark-minervini-stock-around-the-clock): The would-be musician who sold his studio to trade.
- [Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard](https://goodreads.com/book/show/16189528): His SEPA method, and the 220% a year and 33,500% total he reports.
- [Mark Minervini: author biography and quotes](https://www.abebooks.co.uk/author/b00bn1x6ry/mark-minervini): His education business, Minervini Private Access and the Master Trader Program, in his own publisher's words.
- [Mark Minervini's Trend Template: a step-by-step guide](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/stock-screener/technical-analysis-trading-strategies/496-Mark-Minervini-Trend-Template-A-Step-by-Step-Guide-for-Beginners): The Trend Template's tests on price, moving averages, the 52-week range and relative strength.
- [Automating classic market methods: Minervini's Trend Template](https://www.mql5.com/en/articles/22790): The template's conditions, and the 30% (first book) versus 25% (second book) distance from the 52-week low.
- [The Volatility Contraction Pattern: how to spot and trade it](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/technical-analysis/chart-patterns/531-Volatility-Contraction-Pattern-VCP-How-to-Spot-and-Trade-It): Shrinking pullbacks, drying volume and the pivot, counted T1, T2, T3.
- [Mark Minervini: stock trading wizard](https://www.financialwisdomtv.com/post/mark-minervini): His 10% maximum loss and a much smaller average loss.
- [The weekend meltdown of Mark Minervini](https://investinglive.com/news/!/the-weekend-meltdown-of-mark-minervini-was-a-sight-to-behold-20211018): A CNBC interview about Upstart that went badly, and his replies online.
- [93% of individual traders lost money in equity F&O, FY22 to FY24](https://www.sebi.gov.in/media-and-notifications/press-releases/sep-2024/updated-sebi-study-reveals-93-of-individual-traders-incurred-losses-in-equity-fando-between-fy22-and-fy24-aggregate-losses-exceed-1-8-lakh-crores-over-three-years_86906.html): India's regulator on how individual derivatives traders fared over three years.

## Words to know

- **Moving average**: The average closing price over a set number of days, redrawn each day.
- **52-week high/low**: The highest and lowest prices of the past year.
- **Relative strength**: How a stock's price has done compared with other stocks, often as a 1 to 99 rank.
- **Stage 2**: In Stan Weinstein's scheme, the rising phase of a stock's cycle.
- **VCP**: Volatility Contraction Pattern: a pause in which each pullback is smaller than the last.
- **Pivot**: The price level whose breakout is the buy signal.
- **Stop loss**: A preset price at which you sell to limit a loss.
- **SEPA**: Specific Entry Point Analysis, his name for his whole method.

## Sources and scope

Sources: U.S. Investing Championship results (Business Wire, PR Newswire); Investor's Business Daily; Stockopedia; The Wall Street Transcript; Jack Schwager's Stock Market Wizards as summarised online; his books' published descriptions; guides to the Trend Template and VCP by ChartMill; investingLive; SEBI (2024). Lessons are in our own words.

He is a short- to medium-term stock trader, not a long-term investor: he buys fast-rising shares and sells quickly when they fall. Only his contest results are independently verified; his longer record is his own. He also sells trading education. Read the risk note at the top of the page first.

## Disclaimer

- For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
- Records and figures come from the published sources named on this page and may be revised; check the originals before relying on them.
- Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.
- Trading risk: short-term trading can lose money quickly, and futures, options and trading on margin can lose more than the money put in. Most individuals who trade lose money. This page describes one professional's career for education; it is intended for adults aged 18 and over.
- Not registered: this site and its makers are not registered with SEBI, the SEC, the CFTC or any other regulator as an investment adviser, research analyst or commodity trading adviser. Nothing here is a trading signal, a course or a recommendation.
- Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Mark Minervini, Minervini Private Access, Quantech Research Group, the U.S. Investing Championship, Jack Schwager, Stan Weinstein, ChartMill, CNBC, Upstart, SEBI, or any publication named. All trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners. SEPA is a trademark of its owner.
